recipe.title: Pasta ca' le Sardine
recipe.summary: Fresh pasta with sardines, wild fennel, saffron and pine nuts, a Sicilian classic.

items.raw: 400 g fresh sardines, scaled and gutted
150 g wild fennel (fronda di finocchietto), fresh or frozen, chopped

steps.text: Make the pasta: pile the flour on a clean bench, make a well in the centre and crack the eggs into it. With a fork, beat the eggs lightly, then gradually incorporate the flour, mixing with your fingers until a shaggy dough forms. Knead for 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Wrap in plastic wrap and rest for 30 minutes.
While the dough rests, steep the saffron in the warm water until the colour is deep gold, about 5 minutes.
In a small frying pan over medium heat, lightly toast the pine nuts, shaking often, until fragrant, about 3 minutes. Set aside.

Heat the olive oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Add the sliced onion and cook gently, stirring, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Add the chopped garlic and cook for another minute until fragrant.

Add the fresh sardines (or break them into large pieces if very large) to the pan and cook gently, stirring carefully, until the flesh is opaque and beginning to flake, about 5 minutes. Pour in the saffron water and add the chopped wild fennel. Stir gently and simmer for 5 minutes. Season with salt and black pepper. Turn off the heat.
Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil until it is at a rolling, bubbling boil.

Roll out the pasta dough thinly (about 2 mm) on a floured bench. If you have a pasta machine, use it. Cut into long, irregular ribbons or shapes, traditional pasta ca' le sardine is not uniform; think rustic and handmade.
Cook the pasta in the boiling water, stirring gently, until al dente, about 4–5 minutes for fresh pasta. (Test a piece; it should have a slight bite.)
Reserve 200 ml of the pasta cooking water, then drain the pasta.

Gently reheat the sardine sauce over medium-low heat. Add the cooked pasta to the sauce and toss carefully, adding pasta water a little at a time to loosen the sauce and help it coat the pasta. The pasta should look silky, not dry or soupy.
Divide among bowls, scatter the toasted pine nuts over the top, and serve at once.

notes: Wild fennel (fronda di finocchietto) is the leafy fronds, not the seeds. In Australia, you may find it frozen in the Asian or Italian section; if not, a small amount of fresh dill mixed with a pinch of ground fennel seed is an acceptable substitute, though the taste won't be quite the same.
The pasta can be made up to 2 hours ahead and kept covered on the bench. You can also freeze it on a tray, then bag it; cook from frozen, adding 1–2 minutes to the cooking time.
If fresh sardines are hard to find, use tinned sardines in oil (drain well and add them to the sauce at the end, just to warm through, so they don't fall apart).
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Tahdig
recipe.summary: Crispy golden rice crust with butter and yoghurt, the whole point of the pot.

steps.text: Rinse the basmati rice under cold water until the water runs mostly clear. This removes excess starch. Soak in cold water for 30 minutes, then drain.

Bring a large pot of salted water (like the sea) to a boil. Add the drained rice and cook uncovered for about 8 minutes, until the grains are just starting to soften on the outside but still firm in the centre. The rice should be only half-cooked.
Drain the rice well through a fine sieve, shaking gently to remove excess water.
Melt the butter in the same pot over medium heat. Add the drained rice, stirring gently to coat with butter. Spread it in an even layer. Make a well in the centre with the back of a spoon.

Wrap the lid tightly in a clean kitchen towel so the steam stays trapped, then place it firmly on the pot. Reduce the heat to medium-low and cook for 30 minutes. You want to hear a gentle crackling sound after about 15 minutes, that's the tahdig forming.

Remove from heat. Let it rest for 5 minutes with the lid still on. Carefully run a thin knife around the edges of the pot, then place a large serving platter upside-down over the pot and flip everything out in one confident motion. The rice will mound on the platter with the golden tahdig crust on top.
Serve the tahdig hot with cold Greek yoghurt on the side. Break off pieces of the crispy rice and eat it together with a spoonful of yoghurt. This is the prize.

notes: The key is steam. Wrap that lid in a towel, no shortcuts. If your kitchen is very cold, you may need another 5 minutes.
Listen for the gentle crackling around 15 minutes in. That's how you know it's working.
If the tahdig is too dark or burns, it happens. Serve it anyway, bitter tahdig with yoghurt is still tahdig.

recipe.title: Shrimp and Grits
recipe.summary: Creamy stone-ground grits with sautéed shrimp, crispy bacon, and spring onions.

items.raw: 800 g raw shrimp (prawns), peeled and deveined
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Bring the chicken stock to a boil in a saucepan. Slowly whisk in the grits, stirring constantly to avoid lumps. Once combined, reduce the heat to low and cook, stirring often, for 25 to 30 minutes until the grits are creamy and tender and pull away from the sides of the pan.
While the grits cook, fry the bacon in a large cast-iron frying pan over medium heat until crispy, about 8 minutes. Remove to a plate, leaving about 1 tbsp of bacon fat in the pan.
Add the butter to the frying pan with the bacon fat. Once foaming, add the garlic and cook, stirring, for about 1 minute until fragrant.

Season the shrimp well with salt and pepper. Add half to the frying pan in a single layer and cook without stirring for 2 minutes until the underside is pink. Stir and cook for a further 2 to 3 minutes until fully opaque throughout with no translucency. Transfer to a plate and repeat with the remaining shrimp.
Once the grits are creamy, stir in the cream, lemon zest, and cooked bacon. Season to taste with salt, pepper, and lemon juice.

Return all the shrimp to the frying pan and warm through over medium heat for about 1 minute. Top with spring onions and a drizzle of hot sauce if you like. Serve the shrimp alongside the creamy grits.

notes: Cook the shrimp in batches to avoid crowding the pan, this ensures even cooking and a proper sear.
Stone-ground grits take longer than instant grits and have better flavour. Don't skip the low-and-slow cooking.

title: Sheet Pan Chicken Thighs with Root Vegetables

recipe.title: Sheet Pan Chicken Thighs with Root Vegetables
recipe.summary: One-pan roasted chicken thighs with potatoes, carrots and onions.

items.raw: 8 bone-in chicken thighs, skin on (about 1.5 kg)
500 g waxy potato, halved or quartered
400 g carrot, cut into 5 cm pieces
1 large brown onion, cut into wedges
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat oven to 220°C. Pat chicken thighs dry with paper towels and place them skin-side up on a large sheet pan.
Toss potatoes, carrots and onion with olive oil, thyme, oregano, salt and pepper. Scatter around the chicken.

Roast for 35–40 minutes, until the chicken skin is golden and crispy and the internal temperature at the thickest part of the thigh reaches 75°C. The vegetables should be tender and caramelised at the edges.
Let rest for 5 minutes, then serve. A squeeze of lemon over everything is nice if you have it.

notes: Make it ahead: prep the vegetables and pat the chicken dry the night before, then assemble and roast when you get home.
Swap in whatever root veg you have, parsnips, sweet potato or beets all work. Keep the total weight around 900 g.
Leftovers reheat brilliantly at 180°C for 15 minutes, or shred the chicken and toss with the vegetables for a next-day grain bowl.

recipe.title: Crawfish Étouffée
recipe.summary: Crawfish in a thick, spiced brown roux sauce served over rice.

items.raw: 500 g crawfish tail meat, fresh or frozen
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Melt butter in a heavy-based pot over medium heat. Add flour and stir constantly, scraping the bottom, for 12 to 15 minutes until the roux is dark brown and nutty-smelling. This is the foundation, don't rush it or let it burn.
Add the chopped onion, celery and capsicum to the roux. Stir well and cook until soft, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for another minute.
Stir in the cayenne, paprika, oregano and thyme. Cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the chicken stock, stirring to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook for 5 minutes to let the flavours blend.
Add the crawfish and stir gently. Simmer for 8 to 10 minutes until the crawfish is heated through. Season to taste with salt and pepper.
Serve over steamed rice, garnished with spring onion and fresh parsley.

notes: If fresh crawfish isn't available, frozen works just fine, thaw it first.
The roux is everything: low and slow, stirring often. Once it's dark brown, you've got the soul of the dish.
Make this ahead: the étouffée keeps for 3 days in the fridge and tastes even better reheated.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

recipe.title: Żurek
recipe.summary: Sour rye soup with kielbasa and potatoes, a Polish Sunday supper from Kraków.

items.raw: 3 good-quality kielbasa sausages (about 400 g), sliced into thick rounds
1 kg waxy potatoes, peeled and cut into chunks
150 ml żur (Polish sour rye starter, fermented rye flour)
items.note: Polish sour rye starter, fermented rye flour

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large, heavy pot over medium-high heat. Brown the kielbasa slices until the edges are crispy, about 5 minutes. Set them aside on a plate.
In the same pot, sauté the onions until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for another minute until fragrant.
Add the potatoes and stir to coat with oil. Pour in the stock and bring to a simmer. Add the bay leaves and cloves, then cook until the potatoes are tender, about 20 minutes.

Pour the żur into a small bowl and stir it with a little warm stock to loosen it, then pour this mixture back into the pot. Stir well and simmer for 5 minutes, letting the sour flavour meld into the soup.
Return the kielbasa to the pot and simmer for another 5 minutes to warm through and let the flavours combine.
Taste and season with salt and pepper. Ladle into bowls, top each with a spoonful of sour cream and a scatter of fresh dill. Serve with good rye bread.

notes: Żur (sour rye starter) can be found in Polish or Eastern European grocery shops, or made at home by fermenting rye flour in water for 24 hours. It keeps in the fridge for weeks.
Make this a day ahead if you can, the flavours deepen overnight. Reheat gently on the stove, adding a splash of water if needed.
Good kielbasa makes this soup. Don't skip it or use thin sausages; you need that smoky, meaty backbone.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.

recipe.title: Curry Goat
recipe.summary: Fall-apart goat meat in a rich, aromatic curry with potatoes and spring onions.

items.raw: 1.5 kg goat shoulder, cut into 5 cm chunks
4 spring onions, chopped (white and green parts separated)

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large, heavy pot over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the goat meat on all sides, about 3–4 minutes per batch. Remove and set aside.
In the same pot, add the onions and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and ginger, and cook for another minute until fragrant.
Stir in the curry powder, cumin and turmeric, and cook for 2 minutes, stirring constantly, until the spices are dark and fragrant.

Return the goat to the pot. Add the water and crushed tomatoes, scraping up any browned bits from the bottom. Stir in the salt, pepper and thyme. Bring to a gentle simmer until the liquid is bubbling lightly.
Cover with a lid and simmer gently for 45 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the meat is beginning to soften.
Add the potato chunks and the white parts of the spring onions. Simmer, covered, for a further 30–35 minutes until the meat is fall-apart tender and the potatoes are soft. Taste and adjust seasoning.
Stir in the green parts of the spring onions just before serving. Serve hot in a deep bowl with the broth.

notes: Make it a day ahead: the flavours deepen as it sits. Reheat gently on the stove top.
Serve with rice and peas, or plain white rice to soak up the curry.
Can't find goat? Lamb shoulder works, though it cooks faster, check it at 60 minutes.

recipe.title: Paneer tikka
recipe.summary: Paneer marinated in yoghurt and spices, grilled or pan-fried until golden.

items.raw: 200 g paneer, cut into 2 cm cubes

steps.text: Mix yoghurt, ginger-garlic paste, ground coriander, ground cumin, garam masala, cayenne, kashmiri chilli powder, lemon juice and salt in a bowl. Add paneer cubes and stir gently to coat. Set aside for at least 10 minutes (or up to 2 hours in the fridge).
Heat oil in a large frying pan or frying pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers.

Thread paneer, onion and capsicum onto skewers, alternating pieces (or cook them separate in the pan if you don't have skewers). Working in batches, cook until the paneer is golden on all sides and the vegetables are softened and charred, about 8–10 minutes.
Transfer to a serving plate, scatter with fresh coriander and serve hot with lemon wedges and roti or rice.

notes: Marinade the paneer for at least 10 minutes, but up to 2 hours in the fridge makes it taste even better.
Use a good non-stick pan or oil-brushed stainless steel so the paneer doesn't stick. Don't move the pieces around too much, let them get a nice golden crust.
If you have wooden skewers, soak them in water for 30 minutes before threading.

recipe.title: Gyeran Mari
recipe.summary: Rolled egg omelette with vegetables, a banchan that keeps for three days.

steps.text: Blanch the spinach in salted boiling water for 1 minute, then drain and squeeze dry. Mix with the grated carrot and chopped spring onion in a small bowl.
Crack the eggs into a large bowl, add soy sauce, sesame oil and a pinch of salt, then whisk until well combined. Stir the vegetable mixture into the egg.

Heat 1 tbsp neutral oil in a large non-stick frying pan over medium heat. When hot, pour in half the egg mixture and tilt the pan to spread it into a thin, even layer, about 3 mm thick. Cook for 2–3 minutes until the bottom is set but the top is still slightly wet.
Starting from one long edge, roll the omelette tightly towards the opposite edge, using a spatula to help fold as you go. Slide onto a plate and set aside to cool slightly.
Repeat with the remaining 1 tbsp oil and egg mixture to make a second roll.
Once both rolls have cooled to room temperature, wrap them tightly in cling film and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes, this makes them easier to slice.
Unwrap and slice each roll into 1.5 cm thick rounds. Serve chilled or at room temperature.

notes: Keeps in an airtight container in the fridge for 3 days.
Make ahead: prepare and slice the day before; store in an airtight container and eat chilled or bring to room temperature.
For extra fillings, try adding finely chopped mushroom or zucchini, just squeeze out excess moisture first.

title: Beef Mince Tacos with Frozen Veg

recipe.title: Beef Mince Tacos with Frozen Veg
recipe.summary: Quick weeknight tacos with beef mince and frozen corn and capsicum.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring occasionally, until softened, about 3 minutes.
Add the beef mince and cook, breaking it up with a spoon as it browns, until cooked through (no pink remaining), about 5 minutes. Drain off any excess fat if needed.
Stir in the taco seasoning, frozen corn and frozen capsicum until the seasoning is fragrant. Add the water and bring to a simmer until the sauce has thickened and the vegetables are tender.
Cook, stirring occasionally, for 5 minutes or until the vegetables are heated through and the sauce has reduced slightly. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Warm the tortillas in a dry frying pan for 30 seconds each side, or wrap in foil and heat in a 160°C oven for 5 minutes.
Set out the warm tortillas, spiced beef mixture and all the toppings. Let everyone build their own tacos.

notes: Freeze the cooked mince mixture in portions for an even quicker future dinner, just thaw and warm through.
Swap flour tortillas for corn ones, or lettuce leaves if you're out of bread.
Greek yoghurt works just as well as sour cream here.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

recipe.title: Roasted Mushroom and Walnut Pie
recipe.summary: Earthy mushroom and walnut filling in golden butter pastry with local cream.

items.raw: 700 g mixed mushrooms (swiss brown, button, shiitake), halved or quartered
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Make the pastry: rub the cold butter into the flour and salt until it resembles breadcrumbs. Stir in the egg yolk and cold water until the dough just comes together. Shape into a disc, wrap and chill for at least 20 minutes.
While the pastry rests, toast the walnuts in a dry frying pan over medium heat for 3 minutes, stirring until fragrant. Set aside.
Heat the olive oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Cook the onion until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the mushrooms to the pan in batches, cooking until golden and any liquid has evaporated, about 15 minutes total. Stir in the toasted walnuts, thyme, cream, salt and pepper. Let cool slightly.
Preheat the oven to 200°C. Roll out two-thirds of the pastry and line a 23 cm pie dish. Spoon in the mushroom filling.
Roll out the remaining pastry to make a lid. Lay it over the filling, press the edges to seal, then trim and crimp. Brush with beaten egg and make a small slit in the centre.
Bake for 25–30 minutes until the pastry is golden and the filling is bubbling gently at the edges.

notes: Make the pastry up to 2 days ahead and store in the fridge; the filling can also be made a day early and reheated gently before assembling.
If you can't find mixed mushrooms, use whatever is available, button mushrooms alone work just fine, though you'll lose some of that forest-floor flavour.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Tabbouleh
recipe.summary: Bulgur salad with parsley, lemon, tomato and olive oil, fresh, simple and foolproof.

items.raw: 200 g fresh flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Put the bulgur in a large bowl and pour the boiling water over it. Cover with a plate or tea towel and let it sit for 10 minutes until the bulgur is tender and has absorbed the water.
While the bulgur soaks, prepare all your herbs and vegetables: chop the parsley, dice the tomato and onion, and chop the mint.
Once the bulgur is cool enough to handle, fluff it with a fork and add the parsley, tomato, onion and mint.
Pour over the lemon juice and olive oil, then mix everything together gently but thoroughly.
Taste it and season with salt and pepper. Remember: tabbouleh should be bright and tangy, so don't be shy with the lemon.
Let it rest for 10 minutes before serving so the flavours come together. You can eat it at room temperature or chilled.

notes: Make it ahead: tabbouleh keeps in the fridge for up to 2 days in an airtight container. The flavours actually get better the next day.
Swap the fresh mint for dried mint if that's all you have, use about a third of the amount.
Serve with cos lettuce leaves or pita bread for scooping.

recipe.title: Lolo Ika
recipe.summary: Fish simmered in creamy coconut milk with taro leaves and vegetables.

items.raw: 600 g firm white fish fillets, cut into chunks
1 large dalo (taro), peeled and cut into 2 cm chunks
items.prep: peeled and cut into 2 cm chunks

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the onion and garlic, and cook gently until soft and fragrant, about 3 minutes.
Add the dalo chunks and cook for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the edges start to soften.
Pour in the coconut milk and bring to a simmer until it is gently bubbling. Add the salt and stir well.
Add the fish chunks and taro leaves, folding them gently into the coconut milk. Simmer for 15 to 20 minutes, until the fish is cooked through and the dalo is tender.
Taste and adjust the salt and pepper. Serve hot in bowls with the creamy sauce spooned over.

notes: Make ahead: prepare the dalo and taro leaves the day before, stored in separate airtight containers in the fridge.
Swap the white fish for any firm fish, use what's fresh. Trevally, snapper or bream all work beautifully.
Use coconut cream mixed with a little water if you can't find coconut milk, or stir in 2 tbsp grated fresh coconut at the end for deeper flavour.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

recipe.title: Lemon Myrtle Chicken
recipe.summary: Roasted chicken with lemon myrtle leaves, a native Australian citrus with peppery notes.

items.raw: 2 tbsp lemon myrtle leaves, roughly chopped
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Preheat your oven to 200°C.
Pat the chicken dry with paper towels. Season the cavity generously with salt and pepper, then stuff with the lemon myrtle leaves and onion halves.
Brush the outside of the chicken all over with neutral oil, then season the skin with salt and pepper.

Place the chicken breast-side up on a roasting tray. Roast for 60 to 75 minutes, or until the thickest part of the thigh reaches 75°C when tested with a meat thermometer. The skin should be golden and crispy.
Remove from the oven and rest for 10 minutes before carving. Serve with a wedge of lemon or lime on the side if you like.

notes: If you can't find fresh lemon myrtle leaves, dried lemon myrtle powder works well, use about 1 tsp mixed with a little salt and pepper to season the cavity and skin.
The pan juices make a simple sauce: deglaze the hot tray with a splash of water or stock, scraping up the browned bits, and drizzle over the carved chicken.

recipe.title: Gudeg Nangka Muda
recipe.summary: Young jackfruit stewed in coconut milk and spices until tender, a Yogyakarta specialty.

items.raw: 1 kg young green jackfruit, peeled and cut into 2 cm chunks
items.prep: peeled and cut into 2 cm chunks

steps.text: Heat a large, heavy-based pot or dutch oven over medium heat. Add the sliced shallots, garlic, and ginger, stirring constantly until they release their fragrance and soften, about 3 minutes.
Stir in the ground turmeric and coriander, stirring for 1 minute more until the spices coat the aromatics.
Add the jackfruit chunks, stirring well to combine with the spice paste, about 2 minutes.
Pour in the coconut milk and water. Add the bay leaves, makrut lime leaves, and red chillies. Bring to a simmer until gently bubbling and fragrant.

Reduce the heat to low and simmer gently, uncovered, for 75–90 minutes, stirring occasionally. The jackfruit will soften, fray at the edges, and turn golden as it absorbs the coconut and spices. The sauce will thicken and deepen in colour.
Taste and adjust the salt. The gudeg is ready when the jackfruit is very tender and almost dissolving, and the sauce is rich and silky.

notes: Gudeg keeps well in the fridge for up to 3 days and tastes even better the next day as the flavours deepen. Reheat gently on the stove.
Serve with steamed rice and a simple fried chicken or hard-boiled eggs on the side, Yogyakarta style.

recipe.title: Carne Asada
recipe.summary: Grilled marinated beef with citrus and chilli, charred and juicy.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Blend the orange juice, lime juice, minced garlic, cumin, oregano, torn guajillo chillies, salt and pepper in a blender until smooth. Pour in the olive oil and pulse to combine.
Place the skirt steak in a large bowl or a zip-lock bag and pour the marinade over it, making sure all sides are coated. Cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, or overnight for best flavour.
Remove the steak from the fridge 30 minutes before cooking. Preheat your grill to high heat and oil the grates well.
Pat the steak dry with paper towels and season lightly with salt and black pepper on both sides.

Grill the steak for 6–8 minutes on the first side, without moving it, until charred and a crust forms. Flip and grill for 4–6 minutes on the second side for medium-rare (internal temperature of 60°C).
Transfer to a clean board, tent loosely with foil and rest for 5 minutes. This keeps the meat juicy.
Slice against the grain into strips and serve hot with lime wedges, fresh coriander and warm flour tortillas.

notes: The marinade works best overnight. Plan ahead or marinate for at least 4 hours.
Leftover carne asada is great in tacos, quesadillas or over rice the next day.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Bariis iskukaris
recipe.summary: Fragrant Somali spiced rice with cardamom, cinnamon and cloves.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the cardamom pods, cinnamon stick and cloves, stirring for about 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the diced onion and cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and lightly golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the rice and stir to coat in the oil and spices, cooking for 2 minutes.
Pour in the stock and bring to a boil. Stir once, then reduce the heat to low, cover with a tight-fitting lid, and cook for 18–20 minutes until the rice is tender and the liquid is absorbed.
Remove from the heat and let sit, covered, for 5 minutes. Fluff with a fork, season with salt and pepper, and serve.

notes: Make ahead: cook the rice up to 4 hours ahead, then reheat gently with a splash of water in a covered pot over low heat.
This rice holds well in a warm thermos if you're taking it to a family gathering.

recipe.title: Scotch Broth
recipe.summary: A warming barley broth with ham bone, root vegetables and lentils, proper Scottish comfort in a bowl.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Bring the water to a boil in a large pot. Add the ham bone or hock and bay leaf. Skim off any foam from the surface, then reduce the heat and simmer gently for 30 minutes.
Add the pearl barley and brown lentils. Simmer for another 15 minutes.
Add the carrots, parsnips, swede and leek. Stir well and simmer for 20 minutes.
Add the potato and simmer for a further 15 minutes, until all the vegetables are tender and the barley is soft.
Remove the ham bone. If there's any meat clinging to it, shred it and return it to the pot; discard the bone. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Ladle into bowls and scatter with fresh parsley if you like. Serve hot with good bread.

notes: This freezes beautifully, make a double batch and freeze half. Thaw overnight and reheat gently.
Any root vegetables work here: turnip instead of swede, celeriac, or even a bit of cabbage. Swap parsnip for more carrot if that's what you've got.
If you can't find a ham bone, a ham hock works just as well, or use chicken stock and add a splash of ham or bacon for flavour.

recipe.title: Lamb Souvla
recipe.summary: Marinated lamb skewers charred over coals with lemon, oregano and garlic.

items.raw: 2 tbsp fresh oregano, chopped (or 2 tsp dried oregano)
800 g lamb shoulder, cut into 3 cm cubes
2 red onions, cut into 3 cm chunks
2 red capsicums, cut into 3 cm chunks

steps.text: Combine olive oil, lemon juice, garlic, oregano, salt and pepper in a bowl. Add lamb and stir until coated. Cover and marinate in the fridge for at least 2 hours, or overnight.
Thread lamb onto skewers, alternating with onion and capsicum pieces. If using wooden skewers, soak them in water first.
Heat your grill or chargrill to high until very hot, or get your coals hot and glowing, covered in a light grey ash.
Lay skewers on the grill and cook for 20–25 minutes, turning every 2–3 minutes to char evenly on all sides. The lamb is ready when it's charred outside and pink inside.
Rest for 2 minutes, then serve with lemon wedges and extra oregano.

notes: Marinate overnight if you have the time, it'll be even more tender.
Cook over charcoal if you can. It makes all the difference, mate.
Pink lamb is the way. It's not overcooked until it's grey.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

recipe.title: Phở Gà
recipe.summary: Delicate chicken phở with charred ginger and onion, Hanoi-style broth simmered low and slow.

items.raw: 1 kg chicken bones (and pieces such as necks, wings and feet)
items.note: and pieces such as necks, wings and feet

items.raw: 500 g cooked chicken, shredded (or use poached chicken breast)
Fresh herbs: coriander, Thai basil, mint (a big handful altogether)

steps.text: Heat a heavy-based pot or wok over medium-high heat. Place the unpeeled ginger and onion directly on the heat and char them, turning occasionally, until blackened all over, about 8–10 minutes. This gives the broth a subtle, sweet depth. Scrape away the worst of the char if you like, but don't wash it off.

Blanch the chicken bones and pieces: bring a large pot of water to the boil, add the chicken, and simmer for 2 minutes. Drain and rinse the bones under cold water, then scrape away any scum. This keeps your broth clear and clean.

In a clean pot, add 2 litres of water and bring to the boil. Add the blanched chicken bones, charred ginger and onion, star anise, cinnamon stick, garlic, coriander seeds and peppercorns. Bring back to the boil, then reduce the heat to low and simmer, uncovered, for at least 3 hours. The longer you go, the better, Mum simmers hers overnight. Skim off any foam that rises in the first 20 minutes.
About 30 minutes before you want to eat, taste the broth and adjust with fish sauce and salt. Strain the broth through a fine sieve, discarding the solids.
Cook the rice noodles according to packet directions, usually a few minutes in boiling water, until soft and tender but still slightly springy, then drain.

To serve, place a nest of noodles in each bowl. Ladle the hot broth over the noodles, then top with shredded cooked chicken. Scatter with fresh herbs, spring onion and chilli. Serve with lime wedges and extra fish sauce on the side so people can adjust the seasoning.

If you're making this ahead, simmer the broth the night before and refrigerate it. The next day, skim off any fat that has solidified on top, then gently reheat until steaming and bubbling lightly before serving.

notes: Make the broth the night before and chill it; the fat will solidify on top and you can lift it off. This also lets the flavours develop further overnight.
If chicken bones are hard to find, ask the butcher, they'll usually give them to you cheap or free. Chicken feet add real gelatin and depth to the broth.
You can poach a whole chicken breast in the simmering broth for the last 20 minutes, then shred it to serve. Or buy a rotisserie chicken and shred that instead.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

recipe.title: Kleicha
recipe.summary: Crispy-edged, tender cardamom-date shortbread cookies from Iraq.

items.raw: 250 g dried dates, pitted and chopped

steps.text: Make the filling: heat the 2 tbsp ghee in a pan over medium heat. Add the dates and cardamom, stirring often, until the dates soften into a paste, about 5 minutes. Season with salt and set aside to cool.

Make the dough: in a bowl, cream the softened ghee with the sugar until pale, about 2 minutes. Add the flour, cardamom, cinnamon if using, salt and milk. Mix gently with your hands until the dough comes together, it should be soft but not sticky. If too dry, add a touch more milk.
Roll: working with about 1 tbsp of dough at a time, gently roll each piece into a ball. Flatten between your palms into a disc about 6 cm across and ½ cm thick.
Stuff: place a teaspoon of date filling in the centre of each disc. Fold the edges up and gently seal, then flatten again into a thick oval or disc shape.
Mark: using a fork or the tip of a knife, press a gentle pattern into the top of each cookie, traditional kleicha have a decorative crosshatch or lattice. Do this gently so you don't break through.

Heat the oven to 180°C, then bake: place the cookies on a lined baking tray, leaving a little space between each. Bake for 15–20 minutes, until the edges are golden brown but the centres still feel soft to the touch. They will firm up as they cool.
Cool: let them rest on the tray for 5 minutes, then transfer to a wire rack. They'll crisp up at the edges while staying tender inside.

notes: Store in an airtight container for up to 5 days. They're best eaten the day after baking, when they've set but the date filling is still soft.
If your dates are very dry, soak them in a splash of warm water for 10 minutes before chopping.
You can make these ahead and freeze the unbaked cookies for up to a month; bake from frozen, adding 2–3 minutes to the time.

recipe.title: Empanadas de Carne
recipe.summary: Crispy baked beef empanadas with hard-boiled egg and olives.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Make the dough: rub the cold butter into the flour and salt until it resembles breadcrumbs. Make a well, add the egg yolk and 80 ml of the warm water, mix gently with your fingertips until it comes together, adding more water if needed. Knead briefly until smooth, then wrap and rest for 20 minutes.

While the dough rests, cook the filling: heat the oil in a pan over medium heat, add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 6 minutes. Add the beef mince and cook, breaking it up with a spoon, until cooked through and no pink remains, about 8 minutes. Stir in the cumin and paprika, cook for 1 minute, then remove from heat. Let cool slightly, then fold in the hard-boiled egg and olives. Season to taste with salt and pepper.
Preheat the oven to 200°C.
Divide the dough into 12 equal pieces and roll each into a ball. On a floured surface, roll each ball into a circle about 15 cm across and 3 mm thick.
Place 2 tbsp of filling on one half of each circle, leaving a 1 cm border. Fold the dough over to form a half-moon, press the edges to seal, then crimp with a fork.
Place the empanadas on a baking tray lined with baking paper. Brush each with beaten egg.
Bake for 20–25 minutes, until golden and crisp. Serve warm.

notes: Make ahead: prepare the filling and dough the day before, keep both covered in the fridge. Assemble and bake fresh when you're ready.
Freeze: uncooked empanadas freeze well for up to a month. Bake straight from frozen, adding 5–7 minutes to the cooking time.

Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Ahi Poke Bowl
recipe.summary: Soy-ginger ahi tuna over rice with crisp vegetables and sesame seeds.

items.raw: 400 g sashimi-grade ahi (yellowfin tuna), cut into 2 cm cubes

steps.text: In a bowl, whisk together soy sauce, sesame oil, ginger and rice vinegar.
Add the ahi cubes and gently toss to coat. Let sit in the fridge for 5 minutes, until the surface of the fish is lightly coated in the marinade.
Divide the chilled rice between two bowls.
Top each bowl with marinated ahi and its liquid, then layer the cucumber slices and spring onions.
Sprinkle with sesame seeds and serve immediately with lime wedges on the side.

notes: Use only the freshest, sashimi-grade ahi from a reliable fishmonger. Serve immediately after assembly.
Make the rice ahead and chill it completely before building the bowls.
Swap cucumber for daikon radish if you want a bit of crunch and bite.

The fish here is eaten raw or only cured in citrus. Buy sashimi-grade fish from a fishmonger, keep it cold and eat it the same day; skip it for anyone pregnant, very young, elderly or with low immunity.

Food safety: The seafood here is served raw or cured, so buy sashimi-grade, keep it cold and eat it the day it is made; for anyone who should avoid raw fish, cook it until opaque. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.
Feijoada freezes beautifully. Cool completely, then freeze in portions for up to 3 months. Thaw overnight and reheat gently on the stove.
Serve with white rice, orange slices, farofa (toasted cassava flour), and hot sauce on the side.
For a lighter version, use chicken thigh instead of pork shoulder—it will cook in 1.5 hours.
Food safety: cook fresh sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre. Smoked or pre-cooked sausages just need heating right through.

steps.text: Heat oil in a large heavy pot over medium-high heat. Cook the pork shoulder pieces in two batches until browned on all sides, about 5 minutes each batch. Transfer to a plate.
In the same pot, cook the sausage pieces until browned, about 4 minutes. Transfer to the plate with the pork.
Add the chopped onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute more.
Return the pork and sausage to the pot. Add the rinsed beans, bay leaves, and water or stock. Stir well and bring to a boil.
Reduce heat to low, cover, and simmer gently for 2 to 2.5 hours, stirring occasionally. The beans should be completely tender and the pork very soft.
Season with salt and black pepper to taste. The stew should be thick but still saucy—if it looks too dry, add a splash of water. Serve hot.

recipe.title: Feijoada
recipe.summary: Black bean stew with pork and sausage, the Brazilian way.

items.raw: 400 g pork shoulder, cut into 4 cm pieces
200 g pork sausage, cut into 4 cm lengths
2 tsp salt, plus more to taste

title: Steamed Perch with Ginger and Soy

recipe.title: Steamed Perch with Ginger and Soy
recipe.summary: Whole perch steamed until just cooked, topped with ginger, spring onion and soy.

items.raw: 1 whole perch (about 500 g), cleaned and scaled
4 cm piece fresh ginger, peeled and cut into thin matchsticks
items.prep: peeled and cut into thin matchsticks

items.raw: 2 spring onions, cut into 5 cm lengths

steps.text: Remove the perch from the fridge 15 minutes before cooking to bring it to room temperature. This allows the heat to penetrate evenly. Pat dry with paper towel inside and out.

Fill a wok or large pot with water to a depth of about 5 cm and bring to a rolling boil. Set a bamboo steamer rack or metal steaming stand inside, or use a plate on chopsticks to elevate the fish above the water.
Place the perch on a heatproof plate that fits inside your steamer. Season lightly with salt inside the cavity and on the skin.

Carefully transfer the plate to the steamer. Cover with a lid and steam over high heat for 10–12 minutes, until the eye of the fish turns white and cloudy and the flesh is opaque when you gently press it at the thickest part near the backbone.
While the fish steams, warm the neutral oil in a small pan until just smoking, about 2 minutes on medium-high heat.
Remove the fish from the steamer and transfer to a serving plate. Scatter the ginger matchsticks and spring onion lengths over the top.
Pour the light soy sauce over the fish, then immediately pour the hot oil over the ginger and spring onion. The oil will sizzle and release their aromatics. Serve at once.

notes: The key is bringing the fish to room temperature first, it cooks through more evenly. If your perch is larger (750 g), add 2–3 minutes to the steaming time.
If you can't find perch, use any firm white fish whole, about 500 g: bream, snapper, or barramundi work well.
Sashimi-grade fish is not needed here; a regular market-fresh white fish is perfect.

recipe.title: Canh Chua Rau
recipe.summary: Sour tamarind broth with water spinach, tomato and vegetables, a light and tangy vegetarian take on the classic.

items.raw: 200 g water spinach (rau muống), cut into 5 cm lengths
1 medium pumpkin (or squash), peeled and cut into bite-sized pieces
items.prep: peeled and cut into bite-sized pieces

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Mix the tamarind paste with 2 tbsp warm water until loose, then set aside.
Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the garlic and cook, stirring, for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Pour in the vegetable stock and bring to a boil. Add the pumpkin and simmer for 8 to 10 minutes until just tender.
Stir in the tamarind liquid and sugar. Taste and adjust the balance of sour and sweet to your liking.
Add the tomato wedges and water spinach, stirring gently. Cook for 2 to 3 minutes until the spinach wilts and the tomato softens slightly but still holds its shape.
Season with salt and pepper. Pour into bowls and serve with fresh coriander if you wish.

notes: Serve hot for a traditional bowl, or chill it and serve cold on a warm day.
The balance of tamarind and sugar is personal, start with less sugar and add to taste as you simmer.

recipe.title: Stifado
recipe.summary: Beef braised with pearl onions and vinegar until sticky and dark.

items.raw: 800 g beef chuck, cut into 5 cm pieces
500 g pearl onions (or baby onions), peeled
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp olive oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat. Brown the pearl onions, shaking the pot often, until they're coloured on all sides and lightly caramelised, about 8 minutes. Transfer to a plate.
Add the remaining 1 tbsp oil to the pot. Brown the beef in batches, about 3 minutes per batch, until dark all over. Don't crowd the pan. Set aside.
Return all the beef to the pot. Add the crushed garlic and tomato paste, stirring for 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the vinegar and red wine, scraping up any browned bits from the bottom of the pot. Add the tinned tomatoes, bay leaves, and cinnamon. Stir well.
Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cover and braise for 1 hour 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the beef is very tender.

Add the browned pearl onions back to the pot and stir through. Continue to braise, uncovered, for another 30 minutes, until the sauce reduces and becomes sticky and dark, and the onions are completely soft.
Taste and season with salt and pepper. Serve hot, scattered with fresh parsley if you like. This is good with crusty bread or over rice to soak up the sauce.

notes: This tastes better the next day, make it ahead and reheat gently.
If pearl onions are hard to find, use small shallots or just brown onion cut into chunks; the cooking time stays the same.
Serve with crusty bread, rice, or soft polenta to soak up the incredible sauce.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

recipe.title: Bulgogi with Supermarket Steak
recipe.summary: Korean marinated beef steak, sliced and seared until caramelised, ready in 25 minutes.

items.raw: 2 spring onions, white and light green, finely chopped
items.prep: white and light green, finely chopped

items.raw: 800 g beef steak (rib eye, sirloin or rump), thinly sliced

steps.text: Combine soy sauce, mirin, sesame oil, garlic, ginger, sugar and spring onion in a bowl. Stir until the sugar dissolves.
Add the sliced beef to the marinade and toss to coat well. Let it sit for 5 minutes while you heat a large pan or wok over high heat.

Heat the oil in the pan until shimmering. Working in two batches so the beef isn't crowded, sear the sliced steak for 2–3 minutes per side, until caramelised at the edges but still tender. Transfer to a plate.
Pour any remaining marinade into the pan and let it bubble for 30 seconds to thicken slightly, then return the beef to the pan and toss to coat.
Transfer to a serving plate, scatter with sesame seeds and coriander if using, and serve straight away with rice and kimchi.

notes: Slice the steak against the grain, it'll be more tender. If it's too thick, pop it in the freezer for 15 minutes first to make it easier to slice.
Any supermarket steak works: the thinner you slice it, the less time it needs. Rib eye stays juicy, sirloin is leaner.
Make the marinade ahead and marinate the beef for up to 2 hours if you want deeper flavour, just let it come to room temperature before cooking.
Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done.

recipe.title: Egusi Soup
recipe.summary: Melon seed soup with beef and leafy greens, thickened and rich.

items.raw: 2 red chillies, finely chopped (or 1 tsp chilli flakes)
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Add beef and cook, stirring, until browned on all sides, about 10 minutes. Remove and set aside.
In the same pot, add the chopped onions and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add garlic and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 2 minutes, then add the crushed tomatoes. Cook for 3 minutes, stirring to combine.
Return the beef to the pot. Pour in the beef stock and bring to a boil. Reduce heat and simmer, covered, for 30 minutes until the beef is tender.
In a bowl, mix the ground egusi with 250 ml water to form a smooth paste. Slowly stir this into the soup, breaking up any lumps. Add the chillies and maggi cube.
Simmer gently for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking. The soup should thicken and become silky.
Add the spinach, stirring well to wilt it into the soup. Cook for 3 minutes. Taste and adjust salt and pepper to your liking.
Serve hot with fufu, rice or cassava bread to soak up the rich broth.

notes: This soup freezes beautifully and tastes even better the next day. Make a double batch on Sunday and freeze in portions for busy weeknights.
If you can't find egusi, you can substitute with equal parts ground almonds and sesame seeds, though the texture won't be quite the same.
Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done.

title: Soy and Ginger Chicken Thighs with Bok Choy

recipe.title: Soy and Ginger Chicken Thighs with Bok Choy
recipe.summary: Chicken thighs braised in soy, ginger and star anise with quick bok choy on the side.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. Season the chicken thighs with salt and pepper, then place skin-side down in the hot pan. Cook until the skin is golden and crisp, about 6 minutes. Flip and cook for another 2 minutes.
Add the ginger slices and star anise to the pan, stirring for about 1 minute until fragrant. Pour in the soy sauce and chicken stock, then add the caster sugar. Bring to a simmer.
Reduce heat to medium-low, cover, and braise for 12–15 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through (75°C in the thickest part of the thigh). The skin may soften slightly; that's fine.
While the chicken braises, bring a small pot of salted water to the boil. Add the bok choy and cook for 2 minutes until tender-crisp. Drain well.
Transfer the bok choy to serving plates. Remove the chicken from the pan and place on the plates, then spoon the braising liquid (with the ginger and star anise) over the top.

recipe.title: Negima
recipe.summary: Chicken and spring onions skewers brushed with soy-mirin glaze, grilled in a frying pan.

items.raw: 200 g chicken breast, cut into 2 cm pieces
2 spring onion, cut into 3 cm pieces

steps.text: Mix soy sauce, mirin, sugar and garlic in a small bowl.
Heat a frying pan over medium-high heat. Add oil and let it smoke lightly.
Working quickly, add chicken pieces to the pan and cook, stirring occasionally, for 4 minutes until lightly browned on the edges.
Add spring onion pieces and toss to combine. Cook for 1 minute.
Pour the tare over everything and stir constantly for 2–3 minutes until the liquid is sticky and coats the chicken and onion. Check that the chicken is cooked through.
Taste and add salt if needed. Serve hot.

notes: Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

recipe.title: Ugali na Sukuma
recipe.summary: Cornmeal mush with sautéed collard greens, Kenya's everyday plate

steps.text: Bring the water to a boil in a pot with a pinch of salt. Slowly pour in the cornmeal, stirring constantly to avoid lumps, until the mixture thickens, about 5 minutes.
Keep stirring as the ugali cooks and pulls away from the sides of the pot, another 5 to 8 minutes. When it's thick and smooth, press it down and let it sit off the heat.
Meanwhile, heat the oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 3 minutes.

Add the sukuma wiki and stir to coat with oil. Cook for 2 minutes, then add the tomato and chilli, if using. Stir and cook until the greens are tender and the tomato is soft, about 3 to 4 minutes. Season with salt to taste.
Turn the ugali out onto a platter, shape it into a mound with the back of a spoon, and serve the sukuma wiki on the side or spooned over the top.

recipe.title: Larb Moo
recipe.summary: Spiced minced pork salad with lime, fish sauce and toasted rice powder.

items.raw: 2–3 birds eye chillies, finely chopped (or less if you prefer)

steps.text: Toast the rice in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring often, until golden and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Tip into a spice grinder or mortar and pound to a fine powder. Set aside.
Heat the oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. Add the pork mince and cook, breaking it up with a spoon, until cooked through and no longer pink, about 8 minutes.
Remove from the heat and stir through the lime juice and fish sauce. Taste and adjust the balance: it should be hot (spicy), sour and salty in equal measure.
Add the shallots, spring onions, coriander, mint and chillies. Toss to combine. Sprinkle the toasted rice powder over the top and fold through gently.
Transfer to a serving plate. Serve at room temperature with sticky rice and fresh vegetables (lettuce, long beans, cucumber) on the side.

notes: Larb is best served warm or at room temperature. If you can't find toasted rice powder at the markets, toast and grind white rice yourself, it only takes five minutes.
The heat is important: adjust the chillies to your taste, but the dish should have a good kick. Nok doesn't hold back.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

recipe.title: Beef and Guinness Pie
recipe.summary: Rich beef and Guinness stew with a golden pastry crust.

items.raw: 1.2 kg beef chuck, cut into 3 cm pieces
Salt and black pepper, to taste
320 g puff pastry, thawed if frozen

steps.text: Heat oil in a large heavy-based pot over medium-high heat. Season beef with salt and pepper, then brown in batches, about 3 minutes each side. Transfer to a plate.
Add onions and carrots to the pot, cook, stirring, until the onions start to soften, about 5 minutes. Add garlic, cook 1 minute, then dust in flour and stir well.

Pour in Guinness and beef stock, scraping any browned bits from the bottom. Return beef and add bay leaves and thyme. Bring to a simmer, cover, and cook on low heat for 2 hours, until the beef is tender. Stir occasionally. Remove bay leaves and thyme sprigs.
Preheat oven to 200°C. Transfer the beef filling to a large pie dish, about 2 litres capacity. Let it cool slightly.

Roll out pastry to about 3 mm thick and roughly 5 cm larger than your pie dish. Brush the rim of the dish with beaten egg. Lay pastry over the filling, press down on the rim to seal, then trim excess. Cut a few slits in the top for steam to escape.
Brush the pastry with beaten egg. Bake for 25–30 minutes, until golden brown.

notes: Make the filling the day before and refrigerate; assemble and bake just before serving.
Works just as well in the slow cooker: combine all filling ingredients, cook on low for 6–8 hours, then proceed from step 4.

recipe.title: Beef Stew with Dumplings
recipe.summary: Slow-cooked beef stew with herb dumplings, the meat tender enough to eat with a spoon.

items.raw: 1 kg beef chuck, cut into 4 cm chunks
3 celery stalks, cut into 5 cm pieces
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat oil in a large heavy-based pot or slow cooker insert over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the beef all over, about 3 minutes per batch. Set aside.
In the same pot, cook the onion, carrot and celery until softened, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic and tomato paste, stir well, and cook for 1 minute.

Return the beef to the pot. Pour in the wine and stock, and add the bay leaves and thyme. Bring to a simmer, then either cover and transfer to a slow cooker on low for 6 to 8 hours, or cover and braise in a 160°C oven for 4 to 5 hours.
About 45 minutes before serving, add the potatoes and cook until just tender.

While the stew cooks, make the dumplings. In a bowl, combine flour, baking powder, parsley, thyme leaves and salt. Rub in the butter with your fingertips until the mixture resembles breadcrumbs. Make a well in the centre, add the egg and enough cold water to form a soft dough. Mix gently until just combined. Divide into 12 pieces and roll each into a ball.
Once the stew is nearly ready and the potatoes are tender, drop the dumplings into the simmering liquid and cook, uncovered, for 15 to 20 minutes until they float and are cooked through.
Taste and adjust seasoning with salt and pepper. Serve hot.

notes: This stew improves the next day when the flavours have had time to meld. Cool quickly and refrigerate for up to 3 days, or freeze for up to 3 months.
If you don't have wine, use an extra 250 ml beef stock instead.
For camp oven: brown the meat and veg in a big Dutch oven, then pop it straight into the coals for 3 to 4 hours.

Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Carnitas Tostadas
recipe.summary: Crispy tostadas piled high with slow-cooked pork carnitas, pickled onions and fresh coriander.

items.raw: 1 kg pork shoulder, cut into 5 cm chunks
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Preheat oven to 160°C. Put pork chunks in a heavy-based casserole with onion, garlic, cumin, oregano, bay leaf, salt, pepper and water. Cover and cook in the oven for 2.5 to 3 hours, until the pork is tender and falling apart, stirring halfway through.
While the pork cooks, make the pickled onions. Toss red onion with vinegar and salt in a bowl. Let sit for at least 30 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Once the pork is done, drain off as much liquid as you can, reserving it. Shred the pork with two forks.

Heat 5 mm of oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. When hot, lay a tortilla flat and fry for 1 to 2 minutes per side until golden and crisp. Transfer to a plate lined with paper towel. Repeat with remaining tortillas.
Divide tostadas among serving plates. Top each with a generous handful of warm carnitas, a spoonful of pickled onions, and a pinch of fresh coriander. Serve with lime wedges.

notes: Make the carnitas up to 2 days ahead; reheat gently in a low oven or on the stove with a splash of water.
The reserved pork cooking liquid is liquid gold, use it to warm the carnitas or sip as a broth.
No corn tortillas? Flour tortillas work fine, but corn is the real deal.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part.

recipe.title: Gigantes Plaki
recipe.summary: Giant butter beans baked in tomato sauce with herbs and olive oil.

items.raw: 800 g tin giant butter beans (gigantes plaki), drained and rinsed
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large baking dish or shallow ovenproof pan over medium heat. Add the onion and cook gently, stirring, until softened and translucent, about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic and cook, stirring, for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the crushed tomatoes, drained beans, oregano, bay leaves, and chilli flakes. Stir well to combine. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Add 120 ml of water to loosen the sauce slightly, the beans should be mostly submerged in tomato liquid.

Transfer the dish to a 180°C oven (or continue cooking in the pan if it's heatproof). Bake uncovered for 45–50 minutes, until the sauce has thickened and reduced slightly and the flavours have melded. Stir once halfway through.
Taste and adjust seasoning if needed. The beans should be tender and the sauce should coat them richly. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: Gigantes plaki is just as good served at room temperature the next day. The flavours deepen as it sits.
If your tin of beans is particularly large (500 g drained), add a little more tomato sauce or water to keep the proportion balanced.

recipe.title: Gaeng Som Pla
recipe.summary: Central Thai sour curry with barramundi, tomato and herbs from a homemade paste.

items.raw: 500 g white fish fillet, cut into chunks (barramundi or snapper)
Thai basil, small handful, roughly chopped

steps.text: Make the curry paste: pound the garlic, shrimp paste and dried chillies together in a mortar until mostly smooth. Add the ground coriander and turmeric and mix well.
Heat the oil in a large saucepan over medium heat. Add the curry paste and fry, stirring, for 2–3 minutes until fragrant.
Pour in the stock and bring to a gentle simmer. Add the fish sauce, tamarind paste and palm sugar, and stir until the sugar dissolves.
Add the fish and simmer gently for 8–10 minutes, until cooked through and beginning to flake. Do not stir roughly or the fish will break apart.
Add the tomato and simmer for 2 minutes to warm through.
Remove from the heat and stir in the coriander and Thai basil. Taste and adjust with fish sauce, tamarind or lime juice as needed. Serve immediately.

notes: Make the curry paste up to a day ahead and keep it covered in the fridge. Fresh fish is best for this curry, ask your fishmonger what looks good on the day.
Use whatever white fish is fresh and local: snapper, flathead or barramundi all work well.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

recipe.title: Boil-up
recipe.summary: One-pot corned beef, pork bones, potatoes and watercress – kai comfort food.

steps.text: Place the corned beef, pork bones, onions and salt in a large pot. Cover with 3 litres of water. Bring to the boil, then reduce heat and simmer, partly covered, for 45 minutes.
Add the potatoes to the pot. Simmer, partly covered, for another 30 minutes, until the potatoes are tender and the corned beef is cooked through.
Add the watercress and black pepper. Stir gently and cook for 2 minutes until the watercress is just wilted.
Carefully remove the corned beef and pork bones. Slice the corned beef and return to the pot. Serve hot in wide bowls with plenty of the aromatic broth.

notes: Make a bigger batch and cool the broth quickly; it freezes well for up to 3 months.
If you can't find good pork bones, use a ham hock or extra corned beef – the broth won't be quite as rich but it'll still be aroha kai.
Fresh watercress is key. If you can't get it, try silverbeet (spinach) or spring greens – add them the same way, just wilted.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

recipe.title: Yassa au Poulet
recipe.summary: Chicken braised in mustard, lemon and onions, a Senegalese weeknight staple.

items.raw: 800 g chicken pieces (thighs and drumsticks), skin on
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large heavy-based pot over medium-high heat. Season the chicken with salt and pepper, then brown it skin-side down for 4 to 5 minutes until golden. Turn and brown the other side for another 3 minutes. Remove to a plate.

Add the sliced onions to the pot and cook, stirring occasionally, until soft and starting to caramelise, about 8 minutes. Stir in the mustard and turmeric, then add the lemon juice, scraping up any sticky bits from the bottom.

Pour in the stock and return the chicken to the pot, nestling it among the onions. Bring to a gentle simmer, then reduce the heat to low. Cover and braise for 25 to 30 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through (75°C inside) and the onions are very soft.
Taste and adjust the seasoning. Serve warm over rice, spooning the sauce generously over each portion.

notes: Yassa is even better the next day. Cool quickly, cover and refrigerate for up to 3 days, or freeze for up to 3 months. Reheat gently on the stove.
Use thighs and drumsticks rather than breast, they stay moist and the skin crisps beautifully in the pan.

recipe.title: Shanghainese Soup Dumplings
recipe.summary: Delicate wheat dumplings with a pork and gelatin filling, steamed and served in their own rich broth.

items.raw: 50 g gelatine, finely chopped (or 4 leaves gelatine, finely chopped)

steps.text: Make the dough: mix the hot water into the flour and salt with chopsticks or a fork until a shaggy dough forms. Once cool enough to handle, knead for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic. The dough should feel soft and slightly sticky, this high hydration gives you that tender wrapper. Cover and rest for at least 30 minutes.

Make the filling: mix the pork, gelatine, spring onion, soy sauce, sesame oil, shaoxing wine, ginger and sugar in a bowl. Stir until just combined, don't overwork it or it will become dense. Taste and adjust seasoning if needed.

Divide the dough into 16 equal pieces. Roll each into a ball, then use a small rolling pin or your fingers to flatten into a thin disc about 10 cm across, slightly thicker at the edges than the centre.

Place about 1 tbsp of filling in the centre of each wrapper. Bring the edges up and gather at the top, pleating as you go, then twist gently to seal. The dumpling should look like a little purse. Place seam-side up on a small square of baking paper (this stops it sticking to the steamer).
Set up a steamer: bring water to a boil in a wok or large pot, and place a bamboo steamer basket or metal steamer rack above it, making sure the water doesn't touch the base of the basket.

Working in batches, carefully place 4–6 dumplings seam-side up in the steamer, still on their paper squares. Steam over simmering water for 10–12 minutes, until the wrappers are translucent and cooked through. You'll see a slight sheen on them when they're ready.

Transfer the cooked dumplings to a serving platter. Warm the chicken stock gently with the ginger slices and spring onion if using, then ladle into small bowls or a shallow serving dish. Serve the dumplings alongside, with black vinegar and extra stock for dipping.

notes: The dough can be made up to 8 hours ahead and kept covered at room temperature. If it dries out, spritz lightly with water.
The filling can be made several hours ahead and refrigerated. Assemble the dumplings no more than 1 hour before steaming.
If you don't have a bamboo steamer, use a metal steamer rack or even a heatproof plate set on chopsticks above the simmering water, the key is gentle, steady steam.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

recipe.title: Masala Dosa
recipe.summary: Crispy rice and lentil crepe filled with spiced potato curry.

items.raw: 500 g waxy potato, boiled and diced
1 tsp urad dal (white lentils), if you have it

steps.text: Make the potato masala: heat oil in a small pan over medium-high heat. When hot, add mustard seeds and urad dal. Once the seeds crackle (about 30 seconds), add the chopped chilli and curry leaf. Stir for 10 seconds until fragrant.
Add the diced boiled potato, turmeric and cumin. Stir well to coat and warm through, about 2 minutes. Season with salt to taste. Remove from heat and keep warm.
Heat a large non-stick pan or cast-iron griddle (tawa) over medium-high heat for 2 minutes until very hot. Lightly oil the surface.

Pour about 60 ml of dosa batter into the centre of the pan. Using the back of a ladle, spread it in a thin circular motion from the centre outward, working quickly to make a thin crepe about 25 cm across. The thinner the better.
Drizzle a little oil around the edges and under the crepe. Cook until the underside is golden and crispy, about 1–2 minutes. The edges should curl slightly.
Flip the dosa carefully and cook the other side for another 30 seconds until just set. Do not over-cook or it will become chewy instead of crispy.
Slide the dosa onto a plate. Spoon a quarter of the potato masala along one half of the crepe, fold in half, then fold into a triangle if you like.
Repeat with the remaining batter and filling. Serve hot with sambar and coconut chutney for dipping.

notes: Make the dosa batter 1 to 2 days ahead and keep it in the fridge. It ferments and becomes more flavourful. Use it straight from the fridge, don't bring it to room temperature.
If the batter is too thick, thin it with a splash of water. It should pour easily but still coat the pan.
The potato can be boiled and diced an hour ahead.

recipe.title: Karahi Chicken
recipe.summary: Tender chicken in a thick tomato and capsicum gravy, cooked in the karahi with whole spices.

items.raw: 800 g chicken thigh, cut into 4 cm pieces
2 red capsicum, cut into thick chunks

steps.text: Heat the oil in a karahi or heavy-bottomed frying pan over medium heat. Add the cardamom pods, cloves, cinnamon stick and bay leaves. Let them sizzle and colour for about 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft and deep golden, about 8–10 minutes. Add the garlic and ginger, stir and cook for 2 minutes until the raw smell goes.

Increase the heat to medium-high. Add the chicken pieces, salt and black pepper, and cook without stirring for 3 minutes to seal, then stir and cook for another 3 minutes until the chicken is no longer pink on the outside.
Add the ground coriander and turmeric, stir well for 30 seconds.

Pour in the tinned tomatoes and their juice, breaking them up with the spoon. Simmer over medium heat, stirring occasionally, for 12–15 minutes until the sauce is thick and the oil begins to separate from the tomatoes on the surface.

Add the capsicum chunks and green chilli, stir gently, and cook for 5–8 minutes more until the capsicum is tender but still holding its shape and the chicken is cooked through (75°C at the thickest point).
Taste and adjust the salt if needed. Scatter with fresh coriander and serve hot with naan, roti or steamed rice.

notes: This keeps well in the fridge for 2 days and freezes beautifully for up to 3 months. Reheat gently on the stove.
Ayesha's tip: Don't rush the tomato-breaking-down stage. That's where the flavour sits. If you like more heat, add a pinch of dried chilli flakes with the ground spices or more green chilli.

recipe.title: Kinilaw na Tuna
recipe.summary: Raw tuna cured in vinegar and lime, with coconut milk, chilli and ginger.

items.raw: 500 g sashimi-grade tuna, cut into bite-sized cubes
3 spring onions, cut into 3 cm pieces

steps.text: Cut the sashimi-grade tuna into bite-sized cubes and place in a glass or ceramic bowl (not metal, as vinegar will react).
Pour the vinegar and lime juice over the tuna and stir gently to combine. Let it sit in the fridge for 5 minutes so the acid begins to denature the fish.
Add the coconut milk, sliced chillies and julienned ginger, and stir gently to coat everything.
Add the spring onions and taste, adjusting salt as needed. The acid should be balanced by the richness of the coconut milk.
Cover and chill until ready to serve. Kinilaw is best eaten the same day, within a few hours of making it, while the texture is firm and the flavours are fresh.

notes: Use the freshest sashimi-grade tuna available. If you're unsure about the source, ask your fishmonger.
Coconut vinegar adds a more authentic Visayan flavour, but white vinegar works well too.
Eat the same day you make it – the acid cures the fish but doesn't preserve it like cooking does.

The fish here is eaten raw or only cured in citrus. Buy sashimi-grade fish from a fishmonger, keep it cold and eat it the same day; skip it for anyone pregnant, very young, elderly or with low immunity.

Food safety: The seafood here is served raw or cured, so buy sashimi-grade, keep it cold and eat it the day it is made; for anyone who should avoid raw fish, cook it until opaque. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Penang Assam Laksa
recipe.summary: Sour and spicy rice noodle soup with mackerel, tamarind and shrimp paste.

items.raw: 2 cm piece fresh ginger, roughly chopped
2 whole mackerel (about 400 g), cleaned and halved

steps.text: Soak the dried chillies in hot water for 10 minutes until soft. Drain and roughly chop.
Pound the softened chillies, garlic, galangal, ginger, shrimp paste and 2 tbsp tamarind paste together in a mortar until you have a rough paste (or blend in a food processor).
Heat the 2 tbsp oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the laksa paste and fry, stirring, for about 3 minutes until fragrant and darker in colour.
Pour in the fish stock and bring to a gentle simmer. Add the halved mackerel and cook for 8 to 10 minutes until the fish is cooked through, the flesh should flake easily.

Stir in the coconut milk and the extra 2 tbsp tamarind paste. Taste and season with salt and palm sugar if you like a bit of sweetness. Simmer for another 2 minutes. The broth should be spicy, sour and rich.
While the soup cooks, blanch the fresh rice noodles in a large pot of boiling water for 1 to 2 minutes until just tender. Divide among serving bowls.
Carefully remove the mackerel pieces from the soup and divide among the bowls. Ladle the hot broth over the noodles.
Top each bowl with cucumber, pineapple, a hard-boiled egg half, fresh herbs and fried shallots. Serve hot.

notes: The laksa paste can be made the day before and kept in an airtight container in the fridge.
Use the freshest mackerel you can find, the quality makes all the difference. If fresh mackerel is hard to find, try Spanish mackerel or another firm white fish.
The broth can be made ahead and reheated gently; cook the noodles fresh just before serving.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Sugo di Calabria
recipe.summary: Deep red Sunday sauce with pork, garden tomatoes, and Calabrian heat.

items.raw: 600 g pork shoulder, cut into 4–5 large chunks

steps.text: Heat a generous glug of olive oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat. Brown the pork chunks on all sides, about 10 minutes total. Set aside.
Add the onion halves to the same pot and cook until caramelised at the edges, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and whole chillies, stir for 1 minute until fragrant.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 2 minutes, then add the tinned tomatoes and fresh tomatoes with their juices. Return the pork to the pot and add the oregano. Stir well.

Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cover partially and cook, stirring occasionally, for 3 hours. The sauce should reduce by half and become deep red and glossy. The pork will fall apart easily when ready.
Remove the pork chunks and shred them with two forks, discarding any large bones or tough bits. Return the shredded pork to the sauce.
Taste and adjust salt and pepper. The sauce should be rich, thick, and warm with heat from the chillies. Serve over pasta with grated parmesan.

notes: Make this the day before and reheat gently, the flavour deepens overnight.
Freeze the sauce in portions for up to three months.
Serve over fresh pasta, pappardelle, or rigatoni, with a scatter of fresh basil and parmesan.
Cook pork until it reaches at least 70°C in the thickest part (75°C for mince and sausages).

recipe.title: Borscht
recipe.summary: Deep beetroot soup with beef, potatoes and dill, the soup that defines home.

items.raw: 600 g beef chuck, cut into 2 cm pieces
400 g beetroot, peeled and cut into thin matchsticks
items.prep: peeled and cut into thin matchsticks

items.raw: 3 medium waxy potatoes, cut into 1 cm cubes
2 tbsp white vinegar (or apple cider vinegar)
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the beef on all sides, about 3 minutes per batch. Set the beef aside.
Add the onions to the same pot and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute more.
Return the beef to the pot and add the beef stock and bay leaf. Bring to the boil, then reduce the heat and simmer, covered, for 30 minutes until the beef is starting to become tender.
Add the beetroot, potatoes, carrots and tomato paste. Stir well and simmer, covered, for 35–40 minutes until the beef is tender and the potatoes are soft.
Stir in the vinegar, then taste and season with salt and pepper. If you prefer a deeper flavour, add a little more vinegar.
Ladle into bowls and serve hot, topped with fresh dill and a spoonful of sour cream if you like.

notes: Borscht keeps well in the fridge for up to 4 days, and the flavour deepens each day. Reheat gently on the stove.
For a vegetarian version, skip the beef and use vegetable stock instead; the soup will need only 45 minutes on the stove after the vegetables go in.
Some cooks add 200 g cooked kidney beans with the potatoes for a heartier soup.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.
Make the chilli oil ahead: gently warm 2 tbsp neutral oil with 1 tsp chilli flakes and a small pinch of salt, let it cool, then strain. It keeps for two weeks.
Don't stir the tofu vigour​ously or it will break apart—the goal is cubes, not a purée.
The Sichuan peppercorns are essential: they make your mouth tingle gently, not burn. Toast them lightly in a dry pan first for deeper flavour.

steps.text: Heat the neutral oil in a wok or large shallow pan over high heat. Add the pork mince and stir-fry, breaking it apart as it cooks, until it is browned and just cooked through, about 3 minutes.
Reduce the heat to medium. Push the mince to the side and add the doubanjiang to the empty space. Stir it in the oil for 30 seconds to release the flavour, then mix it through the mince.
Add the garlic, ginger and white parts of the spring onions. Stir constantly for 1 minute until fragrant.

Pour in the stock and add the soy sauce and rice vinegar. Bring to a simmer, then gently slide the tofu cubes into the liquid. Simmer for 3 minutes without stirring, so the tofu heats through and the sauce begins to thicken naturally.
Stir the cornflour slurry and pour it into the pan while stirring gently. Simmer for 1 minute until the sauce coats the tofu and thickens slightly.
Remove from heat. Drizzle with the chilli oil, scatter the Sichuan peppercorns and green parts of the spring onion over the top, and serve immediately with steamed rice.

recipe.title: Mapo Tofu
recipe.summary: Silken tofu in a numbingly spiced meat sauce with Sichuan peppercorns and chilli oil.

items.raw: 500 g silken tofu, cut into 1 cm cubes
2 spring onions, white and green separated, thinly sliced
items.prep: white and green separated, thinly sliced

items.raw: 1 tsp cornflour, mixed with 2 tbsp cold water

recipe.title: Lamb and Apricot Bredie
recipe.summary: Spiced lamb and apricot stew, slow-cooked with turmeric and cinnamon.

items.raw: 800 g lamb shoulder, cut into 4 cm chunks

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large, heavy pot over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the lamb on all sides, about 3–4 minutes per batch. Set aside.
In the same pot, cook the onions over medium heat, stirring, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute more.
Add the turmeric, cinnamon, coriander and black pepper. Stir through the onions, cooking gently for 1 minute until fragrant.

Return the lamb to the pot. Pour in the stock and add the bay leaves. Stir in the golden syrup and apricots. Bring to a simmer, then reduce the heat to low, cover, and cook gently for 1 hour, or until the lamb is very tender.
Stir in the lemon juice, taste, and adjust the salt and spices if needed. The stew should be balanced, warm spice, a touch of sweetness from the apricots, and a hint of brightness from the lemon.
Serve hot, spooned over plain boiled rice.

notes: Bredie improves overnight as the spices deepen. Make it the day before and gently reheat it.
If you can't find dried apricots, use dried peaches or a combination of apricots and raisins.
Traditionally made with mutton; lamb shoulder works beautifully and cooks a little faster.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

recipe.title: Kartoffelpuffer mit Lachs
recipe.summary: Crispy potato pancakes topped with smoked salmon and dill crème fraîche.

items.raw: 800 g waxy potato, peeled and coarsely grated
Salt and black pepper, to taste
150 g smoked salmon, sliced or torn

steps.text: Squeeze the grated potato and onion firmly in a clean tea towel to remove as much moisture as possible, this is essential for crispy pancakes.
In a bowl, whisk the eggs, then stir in the drained potato and onion, flour, salt and pepper until combined.

Heat about 5 mm of oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. When the oil is shimmering, carefully spoon the mixture into the pan in loose mounds (about 6 cm across) and flatten them gently with the back of a spatula.

Fry for 4 to 5 minutes until the underside is golden and crisp. Flip and cook the other side for another 3 to 4 minutes until golden. Work in batches and keep cooked pancakes warm on a plate lined with paper towel.
While the pancakes cook, fold the dill into the crème fraîche and season lightly with salt and pepper.
Serve the warm pancakes topped with a spoonful of dill crème fraîche and a few pieces of smoked salmon. Finish with a squeeze of lemon if you like.

notes: Make the potato mixture just before frying, it will start to weep if left to sit. If you must wait, drain and squeeze it again before cooking.
The crème fraîche topping can be made up to a day ahead and kept refrigerated.

recipe.title: Adobong Manok
recipe.summary: Chicken braised in vinegar and soy with garlic and bay leaf, Kapampangan-style.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large heavy pot or deep pan over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the chicken pieces all over, about 5 minutes per batch. Set aside.
In the same pot, add the crushed garlic and peppercorns. Stir constantly for about 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the vinegar and soy sauce, stirring well to combine. Return the chicken to the pot and add the bay leaves and water. Bring to a simmer until the liquid is gently bubbling.
Reduce heat to low, cover, and braise gently for 40–45 minutes, turning the chicken halfway through, until the chicken is very tender and cooked through (the juices should run clear when pierced).
Taste and adjust salt as needed. The sauce should be rich and deeply flavoured.
Serve hot with steamed rice, anak.
