notes: This adobo tastes even better the next day, anak. Keep it in the fridge and warm it gently before serving.
If you don't have calamansi, use fresh lime juice or good white vinegar, both work beautifully.
Corazon always serves this with plain steamed white rice and a simple green vegetable.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

recipe.title: Nasu Dengaku
recipe.summary: Grilled eggplant with warm miso glaze, charred outside and silky within.

steps.text: Score the flesh of each eggplant half with shallow cuts in a crosshatch pattern, being careful not to pierce the skin.
Brush the eggplant flesh generously with oil. Season lightly with salt.
Heat a grill pan or barbecue to medium-high. Grill the eggplants flesh-side down for 6 to 8 minutes, until soft and charred. Turn skin-side down and grill for another 1 to 2 minutes.
While the eggplants cook, whisk together the miso, sugar, mirin, and dashi powder in a small bowl until smooth.
Transfer the grilled eggplants to a serving plate, flesh-side up. Spread the miso glaze generously over the hot flesh, it will warm and soften.
Scatter sesame seeds over the top and serve at once.

notes: The eggplants can be grilled up to 30 minutes ahead; reheat gently in the oven at 180°C for 5 minutes, then glaze and serve.
Red miso gives a deeper colour; white miso is sweeter and milder. Use what you have.
If you don't have a grill pan, use a regular frying pan over medium-high heat, or grill over charcoal if you can.

recipe.title: Cơm Chiên Hải Sản
recipe.summary: Saigon seafood fried rice with squid and prawns, crispy edges and fish sauce

items.raw: 3 cups cooked white rice, cold (about 600 g)
200 g squid tube, cleaned and sliced into thin rings
items.prep: cleaned and sliced into thin rings

items.raw: 2 spring onion, sliced (white and green parts separated)

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp of the oil in a large wok or heavy-based frying pan over high heat until smoking hot. Add the squid and prawns, stirring constantly until cooked through, about 2–3 minutes. Transfer to a plate.
Add the remaining 1 tbsp oil to the wok. Add the garlic and white parts of the spring onion, stirring for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the cold rice, breaking up any clumps with the back of a spatula. Stir-fry for 4–5 minutes, letting some rice stick to the bottom of the wok and char slightly.
Return the squid and prawns to the wok. Add the fish sauce and sugar, tossing everything together. Cook for 1 minute more, letting more rice crisp against the hot pan.
Season with salt and white pepper to taste. Stir through the green parts of the spring onion.
Serve hot from the wok, scraping up those golden, crispy bits from the bottom. Top with fresh coriander if you like.

notes: Cold, leftover rice works best, warm rice gets mushy. Spread it on a tray and refrigerate for at least 2 hours.
The key to those crispy golden bits (cơm cháy) is letting the rice sit untouched on the hot pan for 30 seconds at a time before stirring.
For extra flavour, add a splash of soy sauce or a drizzle of chilli oil after cooking.

Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through. Cool any leftover rice quickly and refrigerate it within an hour; reheat it until steaming hot.

recipe.title: Pasta alla Nduja
recipe.summary: Spaghetti with spicy Calabrian nduja, tomato, garlic and a touch of cream.

items.raw: 150 g nduja, chopped into small pieces
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Bring a large pot of salted water to the boil and cook the spaghetti until just al dente, about 9–10 minutes. Reserve 200 ml of pasta water, then drain.

While the pasta cooks, place the nduja and garlic in a large frying pan over medium-low heat. Stir gently for 2–3 minutes until the nduja starts to break down and release its oils, don't let it brown.
Add the crushed tomatoes to the pan and stir well to combine with the nduja and garlic. Simmer for 4–5 minutes until the sauce thickens slightly.
Pour in the cream and stir through. Season with salt and black pepper to taste. Add a splash of pasta water if the sauce is too thick, it should coat the pasta loosely.
Add the cooked spaghetti to the pan and toss gently to coat every strand. Add a little more pasta water if needed to loosen the sauce.
Divide among four bowls and finish with a generous handful of grated parmesan and a basil leaf, if you like.

notes: Nduja keeps well in the fridge for weeks once opened. Wrap it tightly or keep it in an airtight container.
If you can't find nduja at your local deli, check the Italian section at a good supermarket or order it online, it's worth the hunt.

recipe.title: Tempe Goreng Sambal Matah
recipe.summary: Crispy fried tempeh with raw sambal of shallots, chilli and lime.

items.raw: 250 g tempeh, sliced into 1 cm rectangles

steps.text: Make the sambal matah first: combine the shallots, chillies and garlic in a bowl. Add the lime juice and neutral oil, then taste and add salt. Set aside while you fry the tempeh.
Heat about 1 cm of neutral oil in a frying pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Test with a piece of tempeh, it should sizzle immediately.
Working in batches so you don't crowd the pan, fry the tempeh slices until golden and crispy on both sides, about 3–4 minutes total. Drain on paper towel and sprinkle with salt while still hot.
Arrange the hot fried tempeh on a plate and spoon the sambal matah over the top. Eat straight away, the contrast between the crispy, hot tempeh and the cool, bright sambal is the whole point.

notes: Make a big batch of sambal matah and keep it in the fridge for up to three days, it's brilliant on rice, eggs, or any leftover protein.
If you can't find fresh lime, use lemon or bottled lime juice, but fresh is so much better.
Tempeh keeps in the fridge for ages; fry it whenever you need a quick, protein-packed lunch.

recipe.title: Atsuage
recipe.summary: Thick-fried tofu cutlet with dashi and grated daikon.

items.raw: 300 g firm tofu, drained and cut into 2 thick slices
items.prep: drained and cut into 2 thick slices

steps.text: Pat the tofu slices dry with paper towels. Blot both sides well, this is important for crispy frying.

Heat about 3 cm of oil in a small, deep pan to 160°C. The tofu will sink and then float as it cooks; if you don't have a thermometer, test with a wooden chopstick, bubbles should form steadily around it.
Carefully lower the tofu into the hot oil. Fry for 4 minutes until the surface is golden and crispy, then gently turn it over and fry for another 4 minutes until both sides are golden.
Warm the dashi in a small saucepan. Stir in the soy sauce and mirin.
Transfer the hot tofu to a bowl. Pour the hot dashi over it. Top with the grated daikon and spring onion. Eat while it's still steaming.

notes: The key is drying the tofu well before frying, squeeze it gently between clean cloths to release as much water as you can.
Atsuage is best eaten straight away, while the outside is still crackling and the inside soft.

recipe.title: Bacalao a la Vizcaína
recipe.summary: Salt cod in dark pepper and tomato sauce, the Vizcaya way.

items.raw: 4 dried choricero peppers (or 3 large dried red peppers)
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Soak the salt cod in cold water for 24 hours, changing the water every 6–8 hours. This draws out the salt. After soaking, drain and place in a large pot with 1 litre of fresh cold water. Bring slowly to a gentle simmer, do not boil. Simmer for 8–10 minutes until the flesh is tender and flakes easily. Remove from heat, drain gently, and set aside on a warm plate. Keep the cooking broth.

While the cod simmers, prepare the sauce. Toast the dried choricero peppers briefly in a dry pan over medium heat, about 30 seconds each side, until fragrant. Soak them in 200 ml of warm water for 10 minutes to soften, then drain. Scrape the flesh from the skin with a spoon and discard the skins and seeds. You should have a dark red paste.

Heat the olive oil in a heavy pan over medium heat. Add the chopped onion and cook gently, stirring occasionally, for about 8 minutes until soft and golden. Add the sliced garlic and cook for 1 minute more until fragrant.

Stir in the paprika and cook for 30 seconds. Add the pepper paste you made, the tinned tomatoes, and 2 tablespoons of water. Stir well to combine. Simmer gently for 15 minutes, stirring often, until the sauce darkens and thickens slightly. Season with salt and black pepper to taste.

Carefully place the warm salt cod fillets into the sauce. Pour about 100 ml of the reserved cooking broth around (not over) the cod. Simmer very gently for 5 minutes, the cod will break apart if you're rough with it. The sauce should be rich, dark, and coat the fish.
Serve in deep earthenware bowls with the sauce spooned around the fish. Eat with good bread and a glass of txakoli or dry white wine.

notes: Salt cod must be soaked for 24 hours before cooking. Start the night before.
Choricero peppers are essential, they give the sauce its deep colour and flavour. Find them in Spanish delis or good supermarkets; regular dried peppers work but won't taste the same.
This dish is best made in a heavy earthenware cazuela, but any heavy-bottomed pan works fine.

recipe.title: Quenelles de brochet
recipe.summary: Pike dumplings in creamy shellfish sauce, a lighter Lyonnaise bistro classic.

items.raw: 400 g white fish fillet (pike, perch or barramundi)

steps.text: Pulse the fish fillet in a food processor until very finely minced. Add the softened butter and pulse until you have a pale, creamy paste. Work in the eggs one at a time, then fold in the cream by hand. Season with salt, white pepper and nutmeg. Taste a tiny spoonful by poaching it briefly in a small pan of water to check the seasoning. Chill for 10 minutes.

Bring the stock to a gentle simmer in a large, wide pan. Using two warm wet spoons, shape the pike mixture into quenelle shapes (or simply oval dumplings, don't fuss). Gently slide them into the simmering stock. They'll sink, then float to the surface when cooked through, about 4 minutes. Poach in two batches if needed so they're not crowded. Lift them out with a slotted spoon and keep warm on a plate.

For the sauce: melt the butter in a small pan over medium heat. Whisk in the flour to make a smooth roux and cook, stirring, for 2 minutes. Gradually whisk in the stock, then the cream, stirring until smooth. Simmer for 3 minutes. Stir in the cooked prawn and sherry, season with salt, white pepper and a pinch of cayenne. Taste and adjust.
Arrange the quenelles in a warmed shallow dish or on individual plates. Pour the Nantua sauce over and serve at once.

notes: Make the quenelle mixture up to 2 hours ahead and chill. The sauce can be made while the quenelles poach.
If pike isn't available, perch, barramundi or any firm white fish works well, this is a weeknight dinner, not a pilgrimage.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

recipe.title: Pantry Chicken and Lentil Soup
recipe.summary: Hearty weeknight soup with chicken, lentils and tomato from your pantry cupboard.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add onion and cook, stirring, until soft and starting to colour, about 5 minutes.
Add garlic, carrot and celery. Stir and cook for 2 minutes until fragrant.
Add crushed tomatoes, lentils and stock. Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to medium-low. Cook for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until lentils are very soft.
Stir in the shredded chicken and cook for 5 minutes to warm through. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Divide among bowls and serve hot.

notes: Leftovers keep in the fridge for 3 days. Reheat gently on the stove, adding a splash of water if it's thickened too much.
Use rotisserie chicken, or shredded leftover roast chicken. If you don't have cooked chicken, add 300 g raw chicken breast to the pot with the stock and cook for 12 minutes before adding lentils.
Swap red lentils for brown lentils if you prefer a firmer texture; they'll need the full 25 minutes to cook.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

recipe.title: Katsudon
recipe.summary: Crispy panfried pork cutlet over rice with egg and onions, the weeknight donburi that beats takeout.

items.raw: 2 pork loin cutlets, about 150 g each, pounded thin to 5 mm
items.prep: about 150 g each, pounded thin to 5 mm

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
1 brown onion, halved and thinly sliced
2 cups cooked short-grain white rice, warm

steps.text: Set up your crumbing station: put the flour in one shallow bowl, beaten egg in another, and panko in a third. Season the pork with salt and pepper, then coat in flour, shaking off excess. Dip in beaten egg, then press into panko until fully coated.

Heat 3 tbsp oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. When it's hot and shimmering, carefully lay the pork cutlets in and cook until golden and crisp, 3 to 4 minutes on each side. The pork is done when it reaches 63°C in the thickest part. Transfer to a plate.
In the same pan, reduce heat to medium and add the sliced onion. Cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 4 minutes. Add the mirin, soy sauce and water, and bring to a simmer.
Slice each pork cutlet into strips. Return the pork to the pan, nestled among the onions, and simmer for 2 minutes to warm through and coat with sauce.

Push the pork and onions to the sides of the pan. Pour the beaten eggs into the sauce, and without stirring, let them cook for 1 to 2 minutes until just set but still slightly glossy on top, you want the eggs to stay soft.
Divide the warm rice between two bowls. Carefully slide the pork, onions and egg over the rice, spoon the sauce over top, and scatter spring onions and nori strips if using. Serve immediately.

notes: Make the sauce while the pork cooks: mix mirin, soy sauce and water in a small bowl and you're ready to go.
No fresh pork cutlets? Thin chicken breast works just as well, pound it to 5 mm and it'll cook in the same time.
Leftover rice from lunch? This dish is your friend. Just make sure it's still warm when you serve.

Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system. Cool any leftover rice quickly and refrigerate it within an hour; reheat it until steaming hot.

recipe.title: Braised Pork Rice
recipe.summary: Tender braised pork belly over steamed rice with a jammy egg.

items.raw: 500 g pork belly, cut into 3 cm cubes

steps.text: Blanch the pork belly cubes in boiling water for 5 minutes, then drain and rinse under cold water until the water runs clear. This removes impurities and keeps the braise clean.
Heat the neutral oil in a medium pot over medium-high heat. Add the blanched pork and cook, stirring occasionally, until the surfaces are lightly golden, about 5 minutes.

Add the garlic, ginger, brown onion, dried shiitake, star anise, rock sugar, soy sauce and dark soy sauce. Stir well, then add the water. Bring to a simmer, then lower the heat to low, cover, and braise for 60–70 minutes until the pork is very tender and the sauce is rich and glossy. Stir every 20 minutes.
While the pork is braising, soft-boil the eggs: bring a small pot of water to the boil, gently add the eggs, and cook for 6–7 minutes for a jammy yolk. Transfer to cold water, then carefully peel.

Divide the cooked rice between two bowls. Top each with the braised pork and sauce, and halve a soft-boiled egg over the top. Scatter with spring onion and drizzle with extra soy sauce or chilli oil if you like.

notes: Make the braised pork up to 2 days ahead. It keeps in the fridge in its sauce and tastes even better reheated.
The eggs are best cooked just before serving, but you can boil them ahead and reheat gently in hot water.

Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Chicken and Mushroom Pie
recipe.summary: Creamy chicken and mushroom filling in golden shortcrust pastry, proper comfort food.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Make the pastry: rub the butter into the flour and salt until it looks like breadcrumbs. Mix the egg yolk with cold water, pour it in, and bring it together into a dough with your hands. Wrap in cling film and chill while you make the filling.
Melt the butter in a large heavy-bottomed pan over medium-high heat. Season the chicken with salt and pepper, then brown it in batches, about 3 minutes each side, don't crowd the pan. Set aside.
In the same pan, add the onion and cook until soft, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and mushrooms, stir, and cook until the mushrooms release their liquid and it evaporates, about 8 minutes.

Sprinkle the flour over the veg, stir well, and cook for 1 minute. Pour in the stock and cream, add the mustard, and stir to combine. Return the chicken to the pan, bring to a simmer, and cook gently for 10 minutes. Taste and adjust the seasoning. Let it cool completely, this is important or the pastry will be soggy.

Preheat the oven to 200°C. Pour the cooled filling into a 1.5 litre pie dish. Roll out the pastry on a floured bench to about 5 mm thick and about 2 cm larger than the dish. Lay it over the filling, press the edges down, and trim with a knife. Brush with beaten egg.
Bake for 25–30 minutes until the pastry is golden brown and the filling bubbles at the edges. Rest for 5 minutes before serving.

notes: The filling must cool completely before adding the pastry, or it'll go soggy. Make it the day before if you like.
You can freeze the uncooked pie for up to a month. Bake straight from frozen, adding 10–15 minutes to the cooking time.
Swaps: button mushrooms work fine if you can't get swiss browns, or use a mix. Crème fraîche instead of cream if that's what you've got.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Kimchi-jjim
recipe.summary: Braised pork belly with aged kimchi and ginger, stewed until tender.

items.raw: 800 g pork belly, skin removed, cut into 5 cm cubes
items.prep: skin removed, cut into 5 cm cubes

items.raw: 500 g aged kimchi (napa cabbage), roughly chopped
3 tbsp kimchi juice (reserved from the jar)
2 spring onions, cut into 3 cm pieces

steps.text: Place pork belly cubes in a heavy-bottomed pot or braising pan. Add the water and bring to a boil over medium-high heat. Simmer for 8 minutes, skimming any scum that rises to the surface, until the pork is partially cooked.

Add the aged kimchi, kimchi juice, garlic, ginger, gochugaru, soy sauce, and sugar. Stir well, then return to a simmer. Cover and braise over medium heat for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the pork is very tender and falling apart at the edges.
Taste and adjust the salt if needed. Add the spring onions and stir gently, cooking for 1 minute until just wilted.
Transfer to a serving bowl and scatter with toasted sesame seeds. Serve hot with steamed white rice.

notes: Use well-aged kimchi for the deepest flavour; old kimchi that's been fermenting for months is better than fresh.
Don't skip the skimming step, it keeps the braise clean and clear.
Leftover kimchi-jjim reheats gently on the stove with a splash of water.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part.

recipe.title: Tagine d'Agneau aux Pruneaux
recipe.summary: Slow-cooked lamb with prunes and warm spices, a classic Moroccan tagine.

items.raw: 800 g lamb shoulder, cut into 5 cm pieces
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large heavy pot or tagine over medium-high heat. Season the lamb pieces with salt and pepper, then brown them in batches, 3–4 minutes per side. Set aside.
In the same pot, cook the onion until soft, about 5 minutes. Add the chopped fresh garlic and fresh ginger, and stir for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the ground ginger, cinnamon, and cumin, stirring constantly for 30 seconds until fragrant, to toast the spices.
Return the lamb to the pot and stir well to coat. Pour in the chicken stock and bring to a simmer. Cover and cook gently on low heat for 60 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Add the saffron threads and prunes, and stir. Simmer, covered, for another 20–30 minutes until the lamb is very tender and the sauce has thickened slightly.
Taste and adjust seasoning with salt and pepper. Serve hot, scattered with fresh coriander if you like.

notes: Make it the day before and reheat gently, the flavours deepen. Store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 4 days.
Serve with couscous or warm flatbread to soak up the sauce.
If you can't find saffron, add a pinch of turmeric instead for warmth and colour.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

recipe.title: Sambal Ikan Bilis
recipe.summary: Crispy anchovies coated in a fierce, garlicky sambal that'll make you sweat.

steps.text: Remove the heads and innards from the ikan bilis. Rinse gently under cold water and pat dry well with paper towels.

Heat 2 tbsp of the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Working in batches if needed, fry the ikan bilis until they are golden and crispy, about 5–6 minutes, stirring frequently. Transfer to a plate lined with paper towels.
While the ikan bilis fry, pound the bird's eye chillies and garlic together in a mortar until you have a coarse paste. Mix the tamarind paste with 2 tbsp water.
Heat the remaining 1 tbsp oil in a clean pan over medium heat. Add the chilli-garlic paste and fry, stirring often, until fragrant and the oil is starting to darken around the edges, about 3 minutes.
Pour in the tamarind mixture and stir well. Cook for 1 minute until it comes together into a thick sambal. Taste and add salt as needed.
Add the crispy ikan bilis to the hot sambal and toss quickly to coat evenly. Serve immediately while still warm.

notes: Make the sambal ahead and reheat it just before frying the ikan bilis, the anchovies need to go in hot to stay crispy.
If the ikan bilis are very small, you don't need to clean them; just rinse and fry whole.
For less heat, remove some of the chilli seeds before pounding.

recipe.title: Varenyky
recipe.summary: Soft hand-folded potato and cheese dumplings with caramelised onions and sour cream.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Make the dough. Mix flour and salt in a bowl, then make a well in the centre. Add the egg and half the warm water, then stir to bring the flour in. Add more water a little at a time until a soft, slightly sticky dough forms. Knead for 2 minutes until smooth. Cover and rest for 15 minutes.

While the dough rests, boil the diced potato in salted water until very tender, about 12 minutes. Drain well, then mash with butter until smooth. Stir in the grated cheese, salt and pepper. Set aside to cool.
Caramelise the onions. Heat oil in a large frying pan over medium heat and cook the sliced onions, stirring often, until deep golden and soft, about 15 minutes. Transfer to a plate.
Roll the dough as thin as you can (about 2 mm) on a floured surface. Using a 7 cm glass or cutter, cut out circles. Place 1 tbsp filling just off-centre on each circle.
Fold the dough in half over the filling, then bring the corners together and press to seal into a little purse shape. Place each finished dumpling on a floured tray.

Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Working in batches, add the varenyky and cook until they float to the surface, then cook for another 2 minutes. Remove with a slotted spoon and transfer to a serving dish.
Top the warm varenyky with caramelised onions and serve with a dollop of sour cream. Scatter with fresh dill if you like.

notes: Dough can be made ahead and refrigerated for up to 24 hours. Bring to room temperature before rolling.
Cooked varenyky freeze well for up to 1 month. Reheat by boiling briefly in salted water until they float again, or pan-fry with the caramelised onions.
The filling is traditional, but varenyky are also delicious filled with fried cabbage and mushrooms, or with cherries and sugar for dessert.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Nkatenkwan (Groundnut Soup)
recipe.summary: Ghanaian chicken and groundnut soup with tomatoes and peppers

items.raw: 800 g chicken thigh, bone-in skin-on, cut into chunks
4 medium tomatoes, roughly chopped (or 400 g tin crushed tomatoes)
100 g smooth peanut butter (or 3 tbsp groundnut paste)
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Season the chicken with salt and pepper, then brown it for 3 to 4 minutes per side until golden. Remove and set aside.
In the same pot, fry the onion for 2 to 3 minutes until soft. Add the garlic and tomato paste, stir well and cook for 1 minute.
Add the tomatoes and cook, stirring, for 3 to 4 minutes until they break down slightly.
Pour in the stock and return the chicken to the pot. Bring to a boil, then lower the heat and simmer gently for 15 minutes, skimming off any foam.
Add the red and green capsicum, stir and simmer for another 8 to 10 minutes until the peppers are tender but still bright.

Stir the peanut butter into a small cup with a splash of the hot broth until smooth, then stir this mixture back into the pot. Simmer for a final 5 minutes, stirring gently, until the soup is smooth and the chicken is cooked through (75°C inside). Taste and adjust seasoning.
Serve hot in bowls, scattered with fresh coriander if you like.

notes: Light soup keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days and freezes well for a month. Just reheat gently on the stove.
If you can't find groundnut paste, smooth peanut butter works just fine.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Kol Börek
recipe.summary: Crispy fried yufka rolls filled with spiced meat and cheese.

items.raw: 150 g white cheese (feta or beyaz peynir), crumbled

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp neutral oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. Add the chopped onion and cook, stirring, until softened and golden, about 4 minutes.
Add the beef mince and cook, stirring to break it up, until browned through, about 6 minutes. Drain off any excess fat.
Stir in the cumin, black pepper, salt and parsley. Remove from heat and let cool for 5 minutes.
Fold in the crumbled cheese and stir to combine. Taste and adjust seasoning. Let the filling cool completely.
Lay one sheet of yufka on a clean work surface. Place 3 tbsp of filling along one long edge, leaving a 2 cm border.

Fold the sides in by about 2 cm on each end, then roll tightly away from you, keeping it as firm as you can. The roll should be about 10 cm long and shaped like a tight cylinder. Repeat with remaining yufka and filling.
Heat neutral oil in a large, deep frying pan to 180°C (or until a small piece of yufka sizzles immediately when dropped in).
Carefully place 2 or 3 börek at a time into the hot oil, don't crowd the pan. Fry until deep golden brown all over, about 3 minutes, turning once halfway through.
Transfer to a paper towel to drain. Serve hot.

notes: Make the filling up to 2 hours ahead and chill. Roll the börek just before frying.
If yufka dries out, cover unused sheets with a damp tea towel.
Leftover börek can be reheated in a 180°C oven for 5 minutes to crisp up again.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Dhokla
recipe.summary: Steamed fermented chickpea cake, tangy and light with mustard seeds and curry leaves.

items.raw: 200 g dried chickpeas, soaked overnight in cold water
2 cm piece fresh ginger, roughly chopped
½ tsp citric acid (or lemon juice)

steps.text: Drain the soaked chickpeas well and grind them with the ginger and green chillies in a food processor until smooth, adding a little water if needed. The batter should be fine and creamy.

Transfer to a bowl and stir in the salt and citric acid. Cover loosely with a kitchen towel or cling film and leave to ferment at room temperature for 8 to 12 hours, or overnight. The batter will become slightly fluffy and airy.

Set up a steamer: fill a large pot with water and bring to a simmer. Oil a round cake tin or two loaf tins, or a microwave-safe dish if you prefer. Place them in a steamer basket or on a trivet inside the pot so they sit above the water.
Add the bicarbonate of soda to the fermented batter and stir gently but thoroughly, this will make it light and spongy. Do this just before steaming, as it loses its effect if left to sit.
Carefully pour the batter into the prepared tin(s). Cover with foil or a lid and steam for 15 to 20 minutes, until a skewer inserted into the centre comes out clean and the top feels springy.

While the dhokla steams, make the tadka: heat the oil in a small pan over medium heat until hot. Add the mustard seeds and let them crackle and pop for 30 seconds, then add the curry leaves and asafoetida. Stir for another 10 seconds until fragrant.

Remove the dhokla from the steamer and carefully run a knife around the edges to loosen it. Turn it out onto a serving plate or board. Immediately pour the hot tadka over the top, letting the oil and seeds soak in.
Leave to cool for a few minutes, then cut into squares or wedges and serve warm with chutney if you like. Leftover dhokla can be wrapped and kept in the fridge for 3 to 4 days.

notes: Make ahead: prepare the batter the night before and ferment it. In the morning, add bicarbonate of soda and steam. The whole dish takes about 40 minutes from start to finish the next day.
No fermenting time? Use ½ tsp of instant yeast mixed into the batter with a little warm water, and let it rise for 2 to 3 hours instead.
Serve with sweet chutney, green chutney or a spicy tomato achaar for dipping.

recipe.title: Laksa Ipoh
recipe.summary: Creamy tamarind and coconut laksa with fish cakes and tofu.

items.raw: 200 g firm tofu, cut into cubes

steps.text: Bring a large pot of salted water to the boil and cook the rice vermicelli until tender, about 3 minutes. Drain and set aside.
In a separate pot, heat the laksa paste in a little neutral oil over medium heat, stirring, for about 1 minute until fragrant.

Add the tamarind paste and palm sugar, stirring to combine, then pour in the coconut milk and chicken stock. Bring to a gentle simmer, then reduce to low heat and cook for 10 minutes to let the flavours settle.
While the laksa broth is simmering, heat a separate small pan over medium-high heat and fry the fish cake slices for 2 minutes on each side until lightly coloured. Remove and set aside.
In the same pan, fry the tofu cubes until golden on a few sides, about 5 minutes total. Set aside.
Taste the broth and adjust the salt as needed. The balance should be creamy, tangy and slightly sweet.
Divide the cooked vermicelli among four deep bowls. Top each with the fried fish cakes, tofu, bean sprouts and spring onions.
Ladle the hot laksa broth over the noodles and vegetables. Garnish with red chilli if using, fresh coriander and a generous scatter of fried shallots. Serve immediately.

notes: The laksa paste is the backbone, a good quality one saves time. If you can't find tamarind paste, soak a ball of tamarind pulp in hot water for 10 minutes, then strain.
Make the broth first and it'll wait for you while you fry the tofu and fish cakes. The noodles should be cooked fresh just before serving.
Some people add prawns to this laksa. If you'd like them, toss in 200 g of cooked prawns if that's how you like it.

recipe.title: Sopa de Lentejas
recipe.summary: Red lentil soup with dried chillies, cumin, and lime, a Lenten dish that's good all year.

steps.text: Heat a large pot over medium heat. Toast the cumin seeds, stirring, for about 1 minute until fragrant. Remove and set aside.

In the same pot, warm the neutral oil. Add the guajillo and ancho chillies and toast them, turning gently, until they smell rich and toasted, about 2 minutes. Be careful not to burn them. Remove and set aside.
Add the halved onion and whole garlic cloves to the pot and cook until lightly charred, about 4 minutes. This adds depth to the broth.
Soak the toasted chillies in 250 ml of hot water for 5 minutes until soft, then blend with the soaking water until smooth. Strain through a fine sieve into the pot, pressing the pulp through.

Add the red lentils and vegetable stock to the pot. Crush the toasted cumin seeds and stir them in. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer for 20–25 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the lentils break down completely and the soup thickens.
Season with salt to taste. The soup should be thick but pourable.
Serve hot with lime wedges on the side. Squeeze lime juice into each bowl and scatter coriander over the top if you like.

notes: Makes a generous batch. Keeps in the fridge for up to 4 days or freezes well for a month.
If you can't find guajillo or ancho chillies, use 3–4 dried red chillies of any kind, the technique is what matters.

recipe.title: Mercimek Çorbası
recipe.summary: Silky red lentil soup, finished with crispy onion, hot oil and lemon

items.raw: 1 tsp salt, plus more to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the chopped onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the rinsed lentils and rice to the pot. Stir to coat in the oil, about 1 minute.

Pour in the stock and add the salt. Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat and simmer, uncovered, until the lentils and rice break down completely and the soup becomes creamy, about 25–30 minutes. Stir occasionally.
Blend the soup until smooth and silky using a blender or stick blender. If it's too thick, add a little water. Season with lemon juice, more salt and black pepper to taste.

For the topping: heat the oil in a small pan over medium-high heat. Add the sliced onion and cook, stirring often, until golden and crispy, about 8 minutes. Drain on paper towel. If using butter and Aleppo pepper, warm them together in the same pan.
Ladle the soup into bowls. Top with crispy onion, and drizzle with the hot oil (and butter-pepper mixture if using). Serve with lemon wedges.

notes: If you prefer a thinner soup, add more stock or water before blending.
Make the crispy onion topping ahead and store in an airtight container, it keeps for 3 days and turns any soup into something special.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

title: Galette de blé noir aux moules

recipe.title: Galette de blé noir aux moules
recipe.summary: Buckwheat crêpes topped with mussels, shallots, white wine and cream.

steps.text: Make the galette batter: whisk together buckwheat flour and salt. In another bowl, beat the egg with milk and water until combined. Pour the wet ingredients into the flour, whisking until you have a smooth batter with no lumps. Let it rest for 15 minutes.

Heat a non-stick crêpe pan or 25 cm frying pan over medium-high heat and lightly butter it. Pour in 80 ml batter, tilting the pan so it spreads thinly and evenly. Cook for about 2 minutes until the bottom is lightly golden, then flip and cook the other side for 30 seconds. Transfer to a plate. Repeat with remaining batter to make 2 galettes.
While the batter rests, prepare the topping: melt butter in a large saucepan over medium heat. Add shallots and cook gently for 3 minutes until soft and sweet.
Pour in white wine and bring to a simmer. Add the mussels, cover, and cook for 4–5 minutes, shaking the pan once halfway through, until they open. Discard any that don't.
Pour in the cream and stir gently to combine. Warm through for 1 minute, then taste and season lightly with salt if needed.
Place a galette on each plate, top generously with mussels, shallots and cream sauce, scatter with fresh parsley if you like, and serve at once.

notes: The galette batter can be made up to 4 hours ahead and kept covered in the fridge. Bring to room temperature for 10 minutes before cooking.
Clean mussels well under cold running water, pulling away any beard. Discard any that are open and won't close when tapped.

Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through. Throw away any mussels or clams whose shells stay closed after cooking. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Sapasui
recipe.summary: Samoan chop suey with corned beef, cabbage and onion, the weeknight family favourite.

items.raw: 340 g tin corned beef, broken into chunks
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large frying pan or wok over medium-high heat.
Add the onion and cook, stirring, until softened, about 3 minutes.
Add the cabbage and garlic, and cook, stirring often, until the cabbage is tender but still has a bit of crunch, about 6 minutes.
Add the corned beef and stir to break it up and mix through the veg, about 1 minute.
Add the soy sauce and oyster sauce, and stir to coat everything. Cook for 2 minutes until heated through.
Taste and season with salt and black pepper as needed. Serve hot.

notes: Swap the corned beef for tinned tuna or cooked chicken if that's what you've got.
Serve over rice or with fresh bread to soak up the sauce.
Any leftover veg works here, carrots, green beans, capsicum, whatever's in the crisper.

recipe.title: Hand-Pulled Lanzhou Noodles
recipe.summary: Silky stretched wheat noodles in warm beef and spice broth, topped with coriander and chilli oil.

items.raw: 400 g beef chuck, cut into 3 cm pieces

steps.text: Make the dough: mix flour and salt in a bowl. Add warm water gradually, stirring with your fingers until a shaggy dough forms. Knead on a bench for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Cover and rest for 20 minutes.
While the dough rests, make the broth: heat oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Add beef pieces in batches and brown on all sides, about 6 minutes total. Remove and set aside.
In the same pot, add onion, garlic, and ginger. Stir until fragrant, about 2 minutes. Add doubanjiang and stir constantly for 1 minute until it darkens slightly.

Return beef to the pot. Add sichuan pepper, cloves, star anise, bay leaf, and dried chillies. Stir to coat, then pour in stock. Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cover and cook for 45 minutes until beef is very tender.
Season the broth with soy sauce and salt to taste. Keep warm on a low heat.
Divide the rested dough into two equal pieces. Oil your hands and the bench. Take one piece and stretch it gently into a rough rectangle about 20 cm long.

Fold the rectangle in half, then in half again (folding into quarters), and roll it loosely into a log. Repeat this process two more times, resting 5 minutes between each fold. This builds layers and develops the stretch.

Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Take your final dough log and, holding each end, gently stretch it by pulling away from your body and up over your arm, then back down, this distributes the gluten evenly. Stretch and fold, stretch and fold, until the noodle is about 50 cm long and very thin.
Pull the stretched noodle away from your arm and, using one fluid motion, lay it down into the boiling water. It will curl and coil, this is perfect. Repeat with the second piece of dough.
The noodles will rise to the surface within 2–3 minutes. Let them cook for another 1–2 minutes until they're just tender, then use a strainer to carefully lift them into serving bowls.
Pour hot broth into each bowl with the noodles. Top generously with coriander, spring onion, a drizzle of chilli oil, and white pepper.

notes: The dough can be made up to 4 hours ahead, wrapped and refrigerated. Let it come to room temperature before stretching.
The broth keeps for 3 days in the fridge and tastes even better the next day.
If you're nervous about pulling noodles, you can roll the final dough thin and cut it into thick strands instead, it won't be quite the same, but it'll still be good.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

recipe.title: Tagliatelle al Ragù
recipe.summary: Tagliatelle with Bolognese ragù: slow-cooked ground meat, tomato and milk.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large, heavy-based pot over medium heat. Add the pancetta and cook, stirring, until the fat renders, about 4 minutes.
Add the onion, carrot and celery. Cook, stirring often, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. This is your soffritto, don't rush it.

Increase the heat to medium-high. Add the beef and pork mince, breaking it up with a wooden spoon. Cook, stirring often, until the meat is no longer pink, about 10 minutes. Season with salt and pepper.
Pour in the white wine and scrape the bottom of the pot to lift the browned bits. Let the wine reduce until nearly evaporated, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 1 minute. Add the crushed tomatoes and stir well.
Reduce the heat to low. The ragù should barely simmer, just occasional lazy bubbles. Cook uncovered for 2 hours, stirring every 15 minutes or so. The sauce will thicken and darken.
Pour in the milk and stir well. Continue to simmer on low heat for another 1 hour, stirring occasionally. The sauce will be rich, thick and deep brown. Taste and adjust the salt and pepper.
About 30 minutes before serving, bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Cook the tagliatelle for 2 to 3 minutes, or until tender. Fresh pasta cooks fast.
Drain the pasta, reserving a cup of pasta water. Toss the tagliatelle with the ragù in the pot, adding a splash of pasta water if needed to loosen it. Serve with freshly grated Parmesan.

notes: The ragù freezes beautifully for up to three months. Make a double batch when you have time.
Fresh tagliatelle is essential here. If you can't find it, use dried pappardelle, cook it to packet instructions instead.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

recipe.title: Meen Curry
recipe.summary: Kerala fish curry with roasted spices, coconut milk and curry leaves.

items.raw: 600 g white fish fillets (snapper, barramundi or bream), cut into large chunks

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. When it shimmers, add the cumin and coriander seeds and toast, stirring constantly, until they release their fragrance and darken slightly, about 2 minutes. Watch them closely so they don't burn.
Add the curry leaves, then the onion. Cook, stirring often, until the onion is soft and golden, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the garlic, ginger and green chilli. Cook for another minute until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and cook, stirring occasionally, until they break down and the raw edge is gone, about 5 minutes.
Pour in the coconut milk and stir well. Bring to a gentle simmer, then carefully place the fish pieces into the curry. Season with salt and cook until the fish is opaque and flakes easily.
Simmer gently, uncovered, for 8–10 minutes, until the fish is cooked through and flakes easily. Do not stir aggressively or the fish will break apart; you can gently turn the pieces once if needed.
Taste and adjust salt if needed. Serve hot, scattered with fresh coriander if you like, alongside steamed rice.

notes: This curry tastes even better the next day. Reheat gently on the stove or in the microwave until warm through.
Use any firm white fish you like, snapper, barramundi, bream or cod all work well. Avoid delicate fish that will fall apart.
Serve with steamed rice, appam, or flatbread to soak up the coconut broth.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Pilau ya Nyama
recipe.summary: Fragrant rice with beef and whole spices, a celebration in one pot.

items.raw: 600 g beef chuck, cut into 3 cm cubes

steps.text: Toast the cumin seeds, coriander seeds, cardamom pods, cinnamon sticks and cloves in a large, heavy pot over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until fragrant, about 2 minutes. Remove and set aside.
Heat the oil in the same pot over medium-high heat. Add the beef in batches, browning on all sides, about 8 minutes total. Set the beef aside.
Add the onions to the pot and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Stir in the garlic and ginger and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Return the beef to the pot. Add the toasted spices and bay leaves, stir well, and cook for 2 minutes.
Add the rice, stirring to coat in the oil, and cook for 2 minutes. Pour in the beef stock, add the salt and pepper, and stir once.
Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat to low, cover tightly, and simmer without stirring for 45 minutes, until the rice is tender and the liquid is absorbed.
Remove from the heat and let it rest, covered, for 5 minutes. Fluff with a fork, taste and adjust seasoning. Serve hot with fresh coriander if you like.

notes: Pilau tastes even better the next day. Reheat gently with a splash of water.
If beef chuck is hard to find, use beef shin or any tough cut that braises well.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

recipe.title: Pad Grapow Moo
recipe.summary: Stir-fried minced pork with holy basil and chillies served over rice.

items.raw: Handful of fresh holy basil leaves

steps.text: Heat your wok on high heat until it's smoking hot, about 2 minutes.
Add the oil, then immediately add the minced garlic and sliced chillies. Stir constantly for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the pork mince and break it up with the spatula. Stir-fry, without stirring constantly, for 2–3 minutes until cooked through and starting to caramelize. You want colour on it.
Add the fish sauce and palm sugar. Toss well for 30 seconds to combine.
Pull the wok off the heat. Add the fresh holy basil leaves and fold through gently until just wilted and fragrant, don't let them brown.
Transfer the rice to a bowl or plate. Top with the pad grapow moo. Garnish with fried garlic and a fried egg if you want the real street-stall experience.

notes: If you can't find fresh holy basil, Thai basil works fine, use the same amount. Regular basil will change the flavour but won't ruin it.
Prep everything before you start cooking: mince the garlic, slice the chillies, tear the basil, measure the sauce. Once the wok hits temperature, there's no time to stop.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

recipe.title: Kebab İçli Köfte
recipe.summary: Hand-rolled spiced meatballs stuffed with lamb and pine nuts, pan-fried until golden.

steps.text: Make the filling: heat 1 tbsp of the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Cook the onion until soft, about 3 minutes. Add the lamb mince, pine nuts, pul biber, cumin and salt. Cook, stirring, until the lamb is no longer pink, about 5 minutes. Tip onto a plate to cool slightly.
Make the meatball mixture: combine the beef mince, chopped onion, flour, pul biber, cumin, salt and pepper in a bowl. Mix gently with your hands until just combined.

Roll and stuff: wet your hands with cold water. Take about 2 tbsp of the beef mixture and press it into a thin oval in your palm. Place about 1 tsp of the lamb filling in the centre, then fold and roll gently to enclose the filling, shaping into an even oval meatball about 8 cm long. Repeat with the remaining beef mixture and filling (you'll make about 16).

Pan-fry the köfte: wipe the pan clean. Heat the remaining 1 tbsp oil over medium-high heat until shimmering. Working in two batches, fry the meatballs for 4–5 minutes on each side until deeply golden and cooked through (the filling should be no longer pink inside). Don't crowd the pan.
Serve hot with lemon wedges and fresh parsley, if using.

notes: Make the filling while the onion cooks, so everything comes together quickly.
Keep your hands wet when rolling, it stops the meat from sticking and makes shaping easier.
These freeze well raw; just add a couple of extra minutes to the cooking time straight from the freezer.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

recipe.title: Espinacas con Garbanzos
recipe.summary: Wilted spinach with chickpeas, garlic and olive oil, a simple, generous tapa.

items.raw: 400 g tin chickpeas, drained and rinsed
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Add the sliced garlic and cook, stirring gently, for about 1 minute until fragrant but not coloured.
Add the drained chickpeas and stir to coat with the oil. Cook for 2 minutes, then add the chopped spinach in batches, stirring as it wilts into the pan, this will take about 4–5 minutes in total.
Once all the spinach is wilted and the chickpeas are heated through, season with salt and black pepper to taste. Serve hot or at room temperature with a lemon wedge on the side if you like.

notes: Tastes just as good at room temperature, perfect for setting out on the table while you cook other things.
You can add a pinch of smoked paprika or cumin if you want a little more flavour, but honestly, the simplicity is the point.

recipe.title: Bánh Canh Cua
recipe.summary: Thick tapioca noodle soup with crab, slippery and chewy.

items.raw: 400 g crab meat, freshly cooked or from 1 cooked whole crab
items.prep: freshly cooked or from 1 cooked whole crab

items.raw: Spring onion, thinly sliced, to serve

steps.text: Make the noodle dough: Pour 100 ml boiling water over the tapioca starch in a bowl and stir well. Let it cool for 2 minutes. Add the salt, then gradually add cold water while stirring until the mixture is smooth and has the texture of thick pancake batter, it should be glossy and slightly translucent. Let it rest for 10 minutes.

Bring a large pot of water (at least 2 litres) to a rolling boil. Working in batches, push the noodle batter through a large-holed colander or bánh canh press directly into the boiling water. The noodles should be thick and rope-like, about the width of a finger. Stir gently to prevent sticking. Boil for 3-4 minutes until they float and are tender but still chewy. Remove with a slotted spoon and set aside.
For the broth, heat the chicken stock and water in a large pot over medium heat. Add the crushed garlic and simmer for 3 minutes until fragrant.
Stir in the fish sauce, sugar and crab meat. Simmer for 5 minutes to warm through and let the crab flavour infuse. Taste and adjust with salt and white pepper.
Divide the cooked noodles among four bowls. Pour the hot crab broth over each serving.
Top each bowl with fresh coriander, spring onion, fried garlic and sliced chilli if using. Serve with a lime wedge on the side.

notes: If you can't find fresh crab, use 400 g tinned crab or frozen crab meat, thawed.
The noodle batter can be made up to 2 hours ahead and refrigerated; let it come to room temperature before using.
A bánh canh press makes thick, even noodles, but a large-holed colander works just as well.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

recipe.title: Tumpeng
recipe.summary: Turmeric rice cone with vegetables, egg and chicken, a ceremonial Balinese centrepiece.

items.raw: 300 g chicken breast, cut into 3 cm pieces

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp oil in a pot over medium heat. Add the lemongrass and turmeric, and cook for 1 minute until fragrant. Pour in the stock and bring to a boil.
Add the rice, stir well, and reduce the heat to low. Cover and simmer for 18 minutes until the rice is tender and the liquid is absorbed. Season with salt.

While the rice cooks, season the chicken with salt, pepper, garlic, coriander, cumin and turmeric. Heat 2 tbsp oil in a large pan over medium-high heat, add the chicken, and cook for 8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until golden and cooked through.
In the same pan, add the mushrooms and cook for 3 minutes until soft. Transfer to a serving plate.
Bring a pot of salted water to the boil. Add the green beans and carrots, and cook for 4 minutes until just tender. Add the cabbage and cook for 1 minute more. Drain and transfer to a serving plate.
In a small pan, heat a little oil over medium heat. Crack the eggs into the pan and cook until the whites are set and the yolks are still soft, about 4 minutes. Season with salt and pepper.

Fluff the rice with a fork. Wet a bowl with water, fill it with rice, and turn it out onto a large serving platter to form a cone. Arrange the cooked vegetables, chicken and fried egg around the base. Garnish with coriander and serve with lime wedges.
To eat, each person breaks apart a piece of the rice cone and takes some of each dish, mixing the flavours together.

notes: Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Yakitori Momo
recipe.summary: Grilled chicken thigh skewers with salt and lemon, cooked in a frying pan.

items.raw: 250 g boneless chicken thigh, cut into 3 cm cubes

steps.text: Thread the chicken cubes onto two metal skewers, leaving a small gap between each piece so they cook evenly until cooked through and golden. Pat dry with paper towel.
Heat the neutral oil in a frying pan over medium-high heat until shimmering, about 1 minute.
Place the skewers in the pan and cook without moving them for 4 minutes, until the bottom is golden and slightly charred.
Turn the skewers and cook for another 4 minutes until golden on the second side.
Turn once more and cook for 2–3 minutes, turning as needed, until the chicken is cooked through (no pink inside). The outside should be blistered and charred in patches.
Transfer to a plate, season generously with salt, and serve immediately with lemon wedges to squeeze over.

notes: Use bone-in chicken thighs if you prefer, they stay juicier. Cut around the bone and into cubes.
Presoaking wooden skewers for 30 minutes prevents burning, but metal skewers work best and cook faster.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

recipe.title: Roti with Curried Chickpeas
recipe.summary: Soft roti wrapped around spiced chickpea curry, comfort food the Fiji way.

items.raw: 1 tbsp neutral oil, plus extra for cooking
1 red chilli, finely chopped (or ½ tsp chilli powder, optional)
400 g tin chickpeas, drained and rinsed

steps.text: Make the roti dough first so it can rest while the curry cooks. Combine plain flour and salt in a bowl. Add 1 tbsp oil and rub it through the flour with your fingers until it looks like breadcrumbs. Slowly add warm water, stirring with one hand, until you have a soft dough. Knead gently for 2–3 minutes until smooth. Cover with a damp cloth and set aside.
Heat 2 tbsp oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the chopped onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and ginger, stirring for 1 minute until fragrant.

Add the cumin, coriander, turmeric and chilli. Stir for 1 minute, then add the drained chickpeas and crushed tomatoes. Pour in 1 cup water and add salt. Bring to a simmer and cook, uncovered, for 15–20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the curry is thick and the flavours have come together. Taste and adjust salt if needed.

While the curry simmers, divide the rested dough into 8 balls. On a lightly oiled surface or oiled palms, flatten each ball into a thin circle, about 20 cm across, working gently so the dough doesn't tear.

Heat a large non-stick frypan or tava over medium-high heat with a small amount of oil. Cook each roti one at a time for about 1 minute on each side until light golden and a little puffy. Stack them on a clean tea towel to keep warm and soft.
Serve the warm roti with the curried chickpeas spooned into the middle. Fold and wrap as you eat, with fresh coriander if you like.

Rinse the lentils and rice. In a large pot, bring 750 ml water to the boil, add the lentils and rice, and simmer together for 20–25 minutes, until both are tender and the water is absorbed. Season with salt.
Meanwhile, boil a separate pot of salted water and cook the pasta until al dente, about 8–10 minutes. Drain and set aside.

While the lentils and rice cook, slice the onion thinly. Heat 2 tbsp of the oil in a frying pan over medium heat and fry the onion, stirring occasionally, until deep golden and crispy, about 8–10 minutes. Drain on paper towel and set aside.

In the same pan, heat the remaining 1 tbsp oil over medium heat. Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant. Stir in the tomato paste, cumin, and cayenne, and cook for 1 minute. Add the tinned tomatoes, season with salt and pepper, and simmer for 5 minutes.

To assemble, divide the lentil-and-rice mixture among four bowls or plates. Top each with a portion of the cooked pasta. Pour the warm tomato sauce over the top, then finish with the crispy fried onions.
Serve immediately while hot.

recipe.title: Koshari
recipe.summary: Layers of lentils, rice and pasta topped with spiced tomato sauce and crispy fried onions.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
Fried shallots, to serve (optional but traditional)

recipe.title: Doubles
recipe.summary: Spiced chickpea curry tucked into fried bread, Trinidad's essential street snack.

items.raw: 1 tbsp neutral oil, plus more for frying

steps.text: Make the bread dough: mix flour, baking powder and salt in a bowl. Add oil and stir, then add warm water a little at a time, mixing until you have a soft, slightly sticky dough. Knead for 2 minutes until smooth, then set aside to rest for 15 minutes.
Make the chickpea curry: heat oil in a saucepan over medium heat. Add onion and cook, stirring, until soft, about 4 minutes. Add garlic and ginger and stir for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add turmeric, cumin and asafoetida, stirring constantly for 1 minute to bloom the spices. Add green chillies and salt, then the drained chickpeas and water.

Bring to a simmer and cook for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the curry has thickened slightly and the flavours have come together. The chickpeas should be soft and well coated. Taste and adjust salt and spices. Keep warm.

Divide the dough into 8 equal pieces and roll each into a ball. On a lightly oiled surface, use your hands or a rolling pin to stretch each ball into a thin, roughly rectangular shape about 3 mm thick.

Heat oil in a large, deep pan to 170°C (a piece of dough will sizzle gently when it touches the oil). Working in batches, fry each piece of dough for about 1 minute each side until golden and puffed. Drain on paper towels.

To serve, split a fried bread open or lay two pieces on a plate. Spoon a generous amount of warm chickpea curry into or over the bread. Top with pepper sauce and tamarind chutney if using, scatter with fresh coriander, and eat while it's hot.

notes: The chickpea curry can be made ahead and reheated gently; make the bread fresh just before serving for the best texture.
If your kitchen scales aren't handy, the bread dough works with about 2 cups flour, 1 tsp baking powder, 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp oil, and ¾ cup warm water.
Doubles are best eaten fresh and hot, the contrast between the warm spiced chickpea and crispy-soft bread is half the magic.

recipe.title: Koeksister
recipe.summary: Crispy plaited pastry strips fried and drenched in hot ginger-cinnamon syrup.

steps.text: Make the syrup first so it's ready when you need it. In a small saucepan, combine the sugar, water, ground ginger and cinnamon stick. Bring to the boil, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then reduce the heat and simmer for 5 minutes. Remove from the heat, stir in the lemon juice, and set aside. The syrup must stay hot.
Sift the flour, baking powder and salt into a bowl. Rub in the cold butter with your fingertips until the mixture resembles breadcrumbs. Do this gently, you want the dough light, not worked.

In a small jug, whisk the egg and milk together. Make a well in the centre of the dry ingredients and pour in the egg mixture. Mix gently with a fork until a soft dough forms. Do not knead. If it's too dry, add a few drops more milk.
Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface and shape into a ball. Wrap in cling film and rest for 10 minutes.
Roll the dough out thinly, about 3 mm thick. Using a sharp knife, cut into strips about 2 cm wide and 12 cm long.
Take each strip and plait (braid) it gently, pinching the ends to seal. The plaits should be loose and airy.
Heat the oil in a deep frying pan to 180°C (a cube of bread should brown in 30 seconds). Working in batches so you don't crowd the pan, carefully lower the plaited strips into the hot oil.
Fry for about 1 minute on each side until deep golden. They should be crisp and light. Remove with a slotted spoon.
Immediately dip each hot koeksister into the hot syrup, turning to coat all over. The syrup will cling and caramelize on the outside. Place on a rack or paper towel to cool and set.
Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: The syrup can be made an hour ahead and kept warm in a low oven or over a very low heat. It must be hot when you dip the koeksisters.
Make sure your oil is at the right temperature, if it's not hot enough, the koeksisters will be greasy instead of crisp.
Store cooled koeksisters in an airtight container for up to 2 days, though they're best fresh and warm.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Esqueixada
recipe.summary: Shredded salt cod salad with tomatoes, onions and olives, the Empordà way.

items.raw: 400 g salt cod fillet, soaked overnight (or 24 hours)
100 g mixed olives (green and black), pitted
1 can (400 g) tinned tomatoes (optional, if fresh tomatoes lack flavour)
items.note: 400 g; optional, if fresh tomatoes lack flavour

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Drain the soaked salt cod and check for any remaining small bones. Flake the cod roughly into bite-sized pieces by hand, don't cut it; the irregular shreds are essential to esqueixada.
In a large bowl, combine the flaked salt cod, fresh tomatoes, red onion and olives. If using tinned tomatoes, drain well and add them too.
Dress with the olive oil and red wine vinegar, tossing gently to combine. Taste and adjust seasoning with salt (go easy, the cod is already salty) and a good grind of black pepper.
Let the salad rest at room temperature for 15 minutes, until the tomato juices have mingled with the dressing and the flavours meld, then scatter with parsley if you like and serve.

notes: The salt cod must be soaked overnight or up to 24 hours, changing the water 2–3 times. This is not a shortcut dish.
Esqueixada is best served at room temperature, never chilled. The oil and vinegar need warmth to carry the flavours.
In summer, use the ripest tomatoes you can find. If they're bland, the tinned tomatoes (well-drained) give the dish needed acidity and body.

recipe.title: Frikadeller med rødbeder og kartofler
recipe.summary: Tender Danish meatballs with caramelised onions, pickled beetroot and buttered potatoes

items.raw: 400 g beetroot, peeled and thinly sliced

steps.text: Start the pickled beetroot: layer the beetroot in a bowl. In a small saucepan, heat the vinegar, water, sugar, salt, pepper and bay leaf over medium heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves. Pour over the beetroot and let it cool while you cook the rest.

For the caramelised onions, melt the butter in a large frying pan over medium-low heat. Add the sliced onions and salt, stirring often. Cook for 20 to 25 minutes, until very soft and golden; set aside.
Meanwhile, start the potatoes: cut them into even-sized pieces and place in a pot of cold salted water. Bring to a boil and cook for 12 to 15 minutes, until tender.

While the potatoes cook, make the meatballs. Mix the pork, beef, grated onion, milk, breadcrumbs, egg, salt and pepper gently with your hands until just combined, don't overwork. Shape into 12 to 16 balls about the size of a golf ball.
Heat butter or oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Working in batches if needed, cook the meatballs, turning gently, for 8 to 10 minutes total, until golden and cooked through.
Drain the potatoes and return them to the pot. Add the butter and a pinch of salt, and toss gently to coat.
Divide the potatoes among serving plates. Top with the meatballs and caramelised onions, then serve with the pickled beetroot on the side. Scatter with fresh dill if you like.

notes: The pickled beetroot can be made a day ahead and keeps in the fridge for up to a week.
If you can't find waxy potatoes, use any small firm potatoes and cut them in half.
Frikadeller freeze well uncooked; shape and refrigerate on a tray for 30 minutes, then freeze in a bag for up to three months.

Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Arepa con queso
recipe.summary: Warm, crusty corn arepa filled with melted white cheese, how Andrés starts every morning

items.raw: 150 g white cheese (queso de mano or mozzarella), cut into strips

steps.text: Mix the corn flour, warm water and salt in a bowl, stirring until you have a soft, moist dough. Let it rest for 2–3 minutes.
Wet your hands. Divide the dough into 2 balls and gently flatten each into a thick disc about 8 cm across and 1 cm thick.
Heat a griddle or heavy frying pan over medium heat. Once hot, place the arepas on the griddle.
Cook for 6–7 minutes until the bottom is golden and crusty, then flip and cook the other side for another 6–7 minutes until both sides are golden and the arepa sounds hollow when tapped.
Using a thin knife, carefully cut a pocket into the side of each warm arepa without splitting it open completely.
Stuff each arepa with the cheese strips while the arepa is still warm, the residual heat will melt the cheese slightly. Serve immediately.

notes: Make ahead: Mix the dough and shape the arepas up to 2 hours before cooking, then refrigerate, bring to room temperature before cooking.
Swap: If you can't find queso de mano, fresh mozzarella or even mild cheddar works, though it won't be quite the same.
You can cook arepas on a griddle, heavy-bottomed frying pan, or a cast-iron frying pan, whatever you have. The sound and smell tell you more than the time does.

recipe.title: Kırmızı Mercimekli Köfte
recipe.summary: Spiced lentil and bulgur meatballs, pan-fried until crispy.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Rinse the lentils and place in a saucepan with 500 ml water. Bring to the boil, then simmer for 12 minutes until just soft but not falling apart. Drain well and let cool slightly.

In a large bowl, combine the warm lentils with the bulgur, diced onion, garlic, tomato paste, cumin, Aleppo pepper, cinnamon and parsley. Mix gently but thoroughly until it just comes together. Season with salt and pepper. Let sit for 10 minutes so the bulgur absorbs moisture.
With damp hands, shape the mixture into oval meatballs about 4 cm long. Place on a plate.
Heat a thin layer of oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Once shimmering, carefully add the köfte in batches, don't crowd the pan.
Fry for 3 to 4 minutes on each side until golden and crispy all over. Transfer to a plate lined with paper towel.
Serve warm with lemon wedges and yoghurt on the side.

notes: Make ahead: shape the köfte up to 4 hours ahead and refrigerate on a tray, covered. Fry when ready to serve.
Serve with yoghurt, lemon wedges, and fresh salad, or tuck into flatbread with tomato and onion.

recipe.title: Shiitake Jjim
recipe.summary: Braised shiitake mushrooms with soy and sesame, deep and meditative.

items.raw: 2 spring onions, cut into 3 cm pieces

steps.text: Heat the sesame oil in a large shallow pot or braising pan over medium heat.
Add the shiitake mushrooms, cut side down, and let them sit undisturbed for 2 minutes until they begin to brown.
Turn the mushrooms and cook for another 2 minutes, then pour in the soy sauce, sugar, and water.
Bring to a gentle simmer, then lower the heat and braise, uncovered, for about 15 minutes, until the mushrooms are tender and the liquid has reduced by half.
Taste and adjust the soy sauce or water as needed, the braise should taste rich but not overly salty, with a glossy, slightly thickened sauce and tender mushrooms.
Scatter the spring onions over the top and cook for 1 minute, then transfer to a serving bowl.
Finish with the toasted sesame seeds and a pinch of black pepper. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: Keeps well in the fridge for up to 5 days; reheat gently or eat cold as part of a banchan spread.
The mushrooms release their own moisture, so don't add more water than called for or the dish will taste thin.

recipe.title: Cơm Tấm Chay
recipe.summary: Broken rice with marinated tofu, fresh herbs and fried shallots, everyday southern Vietnamese comfort, vegetarian

items.raw: 400 g extra-firm tofu, pressed and cut into bite-sized pieces
items.prep: pressed and cut into bite-sized pieces

items.raw: 1 cup fresh herbs (mint, coriander, Vietnamese mint), roughly chopped
2 spring onions, cut into 5 cm pieces

steps.text: Combine the tofu, soy sauce, 2 tbsp oil, garlic, ground coriander and black pepper in a bowl. Let sit for at least 15 minutes, turning the tofu gently halfway through.

Meanwhile, rinse the broken rice well under cold water until the water runs clear. Cook in 4 cups water in a saucepan over medium-high heat, stirring occasionally, until tender and the liquid is absorbed, about 15 minutes. Fluff with a fork.
Heat a large non-stick frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the marinated tofu (discarding excess marinade) and cook, turning gently, until lightly golden on all sides, about 8 minutes.
Divide the warm rice among bowls. Top each with a portion of the tofu, cucumber, tomato, herbs and spring onions. Scatter the fried shallots over and serve with lime wedges.

notes: Cook the rice in advance and cool quickly; reheat gently before serving if you like. You can marinate the tofu overnight.
Fried shallots keep in an airtight container for a week.
The marinade ingredients are flexible, add a pinch of chilli flakes or a splash of rice vinegar if you like.

recipe.title: Rugbrød med leverpostej og agurkesalat
recipe.summary: Open rye sandwich with liver pâté, cucumber salad and crispy bacon.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
100 g pâté, preferably Danish liver pâté (leverpostej)

steps.text: Make the cucumber salad: toss the sliced cucumber with the vinegar, sugar, salt and pepper. Set aside for at least 10 minutes so the cucumbers soften and flavour the brine.
While the cucumber sits, cook the bacon in a frying pan over medium-high heat until crispy, about 5–6 minutes. Transfer to a plate lined with paper towel.
Lightly toast the rye bread until just crisp at the edges if you like it warm, or leave it as is.
Spread each slice generously with pâté.
Top each slice with 2 rashers of bacon, then a spoonful of the cucumber salad (drain off excess liquid first). Sprinkle with fresh dill if you have it, and a pinch of flaky salt.
Serve straight away while the bacon is still warm.

notes: The cucumber salad can be made up to 2 hours ahead and kept in the fridge. Drain before serving.
Use the best-quality pâté and bacon you can find, this sandwich lives or dies by those two things.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Cook pork until it reaches at least 70°C in the thickest part (75°C for mince and sausages).

recipe.title: Erbsensuppe
recipe.summary: Thick split pea soup with ham hock and leeks, the way Oma made it in winter.

items.raw: 2 leeks, white and light green parts, sliced into 2 cm rounds
items.prep: white and light green parts, sliced into 2 cm rounds

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Put the split peas, ham hock, bay leaves and water into a large pot. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer, uncovered, for 45 minutes.
Add the carrots and leeks. Stir well and simmer for another 45 minutes, until the peas have nearly dissolved and the soup is thick. Stir occasionally to prevent sticking.
Remove the ham hock. When cool enough to handle, shred any meat and discard the bone and skin. Return the shredded meat to the pot.
Fish out the bay leaves. Season with salt and pepper. If the soup is thicker than you like, add a splash of water. Serve hot.

notes: The soup thickens considerably as it cools. Reheat gently with a little water if needed.
Make it a day ahead, the flavour improves overnight. Store in the fridge for up to 4 days.

recipe.title: Khoresh Fenugreek
recipe.summary: Kidney beans and beef in a dark, aromatic stew with dried fenugreek leaves and lime.

items.raw: 600 g beef chuck, cut into 3 cm pieces
400 g tin kidney beans, drained and rinsed
2 tbsp dried fenugreek leaves, rubbed through your fingers
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat oil in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat. Season beef with salt and pepper. Working in batches, sear the meat until golden on both sides, about 2 minutes per side. Set aside.
Add onions to the pot and cook, stirring occasionally, until soft and translucent, about 8 minutes. Add turmeric and cumin, stirring for 1 minute until fragrant.

Return beef to the pot. Add kidney beans and beef stock. Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low. Add the halved dried limes. Cover and cook for 60 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the beef is tender.

Stir in the dried fenugreek leaves. Simmer, uncovered, for 15 minutes more. The sauce should darken and thicken slightly. Taste and adjust salt and pepper. The stew is ready when the beef is fall-apart tender and the flavour is deep and bitter-herbaceous.

notes: This stew tastes better the next day. Make it ahead and reheat gently on the stove.
Dried limes (omani limes) are available at Middle Eastern grocers; if you can't find them, preserved lemon works but use less, the flavour is more intense.

Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft. If using dried kidney beans, soak them, then boil them hard for at least 10 minutes before simmering, to destroy a natural toxin.

recipe.title: Saucisson braisé aux lentilles
recipe.summary: Braised sausage with lentils, a Lyonnaise bistro classic.

items.raw: 4 sausages (good-quality pork sausage or saucisson de Lyon), about 400 g
items.note: good-quality pork sausage or saucisson de Lyon

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large, heavy-based pot or braising dish over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the chopped garlic and carrot rounds, and cook for another 2 minutes until fragrant.
Stir in the lentils, tinned tomatoes, chicken stock, bay leaf and thyme. Bring to a simmer until gently bubbling, then nestle the whole sausages into the lentil mixture.

Cover and braise over a low heat for 35–40 minutes, until the lentils are tender and the sausages are cooked through. The sausages should be opaque and firm inside (check by piercing with a knife; juices should run clear).
Remove the bay leaf and thyme sprig. Taste and season with salt and black pepper. Serve the sausages on a bed of lentils, spooning the braising liquid over the top.

notes: Leftovers keep, covered, in the fridge for three days and taste even better reheated gently on the stove.
If you can find saucisson de Lyon or a good Lyonnaise sausage, use it; otherwise a quality pork sausage works fine.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

recipe.title: Sigara Börek
recipe.summary: Crispy fried pastry tubes filled with feta and herbs, a Turkish snack that's dangerously easy to eat.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Make the filling: combine feta, parsley, dill, spring onion, half the beaten egg, salt and pepper in a bowl. Mix gently, you want the cheese to hold together, not become mushy. Taste and adjust seasoning.
Set up your workspace: lay one sheet of yufka on a clean bench, long edge closest to you. If the yufka is very large, cut it in half lengthwise to make two strips.

Spoon about 2 tbsp filling along the bottom edge, leaving 2 cm on each side. Fold the sides in over the filling, then roll tightly away from you until you have a long, thin, cigarette-shaped roll. Press gently to seal. The seam should be on the bottom.
Brush the outside lightly with remaining beaten egg to help it seal and get golden. Repeat with remaining yufka and filling.
Heat the oil in a deep heavy-bottomed pan or Dutch oven to 170–180°C. If you don't have a thermometer, test with a small piece of pastry, it should sizzle immediately and brown in about 30 seconds.
Working in batches of 3 or 4, fry the börek seam-side down first until they're golden and crispy, about 2 minutes. Turn carefully and fry the other side until evenly golden, another 1–2 minutes.
Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towel. Keep warm while you fry the rest.
Serve hot, while they're still crispy, with lemon wedges and yoghurt for dipping if you like (though purists like Nonna would serve them plain).

notes: Make the börek up to 4 hours ahead and fry them just before serving. Cooked börek can be reheated in a 180°C oven for about 5 minutes, but they're best fresh.
No yufka? Filo pastry works, but use 2 sheets together and brush between them with melted butter. Not quite the same, but it'll do.
The oil temperature matters. Too cool and they'll be greasy; too hot and they'll burn before the inside heats through.

recipe.title: Arrós a Banda
recipe.summary: Rice cooked in seafood stock with grilled fish, a weeknight Catalan take on the Valencia classic.

items.raw: 750 ml seafood stock (or fish stock), warm
4 white fish fillets, 150 g each (sea bream, sea bass or barramundi)
items.note: sea bream, sea bass or barramundi

items.raw: Sea salt and black pepper, to season

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a wide, shallow pan (a paella pan if you have one) over a medium heat. Add the finely chopped onion and cook, stirring often, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. This is the sofregit, don't rush it, as the sweetness is the soul of the dish.
Add the grated tomato to the sofregit and cook, stirring, until the mixture is thick and darkened, about 5 minutes more. The tomato should lose its rawness and merge into the oil and onion.
Stir in the rice until well coated in the sofregit, about 1 minute. Pour in the warm seafood stock all at once, add the salt and saffron if using, and bring to a simmer.
