recipe.summary: Persian herb stew with kidney beans, black-eyed peas and beef kidney in aromatic broth.

items.raw: 300 g beef kidney, trimmed and cut into 1 cm cubes
items.prep: trimmed and cut into 1 cm cubes

items.raw: 400 g tin kidney beans, drained and rinsed
250 g tin black-eyed peas, drained and rinsed
3 dried limes (loomi), pierced with a knife
30 g fresh fenugreek leaves (kasuri methi), or extra parsley

steps.text: Pat the kidney dry and season with salt and pepper. Heat the oil in a heavy-based pot over medium-high heat and brown the kidney in batches, 2–3 minutes a side. Set aside.
In the same pot, soften the onion over medium heat until golden, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute.
Return the kidney to the pot. Add the kidney beans and black-eyed peas, stirring to combine. Pour in the stock and add the dried limes.
Bring to a gentle simmer, cover, and cook for 45 minutes, until the kidney is tender.
Stir in most of the parsley, fenugreek and coriander, reserving a small handful for garnish. Taste and adjust salt and pepper. Simmer, uncovered, for another 10 minutes.
Serve hot in wide bowls, scattered with the reserved fresh herbs. Eat with steamed white rice, pushing some to the edges of the pot for tahdig if you have the nerve.

notes: Make the stew up to 2 days ahead; the flavours deepen overnight. Reheat gently before serving.
Don't skip browning the kidney, it anchors the stew. If you can't find beef kidney, use lamb kidney (200 g) or omit it and add 100 g more beans instead.
Dried limes are essential to the flavour; they're sold in Middle Eastern grocers and most good supermarkets.

Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done. If using dried kidney beans, soak them, then boil them hard for at least 10 minutes before simmering, to destroy a natural toxin.

title: Choy Sum with Garlic and Oil

recipe.title: Choy Sum with Garlic and Oil
recipe.summary: Tender choy sum with bruised garlic and good oil, finished with high heat for wok hei.

items.raw: 600 g choy sum, cut into 8 cm lengths
60 ml good olive oil (or peanut oil)

steps.text: Get everything ready, the greens washed and cut, garlic bruised and sitting on the bench. High heat and speed matter here.
Heat your wok on high until it just begins to smoke lightly, about 2 minutes. Add the oil and swirl to coat the wok surface.
Add the bruised garlic and stir constantly for 20 seconds until fragrant. You want the oil infused but the garlic not burnt.

Immediately add all the choy sum. Toss and stir briskly, keeping the heat high, for 2 to 3 minutes until the stems are tender and the leaves have some char at the edges. The greens should still be bright.
Season with salt to taste. Serve immediately while the oil is still hot and the choy sum is at its best.

notes: Use oil you actually like the taste of, the simplicity means quality matters. Peanut oil or a fruity olive oil both work.
Don't prep the choy sum too early; it wilts quickly. Cut and dress it just before cooking.
If your stove doesn't run hot enough to get good wok hei, finish the pan under a very hot grill for 30 seconds instead.

recipe.title: Gravad lax med senapssås
recipe.summary: Cured salmon with mustard sauce, a Swedish classic to make when you have time.

items.raw: 800 g sashimi-grade salmon fillet, skin on

steps.text: Mix the salt, sugar, and crushed peppercorn together in a small bowl. Pat the salmon dry with paper towel. Spread half the salt mixture over the flesh side of the salmon, then scatter half the dill on top.

Place the salmon skin-side down on a large piece of plastic wrap or in a shallow dish. Spread the remaining salt mixture and dill over the flesh. If you have a second salmon fillet, lay it flesh-side down on top to make a sandwich (this helps the curing), but a single fillet works fine.
Wrap tightly in plastic wrap or cover with a plate. Place on a tray to catch any liquid, then put in the fridge for 3 days. Turn the package over every day so the cure spreads evenly.
On day 3, unwrap the salmon and rinse off the cure under cold running water. Pat dry and slice thinly at an angle, leaving the skin behind. You should get 8 to 12 slices.
Make the mustard sauce: whisk both mustards, sugar and vinegar together in a bowl. Slowly drizzle in the oil while whisking until emulsified. Stir in the fresh dill. Taste and adjust seasoning.
Arrange the gravad lax on a board with sliced rye bread and the mustard sauce alongside. Serve with lemon wedges if you like.

notes: The salmon can be cured up to 5 days ahead; keep it wrapped in the fridge. Slice only what you need and use the rest within a day or two.
The mustard sauce keeps refrigerated for up to 3 days.
Use the best salmon you can find, it's almost raw, so freshness matters.

The fish here is eaten raw or only cured in citrus. Buy sashimi-grade fish from a fishmonger, keep it cold and eat it the same day; skip it for anyone pregnant, very young, elderly or with low immunity.

Food safety: The seafood here is served raw or cured, so buy sashimi-grade, keep it cold and eat it the day it is made; for anyone who should avoid raw fish, cook it until opaque. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Pāua Fritters
recipe.summary: Golden-fried abalone fritters, crispy outside and tender within.

steps.text: Pound each pāua gently but firmly with a meat mallet on both sides until soft and just starting to flatten. Don't overdo it or you'll tear them. Pat dry with paper towels.
Whisk together the flour, baking powder, salt and pepper in a large bowl. In another bowl, whisk the egg with the milk until combined.
Pour the wet ingredients into the dry and stir gently until just combined, the batter should be a little lumpy, not smooth.
Heat about 2 cm of neutral oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat until shimmering. Test with a drop of batter; it should sizzle and float.
Dip each pāua into the batter, coating both sides, then carefully place into the hot oil. Fry in batches of 2 or 3 so you don't crowd the pan, about 2 minutes each side until golden and crispy.
Drain on paper towels and serve hot with a squeeze of fresh lemon.

notes: If you can't find fresh pāua, tinned pāua from a specialist kai moana supplier works well, just drain and pound before battering.
Keep finished fritters warm in a low oven (120°C) while you fry the rest.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Ful Medames
recipe.summary: Slow-cooked broad beans with garlic, lemon and olive oil, a Lebanese vegan breakfast staple.

items.raw: 800 g tin broad beans, drained and rinsed
60 ml olive oil, plus extra to serve
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the minced garlic and cook, stirring, until fragrant and just starting to turn golden, about 1 minute. Don't let it brown.
Add the drained broad beans and stir to coat with the oil and garlic. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 5 minutes.

Add 250 ml water and the ground cumin. Bring to a gentle simmer, then reduce the heat to low. Cook, uncovered, stirring often and mashing some of the beans against the side of the pot as they soften, for 35–40 minutes. The beans should break down into a creamy, chunky sauce.
Add the lemon juice and taste. Season with salt and pepper to your liking. If the mixture is too thick, stir in a splash more water.
Transfer to a serving bowl and make a well in the centre. Drizzle generously with extra olive oil. Serve warm with pita, and top with parsley and halved hard-boiled egg if you like.

notes: Ful keeps well in the fridge for up to 3 days. Reheat gently with a splash of water to loosen it back up.
If using dried broad beans instead, soak overnight, then simmer for about 90 minutes until completely tender before following the rest of the method.

recipe.title: Burrata, Freekeh and Charred Greens
recipe.summary: Creamy burrata, chewy roasted freekeh and bitter charred silverbeet with lemon dressing.

items.raw: 200 g silverbeet, leaves and stems separated
2 tbsp olive oil, plus extra for drizzling
1 ball fresh burrata, at room temperature
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Bring the vegetable stock to a boil in a medium saucepan. Add the freekeh, reduce to a simmer, and cook until tender and the liquid is absorbed, about 20–22 minutes. Season with salt and pepper, then set aside.
While the freekeh cooks, separate the silverbeet stems from the leaves. Roughly chop both stems and leaves.

Heat 1 tbsp olive oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the silverbeet stems and cook for 3 minutes, stirring occasionally, until they soften. Add the silverbeet leaves and cavolo nero, and cook for another 4–5 minutes, stirring often, until the greens are tender and the leaves have some charred edges.
Squeeze the juice from one lemon half over the greens and toss. Season with salt and pepper. Transfer to a plate.

Divide the warm freekeh between two bowls. Top each with the charred greens. Place half the burrata in each bowl, then drizzle everything with a good glug of olive oil and a squeeze from the remaining lemon half.
Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt and black pepper, and serve.

notes: The freekeh can be made up to 2 days ahead and reheated gently. The greens are best charred fresh, but leftovers keep in the fridge for a day.
Burrata is best at room temperature. Pull it out of the fridge 10 minutes before serving.

recipe.title: Spam Musubi
recipe.summary: Grilled spam between seasoned rice and nori, a Hawaiian plate lunch classic in one hand

items.raw: 1 tin (340 g) canned luncheon meat, sliced into 8 pieces

steps.text: While the rice is still warm, mix the rice vinegar, caster sugar and salt together, then fold gently through the rice until well combined. Set aside to cool slightly.

Heat the neutral oil in a frying pan over medium-high heat. Fry the luncheon meat slices for 2–3 minutes each side until the edges are golden and crispy. Brush with kecap manis while still in the pan.
Place a sheet of nori shiny side down on a clean work surface. Wet your fingers and spread about 1 cup of seasoned rice firmly across the nori, leaving a 1 cm border at the top.
Place a slice of fried luncheon meat across the centre of the rice.
Starting from the bottom, roll the nori tightly, using the border at the top to seal. Slice in half crosswise with a sharp, wet knife.
Repeat with the remaining nori sheets, rice and meat. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: Make ahead: prepare the musubi the morning before and keep wrapped in the fridge. Bring to room temperature before eating, or warm gently in the microwave.
Swap the sweet soy sauce for tamari or regular soy sauce if that's what you've got, the musubi will taste less sweet but still good.
Any leftover seasoned rice can be used to make onigiri or fried rice.
Food safety: Cool any leftover rice quickly and refrigerate it within an hour; reheat it until steaming hot.

recipe.title: Milanesa de Ternera
recipe.summary: Thin-pounded veal cutlet, breaded and fried golden, served with lemon and chimichurri.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
15 g fresh oregano, finely chopped (or 1 tsp dried oregano)
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Make the chimichurri first: whisk together the olive oil and red wine vinegar, then stir in the parsley, oregano, garlic, chilli flakes, salt and pepper. Set aside.
Place each veal escalope between two sheets of plastic wrap and pound with a meat mallet or rolling pin until very thin, about 3 mm. Season both sides with salt and pepper.

Set up three shallow bowls: one with flour, one with beaten eggs, and one with breadcrumbs. Coat each escalope in flour, shaking off excess, then dip in egg, then press firmly into the breadcrumbs on both sides.
Heat about 1 cm of neutral oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Test with a small piece of bread, it should sizzle and brown quickly.
Carefully lay the breaded veal into the hot oil and fry for 2–3 minutes until golden brown. Turn and fry the other side for another 2–3 minutes until crispy and golden. Do not overcrowd the pan.
Transfer to a plate lined with paper towel to drain. Serve hot with lemon wedges and chimichurri on the side, with optional fresh parsley garnish.

notes: Use veal or beef. Veal is more tender, but a thin beef cutlet works just as well.
Don't skip the meat mallet. The escalopes must be thin so they cook through before the breadcrumb coating burns.
Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done.

recipe.title: Brik aux Oeufs
recipe.summary: Crispy fried pastry envelope with egg, tuna and harissa.

items.raw: 4 sheets filo pastry (or malsouka if you can get it)
items.note: or malsouka if you can get it

steps.text: Set up a work station with one sheet of filo pastry in front of you, and have a small bowl of water nearby for sealing. In a small bowl, mix the drained tuna with the harissa, coriander and capers. Taste it and adjust the harissa and salt to your liking.
Take the first filo sheet and brush it lightly with oil on both sides. Fold it in half to create a rough square.

Spoon about 1 tbsp of the tuna mixture into the centre of the folded pastry, leaving a margin around the edges. Make a small well in the tuna mixture, then crack an egg directly into it. Season with a pinch of salt and pepper.

Fold the pastry over the filling to create a triangle or envelope, sealing the edges by pressing firmly or brushing them with a little water. The egg should be mostly contained but might leak slightly during cooking, this is normal.
Heat about 3 cm of oil in a deep frying pan to 180°C (or until a small piece of bread browns in about 30 seconds). Carefully place the first brik into the hot oil, seam-side down.

Fry for 2–3 minutes, turning once halfway, until the pastry is golden and crispy on both sides. The egg inside should still have a soft yolk. Use a slotted spoon to remove it and drain on paper towels.
Repeat with the remaining briks, making sure the oil returns to temperature between batches.
Serve hot, on their own or with a squeeze of lemon and extra harissa on the side!

notes: The yolk should be soft when you bite in, if you prefer it cooked through, fry for an extra minute, but you'll lose some of the magic!
If the pastry is splitting, brush the edges with a paste of flour and water to seal them better.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Shorshe Ilish
recipe.summary: Hilsa fish in pungent mustard paste, the most Bengali of celebrations

items.raw: 800 g hilsa fillets (ilish), skin on, or 600 g fresh pomfret or mackerel fillets
items.prep: skin on, or 600 g fresh pomfret or mackerel fillets

items.raw: 4 tbsp mustard seeds, black and yellow mixed

steps.text: Soak the mustard seeds in a little water for 10 minutes, then grind to a coarse paste with the green chillies, turmeric and salt. The paste should be lumpy and pungent, not smooth.
Heat the mustard oil in a wide, shallow pan over medium-high heat until it just smokes, about 2 minutes. This is essential, the burnt edge of the oil gives shorshe ilish its character.
Gently lay the fish fillets skin-side up in the hot oil. Cook for 2–3 minutes without moving them, until the flesh begins to turn opaque at the edges.
Spread the mustard paste over the fish, then add 150 ml water around (not over) it. The sauce should be loose and gravy-like.

Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cook, uncovered and barely disturbing the fish, for 15–18 minutes, until the flesh is cooked through and flakes easily when tested at its thickest point. The sauce should reduce and thicken slightly.
Taste and adjust salt. Stir in the jaggery if using, a hint of sweetness balances the mustard's heat. Serve hot, with rice to soak up the sauce.

notes: Shorshe ilish is traditionally made during spring when hilsa is in season (March–May). If hilsa is unavailable, use fresh pomfret or mackerel, both have the oily texture this dish demands.
Prepare the mustard paste fresh; it loses its pungency if made too far ahead. The dish can be made a few hours in advance and gently reheated.

recipe.title: Rendang Daging Sapi Padang
recipe.summary: Slow-cooked beef in a rich coconut and spice paste, the signature dish of Padang.

items.raw: 1 kg beef chuck, cut into 4 cm chunks
5 cm piece ginger, peeled and chopped
3 stalks lemongrass, white part only, bruised

steps.text: Blend the garlic, ginger, red chillies, shallots and macadamias with 60 ml of the coconut milk until you have a smooth, thick paste. This is your spice foundation, don't rush it.
Heat the oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the lemongrass and bruise it gently with a wooden spoon to release its oils, about 1 minute.
Add the spice paste and cook, stirring constantly, until it darkens and the raw smell fades, about 8–10 minutes. The paste should start to break apart and release its fragrance.
Add the beef chunks and stir well to coat in the paste. Cook for about 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the beef is sealed on the outside.
Pour in the remaining coconut milk. Stir well, then bring to a gentle simmer, until small bubbles appear at the edges. Do not boil. Reduce the heat to low.

Simmer, uncovered, for about 60–70 minutes, stirring every 15 minutes or so. The coconut milk will gradually reduce and the sauce will thicken and darken. By the end, the beef should be very tender and the sauce should be thick and cling to the meat, not swim in liquid. This is where patience matters, watch that the heat stays gentle so the coconut doesn't split.
Taste and season with salt. If the rendang feels too sharp, stir in the palm sugar. Remove the lemongrass stalks.
The rendang is ready when the sauce is nearly absorbed, glossy and deep reddish-brown, and the beef is so tender it breaks easily with a spoon. Serve warm.

notes: Rendang improves overnight as the flavours marry. Make it a day ahead and gently reheat, or store in the fridge for up to 4 days.
Use a heavy-bottomed pot so the heat stays even and the sauce doesn't catch at the bottom.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

recipe.title: Cabbage Thoran
recipe.summary: Shredded cabbage stir-fried with grated coconut, mustard seeds and curry leaves.

items.raw: ½ head cabbage (about 500 g), finely shredded
200 g fresh grated coconut (or 150 g desiccated coconut, rehydrated in 80 ml warm water for 10 minutes)
items.note: or 150 g desiccated coconut, rehydrated in 80 ml warm water for 10 minutes

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large frying pan or kadai over medium-high heat.
Once shimmering, add the mustard seeds. As soon as they pop and crackle, add the halved red chilli and curry leaves. Fry for 30 seconds, stirring, until fragrant.
Add the shredded cabbage and salt. Stir well to coat in the oil and spices.
Cook, stirring often, for 5–6 minutes. The cabbage should soften and turn glossy but stay bright; if water beads on the pan, keep stirring until it evaporates.
Add the grated coconut and toss to combine. Cook for 1–2 minutes, stirring constantly, until the coconut is warm and the cabbage is tender but still has a slight bite.
Taste and adjust salt if needed. Serve hot as a side to rice and curry.

notes: Make ahead: prepare the cabbage and coconut the morning before, store them separately in the fridge, and cook just before serving.
Swap: if fresh coconut is hard to find, use desiccated coconut rehydrated in warm water as given above.
Use waxy cabbage if possible; savoy can release more water and make the dish wetter.

recipe.title: Slow-Roasted Gemista
recipe.summary: Tomatoes and peppers stuffed with rice and herbs, slow-roasted until they collapse into themselves.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Cut the top off each tomato and set aside. Using a spoon, scoop out the insides, leaving about 1 cm of flesh around the walls. Chop the scooped flesh and set aside. Cut the capsicums in half and remove the seeds.
Heat 2 tbsp of the olive oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Cook the onion until soft, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for another minute, stirring.
Add the rice and stir for 2 minutes to toast it lightly. Add the chopped tomato flesh, parsley, mint, oregano, and a pinch of salt and pepper. Stir well and remove from heat. Let cool slightly.

Arrange the tomato shells and capsicum halves in a large baking dish, cut-side up. Divide the rice mixture evenly among them, pressing gently and mounding slightly, they'll settle as they cook until the rice is tender and the tops are lightly golden.
Drizzle the remaining 2 tbsp olive oil over everything. Pour the water into the dish around (not over) the vegetables. Replace the tomato tops. Season with salt and pepper.

Roast, uncovered, at 180°C for about 60 minutes, until the tomatoes and capsicums are very soft and the edges are slightly charred. The rice will have absorbed most of the liquid. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: These are best served warm or at room temperature, not hot, the flavours settle beautifully as they cool.
You can make them a few hours ahead and reheat gently in a 150°C oven for 15 minutes.
If your tomatoes are not very ripe, add a tbsp of tomato paste to the rice mixture for more depth.

recipe.title: Hijiki No Nimono
recipe.summary: Hijiki seaweed simmered with carrots, burdock and abura-age, a traditional bento side.

items.raw: 80 g burdock (gobo), cut into thin matchsticks
2 abura-age (fried tofu pockets), cut into thin strips

steps.text: Soak the dried hijiki in 200 ml room-temperature water for 5 minutes until soft and pliable. Drain well and squeeze gently to remove excess water.
Heat the oil in a wide shallow pan over medium heat. Add the carrot and burdock and cook, stirring, until they soften slightly, about 3 minutes.
Add the drained hijiki and the abura-age strips to the pan. Stir to combine.

Pour in the chicken stock, soy sauce, mirin and sugar. Bring to a simmer, then reduce the heat to low. Cook, uncovered, stirring occasionally, until almost all the liquid has been absorbed and the vegetables are very tender, about 15 minutes.
Remove from the heat and let cool. Serve at room temperature, or pack into bento boxes.

notes: This keeps well in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 5 days, making it perfect for bento prep.
If you can't find burdock, use parsnip cut into thin matchsticks; it cooks a little faster but has a similar sweetness.
Hijiki expands as it soaks, so don't skip that step, the texture will be much better.

title: Chopped Salad with Feta and Oregano

recipe.title: Chopped Salad with Feta and Oregano
recipe.summary: Tomato, cucumber, red onion and feta tossed with oregano and lemon.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Chop the tomatoes, cucumber and red onion into roughly the same size pieces. Put them in a big bowl.
Add the olive oil, lemon juice and oregano. Toss everything together and season with salt and pepper.
Let it sit for 2 minutes, until the salt has drawn out a little juice and the vegetables are glossy, so the flavours come together.
Scatter the feta on top and toss through gently. Serve straight away.

recipe.title: Hobak Bokkeum
recipe.summary: Stir-fried zucchini with perilla leaf and sesame, bright, delicate banchan.

items.raw: 600 g zucchini, halved lengthwise and sliced into half-moons about 3 mm thick
items.prep: halved lengthwise and sliced into half-moons about 3 mm thick

items.raw: 8–10 perilla leaves (kkaenip), torn or cut into bite-sized pieces
items.prep: torn or cut into bite-sized pieces

steps.text: Heat the sesame oil in a large wok or wide frying pan over medium-high heat.

Add the zucchini and salt. Stir-fry, tossing gently and frequently, until the zucchini is tender but still holds its shape and the edges are lightly caramelised, about 6–8 minutes. The zucchini will release a little moisture; let it cook off.
Remove from the heat and allow to cool for a minute. Add the perilla leaves and toss gently to combine.
Transfer to a serving bowl, scatter with the sesame seeds and black pepper, and serve at room temperature or slightly warm.

notes: Hobak bokkeum is best served at room temperature as part of a banchan spread, but it's also good warm.
Make it ahead and reheat gently, or prepare up to the stir-frying step and add the perilla leaves just before serving.

recipe.title: Causa Limeña
recipe.summary: Layered potato terrine with ají amarillo, chicken and avocado, Lima's most elegant potato dish.

items.raw: 1 kg waxy potatoes, peeled and chopped

steps.text: Boil the potatoes in salted water until just tender, about 15 minutes. Drain well.
Mash the hot potatoes with the ají amarillo paste, oil and lime juice. Season with salt and pepper. Let cool to room temperature.
In a bowl, combine the shredded chicken with mayonnaise, spring onions, chilli and lime juice. Season with salt and pepper.
Line a 1 litre loaf tin with plastic wrap. Spread half the potato mixture evenly on the bottom, smoothing it level.
Spread the chicken salad evenly over the potato layer. Top with the remaining potato mixture, smoothing it level.
Refrigerate for at least 2 hours, or until completely set and chilled.
Invert the terrine onto a serving plate and gently peel away the plastic wrap.
Arrange the avocado and egg slices on top, scatter with olives, and garnish with fresh coriander. Slice at the table and serve.

notes: Make up to 24 hours ahead: unmould, wrap gently in plastic and refrigerate. Add avocado and toppings just before serving.
For the cooked chicken, use a store-bought rotisserie chicken or leftover roast chicken.
Ají amarillo paste is available from Latin American grocers or online; it's worth seeking out for its distinct fruity heat, but yellow chilli paste works in a pinch.

recipe.title: Pad Cha Het
recipe.summary: Stir-fried wild mushrooms with fresh chilies and garlic, a simple northern Thai favourite.

items.raw: 500 g mixed mushrooms (cremini, oyster, shiitake), torn into bite-sized pieces

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large wok or frying pan over high heat until shimmering.
Add the mushrooms and cook, stirring occasionally, for 4–5 minutes until they begin to soften and release their liquid.
Add the garlic and chillies, stirring constantly for about 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the soy sauce and palm sugar, tossing everything together until the mushrooms are coated and tender, about 2 minutes more.
Taste and adjust the seasoning if needed.
Transfer to a serving plate, top with fresh Thai basil, and serve with a lime wedge on the side.

notes: If you can't find Thai basil, regular basil works well too.
For a deeper savoury note, replace soy sauce with tamari or add a teaspoon of coconut aminos.
Use whatever fresh or dried mushrooms you have; this dish works beautifully with any combination.

title: Smashed Avocado on Sourdough with Za'atar

recipe.title: Smashed Avocado on Sourdough with Za'atar
recipe.summary: Thick-cut sourdough topped with smashed avocado, crispy za'atar and lemon juice.

steps.text: Toast the sourdough until golden and crispy, about 3 minutes.
While the bread toasts, scoop the avocado into a small bowl and mash roughly with a fork, leaving it chunky. Season with a pinch of salt and pepper.
Divide the smashed avocado between the two warm toasts and spread gently.
Sprinkle 1 tsp za'atar over each slice.
Squeeze lemon juice over the top and serve straight away.

notes: Use a ripe but not over-soft avocado for the best texture.
Make it a full breakfast by adding a squeeze of hot sauce or fresh chilli if you want more heat.

recipe.title: Pico de Gallo
recipe.summary: Fresh tomato, white onion, coriander and lime salsa, the real deal, made in five minutes.

items.raw: 1 small handful fresh coriander, finely chopped

steps.text: Dice the tomatoes into small, even pieces, about the size of a pea. If they release a lot of juice, drain them slightly.
Dice the white onion into small pieces the same size as the tomato.
Chop the fresh coriander roughly, then go over it once more with the knife so it's fine.
Combine the tomato, onion and coriander in a bowl.
Squeeze the lime juice over, add a pinch of salt, and stir gently until the tomato is glossy and lightly coated in juice. Taste and adjust salt and lime.
Serve right away, or cover and keep in the fridge for up to an hour.

notes: Make it no more than an hour ahead; after that it gets watery.
If your tomatoes are mealy, add a tiny pinch of sugar to wake them up.

recipe.title: Bún Riêu
recipe.summary: Crab and tomato noodle soup with crab paste, tangy and rich.

items.raw: 200 g fresh crab meat (or 150 g tinned crab)
3 tbsp crab paste (cua cốt, or more crab meat)
items.note: cua cốt, or more crab meat

items.raw: 2 tbsp fish sauce, plus extra to taste
300 g rice vermicelli, soaked in room-temperature water until pliable (about 10 minutes)
items.prep: soaked in room-temperature water until pliable

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Add garlic and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Add tomato paste and stir for 30 seconds.
Add the chopped tomatoes and cook, stirring occasionally, until they begin to break down, about 5 minutes.

Pour in the chicken stock and bring to a simmer. Add the crab meat (if using fresh or tinned), caster sugar, and 2 tbsp fish sauce. Simmer gently for 20 minutes to let the flavours meld and the tomato dissolve into the broth.
In the last 5 minutes of simmering, stir in the crab paste gradually, letting it warm through without boiling. Taste and adjust with extra fish sauce and salt as needed.
Bring a separate pot of water to a boil. Add the soaked rice vermicelli and cook for 2–3 minutes, then drain well.
Divide the noodles between two bowls. Ladle the hot broth and crab over the top. Scatter spring onion, fresh coriander, and fried shallots over each bowl. Serve at once.

notes: Make the broth ahead and reheat gently; it keeps for 3 days in the fridge. Cook the noodles fresh just before serving.
No fresh crab? Use a good tinned crab in brine (drain well), or substitute more crab paste with a little extra stock to thin it.
The fried shallots are worth finding at any Vietnamese or Asian grocer, they're the difference between good and the stall version.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

recipe.title: Ayam Goreng Yogyakarta
recipe.summary: Golden fried chicken with sweet soy and garlic, a Yogyakarta workshop lunch favourite.

items.raw: 1 kg chicken pieces (thigh and drumstick), skin on

steps.text: Mix the crushed garlic, sweet soy sauce, oil and salt in a bowl to make the marinade. Add the chicken pieces and turn to coat well. Cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, or overnight if you have the time.
Remove the chicken from the refrigerator 20 minutes before cooking to bring it closer to room temperature.
Heat 5 cm of neutral oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pan or wok to 160–170°C. If you don't have a thermometer, the oil is ready when a cube of bread browns in about 45 seconds.

Working in batches to avoid crowding the pan, carefully slide the chicken pieces into the hot oil, skin side down. Fry for 12–15 minutes, turning halfway through, until the skin is deep golden brown and the thickest part of the thigh reaches 75°C inside.
Transfer the cooked chicken to a paper-lined plate to drain. Serve hot with the pan juices spooned over.

notes: Marinate the chicken overnight for best flavour, it's worth the patience.
Use bone-in, skin-on chicken; it stays juicier and develops that crackling skin Yogyakarta style.
Serve at room temperature with steamed rice and sambal if you like heat.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Snapper and Sambal Oelek Pasta
recipe.summary: Pan-seared snapper with sambal oelek, garlic and parsley tossed through pasta.

items.raw: 2 snapper fillets (about 150 g each), skin on
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Bring a large pot of salted water to the boil and cook the pasta until al dente, about 10 minutes. Drain, reserving 150 ml of pasta water.
While the pasta cooks, pat the snapper fillets dry and season with salt and pepper on both sides. Heat 2 tbsp olive oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat.
Place the snapper skin-side down in the hot pan and cook for 4 minutes until the skin is crispy. Flip and cook for another 2 minutes until just cooked through. Transfer to a plate.
In the same pan, add the sliced garlic and cook over medium heat for 1 minute until fragrant. Stir in the sambal oelek and cook for another 30 seconds.
Add the cooked pasta to the pan with 100 ml of the reserved pasta water. Toss gently for 1–2 minutes, adding a little more pasta water if needed to coat the pasta lightly.
Break the snapper into large flakes and fold through the pasta gently. Squeeze over the lemon juice, scatter with parsley and serve immediately.

notes: Snapper is the go-to, firm, sweet, cooks quickly. Sub any fresh white fish fillet.
Make it vegetarian: swap the fish for 250 g firm tofu, cut into thick slices, pan-seared until golden.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Tonga Pumpkin & Coconut
recipe.summary: Roasted pumpkin simmered in coconut milk with onions and garlic.

items.raw: 1 kg jap pumpkin, cut into 5 cm chunks

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat. Working in batches, roast the pumpkin chunks until golden brown on all sides, about 10 minutes total. Set aside.
In the same pot, soften the onions over medium heat, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and cook, stirring, for 1 minute until fragrant.
Return the pumpkin to the pot. Pour in the coconut milk and chicken stock, then season with salt and pepper.

Bring to a gentle simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cover and simmer until the pumpkin is completely soft and starting to break down, about 20 minutes. Stir occasionally and taste, adding more salt if needed.
Serve warm with fresh coriander if you like. Feeds the whole family on a weeknight.

notes: Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

recipe.title: Molokhia
recipe.summary: Egyptian leafy green stew with garlic and coriander, served over rice.

items.raw: 400 g fresh molokhia leaves, roughly chopped (or 200 g dried molokhia, crushed)

steps.text: Bring the vegetable stock to a boil in a large pot, until it bubbles steadily.
Add the chopped molokhia leaves and stir to combine. Simmer for 5 minutes until the leaves start to break down.
While the molokhia simmers, heat a tablespoon of oil in a small pan over medium heat. Add the chopped garlic and fry gently, stirring often, until golden and fragrant, about 3 minutes.
Crush the fried garlic with the salt using the back of a spoon or a mortar and pestle until it forms a paste.
Stir the garlic paste and ground coriander into the molokhia. Simmer for a further 3 to 5 minutes until the stew is thick and cohesive.
Serve the molokhia over a bed of steamed rice, with lemon wedges on the side for squeezing.

notes: Fresh molokhia is best and usually the cheapest; dried molokhia works too, use half the weight and crush it into a powder before adding. Frozen molokhia is also fine.
If you can't find molokhia, spinach is the closest substitute, though it's leafier and less slimy. Don't overcook spinach or it falls apart.
The stew thickens as it cools; add a splash more stock when reheating if needed.

recipe.title: Fava
recipe.summary: Silken yellow split pea purée from the Greek islands, dressed with olive oil and lemon.

items.raw: 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, to serve

steps.text: Rinse the yellow split peas under cold water, then tip into a large pot with the water and quartered brown onion. Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat and simmer gently, uncovered, for about 50 minutes, stirring often, until the peas have broken down completely into a thick purée.
When the peas are very soft and falling apart, remove from the heat and discard the onion pieces. Season generously with salt.
Whisk in the olive oil, a little at a time, beating to incorporate air and make the purée smooth and pale. This will take 3–4 minutes of steady whisking.
Stir in the lemon juice, then taste and adjust the seasoning, you want salt, brightness and richness in balance.
Divide among four bowls and top each with a handful of raw red onion slices and a crack of black pepper. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: Fava keeps well for 3 days in the fridge, covered. Reheat gently with a splash of water to loosen it back to a purée consistency.
This is also lovely cold, straight from the fridge, with toasted bread and a scatter of caper berries or olives.

recipe.title: Tarhana Çorbası
recipe.summary: Tangy fermented grain and yoghurt soup, warming and sour, Anatolian comfort food.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Melt the butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook, stirring often, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the ground cumin and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the stock and bring to a simmer. Whisk the tarhana paste with a small cup of warm water until smooth, then slowly pour it into the simmering stock, whisking constantly so no lumps form.
Simmer gently for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the soup has thickened slightly and the flavours have melded. Taste and season with salt and pepper.
Ladle into bowls and scatter with fresh mint if you like. Serve hot.

notes: If you can't find ready-made tarhana paste, you can order it online. Turkish delis often stock it.
Tarhana keeps for months in an airtight jar, so it's worth having on hand.
A dollop of yoghurt stirred in at the end is traditional, use about 1 tbsp per bowl.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

recipe.title: Chikni Dal
recipe.summary: Smooth, silky split pea dal with fried garlic and green chilli, served with roti.

steps.text: Rinse the lentils under cold water until the water runs clear. Put them in a large pot with the halved onion, turmeric, salt and water. Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat to a simmer.

Cook, stirring occasionally, for 35–40 minutes, until the lentils have completely broken down and the mixture is smooth and thick. If it's too thick, add a splash of water. Remove and discard the onion.

While the dal is cooking, heat the oil in a small frying pan over medium heat. Add the garlic slices and cook, stirring, for 2–3 minutes, until golden and fragrant. Stir in the green chilli and cook for another 30 seconds.
Pour the hot garlic and chilli oil over the dal and stir through. Taste and add more salt if needed. Serve hot with roti, garnished with fresh coriander if you like.

notes: Make it ahead: the dal keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days. Reheat gently on the stove with a splash of water if needed.
The garlic and chilli tempering can be made while the dal cooks and kept warm, or made fresh just before serving.

recipe.title: Pol Sambol
recipe.summary: Fresh coconut, lime, chilli and dried fish, a Sri Lankan sambol to eat with rice and curry.

items.raw: 1 fresh coconut, or 400 g freshly grated coconut
1 small red onion, very finely chopped

steps.text: If using a whole coconut, pierce the eyes and drain the liquid. Crack open the shell and peel away the brown skin with a vegetable peeler. Grate the white flesh on a fine grater or microplane until you have about 400 g of fine, fluffy coconut.
Put the grated coconut into a bowl and add the lime juice, chopped chillies, pounded dried fish, and red onion.
Mix gently but thoroughly until every grain of coconut is coated and the flavours are even.
Taste and adjust the seasoning with salt. The sambol should be bright, sharp, and hot, not timid.
Serve immediately alongside hot rice and curry.

notes: Make it up to 2 hours ahead and keep covered at room temperature; the coconut will soften slightly and the flavours will deepen.
If you can't find fresh coconut, use a block of frozen grated coconut, thawed, or good-quality desiccated coconut rehydrated in a little warm water and squeezed dry.
Ikan bilis (dried anchovies) are sold in Asian grocers; if you can't find them, use a small tin of anchovy fillets in oil, drained and mashed.

recipe.title: Pierogi Ruskie
recipe.summary: Potato and cheese dumplings with caramelized onions and sour cream.

items.raw: 500 g waxy potato, peeled and chopped into 2 cm pieces
items.prep: peeled and chopped into 2 cm pieces

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Make the dough: mix flour and salt in a bowl. In another bowl, whisk the egg, then stir in the sour cream. Pour the wet mixture into the flour and mix until you have a soft, slightly sticky dough. Knead for 5 minutes until smooth and elastic. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

Meanwhile, make the filling: boil the potato pieces in salted water until very tender, about 12 minutes. Drain well and mash roughly, you want some small lumps. Fry the chopped onion in 2 tbsp butter over medium heat until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Stir the onion and butter into the potato, then fold in the cheese. Season to taste with salt and pepper. Let cool.

Make the caramelized onions for serving: slice the 2 onions thinly. Melt 3 tbsp butter in a wide pan over medium heat and cook the onions, stirring often, until they're golden and soft, about 15 minutes. Set aside.

Roll the pierogi: flour your work surface lightly. Roll the dough out to about 2 mm thick. Using a 7 cm round cutter or a glass, cut out circles. Place a heaped teaspoon of filling on each circle, fold in half, then press the edges to seal, fold the corner of the half-moon up and over itself to make a small curved seal (this is the traditional shape). Oil your hands if the dough sticks.

Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Working in batches, drop the pierogi in. They'll sink at first, then float to the surface when they're nearly done, about 2 minutes. Boil for another 30 seconds after they float, then lift out with a slotted spoon.
Serve the pierogi warm with the caramelized onions spooned over the top and a dollop of sour cream. Scatter with fresh dill if you like.

notes: Make the filling and dough ahead: the filling keeps for 2 days in the fridge, and the dough keeps for up to 4 hours. You can freeze uncooked pierogi on a tray, then boil them straight from frozen (add 1 extra minute to the boiling time).
A potato ricer or food mill makes a smoother filling if you don't like lumps, though a rustic texture is traditional too.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Curry Rice with Sambals
recipe.summary: Fragrant turmeric rice with Cape Malay curry and fresh homemade sambals.

items.raw: 500 g beef mince (or lamb shoulder), cubed

steps.text: Make the sambals first: combine tomatoes, red onion, red chilli and coriander in a small bowl. Add lime juice and salt. In another bowl, combine cucumber, green chilli, mint, lime juice and salt. Set both aside.

For the curry rice, heat oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add onion and cook, stirring, until softened and golden, about 5 minutes. Add garlic and ginger, stirring constantly for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add turmeric and stir for 30 seconds, then add rice, stirring to coat each grain in the oil and spices, about 2 minutes.
Pour in stock and add bay leaves. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat to low, cover and simmer for 15–18 minutes until the rice is tender and liquid is absorbed. Taste and adjust salt.

If making the suggested curry: heat oil in a separate pot over medium-high heat. Brown the meat in batches, set aside. In the same pot, cook onions until soft, about 5 minutes. Add curry powder and tomato paste, stirring for 1 minute. Return meat to pot, add stock and potatoes. Simmer, covered, for 20–25 minutes until potatoes are tender and sauce is thick. Season to taste.
Fluff the rice with a fork and remove bay leaves. Transfer to a serving dish, top with curry if using, and serve with both sambals on the side.

notes: The curry can be made a day ahead and reheated gently. The sambals are best made an hour or two before serving so the flavours meld.
Use leftover roast chicken or vegetables instead of making the curry, a generous spoonful stirred through the rice works just as well.
The rice can also be cooked in a rice cooker: fry the onion, garlic and ginger in a pot, add turmeric and rice to coat, then transfer to the rice cooker with the stock and bay leaves.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Tarte à la praline
recipe.summary: Pink praline tart, a Lyon specialty that's simpler than it looks.

steps.text: Make the pastry: rub the cold butter into the flour with your fingertips until it looks like breadcrumbs, then stir in the caster sugar and salt. Beat the egg yolk with the cold water and mix into the flour until just combined. Form a disc, wrap in cling film and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes.

Preheat the oven to 200°C. Roll out the pastry between two sheets of baking paper to about 3 mm thick. Press into a 24 cm tart tin, trim the edges and prick the base. Blind bake with baking paper and beans for 12 minutes, then remove the paper and beans and bake for another 5 minutes until just set. Set aside to cool slightly.
Roughly crush about three-quarters of the pink pralines with the back of a spoon, you want some texture, not a smooth paste. Stir the softened butter through the crushed pralines.
Whisk the cream, milk, egg yolks and vanilla together until smooth. Fold in the praline mixture, then pour into the cooled pastry shell. Scatter the remaining whole pralines over the top.

Bake at 180°C for about 10 minutes, until the filling is just set but still trembling slightly in the centre. The tart will continue to set as it cools. Chill for at least 4 hours, or overnight, before serving.

notes: Make this a day ahead: the pralines soften beautifully overnight and the flavours deepen.
Pink pralines are a Lyon specialty and worth hunting down in good delis or online. They're crunchy, delicately flavoured hazelnut pralines and not like anything else.
If your oven runs hot, tent the tart loosely with foil if it's browning too quickly.
Food safety: The eggs are cooked until just set. For pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system, cook them until firm all the way through.

title: Kokt torsk med gräslök och smör

recipe.title: Kokt torsk med gräslök och smör
recipe.summary: Poached cod with chives and brown butter, a simple West Coast Swedish dinner.

items.raw: 4 white-fish fillets, about 150 g each (cod or similar)

steps.text: Pour the stock or water into a wide, shallow pan and add the bay leaf. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat, until the surface is barely trembling with tiny bubbles and not boiling.
Pat the fish fillets dry with paper towel and season lightly with salt on both sides.

Slide the fish into the simmering stock. The liquid should barely cover them. Poach gently, the surface should barely tremble, for about 8 minutes, until the fish is cooked through and flakes easily when tested with a fork.
Carefully lift the fish onto warm plates using a slotted spatula, leaving the poaching liquid behind.
Melt the butter in a small pan over medium heat, swirling occasionally, until it turns a light golden brown and smells nutty, about 3 minutes. Watch it carefully so it doesn't burn.

Drizzle the brown butter, which should smell nutty and be golden brown, over each fillet, which should be opaque and flake easily. Scatter the chives over the top, and finish with a grind of black pepper. Serve at once.

notes: The whole point is freshness and gentleness. Don't rush the poaching, low heat keeps the fish tender. If your fillets are very thick, give them an extra minute.
Brown butter can be made ahead and kept warm; reheat gently before serving.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Spring onion Pancakes
recipe.summary: Laminated flatbread layered with oil and spring onions, flaky and crispy outside.

items.raw: 3 tbsp neutral oil, plus extra for brushing
4 spring onions, white and light green parts, finely chopped
items.prep: white and light green parts, finely chopped

items.raw: 1 tsp coarse sea salt, for finishing

steps.text: Mix the boiling water into the flour and salt with a wooden spoon or chopsticks until shaggy. Let cool for 5 minutes, then knead by hand until smooth and soft, about 8 minutes. The dough will be slightly sticky, this is right. Cover with a damp cloth and rest for 20 minutes.
Divide the dough into 4 equal pieces. Roll each piece into a ball, brush all over with a little oil, and rest for 10 minutes covered.

On an oiled work surface, roll one ball into a thin rectangle about 30 cm × 20 cm. Brush generously with oil, scatter a quarter of the chopped spring onion evenly over the surface, then tightly roll up from one long edge into a log. Coil the log into a spiral, tucking the end underneath. Press gently to flatten slightly into a disc about 1 cm thick. Repeat with the remaining dough balls, spring onion and oil. Let rest for 5 minutes.
Roll each disc into a round about 20 cm across, being gentle so the layers stay distinct. If the dough springs back, let it rest for a minute and try again.

Heat 1½ tbsp oil in a large non-stick frying pan over medium heat. Once shimmering, place one pancake in and cook for 2–3 minutes until the underside is golden and crispy. Flip and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes until speckled and cooked through.
Transfer to a plate and immediately sprinkle with a pinch of coarse sea salt. Repeat with the remaining pancakes, adding a little more oil to the pan as needed. Serve warm, torn into pieces.

notes: The dough keeps well: store finished pancakes in an airtight container for 2 days, then reheat briefly in a dry frying pan. You can also freeze uncooked rested discs for up to a month, then cook straight from frozen (add 2 minutes to the cooking time).
Hydration is key here, 75% feels sticky at first, but it's what gives you those delicate, shattering layers. Don't add extra flour.

recipe.title: Frittata di Cipolla e Peperoncino
recipe.summary: Caramelised onions and fresh chilli eggs, best at room temperature with bread and a story.

items.raw: 2 fresh red chillies, deseeded and finely sliced

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a 25 cm non-stick frying pan over medium heat. Add the onions and a pinch of salt, and stir often until they're golden and soft, about 15 minutes. You want them sweet, not brown and crispy.
Scatter the chilli through the onions and cook for another 2 minutes, then taste and adjust the salt and pepper.
While the onions are cooking, crack the eggs into a bowl, whisk them together well, and set aside.
Turn the heat to medium-low. Pour the eggs over the onions, stir gently to distribute them, then leave it alone. Cook until the edges are set and the top is still a little soft, about 10 minutes.
Slide the frittata onto a plate and let it cool to room temperature. Scatter with parsley if you like, cut into wedges, and serve with good bread.

notes: Keep in the fridge for up to 3 days and serve cold, or reheat gently in a 180°C oven.
No chilli in the house? Use a pinch of dried oregano instead, or just the onions. The frittata doesn't need much.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Rice and Peas
recipe.summary: Creamy coconut rice studded with red kidney beans and thyme, the everyday side that turns a plate into a meal.

items.raw: 400 g tin kidney beans, drained and rinsed
1 sprig fresh thyme (or 1 tsp dried thyme)

steps.text: Pour the coconut milk into a large measuring jug and add water to make 600 ml total. Stir well to combine.
Heat the oil in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until softened and fragrant, about 3 minutes.
Add the garlic and cook, stirring, for 1 minute more.
Add the rice, stirring to coat in the oil, about 1 minute.
Pour in the coconut milk mixture and stock, then add the kidney beans, thyme, salt and pepper. Stir well and bring to a boil until the liquid is bubbling steadily.
Once boiling, reduce the heat to low, cover with a tight-fitting lid, and cook for 18 to 20 minutes, until the rice is tender and the liquid is absorbed. Do not lift the lid during cooking.
Remove from the heat and let it rest, covered, for 2 minutes. Fluff with a fork, discard the thyme sprig if using fresh, and scatter with spring onion if you like.

notes: Make it ahead: cook it the day before, cool quickly, and refrigerate in an airtight container for up to 3 days. Reheat gently in the pot with a splash of water.
This is Jamaican rice and peas, which uses kidney beans, not the peas you might find elsewhere in the Caribbean.

recipe.title: Marmitako
recipe.summary: Basque fisherman's stew with tuna, potatoes and peppers.

items.raw: 600 g fresh tuna, cut into chunks
500 g floury potato, cut into large dice
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large, heavy pot over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic and paprika, stir well, and cook for 1 minute.
Add the potatoes and stir to coat in the oil. Pour in the stock and bring to a boil. Cook for 15 minutes until the potatoes are nearly tender.
Add the red and green capsicum and simmer for 5 minutes.
Add the tuna chunks and stir gently. Simmer for 8–10 minutes, until the tuna is just cooked through and the potatoes are tender. Don't overcook the tuna.
Season with salt and black pepper to taste. Serve hot in bowls.

notes: Use good-quality fresh tuna; frozen won't give you the same result.
Don't stir too much once the tuna is in, you want to keep the chunks intact.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

recipe.title: Waakye
recipe.summary: Millet and beans with rice, Ghana's beloved street breakfast made at home.

items.raw: 200 g dried brown beans (or tinned kidney beans)
1 litre water (or more, for tinned beans)

steps.text: If using dried beans, soak them in cold water for at least 2 hours or overnight. Drain and rinse. (Skip this if using tinned beans.)

In a large pot, bring water to the boil. Add the beans, bay leaves, ginger and onion. Simmer for 40 minutes if using dried beans, or 15 minutes if using tinned beans, until the beans are soft but not falling apart.
Add the millet to the pot. Stir well and cook for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Add the rice, stir, and bring back to a simmer. Cook, covered, for 20 to 25 minutes until the rice is cooked through and most of the liquid is absorbed. The mixture should be moist but not soupy.
Taste and add salt as needed. Remove the bay leaves.
Serve hot with your choice of toppings: grated hard-boiled egg, fried plantain, avocado, hot shito sauce, or a rich stew.

notes: If you can't find millet, substitute with 150 g of pearl barley or extra rice, though the texture won't be quite the same.
Make it the night before and reheat gently with a splash of water, the flavour deepens overnight.
The best toppings are fried plantain, avocado slices, grated hard-boiled egg, and a spoonful of hot shito (pepper) sauce on the side.

recipe.title: Smoked Mackerel with Horseradish Cream
recipe.summary: Smoked mackerel with sharp horseradish cream and buttered new potatoes.

items.raw: 2 tbsp fresh horseradish, finely grated (or 3 tbsp prepared horseradish)
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Put the potatoes in a large pot of cold salted water and bring to the boil. Cook for 12 to 15 minutes until just tender when pierced with a knife, then drain well.
While the potatoes cook, make the horseradish cream: whip the cold cream to soft peaks, then gently fold in the horseradish, lemon juice, sugar and a pinch of salt and pepper.
Return the warm potatoes to the pot, add the butter and toss until coated and glossy. Season to taste.

Warm the smoked mackerel fillets gently by placing them skin-side up on a plate and letting them sit near (not on) a warm part of the stove for 2 to 3 minutes, or arrange them on a baking tray and warm through in a 160°C oven for 5 minutes.
Divide the potatoes among four plates, place a mackerel fillet alongside each portion, and top with a generous spoonful of horseradish cream. Scatter with fresh parsley if you like and serve at once.

notes: The horseradish cream can be made up to 2 hours ahead and kept in the fridge.
Use the best smoked mackerel you can get, local fishmonger quality makes all the difference.

recipe.title: Lancashire Hotpot
recipe.summary: Layered lamb, potatoes and onions, baked low and slow until the potatoes crisp on top.

items.raw: 800 g lamb shoulder, diced into 3 cm pieces
700 g waxy potato, thinly sliced (about 3 mm)
2 tbsp butter, plus extra for dotting
1 tsp fresh thyme leaves (or ½ tsp dried thyme)

steps.text: Heat oven to 160°C. Layer half the potatoes in the bottom of a deep baking dish or casserole (about 2 litre capacity), then half the onions.
Add all the lamb pieces, then layer the remaining onions and remaining potatoes on top, seasoning each layer with salt, pepper and thyme as you go.
Warm the chicken stock and pour it over everything, it should come about three-quarters of the way up the dish. Dot the top with small pieces of butter.
Cover tightly with foil and bake for 2 hours at 160°C, until the lamb is completely tender.
Increase oven to 200°C, remove the foil, and bake uncovered for a further 15 minutes until the potato tops are golden and crispy.
Rest for 5 minutes before serving. The gravy should come from the lamb and stock, you don't need to make it separately.

notes: Make it the day before and refrigerate, it actually improves. Just add 10 minutes to the baking time if cooking from cold.
Lamb neck fillet works just as well as shoulder and gives you more flavour for the gravy.
Don't skip the second blast at high heat, that's what gets the potatoes crispy.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Shakshuka Tunisienne
recipe.summary: Eggs poached in fiery harissa tomato sauce with caraway and preserved lemon.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large shallow pan over medium heat. Add the chopped onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the minced garlic and cook for 1 minute until fragrant. Stir in the harissa and cook for another minute.

Pour in the crushed tomatoes and bring to a simmer. Add the preserved lemon and caraway seeds. Simmer for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce is thick and the flavours have melded. Season with salt and pepper.
If using it, drizzle the extra harissa over the surface of the sauce.

Make 8 small wells in the sauce by pushing it gently to the sides. Crack an egg into each well. Cover the pan and cook over medium-low heat for 6–8 minutes, until the egg whites are set but the yolks are still soft.
Scatter fresh coriander over the top and serve straight from the pan.

notes: Serve with torn bread to soak up the sauce.
Make the sauce ahead and reheat gently before poaching the eggs.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Salatit al-Khudar
recipe.summary: Simple Palestinian chopped salad of tomatoes, cucumber, parsley and lemon.

items.raw: 1 bunch fresh parsley, finely chopped (about 1 cup loosely packed)

steps.text: Dice the tomatoes into small, even pieces about the size of a pea, working over a bowl to catch the juice.
Dice the cucumber to the same size as the tomato.
Finely chop the parsley, removing the coarse stems and using mostly the leaves.
Combine the tomato, cucumber and parsley in a bowl.
Pour the lemon juice and olive oil over the vegetables and toss gently but thoroughly so everything is well coated.
Taste and add salt until it's right, not too much, just enough to bring out the flavour of the vegetables.
Serve straight away with warm bread to eat it with.

notes: Make this salad just before eating, if it sits too long, the vegetables release water and it becomes watery.
The dice should be fine and even. This isn't just cutting vegetables small; it's about texture, so every piece sits together in the bowl.

recipe.title: Thieboudienne
recipe.summary: Senegal's national dish: fish and rice slow-cooked with caramelized vegetables and tomato.

items.raw: 1 kg whole white fish (barramundi or snapper), scaled and gutted
1 medium sweet potato, cut into chunks
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Pat the fish dry and season inside and out with salt and pepper. Set aside.
Heat the oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat. Add the sliced onions and cook, stirring often, for 8–10 minutes until deeply golden and caramelized.
Stir in the garlic and tomato paste, cooking for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the crushed tomatoes and let them simmer for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the mixture darkens and thickens slightly.

Pour in the fish stock and bring to a simmer. Gently lay the whole fish into the liquid, then arrange the carrot, sweet potato, pumpkin and celery around it. Simmer gently for 15 minutes until the fish is just cooked through.
Carefully remove the fish and all vegetables to a plate. Cover loosely to keep warm.
Add the rice to the cooking liquid, stirring once, and bring back to a gentle simmer. Cook uncovered for about 20–25 minutes until the rice is tender and has absorbed most of the liquid.

Return the vegetables to the pot to warm through, then taste and adjust the seasoning. Serve the rice on a platter with the fish and vegetables arranged on top, scattered with fresh parsley if you like.

notes: Thieboudienne can be made a day ahead: cook the fish and vegetables up to step 5, cool and refrigerate, then finish the rice and reheat gently before serving.
If you can't find a whole fish, use thick fish steaks (about 200g each) and add them after the rice has cooked for 15 minutes, so they don't break up.
The caramelized onion base is everything, don't rush it. The darker and deeper the onions, the better the dish.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

recipe.title: Pastitsada
recipe.summary: Rabbit or chicken stewed in tomato and red wine until very tender, served over pasta, a Cretan Sunday dish.

items.raw: 1 whole rabbit (about 1.2 kg), or 1.2 kg chicken thigh, cut into pieces
items.prep: or 1.2 kg chicken thigh, cut into pieces

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Season the rabbit or chicken pieces with salt and pepper. Heat the olive oil in a large heavy pot over medium-high heat and brown the meat in batches, about 4 minutes each side, until golden. Set aside.
Add the diced onion to the same pot and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add the crushed garlic and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Return the meat to the pot. Pour in the red wine and scrape up any brown bits from the bottom. Let it bubble for 2 minutes, then add the crushed tomatoes, oregano and bay leaves.

Bring to a gentle simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cover partially and cook, stirring occasionally, until the meat is very tender and falls easily from the bone, about 2 hours. The sauce should be rich and concentrated.
Taste and adjust salt and pepper as needed. Remove bay leaves.
Cook the pasta in salted boiling water until al dente, about 10 minutes (or as the packet says). Drain well.
Divide the pasta among bowls and top with the rabbit or chicken and its sauce.

notes: This keeps well in the fridge for 3 days, or freeze for a month. The flavour deepens as it sits.
Yiayia's notebook says rabbit is traditional, but chicken thigh works beautifully and is easier to find.

recipe.title: Pancit Lomi
recipe.summary: Creamy egg noodle soup with chicken liver and greens, a Kapampangan birthday staple.

items.raw: 200 g chicken liver, cleaned and cut into bite-sized pieces
items.prep: cleaned and cut into bite-sized pieces

items.raw: 2 tbsp cornflour, mixed with 3 tbsp water

steps.text: Heat oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Fry the liver, stirring gently, until just cooked through, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.
In the same pot, sauté the onion and garlic until fragrant, about 2 minutes. Add the chicken breast and cook, stirring, until no longer pink, about 5 minutes.
Pour in the chicken stock and bring to a boil. Add the fresh egg noodles and cook until tender, about 5 minutes. Add the bok choy and spring onion.
Slowly pour the cornflour slurry into the simmering broth, stirring constantly until the soup thickens and turns creamy, about 2 minutes.
Return the cooked liver to the pot. Slowly drizzle in the beaten eggs while stirring gently to create egg ribbons, about 1 minute.
Season with salt and white pepper to taste. Serve hot.

notes: The chicken liver must not be overcooked or it becomes tough. Add it back to the pot at the very end.
Fresh egg noodles cook much faster than dried; if using dried noodles, add them earlier and cook for 8–10 minutes.
The cornflour slurry must be stirred in slowly to avoid lumps.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

recipe.title: Nyama Choma
recipe.summary: Grilled meat with lime and salt, charred and tender, the Kenyan way.

items.raw: 800 g beef chuck steak (or beef ribs), cut into 5 cm chunks

steps.text: Heat your grill or barbecue to hot. If using charcoal, wait until the coals are white and glowing; if gas, get it smoking.
Pat the beef dry with paper towel until the surface is no longer wet. This helps it char, not steam.
Rub the meat lightly with oil, then season generously with salt on both sides.
Lay the meat on the grill in a single layer. Don't move it for the first 4 minutes, you want a good char.
Flip and cook the other side for another 4 minutes. The meat should have a dark crust but still be pink inside (about 55°C on a meat thermometer).
Transfer to a warm plate. Squeeze lime over the hot meat, it'll sizzle and the juice will run into all the crevices.
Let it rest for 2 minutes, then serve with extra lime wedges and salt on the side for dipping.

notes: Beef ribs (short ribs or beef back ribs) cook beautifully the same way, just allow an extra 2–3 minutes per side.
No grill? A heavy cast-iron pan on the stove over high heat works. You won't get the same char, but the flavour will be there.
Best eaten straight off the heat with your flatmates and cold beers.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Enchiladas Verdes
recipe.summary: Corn tortillas filled with chicken and cheese, smothered in green salsa and sour cream, then baked until golden.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 180°C. Pour half the salsa verde into the bottom of a 20×30 cm baking dish.
In a bowl, mix the shredded chicken with 100 g of the tasty cheese and a pinch of salt.
Warm the tortillas briefly (so they don't crack when rolling): hold each one over a gas flame for a few seconds, or wrap them in a clean tea towel and microwave for 30 seconds.
Fill each tortilla with a generous spoonful of the chicken mixture and roll tightly. Lay seam-side down in the baking dish.
In a small bowl, stir the remaining salsa verde with the sour cream until smooth. Pour this mixture over the enchiladas, spreading it evenly.
Scatter the remaining cheese on top and bake for 20–25 minutes, until bubbling at the edges and the cheese is golden.
Let rest for 2 minutes. Top with spring onions and coriander if you like, then serve.

notes: Use a rotisserie chicken from Coles if you don't have cooked chicken on hand, shred the meat, skip the skin.
Salsa verde comes in jars in most supermarkets (Coles has it). If you can't find it, blend canned green tomatoes (tomatillos) with a jalapeño, coriander, and lime juice.
Make ahead: assemble the dish, cover with foil, and refrigerate up to 24 hours. Bake for an extra 5 minutes if cooking from cold.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

recipe.title: Tortellini in Brodo
recipe.summary: Hand-folded tortellini in clear broth, a Sunday project with a pork and cheese filling.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
1 l good chicken stock (or beef stock)

steps.text: Make the pasta: mound flour on a bench, crack eggs into centre, add a pinch of salt. Work with a fork until shaggy, then knead by hand for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Wrap and rest 30 minutes.

Make the filling: fry pork mince in a pan over medium heat, breaking it up, until it loses its colour, about 5 minutes. Cool completely, then mix with ham, parmesan, breadcrumbs, egg yolk, nutmeg, salt and pepper. Taste and adjust.

Roll the pasta: divide dough into 4 pieces. Working with one at a time (keep others covered), roll very thin on a lightly floured surface, thin enough to read through. Using a 5 cm cutter or glass, cut circles.

Fill and fold: place ½ tsp filling slightly off-centre on each circle. Fold in half to make a half-moon, press edges firmly. Bring the two points of the half-moon together to seal into a ring. Place on a tray lined with baking paper, well spaced. Repeat until done.
Chill the tortellini on the tray, uncovered, for at least 30 minutes (or up to 4 hours before cooking).

Bring stock to a steady simmer in a large pot. Carefully drop in tortellini, a few at a time so the broth stays moving. They'll sink, then float to the surface; simmer for 2–3 minutes after they float.
Serve in bowls with hot broth, grated parmesan, a crack of black pepper, and parsley if you like.

notes: Make the filling and dough a day ahead; chill separately. Roll and fold the morning of, then chill on the tray.
Freeze uncooked tortellini on a tray, then transfer to a freezer bag. Cook from frozen, adding 1–2 minutes to the simmer time.
The filling should taste bold, it seasons the broth. Don't be shy with salt, pepper, and nutmeg.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Gyutan
recipe.summary: Grilled sliced beef tongue with salt and lemon, izakaya-style.

items.raw: 300 g beef tongue, thinly sliced (about 3 mm)

steps.text: Bring the beef tongue to room temperature, about 10 minutes, while you heat a frying pan over high heat until it's very hot.
Add the oil to the pan. Once smoking, add the beef tongue slices in a single layer. Don't stir; let them sit for 1 to 2 minutes until lightly charred underneath.
Flip and cook for another 1 to 2 minutes on the second side. The meat should be just cooked through, still tender.
Transfer to a plate. Season generously with salt while the meat is still hot.
Serve with lemon wedges. Squeeze over each bite.

notes: Beef tongue keeps well raw for 2 days in the fridge, wrapped. Ask your butcher to slice it thin on the deli slicer, or freeze for an hour and slice yourself with a sharp knife.
Cooked tongue is best eaten fresh, but any leftovers are good cold the next day.
Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done.

recipe.title: Canh Chua Cá
recipe.summary: Sour soup with white fish, pineapple and okra, bright and tangy with herbs.

items.raw: 500 g white fish fillet (barramundi or snapper), cut into large chunks
200 g fresh pineapple, cut into chunks

steps.text: Bring the stock to a gentle simmer in a large pot. Stir in the tamarind paste, fish sauce and sugar until the paste dissolves and everything is combined.
Add the pineapple and okra, and simmer for 5 minutes until the okra is just tender.
Gently slide the fish pieces into the broth. Simmer for 3–4 minutes until the fish is cooked through and opaque.
Add the tomato wedges and chilli, if using, and warm through for 1 minute.
Divide the soup among bowls and scatter with dill, coriander and mint before serving.

notes: If you can't find fresh tamarind paste, use 1½ tbsp tamarind concentrate or 2 tbsp lime juice for a lighter sour note.
The herbs are not optional, they're what makes it sing. Vietnamese mint (laksa leaf) is traditional, but use whatever fresh herbs you have.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Fafda-Jalebi
recipe.summary: Fried gram flour noodles and crispy vegetables with sweet jalebi and garlic chutney.

items.raw: 2 tbsp water (or more to reach piping consistency)
items.note: or more to reach piping consistency

items.raw: 2 tbsp neutral oil, plus 1 litre for deep frying

steps.text: Make the jalebi syrup first: In a heavy-bottomed saucepan, combine the caster sugar and 300 ml water. Bring to a boil, stirring until the sugar dissolves completely. Add the lemon juice and crushed cardamom pods. If using saffron, crumble it into the syrup. Simmer for 10 minutes until the syrup thickens slightly and coats the back of a spoon. Set aside to cool completely.

Make the jalebi batter: In a bowl, whisk together the plain flour and bicarbonate of soda. Add the yoghurt and water, stirring until you have a smooth, lump-free batter with a consistency like double cream, thin enough to flow through a piping bag, but not watery. If using saffron, crumble it into the batter. Stir in the 2 tbsp of neutral oil. Set aside for 15 minutes to rest.
Make the garlic chutney: Blend all the ingredients together in a food processor or with a mortar and pestle until you reach a smooth paste. Transfer to a small bowl and set aside.

Make the fafda batter: In a large bowl, whisk together the gram flour, yoghurt, salt, turmeric and cumin. Add the chopped green chilli. Gradually add the 200 ml water, stirring until you have a thick, smooth batter, it should be slightly thicker than the jalebi batter, dropping slowly from a spoon. Gently fold in the carrot, peas and red onion. Let the batter rest for 10 minutes.

Heat the 1 litre of neutral oil in a heavy-bottomed, deep saucepan or wok to 170°C. You can check the temperature with a thermometer; if you don't have one, a small piece of batter should sizzle gently and brown in about 60 seconds.

Fry the jalebi: Transfer the jalebi batter to a piping bag fitted with a thin nozzle (about 5 mm). Carefully squeeze the batter into the hot oil in spiral shapes, starting from the centre and spiralling outward, making each jalebi about 5 cm across. Fry 3–4 at a time so they don't touch. Fry for about 90 seconds until deep golden and crisp, then turn gently and fry the other side for another 30–45 seconds. Remove with a slotted spoon and immediately place in the cool jalebi syrup. Repeat until all the batter is used. Set the jalebi aside in the syrup.

Fry the fafda: Once the oil returns to 170°C, carefully lower a fafda mould (or use a kitchen spoon or ladle) into the oil if you have one. Alternatively, use your hands or two spoons to shape the batter into loose, irregular nests about 10 cm across, don't make them perfectly compact; fafda should be airy and crispy. Fry 2–3 at a time for 3–4 minutes, turning halfway, until golden and crispy all over. The edges should be lacy and crackly. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towel.
Serve the fafda warm with a jalebi on the side, a spoonful of garlic chutney, and a small bowl of the syrup for dipping.

notes: Make the jalebi syrup and batter the day before if you like, this takes the stress out of frying day. Keep both in airtight containers at room temperature.
The garlic chutney keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days.
Fafda is best eaten warm and fresh, but jalebi will keep in the syrup for up to 2 days.

recipe.title: Boerewors with Pap
recipe.summary: Homemade spiced sausage grilled over open flame, served with creamy maize porridge.

items.raw: 120 ml full-cream milk (optional, for creamy pap)

steps.text: Toast the coriander seeds, cumin seeds, peppercorns and cloves in a dry pan over medium heat for 2 minutes until fragrant, then grind to a coarse powder.
Place the pork mince, pork belly, ground spices, garlic, salt, ginger and turmeric in a bowl. Mix gently but thoroughly, then add the ice water and mix again. Keep everything cold while you work.

Soak the sausage casings in warm water for 15 minutes. Fit a casing onto a sausage maker, leaving a 5 cm tail. Fill slowly and evenly, twisting into 10 cm lengths. Prick any air pockets with a needle. Refrigerate until ready to grill.

For the pap: bring water or stock to the boil in a large pot. Slowly whisk in the maize meal, stirring constantly to avoid lumps. Reduce heat to low and stir often for 10–12 minutes until thick and creamy.
Stir in salt and butter. If you like it creamier, add the milk at the end and stir until smooth. Keep warm on the stove.
Heat your braai or barbecue to medium-high. Grill the boerewors for 12–15 minutes, turning regularly, until cooked through (internal temperature 75°C) and golden brown with a few charred spots.
Rest the wors for 2 minutes, then serve over the hot pap with lemon wedges and hot sauce on the side.

notes: Make the wors up to 2 days ahead and store in the fridge. They freeze beautifully too.
If you don't have natural casings, make pattie wors instead: shape the mixture into thick patties and braai or pan-fry them.
Pap reheats well, if it thickens too much overnight, loosen it with a splash of water or milk on the stove.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Eggplant with Garlic and Doubanjiang
recipe.summary: Soft eggplant in a savory-spicy doubanjiang sauce, a quiet Sichuan classic that needs no meat.

items.raw: 600 g eggplant, cut into 4 cm pieces
2 spring onions, white and green parts separated, sliced
items.prep: white and green parts separated, sliced

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp of neutral oil in a large wok or wide pan over high heat until shimmering. Working in two batches, fry the eggplant pieces, turning occasionally, until golden and softened, about 8 minutes per batch. Transfer to a plate.
Add the remaining 1 tbsp oil to the pan. Lower the heat to medium and add the minced garlic, stirring for about 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the doubanjiang, breaking it up with the back of your spatula, and cook for 1 minute until the paste darkens slightly and releases its aroma.

Return all the eggplant to the pan. Add the soy sauce, sugar, white pepper, and water, stirring gently to coat the eggplant evenly. Cook for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce has reduced and clings to the pieces.
Turn off the heat. Stir in the white parts of the spring onions and the sesame oil. Scatter the green parts over the top and serve immediately with rice.
