Resist the urge to stir; instead, tilt the pan gently so the unmelted sugar slides into the liquid. When all the sugar has dissolved and turned a deep amber, about 8 minutes, remove from heat. It should smell like caramel, nutty and rich.
Working quickly, dot the 60 g butter over the caramel in small pieces. Stir in the vanilla extract.

Arrange the apple halves cut-side up in concentric circles, starting at the outside and working towards the centre. They will fit snugly and overlap slightly. The apples will release their juice and seem to fill the pan; this is normal.
Return the pan to medium heat and cook, without stirring, for 15 minutes. The apples will soften and the caramel will darken further. Tilt the pan occasionally to ensure even cooking.
Roll out the puff pastry to a circle slightly larger than the pan. Lay it over the apples, tucking the edges down inside the pan. If the handle is not ovenproof, wrap it in foil.
Bake for 20 to 25 minutes, until the pastry is golden and puffed. The edges will brown before the centre, this is fine.

Remove from the oven and let rest for 5 minutes. Place a serving plate over the pan, then quickly and confidently invert the tart onto the plate. If any apples stick, gently replace them. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: Tarte tatin is best served warm or at room temperature on the day it is made, though it can be gently reheated. Once cooked, do not refrigerate, the pastry will lose its crispness.
The apples can be prepared an hour ahead; keep them in a bowl of lemon water to prevent browning, then pat dry before arranging in the pan.
If your pan handle is not ovenproof, wrap it in foil before the tart goes into the oven.

recipe.title: Pappardelle al Ragù di Maiale
recipe.summary: Wide ribbon pasta with slow-cooked wild boar ragù, rustic Tuscan comfort.

items.raw: 600 g pork shoulder, cut into rough chunks
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the pork on all sides, don't crowd the pan. Set aside, about 10 minutes total.
Lower the heat to medium. Add the carrot, celery and onion to the same pot and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 12 minutes. This is your soffritto; don't skip it.
Return the pork to the pot. Pour in the wine and let it bubble away, scraping up the brown bits, about 2 minutes. Add the tomatoes, stock and bay leaves. Stir.
Bring to a gentle simmer. Partially cover and cook for 3 hours, stirring occasionally. The ragù is done when the meat falls apart and the sauce is thick and dark. Season with salt and pepper.
Twenty minutes before serving, bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Cook the pappardelle until al dente, about 3 minutes for fresh pasta. Reserve a cup of pasta water.
Drain the pappardelle and add directly to the ragù. Toss, adding pasta water a splash at a time until the sauce coats the ribbon. Serve with grated Parmesan.

notes: Make the ragù the day before and reheat gently. It improves overnight.
If you can't find pork shoulder, beef chuck works just as well.
Cook pork until it reaches at least 70°C in the thickest part (75°C for mince and sausages).
Food safety:

recipe.title: Mì Vàng Xào Mềm
recipe.summary: Soft egg noodles stir-fried with chicken and aromatics, ready in 30 minutes.

items.raw: 2 spring onions, cut into 4 cm pieces
150 g choy sum, cut into 5 cm lengths

steps.text: Bring a large pot of water to the boil. Add the egg noodles and cook for 2 minutes until just softened but still a little firm, they'll cook a bit more in the pan. Drain well in a colander.
Heat 1 tbsp of the neutral oil in a large wok or frying pan over high heat. Add the chicken and cook, stirring, for 4 to 5 minutes until cooked through. Transfer to a plate.

Add the remaining oil to the pan. Add the garlic and cook, stirring, for 30 seconds until fragrant. Add the spring onions and choy sum, and stir-fry for 2 minutes until the choy sum is tender and bright.

Return the chicken to the pan. Add the cooked noodles, soy sauce, oyster sauce and sesame oil. Toss everything together, stirring gently but constantly, for 2 minutes until heated through and well mixed. Taste and adjust the seasoning with salt and white pepper.
Divide between bowls and top with fried shallots if you like.

notes: Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

title: Pasta con Broccoli, Aglio e Peperoncino

recipe.title: Pasta con Broccoli, Aglio e Peperoncino
recipe.summary: Calabrian pasta with crispy broccoli, garlic and chilli

items.raw: 1 red chilli, thinly sliced (or 1 tsp chilli flakes)

steps.text: Heat a large frying pan over high heat without any oil. Add the broccoli and toss it around for 5–6 minutes, stirring often, until the florets are brown and crispy on the edges and tender inside. Tip onto a plate.
In the same frying pan, warm the olive oil over low-to-medium heat. Add the sliced garlic and chilli, stirring gently for 1–2 minutes until fragrant but not brown. The oil will flavour as it warms.
While the oil and garlic warm, bring a pot of salted water to a boil and cook the pasta until just al dente, about 10–12 minutes.
Drain the pasta, reserving a cup of the cooking water. Add the hot pasta to the frying pan with the garlic oil, tossing gently to coat. Add the crispy broccoli back in and toss again.
If it looks dry, splash in a splash of the pasta water to loosen it, you want it silky, not oily. Taste and add more salt and chilli if you like. Serve straightaway.

notes: This is best eaten fresh, the moment it comes off the stove, the broccoli stays crispest that way.
If you don't like chilli heat, leave it out or just use half a slice. It's your table.

recipe.title: Rasam
recipe.summary: Peppery tamarind and tomato soup, quick and warming, a Tamil dinner staple.

items.raw: 1 dried red chilli, broken in half

steps.text: Dry-roast the cumin seeds, black peppercorns and dried red chillies in a small pan over medium heat for 2–3 minutes, stirring, until fragrant. Grind to a fine powder in a spice grinder or mortar and pestle.

Bring the stock to a boil in a large pot. Add the chopped tomatoes, tamarind paste, ground spices and turmeric. Simmer for 8–10 minutes until the tomatoes are soft and the flavours meld. Taste and adjust the salt.

While the rasam simmers, heat the oil in a small pan over medium heat. Add the mustard seeds and let them crackle (about 30 seconds). Add the broken chilli and curry leaves, and fry for another minute until the curry leaves darken slightly.
Pour the tempering into the pot of rasam, stir through, and serve hot with rice, dosa or a simple bread. A sprig of fresh coriander on top is nice, if you have it.

notes: If you don't have tamarind paste, use ½ tsp tamarind concentrate or a squeeze of lemon juice, adjust to taste.
Rasam keeps well in the fridge for 2–3 days. Reheat gently on the stove; make the tempering fresh each time for maximum crackle.

recipe.title: Ojingeo Bokkeum
recipe.summary: Spicy stir-fried squid with gochugaru, garlic and sesame, a banchan that keeps all week.

items.raw: 500 g calamari, cleaned, cut into thin rings and 5 cm pieces
items.prep: cleaned, cut into thin rings and 5 cm pieces

items.raw: 1 spring onion, white and green parts separated, sliced
items.prep: white and green parts separated, sliced

steps.text: Blanch the calamari in boiling water for 1 minute, then drain and set aside, this stops it toughening when you stir-fry it.
Heat the sesame oil in a large pan or wok over medium-high heat. Add the garlic and fry, stirring, for about 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the gochugaru and stir for another 30 seconds to bloom the spice. Pour in the soy sauce and sugar.
Add the calamari and the white parts of the spring onion. Stir-fry for 2–3 minutes until everything is coated and heated through. Don't overcook or the squid will be rubbery.
Remove from heat. Fold through the green parts of the spring onion and sprinkle with sesame seeds.
Let it cool to room temperature, then transfer to a clean jar. It keeps covered in the fridge for 5 days.

notes: Make a double batch on Sunday: divide into two jars and it lasts the week. The flavour deepens after day two.
Serve cold or at room temperature with white rice and other banchan.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

recipe.title: Apple and Cider Pork Braise
recipe.summary: Pork shoulder slow-cooked with cider, Tasmanian apples and thyme until it falls apart.

items.raw: 1.5 kg pork shoulder, skin and excess fat trimmed, cut into 5 cm chunks
items.prep: skin and excess fat trimmed, cut into 5 cm chunks

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
3 sprigs fresh thyme (or 1 tsp dried thyme)
4 medium Tasmanian apples, peeled, cored and quartered

steps.text: Heat the oven to 160°C. Pat the pork dry and season generously with salt and pepper.

Heat the oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the pork for 2–3 minutes on each side, then set aside on a plate. Don't crowd the pan, you're looking for a good golden colour, not steam.

In the same pot, cook the onions and garlic until the onions soften and just begin to colour, about 5 minutes. Pour in the cider, scraping up the browned bits at the bottom, and let it bubble for a minute.
Return the pork to the pot, add the stock, thyme and bay leaves. Bring to a simmer, then cover and transfer to the oven for 2 hours, stirring occasionally.
Add the apples and stir through. Return to the oven, uncovered, for another 30 minutes, until the pork is very tender and the apples have softened into the sauce.
Taste and adjust the seasoning. If you like, stir through the honey for a little sweetness. Serve with crusty bread or mashed potato.

notes: Make this a day ahead and reheat gently; the flavours deepen overnight. Serve with mashed potato, crusty bread or steamed greens.
A dry Tasmanian apple cider works best, but you can use any dry cider. If you only have sweet cider on hand, reduce the honey.
Leftovers keep in the fridge for up to 4 days and freeze well for a month.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part.

title: Blistered Shishito Peppers with Sesame and Fish Sauce

recipe.title: Blistered Shishito Peppers with Sesame and Fish Sauce
recipe.summary: Quick pan-charred peppers with a Southeast Asian dressing of fish sauce and toasted sesame.

steps.text: Heat the neutral oil in a large pan over high heat until it's shimmering. Working in batches if needed, add the shishito peppers and let them sit undisturbed for 1 to 2 minutes until the skin blisters and blackens in spots.
Toss the peppers and cook for another minute or two, shaking the pan occasionally, until they're soft and blistered all over. Transfer to a serving bowl.
While the peppers are still hot, whisk together the sesame oil, fish sauce, lime juice and caster sugar. Pour over the warm peppers and toss gently to coat.
Taste and add a pinch of salt if needed. Scatter the toasted sesame seeds over the top and serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: If you can't find shishitos, long green chillies work fine, just halve them lengthways so they cook through faster.
Make the dressing ahead of time if you like, but toss the peppers while they're still hot so they soak up the flavours.

recipe.title: Moi Moi
recipe.summary: Steamed bean pudding with hard-boiled eggs tucked inside, served warm with bread or rice

steps.text: Boil the 2 eggs for 8 minutes until just hard-boiled, then peel and set aside.

In a blender, combine the drained black-eyed peas, red onion, red chillies, garlic, raw egg, oil, ginger, salt and pepper. Blend until completely smooth, 2–3 minutes; the batter should be light and silky.
Lightly oil four small ramekins (about 200 ml each) or line four coffee cups with plastic wrap.
Divide one-third of the batter among the ramekins. Place a hard-boiled egg in the centre of each, then top with the remaining batter until each ramekin is three-quarters full.
Pour water into a large pot to a depth of 3 cm. Place a trivet or heat-proof saucer in the bottom. Bring to a boil until the water is bubbling steadily and steam is rising.

Carefully place the ramekins on the trivet. Cover the pot with a lid and steam over medium heat for 40 minutes, until the moi moi is set and springs back when lightly touched. Refill the water if it falls below the level of the trivet.
Remove from the pot and let rest for 5 minutes. Run a knife around the edge of each ramekin and turn out onto a plate (if using ramekins) or unwrap carefully. Serve warm with bread or rice.

notes: Make ahead: Prepare the batter up to 4 hours before steaming and keep chilled. Assemble and steam when ready.
Banana leaves: If you have fresh or frozen banana leaves, wrap each portion in a leaf before steaming for that authentic texture.
This uses raw or lightly cooked egg. Use fresh, clean, uncracked eggs (pasteurised if you can get them), keep it cold, and skip it for anyone pregnant, very young, elderly or with low immunity.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Spiced Potato Roti Filling
recipe.summary: Mashed potatoes with cumin and green chilli for stuffing roti, a weeknight Indo-Fijian favourite.

items.raw: 800 g floury potato, peeled and cut into chunks
Freshly ground black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Boil the potato in salted water until tender, about 15 minutes. Drain well.
While the potato cooks, heat the oil in a large pan over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and let them crackle for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the diced onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the chopped green chillies and cook for another minute, until fragrant and the chillies have softened slightly.
Tip the hot potato into the pan and mash gently with the back of a wooden spoon, breaking it into floury pieces rather than a smooth paste. The potato should be chunky and still slightly warm.
Mix in the salt and pepper to taste. Set aside to cool slightly before using to fill roti.

notes: Make the filling up to 3 hours ahead and reheat gently before using. It's best warm but not piping hot when you wrap it.
Use waxy potato if floury is hard to find, it'll be a bit stickier but still work fine.

recipe.title: Grilled Octopus with Charred Lemon
recipe.summary: Tender grilled octopus with charred lemon, olive oil and oregano

items.raw: 1 kg whole octopus, fresh or thawed
1 tbsp fresh oregano, leaves (or 1 tsp dried oregano)
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil. Add the octopus, onion and bay leaves. Simmer gently for 45–60 minutes, until the octopus is tender, a fork should pierce it easily. Drain and let cool slightly.
Cut the octopus in half lengthwise, then cut each half into 4 or 5 pieces. Pat dry with paper towel.
Heat your grill to high until very hot and smoking lightly. Brush the octopus pieces with a little olive oil and season with salt and pepper.
Grill the octopus for 3–4 minutes each side until charred and crispy on the outside. Transfer to a plate.
Place the lemon halves cut-side down on the grill and char for 2–3 minutes until dark and caramelised.
Arrange the octopus on a serving platter. Drizzle generously with olive oil, scatter with oregano, squeeze the charred lemon juice over everything and season with more salt and pepper. Serve warm.

notes: You can prep the octopus the day before: boil it, cool, cut it, and store it in the fridge. Grill it fresh on the day.
Charring the lemon is crucial, don't skip it. The bitterness and colour make the dish.
If you can't find whole fresh octopus, use frozen. Thaw it overnight in the fridge first.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

recipe.title: Egg White Soup with Crab
recipe.summary: Silken egg white ribbons in delicate crab and chicken broth.

items.raw: 200 g crab meat, fresh or tinned, drained
2 tsp cornstarch, mixed with 3 tbsp water
2 spring onions, green parts only, finely sliced (optional)

steps.text: Bring the chicken stock to a gentle boil in a large saucepan over medium-high heat. Add the crab meat and simmer for 2 minutes, stirring gently, until the crab has warmed through.

In a small bowl, beat the egg whites lightly with a fork until just combined and slightly foamy. Pour the beaten egg white in a thin, steady stream into the simmering broth while stirring gently in one direction with a wooden spoon. The egg white will form delicate, silken ribbons as it cooks, about 1–2 minutes. Don't stir aggressively or the ribbons will break into small pieces.
Give the cornstarch slurry a quick stir and pour it slowly into the soup while stirring gently. The broth should thicken slightly and become translucent, about 1 minute.
Taste and season with salt and white pepper. Stir in the sesame oil.
Pour into serving bowls and scatter the spring onion greens on top, if using. Serve immediately while the soup is hot.

notes: Use sashimi-grade or very fresh crab meat if available; tinned crab in brine works too.
White pepper, not black, keeps the soup's refined appearance, no dark specks.
Don't let the broth boil hard when pouring the egg white, or it will scramble into lumps instead of forming ribbons.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

recipe.title: Smørrebrød med roastbeef og remoulade
recipe.summary: Classic Danish open sandwich with roast beef, sharp remoulade, crispy onions and pickled cucumber on dark rye.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
150 g good-quality roast beef, thinly sliced

steps.text: Make the remoulade: whisk together mayonnaise, Dijon mustard and wholegrain mustard until smooth. Fold in the capers and pickled gherkin. Add lemon juice and season with salt and pepper. Taste and adjust the mustard or lemon if needed.
Lightly butter each slice of bread, spreading it all the way to the edges.
Lay the roast beef slices on top of the butter in a slightly overlapping layer, until the bread is fully covered and the beef is soft and draped.
Spoon remoulade generously over the beef.
Top with pickled cucumber slices and a handful of crispy fried onions.
Garnish with a small sprig of fresh parsley and serve immediately.

notes: Make the remoulade up to 3 days ahead and keep it in the fridge.
Use really good-quality roast beef sliced thin from the deli counter, it makes all the difference.
Assemble the smørrebrød just before serving so the bread stays crisp and the onions don't soften too much.
Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done.

title: Sweet Potato and Kale Sheet Pan with Tahini Drizzle

recipe.title: Sweet Potato and Kale Sheet Pan with Tahini Drizzle
recipe.summary: Roasted sweet potato wedges and massaged kale with tahini, garlic and lemon dressing.

items.raw: 700 g sweet potato, cut into thick wedges

steps.text: Heat oven to 220°C. Toss the sweet potato wedges with 2 tbsp oil, salt and pepper. Spread on a large sheet pan and roast for 15 minutes until starting to soften and colour.
While the sweet potato cooks, whisk together tahini, minced garlic, lemon juice and 1 tbsp oil in a bowl with 3 tbsp water until smooth and pourable. Season with salt and pepper.

Toss the kale with a pinch of salt and massage with your hands for 1 minute until it softens slightly. Push the kale to the sides of the pan, then add it to the sweet potato. Toss everything together.
Roast for another 5 minutes until the kale is tender and the sweet potato is golden and crispy at the edges.
Divide between bowls and drizzle with the tahini dressing. Serve hot.

recipe.title: Gotamba
recipe.summary: Sweet crispy fried dough with banana and jaggery, a Sri Lankan street breakfast.

items.raw: 60 ml neutral oil, plus extra for frying

steps.text: Mix flour and salt in a bowl. Add 60 ml oil and rub between your fingers until the mixture is crumbly, about 2 minutes. Add warm water a little at a time, mixing with your hand until you have a soft, sticky dough. Knead gently for 1 minute and set aside to rest for 5 minutes.
Divide the dough into 2 portions. On a lightly oiled surface, stretch and flatten each portion into a thin rectangle, about 3 mm thick.

Scatter half the banana slices over each rectangle, then sprinkle with jaggery. Roll up tightly from one end, then coil the roll back on itself to make a tight spiral. Flatten slightly with the heel of your hand to about 1 cm thick.
Heat 2–3 cm neutral oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers, about 3 minutes. When a small piece of dough sizzles immediately, it's ready.

Carefully slide one gotamba into the oil. Fry for 3–4 minutes until golden and crispy, then flip. Fry the other side for another 2–3 minutes until deep golden brown. The jaggery will caramelize and stick to the dough.
Transfer to a plate lined with paper towel. Repeat with the second gotamba.
Serve while still warm and crispy, within a few minutes of frying.

notes: Best eaten hot and crispy. If making ahead, you can prepare the dough and filling the evening before and fry just before serving.
If the oil isn't hot enough, the gotamba will be oily and soggy. Let it come to a proper shimmer before you start frying.

recipe.title: Teh Tarik
recipe.summary: Pulled tea with condensed and evaporated milk, a nostalgic Malaysian mamak-stall favourite.

items.raw: 3 tbsp black tea leaves, or 3 black tea bags

steps.text: Boil the water in a kettle or small saucepan until it reaches a rolling boil with large bubbles.
Place the black tea leaves in a small pot or teapot. Pour the boiling water over the leaves and let steep for 2–3 minutes until the tea is very strong and dark.
Strain the tea into a large jug, leaving behind the leaves (or remove the tea bags).
Pour the condensed milk and evaporated milk into two glasses or cups.
Carefully pour the hot tea into each glass over the milk, stirring well to combine. If you're feeling brave, pour the tea from a height to create the signature foam and mix.
Taste and add a pinch of salt if you like. Serve hot, and drink while the foam is still there.

notes: The 'tarik' (pull) is what creates the signature smooth texture and foam. At home, a careful pour from height into the glass works; the mamak masters pour between two vessels for even more drama.
Use a strong black tea, English Breakfast or Assam works perfectly. The tea needs to be robust enough to stand up to the milk.
Drink it straight away while hot and foamy; it's not the same when it cools down.

recipe.title: Shrimp and Bamboo Shoot Dumplings
recipe.summary: Tender wheat dumplings filled with cooked prawns and bamboo shoots, served with a light soy dipping sauce.

items.raw: 200 g tinned bamboo shoot, drained and finely chopped
2 spring onions, white parts finely chopped

steps.text: Make the dough: combine flour and salt in a large bowl. Slowly add warm water while stirring with chopsticks or a fork until shaggy crumbs form. Knead by hand for 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Cover and rest for at least 20 minutes.
Meanwhile, make the filling: combine cooked prawns, bamboo shoots, spring onions, soy sauce, sesame oil, and ginger in a bowl. Season with salt and white pepper to taste.

Divide dough into 16 equal pieces. Roll each into a ball, then flatten with your palm. Use a rolling pin to roll each into a thin circle about 8 cm across, keeping edges slightly thicker than the centre.
Place 1 tbsp filling in the centre of each wrapper. Fold in half and pinch the edges to seal, then bring the two ends together and press to form a crescent or tortellini shape.
Bring a large pot of water to a boil. Working in batches, add dumplings and stir gently. Once they float, simmer for 2 minutes, then remove with a slotted spoon.
While dumplings cook, mix soy sauce, rice vinegar, and sesame oil in a small bowl. Top with sliced chilli if using.
Serve dumplings with the dipping sauce on the side.

notes: Make the dough up to 2 hours ahead and keep it covered at room temperature.
You can fill and shape the dumplings up to 4 hours ahead; lay them on a floured tray, cover with plastic wrap, and refrigerate.

recipe.title: Tacos al Pastor
recipe.summary: Spit-marinated pork tacos with pineapple and a pantry-made achiote marinade.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
800 g pork shoulder, cut into 2 cm thick slices
250 g fresh pineapple, cut into chunks

steps.text: Make the marinade: combine achiote paste, vinegar, honey, garlic, cumin, cinnamon, cayenne, salt and pepper in a bowl. Stir until smooth.
Add pork slices to the marinade and mix well, making sure each piece is coated. Cover and refrigerate for at least 2 hours (or overnight if you have time).

Heat a large heavy-based frying pan over high heat. Working in batches, cook the marinated pork slices for 3–4 minutes per side until the edges are caramelised and crispy and the pork is cooked through. Transfer to a plate.
In the same pan, cook the pineapple chunks over medium-high heat for 2–3 minutes, stirring, until golden and warmed through.
Shred or chop the cooked pork into bite-sized pieces.
Warm the tortillas in a dry frying pan or directly over a gas flame for about 30 seconds each side.
Assemble tacos: place pork on each tortilla, top with a piece of caramelised pineapple, diced onion and coriander. Serve with lime wedges.

notes: The pork can marinate for up to 24 hours, the longer, the better the flavour.
If you can't find achiote paste, use the annatto seed swap, or swap in 1 tbsp smoked paprika plus ½ tsp ground turmeric for a different but still delicious flavour.
Leftover cooked pork keeps in the fridge for 3 days and makes a great burrito filling.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part.

recipe.title: Sopa de Nopales
recipe.summary: Tender cactus paddle soup with tomato, garlic, and coriander in a light, vegetable-forward broth.

items.raw: 500 g nopales (cactus paddle), cleaned, trimmed and diced (about 2 cm pieces)

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the quartered onion and crushed garlic, cooking gently until softened and fragrant, about 4 minutes.
Add the diced nopales to the pot, stirring to coat in the oil. Cook for 3–4 minutes; the nopales will release a slight mucilage, which is normal and helps thicken the broth.
Pour in the tinned tomatoes and vegetable stock, breaking up the tomatoes gently. Bring to a simmer until the soup is bubbling gently.
Simmer, uncovered, for 15–18 minutes until the nopales are tender and the broth has developed flavour. Taste and season with salt and black pepper.
Ladle into bowls. Serve hot, scattered with fresh coriander and a lime wedge on the side.

notes: Nopales prep: Remove the spines carefully with a sharp knife or peeler, then trim the base. If you can't find fresh nopales, jarred or tinned ones work, just drain and rinse before use, and reduce simmering time to 5–8 minutes.
This soup keeps well in the fridge for 3 days and can be frozen for up to a month.

recipe.title: Makki di roti
recipe.summary: Warm cornmeal flatbread, crumbly and buttery, that even fussy kids will eat when wheat roti gets a no.

items.raw: 2 tbsp ghee (or butter), plus extra for serving

steps.text: Mix the cornmeal, green chilli and salt in a large bowl.
Pour in the warm water slowly, stirring with your fingers until you have a soft, sticky dough that just comes together. It should feel wetter than wheat dough, don't try to knead it smooth.
Heat a cast iron tawa or non-stick frying pan over medium-high heat until a drop of water sizzles and disappears in a second.
Wet your hands with water. Take a golf-ball-sized piece of dough and flatten it between your palms into a rough circle about 5 mm thick. It won't be perfect and it doesn't need to be.
Carefully lay it on the hot tawa and cook for 1 to 2 minutes, until the bottom is pale golden and starting to blister. It will look fragile but it's not.
Flip gently and cook the other side for another 1 to 2 minutes until golden and speckled brown. The roti will stay soft and slightly crumbly.
Transfer to a plate and dot with a tiny bit of ghee or butter. Serve hot, while they're still warm enough to tear easily.

notes: Make these just before serving, they're best eaten warm straight off the tawa.
Pair with sarson da saag, a dollop of yoghurt and sliced onion.

recipe.title: Torshi
recipe.summary: Quick-pickled vegetables, cauliflower, turnips and chillies, the tangy condiment that lives in every Lebanese fridge.

items.raw: 4 small turnips, peeled and cut into thin wedges or batons
items.prep: peeled and cut into thin wedges or batons

items.raw: 3–4 red chillies, halved lengthwise, seeds left in
1 cup white vinegar (or apple cider vinegar)

steps.text: Pack the cauliflower florets, turnip wedges, chillies and smashed garlic into a large sterilised jar, layering them loosely.
In a saucepan, combine the water, vinegar, salt and peppercorns. Bring to a boil, then remove from heat and let cool for 2 minutes.
Pour the hot brine over the vegetables until they are completely submerged. If needed, weigh them down with a smaller jar to keep them under the liquid.
Cover loosely and let cool to room temperature, about 1 hour.
Once cool, seal the jar and refrigerate. The torshu will keep for up to 3 months, and tastes better after a day or two when the flavours have settled.

notes: Make it a day ahead; the flavour deepens as it sits.
Use sterilised jars, run them through the dishwasher on a hot cycle or boil them for 10 minutes.
Serve as a side to mezze, with fresh bread, or alongside grilled vegetables and legumes.

recipe.title: Ika Samoa
recipe.summary: White fish in coconut cream with tomatoes and silverbeet.

items.raw: 600 g white fish fillet, cut into chunks
250 g silverbeet, roughly chopped (stem and leaves separated)
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pan over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic and stir for 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the coconut milk and crushed tomatoes. Stir to combine and bring to a gentle simmer until the sauce is bubbling lightly.
Add the silverbeet stems and cook for 3 minutes. Then add the silverbeet leaves and stir through.
Gently add the fish chunks to the pan, stirring carefully to distribute them evenly. Simmer for 10 to 12 minutes, until the fish is cooked through and flakes easily.
Season with salt and black pepper to taste. Serve hot with rice or taro.

notes: Serve with steamed white rice, taro or fresh soda bread to soak up the coconut broth.
You can use any firm white fish: barramundi, snapper, flathead or basa all work well.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Mentaiko Pasta
recipe.summary: Spaghetti tossed with spicy cod roe, butter and nori.

items.raw: 1 sheet nori, torn into bite-sized pieces

steps.text: Bring a pot of salted water to a boil and cook the spaghetti until al dente, about 9 minutes. Reserve 60 ml of pasta water, then drain.
While the pasta cooks, scoop the mentaiko into a large bowl with the butter.
Add the hot drained pasta to the bowl with the mentaiko and butter. Toss gently, adding pasta water a little at a time, until the roe coats the strands and forms a silky sauce, about 1 minute.
Divide into a bowl, top with nori and spring onion, season with a pinch of salt and pepper, and serve straight away.

recipe.title: Khao Sticky Rice
recipe.summary: Properly steamed glutinous rice, the foundation of every Isaan meal.

steps.text: Rinse the glutinous rice in a sieve under cold running water until the water runs clear, about 30 seconds. Transfer to a bowl.
Cover the rice with 500 ml cold water and leave to soak for at least 8 hours, or overnight.
Drain the rice well in a sieve. Add the 350 ml water to the bamboo steamer basket or the top part of a sticky-rice cooker.
Tip the drained rice into the steamer and stir gently. Steam for 15 minutes, or until the rice is tender and the water is absorbed.

Turn the rice out into a bamboo sticky-rice basket (kratip) lined with a clean damp cloth. Fold the cloth over the top and let it rest for 5 minutes before serving. If you don't have a kratip, wrap the hot rice loosely in a damp cloth for the same effect.

notes: Make ahead: soak the rice overnight, then steam and serve fresh.
Keep the rice warm: wrapped in a damp cloth in the bamboo basket for up to an hour.
No sticky-rice basket? A covered bamboo steamer or any covered pot works fine, just keep it warm and wrapped.

recipe.title: Quandong Pavlova
recipe.summary: Crispy meringue nest topped with whipped cream and tart native quandongs.

items.raw: 250 g quandong, pitted and halved (or whole if small)

steps.text: Preheat oven to 130°C. Line a large baking tray with baking paper.
Whisk egg whites in a clean, dry bowl until stiff peaks form, about 5 minutes. Gradually add caster sugar while whisking until thick and glossy, about 8 minutes.
Fold in vinegar and cornflour gently until just combined.
Spoon the meringue onto the prepared tray in a single large nest shape (about 20 cm across), or make four smaller individual nests. Use the back of a spoon to create a slight well in the centre.
Bake for 90 minutes until crisp and pale. Turn off the oven and let the meringue cool completely in the oven for at least 30 minutes, then transfer to a wire rack.
Just before serving, whip cream with icing sugar until soft peaks form.
Top the meringue nest(es) with whipped cream and scatter quandong halves over. Serve immediately.

notes: The meringue base can be made up to 2 days ahead and kept in an airtight container.
Quandongs are tart stone fruit sourced locally in Central Australia; if unavailable outside the region, use fresh or lightly stewed stone fruit like peaches, nectarines or apricots.
Assemble just before serving so the meringue stays crisp.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Papa a la Huancaína
recipe.summary: Boiled potatoes with silky ají amarillo and cheese sauce, Peru's most iconic potato dish.

items.raw: 200 g queso fresco (fresh cow cheese), crumbled
Boiled egg, hard-boiled and sliced, to serve

steps.text: Cut potatoes into large chunks and place in a pot of cold salted water. Bring to a boil and cook until tender but still holding their shape, about 15–20 minutes. Drain well.

While potatoes cook, make the sauce: in a blender, combine ají amarillo paste, evaporated milk, queso fresco, crushed crackers, garlic, neutral oil and lime juice. Blend until silky and smooth, about 1 minute. Season with salt to taste.
Arrange warm potatoes on a serving plate. Pour the sauce generously over the top.
Garnish with sliced hard-boiled egg, olives and fresh coriander if you like. Serve at room temperature or chilled.

notes: Make ahead: boil potatoes the night before and keep in the fridge. The sauce also keeps for 2 days. Warm gently and serve at room temperature.

If you can't find ají amarillo paste, look for it in the Latin or South American aisle of your supermarket, or online. It's worth seeking out, it has a distinctive mild heat and fruity flavour unique to Peruvian cooking.

recipe.title: Nabak Kimchi
recipe.summary: Summer radish water kimchi: crisp, refreshing and lightly fermented in its own brine.

items.raw: 600 g daikon (white radish), peeled and thinly sliced
4 spring onions, cut into 5 cm lengths

steps.text: Place the sliced daikon in a large bowl. Add 1 tbsp salt and toss gently but thoroughly until every slice is coated. Set a timer: salt the radish for exactly 20 minutes, this is crucial. The radish should release its water and become pliable but still crisp.

While the radish salts, prepare the brine: dissolve 2 tbsp salt in 1 litre of cold water in a separate bowl. Stir in the fish sauce and sugar until dissolved. Taste and adjust the salt if needed, it should taste pleasantly salty, like a good broth.
After 20 minutes, gently rinse the radish under cold running water, pressing softly to remove excess salt and liquid. Drain well in a colander for 2 minutes.
Transfer the drained radish to a clean container or bowl. Add the gochugaru, garlic, ginger and spring onions, tossing gently to combine.
Pour the cold brine over the vegetables until they are just covered. Press a piece of plastic wrap or a small plate onto the surface to keep everything submerged.

Cover and refrigerate for at least 2 hours before serving. The nabak kimchi will taste good cold from the fridge and will keep for up to 2 weeks. The flavour deepens as it ferments; after 3–4 days in the fridge, it develops a gentle fizz and tang.

notes: Nabak kimchi must be served ice-cold. Keep it in the coldest part of your fridge.
The radish salting time is exact: 20 minutes softens it just enough while keeping it crisp. Less time leaves it too raw; more time makes it mushy.
This keeps for up to 2 weeks refrigerated, and actually tastes better after 3–4 days when the brine develops a gentle fizz.

recipe.title: Agedashi Dofu
recipe.summary: Silken tofu dusted and fried golden, swimming in hot dashi with spring onion.

steps.text: Pour the dashi into a small pot. Add soy sauce and mirin, and bring to a simmer over medium heat until small bubbles form at the edge and the mixture is fragrant. Keep it warm.
Cut the chilled tofu into 4 cubes, patting them dry very gently with paper towel, moisture is the enemy of crispness.
Put cornflour in a shallow dish and season lightly with salt. Coat each tofu cube gently on all sides.
Heat a thin layer of neutral oil in a small frying pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers. It should be hot but not smoking.
Carefully place the tofu cubes in the oil and cook for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until the outside is golden and crisp all over.
Divide the hot dashi between two bowls. Gently place two tofu cubes into each bowl.
Top with spring onion and ginger, and serve at once, while the dashi steams and the tofu still has its gentle warmth.

notes: The tofu must be very cold and very dry before frying; buy it as close to cooking time as you can.

recipe.title: Arroz Blanco
recipe.summary: Simple, fluffy white rice with onion and bay leaf, the perfect side for any table.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the rice and stir constantly until it turns pale golden and smells toasted, about 3 minutes.
Add the onion halves and bay leaf, then pour in the chicken stock. Stir once, then bring to a boil until the stock is bubbling steadily.
Once boiling, reduce the heat to low, cover with a tight-fitting lid, and cook without lifting the lid for 15 minutes, until the rice is tender and the liquid is absorbed.
Remove from the heat and let it rest, covered, for 2 minutes. Remove the onion halves and bay leaf, fluff the rice with a fork, season with salt to taste, and serve.

notes: Make it ahead: cook completely and store covered in the fridge for up to 3 days. Reheat gently with a splash of water to loosen the grains.
Swap the chicken stock for vegetable stock if you prefer, or use water in a pinch.

recipe.title: Slow Cooker Oxtail Stew
recipe.summary: Tender oxtail braised with carrots and onions until falling off the bone.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the oxtail pieces on all sides, about 3 minutes per batch. Transfer to your slow cooker.
Add the onions, carrots, and garlic to the same frying pan and cook, stirring, for 5 minutes until softened. Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 1 minute more.
Pour in the red wine, scraping up any browned bits from the pan, then transfer everything to the slow cooker with the oxtail.
Add the beef stock, bay leaves, and thyme. Stir well and season with salt and pepper.
Cover and cook on low for 8 to 9 hours, or until the oxtail is tender and the meat falls easily from the bone.
Discard the bay leaves and thyme sprigs. Skim any excess fat from the surface if needed. Taste and adjust seasoning. Serve hot.

notes: Make it a day ahead. The flavour only gets better sitting in the fridge overnight.
Serve with crusty bread, mash, or over rice to soak up the gravy.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

recipe.title: Lumpiang Shanghai
recipe.summary: Crispy fried spring rolls stuffed with pork, shrimp and veggies, party food that hits different on a weeknight

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp neutral oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. Add the garlic and cook for about 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the pork mince and cook, breaking it apart with a spoon, for about 4 minutes until cooked through. Add the chopped prawns and cook for another 2 minutes.

Stir in the cabbage, carrot, and spring onions. Cook for about 5 minutes, stirring often, until the vegetables are soft and any excess liquid has evaporated. Add soy sauce, oyster sauce, and a pinch of black pepper. Taste and adjust seasoning if needed. Let the filling cool to room temperature, about 10 minutes.

Set up a clean work surface. Place one lumpia wrapper on it in a diamond shape. Put about 2 tbsp of filling on the lower third of the wrapper. Fold the bottom corner up over the filling, then fold in the left and right corners. Roll tightly upwards, then seal the top corner with a little water. Repeat with remaining wrappers and filling.
Fill a wok or large, deep pan with neutral oil to about 5 cm depth. Heat over medium-high until a small piece of wrapper sizzles immediately when dropped in (about 170°C).

Working in batches, carefully lower the lumpia into the hot oil. Fry for about 2 minutes, turning halfway through, until golden brown and crispy. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towels. Serve hot with sweet chilli sauce or vinegar for dipping.

notes: Make ahead: Assemble the lumpia up to 4 hours ahead and refrigerate on a tray before frying. Fry just before serving.
Oil temperature is key, too cool and they'll be greasy; too hot and they'll burn. Use a thermometer or the wrapper test.
Serve with sweet chilli sauce, vinegar, or a quick dipping sauce made from soy sauce and a squeeze of lemon.

Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C. Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

recipe.title: Chongqing Chicken
recipe.summary: Crispy fried chicken buried under dried chilies and Sichuan peppercorns, intense and numbing.

items.raw: 750 g chicken thigh, cut into 2 cm pieces
3 spring onion, cut into 2 cm pieces

steps.text: Toss the chicken with soy sauce, rice wine, cornflour, garlic and ginger. Let sit for 10 minutes.
Heat 250 ml oil in a wok or large frying pan over medium-high heat. Working in batches, fry the chicken until golden and cooked through, about 8 minutes per batch. Drain on paper towel.
Pour off all but 1 tbsp of oil from the wok. Add the dried chilli and Sichuan peppercorn and toast, stirring, for 1 minute until fragrant.
Return the chicken to the wok with the spring onion, salt and white pepper. Toss over medium heat for 2 minutes until everything is coated and hot. Serve at once.

notes: Make ahead: marinate the chicken up to 4 hours. Fry it just before serving so it stays crispy.
The numbing heat comes from Sichuan peppercorn, the burn from dried chilies. Neither are mistakes, they're the point.
Serve with plain steamed rice or congee to cool your mouth between bites.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

recipe.title: Shiro
recipe.summary: Creamy chickpea flour paste with onions and berbere, vegan and deeply satisfying.

items.raw: 2 tbsp niter kibbeh (Ethiopian spiced butter), or neutral oil

steps.text: Heat the niter kibbeh in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the chopped onions and cook, stirring often, until they are soft and golden, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the berbere and cook for 1 minute, stirring constantly, until fragrant.
Whisk the chickpea flour into the water or stock until smooth, breaking up any lumps. Slowly pour this mixture into the pot, stirring constantly to avoid lumps forming.

Reduce the heat to low and simmer, stirring frequently with a wooden spoon, for 20 to 25 minutes. The shiro should thicken gradually and smell sweet and nutty. Keep stirring to prevent it from sticking to the bottom.
Taste and season with salt. The shiro is ready when it is thick, creamy, and pulls away from the sides of the pot slightly as you stir.
Serve warm on injera, or alongside it.

notes: Shiro keeps for 3 days in the fridge. Reheat gently with a splash of water or stock, stirring often.
Shiro is a classic Ethiopian fasting dish: vegan, filling and humble.

recipe.title: Gaeng Panang Gai
recipe.summary: Rich, mild red curry with chicken and peanuts, creamy and comforting in one pan.

steps.text: Heat oil in a wok or wide pan over medium-high heat until shimmering, about 1 minute.
Add curry paste and cook, stirring, for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add chicken and stir-fry until the edges turn opaque, about 3 minutes.
Pour in coconut milk and bring to a simmer, stirring gently, until the sauce is bubbling lightly and thickens slightly.
Add peanut butter, fish sauce and palm sugar. Stir until peanut butter dissolves, about 2 minutes.
Tear in the makrut lime leaf and simmer for 5 minutes until chicken is cooked through (75°C inside) and sauce is thick and glossy.
Taste and adjust fish sauce or palm sugar to balance salty and sweet.
Serve in a bowl with jasmine rice, topped with fresh Thai basil and chilli if using.

notes: Serve over jasmine rice. One batch feeds one person with rice.
Make ahead: the curry keeps in the fridge for 3 days and reheats gently on the stove.
Swap peanut butter for ground peanuts (2 tbsp) stirred in at the end if you prefer texture.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Mì Gà Cốt Dừa
recipe.summary: Silky turmeric chicken noodles in coconut broth, Saigon street food at home.

items.raw: 2 spring onions, cut into 3 cm lengths

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the turmeric and crushed garlic, stirring for 30 seconds until fragrant and the oil turns golden yellow.
Pour in the stock and coconut milk, stirring to combine. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat until the broth is bubbling gently and steaming.
Add the fish sauce and stir. Add the chicken slices and simmer gently for 8–10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the chicken is cooked through.
While the chicken cooks, bring a large pot of water to the boil. Add the noodles and cook according to packet directions until just tender. Drain well.
Divide the noodles between two bowls. Ladle the hot broth and chicken over the top.
Scatter the spring onions over each bowl. Serve with a lime wedge and fresh coriander on the side if you like. Squeeze the lime in before eating.

notes: Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

recipe.title: Gaeng Hang Lay
recipe.summary: Rich mushroom curry in the style of the classic pork belly dish, with layers of spice and tender mushrooms.

items.raw: 3 tbsp red curry paste (or gaeng hang lay paste)
600 g mixed mushrooms, halved or quartered (shiitake, oyster, button)
1 tsp salt, plus more to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot or deep pan over medium heat. Add the curry paste and cook, stirring, for 2 minutes until fragrant.
Add the ginger and garlic, cook for another minute until fragrant, then pour in the coconut milk and stir well to combine.
Add the mushrooms and stir to coat with the curry mixture. Cook for 5 minutes until they start to soften.
Pour in the vegetable stock, tamarind paste and palm sugar. Stir until the sugar and tamarind dissolve, about 2 minutes.

Bring to a gentle simmer and cook uncovered for 25–30 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the mushrooms are very tender and the curry has reduced and darkened. The sauce should coat the back of a spoon.
Taste and adjust salt and sourness if needed. Serve hot with jasmine rice.

notes: Make it ahead: the curry tastes better the next day. Store in the fridge for up to 3 days, or freeze for a month.
Use whatever mushrooms you have, cremini, button, portobello all work. Firmer varieties hold their shape better in the long simmer.

recipe.title: Involtini di Melanzane
recipe.summary: Eggplant rolls filled with breadcrumbs, cheese and herbs, baked in tomato sauce.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Slice the eggplants lengthways into thin strips, about ½ cm thick. Lay them on paper towels, salt generously, and let sit for 15 minutes to draw out moisture; pat dry.
Heat 2 tbsp olive oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Working in batches, fry the eggplant strips until golden on both sides, about 2 minutes per side. Set aside on paper towels.
In a bowl, combine breadcrumbs, parmesan, pine nuts, garlic, parsley, basil, egg, and a good pinch of salt and pepper.
Lay an eggplant strip on the bench. Spoon a tablespoon of filling along one end, then roll tightly. Place seam-side down in a baking dish. Repeat with remaining strips and filling.
Pour crushed tomatoes over the rolls, drizzle with remaining olive oil, and season with salt and pepper.
Bake at 180°C for 35–40 minutes, until the sauce is bubbling and the rolls are heated through.

notes: Make them ahead: assemble the rolls, refrigerate up to 4 hours, then bake as directed.
The eggplants need to lose their water first – salt them well and don't rush this step.
For a vegetarian version, use a vegetarian hard cheese (made without animal rennet).

recipe.title: Karaage
recipe.summary: Japanese fried chicken thighs marinated in soy, ginger and garlic, crispy outside and juicy inside.

items.raw: 800 g chicken thighs, skin-on bone-in, cut into bite-sized pieces
items.prep: skin-on bone-in, cut into bite-sized pieces

steps.text: Combine soy sauce, mirin, garlic, ginger and sesame oil in a bowl. Add the chicken pieces and toss to coat well. Cover and marinate in the fridge for at least 2 hours, preferably overnight.
When ready to cook, remove the chicken from the marinade and place on paper towel. Pat dry thoroughly, this is important for crispiness. Reserve the marinade.
Mix potato starch and plain flour together on a plate. Season the chicken pieces lightly with salt and white pepper, then coat each piece in the starch mixture, shaking off any excess.
Heat neutral oil in a deep-sided pan or wok to 170°C. Working in batches so the pan isn't crowded, carefully lower the chicken into the oil.
Fry for 8 to 10 minutes, turning halfway through, until the coating is golden and the thickest pieces are cooked through (75°C inside). Transfer to a paper towel to drain.
Serve hot with lemon wedges and fresh coriander if you like. Any leftovers keep well cold in a bento box for the next day.

notes: Make ahead: marinate the chicken overnight in the fridge for deeper flavour and better texture.
Leftovers: keeps in an airtight container in the fridge for 3 days; serve cold in bento or reheat gently.
Oil temperature matters: use a thermometer if you have one; too cool and it will be oily, too hot and the outside burns before the inside cooks.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Sambusa
recipe.summary: Crispy triangular pastries with spiced meat filling, a quick snack and gathering staple.

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. Add onion and cook, stirring, until softened and starting to colour, about 4 minutes.
Add garlic and cook for 1 minute. Add beef mince and cook, breaking it apart as it browns, until cooked through, about 5 minutes.
Stir in cardamom, black pepper and salt. Add 2 tbsp water and cook, stirring, until the liquid evaporates, about 2 minutes. Taste and adjust the seasoning. Let cool slightly.
Lay out one filo sheet. Brush lightly with melted butter or oil. Cut it in half lengthwise to make two long strips.

Place about 1 tbsp of filling on one end of a filo strip, just off centre. Fold the corner diagonally to cover the filling and form a triangle. Continue folding along the length of the strip, keeping the triangular shape. Trim any excess pastry. Repeat with remaining sheets and filling.

Heat about 2 cm of oil in a deep frying pan over medium heat. When shimmering, carefully lay in sambuusas a few at a time and fry until golden on the first side, about 2 minutes. Flip and fry the other side until golden, about 1–2 minutes. Do not overcrowd the pan.
Transfer to a plate lined with paper towel and serve warm.

notes: Make the filling up to a day ahead; store in the fridge. Assemble sambuusas up to 2 hours before frying.
If filo dries out as you work, cover the sheets with a damp tea towel.
Freeze uncooked sambuusas on a tray, then transfer to a container. Fry from frozen, adding a minute or two to the cooking time.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

recipe.title: Buttermilk Biscuits
recipe.summary: Tall, flaky biscuits made with cold butter and buttermilk, baked in cast iron until golden.

steps.text: Preheat oven to 200°C. Place a 25 cm cast-iron frying pan in the oven to heat.

Whisk together flour, baking powder and salt in a large bowl. Add the cold butter cubes and use your fingertips to rub the mixture until it resembles coarse breadcrumbs with some pea-sized pieces of butter remaining.
Make a well in the centre and pour in the cold buttermilk. Using a fork, gently mix until a shaggy dough just comes together, don't overwork it or the biscuits will be tough.
Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured bench and gently pat it into a 2 cm thick round. Using a 7 cm biscuit cutter dipped in flour, cut out biscuits, pressing straight down without twisting.
Carefully remove the hot frying pan from the oven and brush lightly with melted butter. Arrange biscuits in the pan, they should just touch each other.
Brush the tops with a little more melted butter. Bake for 12–15 minutes, until golden brown on top and cooked through.
Let cool in the pan for 2 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack. Serve warm.

notes: Biscuits are best served warm from the oven. Leftovers can be split and toasted the next day.
For extra tender biscuits, chill the dough for 15 minutes before cutting and baking.
Make sure your butter and buttermilk are cold, this is what gives the biscuits their flaky layers.

title: Beef and Spring Onion Stir-Fry Rice

recipe.title: Beef and Spring Onion Stir-Fry Rice
recipe.summary: Minced beef with Sichuan peppercorns, spring onion and white pepper over fried rice.

items.raw: 2 cups cooked white rice, cooled (day-old or chilled)
4 spring onion, cut into 3 cm lengths (white and green parts)

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp oil in a large pan over high heat. When it's smoking, add the beef mince and cook, breaking it up with a spoon, until browned and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Stir through the soy sauce, white pepper and Sichuan peppercorn. Transfer to a plate.
Add the remaining oil to the pan over high heat. Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the rice, breaking up any clumps with the back of a spoon. Stir-fry until heated through and the rice grains are separated, about 4 minutes.
Return the beef to the pan. Add the spring onion and toss everything together over the heat for 1 minute until the spring onion just softens. Taste and add salt if needed. Serve immediately.

notes: Use day-old or chilled rice, fresh hot rice gets mushy. If you only have hot rice, spread it on a plate to cool first.
Toast the Sichuan peppercorns in a dry pan for 1 minute before grinding for deeper flavour.
Leftovers keep in the fridge for 2 days and reheat well in a hot pan.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

recipe.title: Maklouba
recipe.summary: Upside-down rice with spiced vegetables and yoghurt, served with a crispy golden layer on top.

items.raw: 2 medium eggplants, cut into 5 mm thick slices
2 medium potatoes, peeled and cut into thin matchsticks
items.prep: peeled and cut into thin matchsticks

items.raw: 1 small cauliflower head, cut into small florets
750 ml chicken stock (or vegetable stock), warm
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Fry the eggplant slices in batches in hot oil until golden on both sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate lined with paper towel. This step is crucial, the eggplant will soften in the steam, so frying it first keeps its shape and flavour.

In the same oil, fry the potato matchsticks in batches until just starting to turn golden, about 3 minutes. You want them still a bit firm because they'll cook further in the rice. Transfer to the paper towel plate.
Fry the cauliflower florets until lightly golden, about 3 minutes. Set aside. You should have about 3 tablespoons of oil left in the pot; if not, add a little more.
In the same pot, cook the sliced onions over medium heat, stirring, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute more until fragrant.

Stir in the cumin, coriander, cardamom and cinnamon, cooking for 1 minute. You'll smell the spices bloom, this is when their flavour becomes most alive. Add the rice and stir to coat it in the spiced oil, cooking for 2 minutes.

Layer the rice mixture back into the pot in this order: half the rice on the bottom, then the eggplant, potato and cauliflower mixed together, then the remaining rice on top. Press down gently to compact the layers. Pour the warm stock over carefully.

Bring to a boil, then reduce heat to low. Cover with foil, then place the lid on top, the foil traps steam, which cooks the rice evenly. Cook for 20 minutes until the rice is tender and the stock is absorbed. Listen: when the liquid stops bubbling, you're done.

Let it rest, covered, for 5 minutes. Run a thin knife around the edges of the pot to loosen it. Place a large platter over the pot, and in one confident motion, flip the pot onto the platter. Lift the pot away slowly. You should see a golden crust on top.
Serve warm with generous dollops of Greek yoghurt and fresh parsley if you like. Eat it while the crust is still crispy.

notes: Maklouba keeps well in the fridge for up to 3 days. Reheat gently in a low oven wrapped in foil, or flash it in a hot pan to recrisp the bottom layer.
Use a non-stick or well-seasoned pot, this makes the flip much less stressful.
The spice blend is forgiving. If you don't have cardamom, add a pinch more cumin. If you don't have cinnamon, leave it out entirely.

recipe.title: Fesenjan
recipe.summary: Pomegranate and walnut stew with chicken, sweet and deep and meant for rice.

items.raw: 1 kg chicken thighs, bone-in and skin-on
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large, heavy pot over medium-high heat. Season the chicken generously with salt and pepper. Working in batches, brown the chicken skin-side down for 5 minutes, then turn and brown the other side for 3 minutes. Set aside.
In the same pot, add the onion halves and cook, stirring occasionally, until they soften and colour, about 8 minutes. Add the tomato paste and cook for 1 minute, stirring.
Stir in the walnuts, cinnamon and turmeric. Cook for 2 minutes until fragrant.

Pour in the pomegranate juice and pomegranate molasses, scraping up any brown bits from the bottom of the pot. Return the chicken to the pot, skin-side up. Bring to a simmer until the sauce is bubbling gently and starting to thicken.

Cover and cook on low heat for 50–60 minutes, until the chicken is tender and cooked through and the sauce has deepened in colour and thickened slightly. Taste and adjust the salt, pepper, and balance of sweet and sour as needed.
Remove the onion halves. Serve over rice, with fresh coriander if you like it.

notes: Fesenjan tastes better the next day. Make it ahead and reheat gently.
If you can't find pomegranate molasses, use equal parts pomegranate juice and lemon juice reduced in a pan until syrupy, or use a mix of pomegranate juice and balsamic vinegar.
Serve with tahdig, rice cooked until the bottom catches and caramelizes in a thin, crispy layer.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

recipe.title: Seafood Jambalaya
recipe.summary: Shrimp, crab, and oysters stirred into rice with sausage, peppers, and Cajun spices all in one pot.

items.raw: 300 g andouille sausage, sliced into coins
200 g raw prawn, peeled and deveined
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the flour and stir constantly for 8 to 10 minutes, until the roux is deep golden brown, this is the foundation of everything. Don't rush it; if it starts to burn, pull it off the heat for a moment.
Add the onion, capsicum, and celery to the roux. Stir well and cook for about 5 minutes, until the vegetables soften and release their flavour. This is the holy trinity, cher.
Push the vegetables to the side, add the sausage, and let it sear for 2 to 3 minutes. Stir in the garlic, cayenne, paprika, thyme, and oregano, cooking for 1 more minute until fragrant.

Pour in the crushed tomatoes and chicken stock. Scrape the bottom of the pot to loosen any browned bits. Bring to a gentle boil until bubbling, then reduce the heat to medium-low. Stir in the rice, making sure it's covered by liquid.
Simmer, stirring occasionally, for about 20 minutes, until the rice is nearly tender and most of the liquid is absorbed.
Gently fold in the prawns, crab, and oysters (if using). Cook for 3 to 4 minutes, until the prawns are pink and cooked through and the oysters have just firmed up.
Season to taste with salt and pepper. Serve hot, scattered with fresh parsley if you like.

notes: Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

recipe.title: Uttapam
recipe.summary: Thick savoury pancake topped with onion and tomato, made from dosa batter in minutes.

steps.text: Heat a non-stick griddle or heavy-bottomed pan over medium heat and lightly oil it.
Pour 1/4 cup of batter onto the griddle and gently spread into a thick round, about 8 cm across. Don't thin it out like a dosa, keep it thick and spongy.
Let it cook, undisturbed, for about 2 minutes until the bottom is golden and set.
Sprinkle a small handful of chopped onion, tomato, green chilli and coriander (if using) over the top. Press gently into the batter.
Flip carefully and cook the other side for another 2 minutes until golden. If the top toppings aren't cooked enough, cover the pan with a lid for 30 seconds.
Transfer to a plate and repeat with the remaining batter and toppings.
Serve hot with sambar, rasam or fresh coconut chutney.

notes: Make sure your dosa batter is at room temperature; cold batter won't spread and cook evenly.
If your batter is too thick, add a splash of water, it should be pourable but thicker than a dosa batter.
Uttapam keeps for a day in an airtight container and reheats well in a toaster or griddle.

recipe.title: Suya
recipe.summary: Grilled seasoned beef skewers coated in spiced peanut powder.

items.raw: 600 g beef sirloin, cut into 2 cm cubes

steps.text: Thread the beef cubes onto skewers, packing them tightly together. Rub with oil, salt, black pepper and ground ginger.

Pulse the roasted peanuts in a food processor until they're finely ground but still have some texture, not a smooth butter. Tip into a shallow bowl and stir through the cayenne, paprika, ground ginger, salt, black pepper and garlic.

Heat a griddle, grill or large frying pan over high heat until very hot. Working in batches, sear the skewers for 3 to 4 minutes, turning to cook all sides until the beef is deeply browned and cooked through (the meat should reach 75°C inside).
Immediately after cooking, while still hot, roll each skewer in the suya spice mixture until generously coated on all sides.
Serve hot, straight away.

notes: Soak wooden skewers in water for 30 minutes before threading if using them instead of metal ones.
Make the suya spice ahead and store in an airtight container for up to two weeks.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Potjiekos
recipe.summary: One-pot stew of meat, potatoes and veg cooked low and slow in cast iron on the braai.

items.raw: 800 g beef chuck, cut into 3 cm cubes
600 g waxy potato, cut into chunks
1 large brown onion, cut into thick wedges
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Place a 7-litre cast iron potjie (or large heavy-based pot) over medium coals on the braai. Heat the oil until shimmering, then add the beef in batches. Brown on all sides, about 8 minutes per batch, then remove and set aside.
Reduce the heat to low coals (move the pot away from the hottest part of the braai). Add the onion to the pot and cook, stirring, for 3 minutes until slightly softened.
Add the browned beef back to the pot, then layer in the carrots and potatoes. Sprinkle with garlic and thyme, then season with salt and pepper.

Pour the beef stock over everything. Cover with the lid and let it cook on low heat for about 1 hour, until the potatoes and beef are almost tender. Resist lifting the lid too often, you want to keep the heat in.
Add the cabbage wedges, nestling them into the liquid. Replace the lid and cook for another 20 minutes until the cabbage is tender and the beef is cooked through.
Taste and adjust the seasoning. Serve straight from the pot, family-style, with crusty bread to soak up the liquid.

notes: A potjie needs at least 45 minutes on low, steady heat. If your braai is too hot, move the pot to the edge and add less frequent wood.
You can prep all the veg at home and bring it in containers to the braai for faster assembly.
Leftover potjiekos reheats beautifully the next day.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

recipe.title: Teriyaki Chicken Plate
recipe.summary: Sticky-glazed chicken thighs with two scoops of rice and macaroni salad, Hawaiian plate lunch style.

steps.text: Cook the macaroni according to packet directions until al dente, then drain and rinse under cold water. In a bowl, mix the mayonnaise, rice vinegar, sugar, carrot, and onion. Toss the cooled pasta through. Season to taste with salt and pepper. Chill while you cook the chicken.
In a small bowl, whisk together the soy sauce, brown sugar, mirin, garlic, and ginger. Set aside.

Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Season the chicken thighs with salt and pepper on both sides. Place skin-side down in the pan and cook for 6–7 minutes until the skin is golden and crispy.
Turn the thighs skin-side up and cook for another 4–5 minutes until cooked through (internal temperature 75°C). Pour off most of the fat from the pan, leaving about 1 tbsp.

Pour the teriyaki sauce over the chicken. Mix the cornflour with the water until smooth, add to the pan, and stir gently. Simmer for 2–3 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce thickens and coats the chicken.
Divide the rice between four plates, making two scoops per plate. Top with the glazed chicken thighs and any sauce. Serve the macaroni salad on the side and garnish with spring onion if you like.

notes: Make the macaroni salad ahead: it's even better the next day.
If you can't find mirin, use 2 tbsp honey instead.
Leftover chicken keeps for three days in the fridge; reheat gently with a splash of water.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Perkedel Kentang
recipe.summary: Soft potato fritters with garlic, nutmeg and a golden crust, best eaten warm.

items.raw: 800 g floury potato, peeled and halved

steps.text: Boil the potato in salted water until soft and cooked through, about 15 minutes. Drain well and let cool completely, at least 15 minutes.
Mash the cooled potato until smooth and lump-free. Stir in the garlic, egg, nutmeg and salt until well combined.
With damp hands, shape the mixture into oval fritters, about 8 cm long, working gently so they stay tender. You should have about 12 fritters.
Heat about 2 cm of oil in a shallow pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Working in batches, fry the perkedel until golden brown all over, about 2 minutes each side. Do not crowd the pan.
Drain on paper towel and serve warm.

notes: Perkedel is best served warm. You can make the fritters ahead and reheat them in a moderate oven (180°C) for 8 minutes.
Let the boiled potato cool completely, warm potato breaks down when you fry it and won't stay soft inside.
Serve with sambal or sweet soy sauce for dipping.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Dal with Crispy Onions
recipe.summary: Split red lentils cooked soft with spice, topped with crispy fried onions.

steps.text: Heat 1½ tbsp oil in a small frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the sliced onions and cook, stirring often, until they're dark golden and crispy, about 10 minutes. Transfer to a plate lined with paper towel and set aside.
In a large pot, heat the remaining 1½ tbsp oil over medium heat. Add the garlic and ginger, and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 1 minute.
Add the turmeric, cumin and chilli powder. Stir for 30 seconds to bloom the spices.

Add the lentils, water (or stock) and crushed tomatoes. Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the lentils have broken down and the dal is creamy, about 25 minutes.
Season with salt to taste.
Spoon the dal into bowls and top with the crispy onions. Scatter with fresh coriander if you like.

recipe.title: Buri Gochu Jjim
recipe.summary: Glazed dried peppers and mushrooms braised until caramelized and tender.

items.raw: 200 g mixed mushrooms (shiitake, oyster, button), halved

steps.text: Soak the dried chillies in 120 ml warm water for 5 minutes until softened. Leave them whole.

Heat the sesame oil in a large heavy-bottomed pan or shallow braising vessel over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms in a single layer and cook, stirring occasionally, until they begin to colour and release their moisture, about 5 minutes.
Add the drained chillies to the pan (discard the soaking water or save it for stock). Stir gently to combine.
In a small bowl, whisk together the soy sauce, rice vinegar, maple syrup and gochugaru. Pour this over the mushrooms and chillies, then add 60 ml fresh water. Stir gently.

Lower the heat to medium and simmer, uncovered, for 12–15 minutes, stirring occasionally. The liquid will reduce, thicken and glaze the mushrooms and chillies. They should be tender and glossy, with most of the liquid absorbed or caramelized onto their surfaces.
Taste and adjust the seasoning with salt and a touch more soy sauce if needed. The flavour should be balanced between salty, slightly sweet and the subtle heat from the gochugaru.
Transfer to a serving dish and scatter with toasted sesame seeds. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: This keeps in the fridge for 3 days and tastes better the next day as the flavours deepen. Serve it cold as banchan or gently reheat.
You can use any dried chillies you have, guajillo or ancho work well too, though the flavour will shift. Stay with long varieties if you can; they soften into beautiful strands.

recipe.title: Lugaw
recipe.summary: Creamy rice porridge topped with boiled egg and crispy fried garlic, a comfort breakfast for grandchildren.

steps.text: Bring the chicken stock to a boil in a large pot until bubbling steadily. Add the rice and salt, stir well, and return to a boil.
Reduce heat to low, cover partly, and simmer, stirring often, for 40 minutes. The rice should break down and the porridge should be creamy and thick.
While the lugaw cooks, boil the eggs in a separate pot for 10 minutes until hard-boiled. Cool, shell, and halve them.
Heat the neutral oil in a small frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the sliced garlic and fry, stirring, until golden and crispy, about 3 minutes. Drain on paper towel.
Divide the lugaw among serving bowls. Top each with a halved egg, crispy fried garlic, and spring onion if using. Serve warm.

notes: Lugaw keeps in the fridge for 2 days; reheat gently with a little extra stock to loosen it.
Add crispy fried garlic and egg just before serving so the garlic stays crunchy.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

recipe.title: Kleftiko
recipe.summary: Lamb shoulder wrapped in parchment and slow-roasted until it melts, the way yiayia cooked it on special occasions.

items.raw: 2 tbsp fresh oregano (or 1 tbsp dried oregano)
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Pat the lamb dry and season generously inside and out with salt and pepper.
Tear off a sheet of baking paper about 1 m long. Place the lamb in the centre and scatter the onion, garlic, tomatoes, feta and oregano around and over it.
Drizzle with olive oil, then fold the paper up and over the lamb, folding and creasing the edges to seal it completely, the parcel should be airtight.
Place the parcel on a large roasting tray and roast at 160°C for 4 to 5 hours. The lamb is done when a fork slides through the meat like butter.
Carefully open the paper (steam will billow out). Transfer the lamb to a serving platter and let it rest for 10 minutes while you pour the cooking liquid into a small saucepan.
Skim the fat from the surface of the liquid and warm it gently over medium heat. Season with salt, pepper and lemon juice to taste, then pour over the lamb and serve.

notes: Make ahead: prepare the parcel up to 4 hours before roasting.
The cooking liquid makes a silky pan sauce, don't skip it. Serve with horta (simply boiled greens) or crusty bread to mop it up.
Leftovers shred beautifully and work in pies or as a filling for spanakopita.
Food safety:

recipe.title: To'ona'i Sunday Spread
recipe.summary: A Samoan feast spread for twenty with pisupo, taro, coconut bread and fresh fruit.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
3 kg taro, peeled and cut into chunks
3 fresh pineapples, peeled and cut into spears

steps.text: Start the taro: bring a large pot of salted water to the boil. Add taro chunks and simmer for 25–30 minutes until tender and cooked through. Drain well and place in a serving bowl. Keep warm.

While the taro cooks, heat oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Add onions and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Add corned beef, breaking it up with a wooden spoon, and stir-fry for 5–8 minutes until warmed through. Season with salt and pepper. Transfer to a serving platter.

Make the coconut bread: preheat oven to 180°C. Sift flour, baking powder and salt into a large bowl. In another bowl, whisk together sugar, coconut milk, desiccated coconut, eggs, oil and vanilla. Pour wet ingredients into dry ingredients and stir until just combined, don't overmix.

Divide batter between two greased 20 cm loaf tins and bake for 35–40 minutes until a skewer inserted in the centre comes out clean. Cool in tins for 5 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack. Slice and arrange on a platter.
Arrange all fruit on platters, keeping different types separate so people can choose.
Set the table with pisupo, taro, coconut bread and fruit platters. Serve family-style, with everyone helping themselves.

notes: The coconut bread keeps wrapped for two days. Taro and pisupo are best made the day of, but can be reheated gently.
Scale up easily for bigger gatherings: add another tin of pisupo and kg of taro for every five extra people.
Let everyone build their own plate, the mains are flexible, and plenty of fruit rounds it out for those with lighter appetites.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Sai Oua
recipe.summary: Isaan grilled sausage packed with pork, herbs and spices, coiled on the barbecue.

items.raw: 2–3 birds eye chilli, finely chopped (add more if you like heat)
items.note: add more if you like heat

items.raw: 2 m pork sausage casing, rinsed and soaked

steps.text: Mix the pork mince with coriander, garlic chives, spring onion, chilli, fish sauce, ground cumin and ground coriander in a bowl until just combined.

Fit a sausage casing onto a sausage stuffer or piping bag fitted with a large plain nozzle. Pipe the filling into the casing, pushing gently so it's loosely packed until the sausage is plump but not tight, which stops it bursting on the grill. Tie the end.
Heat your barbecue or grill plate to medium-high until hot and sizzling when a little oil hits it, and oil the grates.

Coil the sausage onto the hot grill. Cook for 12 minutes, turning every couple of minutes to colour all sides evenly. The casing should be dark brown and crackling, and the meat cooked through when you press it.
Transfer to a plate and let it rest for a minute. Serve with sticky rice, lime wedges and fresh coriander and chilli on the side.

notes: Make the sausages up to a day ahead and refrigerate on a tray before grilling.
Pork sausage casings are in the meat section at good butchers and some larger supermarkets. Soak them in water for 30 minutes before filling so they're easier to work with.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

title: Charred Broccoli and Crispy Chickpea Salad

recipe.title: Charred Broccoli and Crispy Chickpea Salad
recipe.summary: Big salad with roasted chickpeas, charred broccoli, and tahini-lemon dressing.

items.raw: 400 g tin chickpeas, drained and dried on paper towel
items.prep: drained and dried on paper towel

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Pat the chickpeas completely dry with paper towel. Toss with 2 tsp olive oil, salt, pepper and smoked paprika.
Heat 1 tbsp olive oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the chickpeas in a single layer and cook, stirring occasionally, until golden and crispy, about 8 minutes. Set aside.

Add remaining 1 tbsp oil to the same pan. When hot, add broccoli florets and cook without stirring for 3 minutes until the bottoms char. Toss and cook for another 2 minutes until tender-crisp. Season with salt and pepper.
While the broccoli cooks, make the dressing: whisk together tahini, lemon juice, minced garlic, water, salt and pepper until smooth.
Toss the salad leaves, cherry tomatoes and red onion in a large bowl. Drizzle half the dressing and toss gently.
Divide the salad between two bowls. Top with charred broccoli and crispy chickpeas. Drizzle with remaining dressing and scatter sesame seeds if using.

recipe.title: Horta Vrasti
recipe.summary: Boiled greens with olive oil and lemon, the plainest and most essential Greek dish.

items.raw: 1 kg mixed greens (spinach, chard, beetroot leaves, or cicory), roughly chopped
