notes: The broth can be made up to 3 days ahead and stored in the fridge, or frozen for up to 3 months. Matzo balls can be cooked and frozen separately for up to 1 month.
For a lighter broth, use chicken breasts instead of bones; reduce cooking time to 45 minutes. For richer broth, add extra chicken fat (schmaltz) when serving.
The soda water is key to light, fluffy matzo balls, don't skip it. And cold hands matter more than you'd think; it keeps the batter from getting tough.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Barbacoa
recipe.summary: Slow-cooked beef brisket wrapped in agave leaves, shredded until tender for tacos.

items.raw: Agave leaves (or banana leaves), for wrapping

steps.text: Heat the oven to 120°C. Toast the dried guajillo and chipotle chillies in a dry pan for 2 minutes until fragrant, then transfer to a bowl and cover with hot water. Let sit for 15 minutes until soft.

Drain the rehydrated chillies, then blitz them in a blender with garlic, cumin, oregano, cloves, beef stock, vinegar and salt until smooth. Strain through a sieve if you want a silky paste; for rustic texture, leave it coarse.
Pat the brisket dry. Rub all over with the chilli paste until well coated. Wrap tightly in agave or banana leaves and then in foil, sealing the edges.
Place the wrapped brisket in a heavy-based pot or Dutch oven. Cover and braise in the oven for 7 to 8 hours, until the meat shreds easily with a fork.
Remove from the oven and let rest for 15 minutes. Unwrap carefully, watch out for steam, and shred the beef using two forks, pulling it apart along the grain.
Strain the braising liquid into a jug. Skim any fat from the surface and season with salt to taste. Toss the shredded beef with a few tbsp of the braising liquid to keep it moist.

notes: Make ahead: cook the barbacoa the day before, then shred and reheat gently in the braising liquid. Keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days.
Serve on warm flour tortillas with diced onion, fresh coriander and lime wedges.
This is a weekend cook: take your time and let the low heat do the work.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Bariis iyo Caano
recipe.summary: Broken rice cooked soft with milk and cardamom, a comforting Somali breakfast.

items.raw: 250 g broken rice (or short-grain white rice, lightly crushed)
items.note: or short-grain white rice, lightly crushed

steps.text: Heat the ghee in a large pot over medium heat. Add the crushed cardamom pods and warm until fragrant, about 1 minute.
Add the broken rice and stir constantly for 2 minutes, toasting it lightly.
Pour in the water and bring to a boil. Cook, stirring often, until the water is mostly absorbed, about 10 minutes.
Reduce the heat to low and pour in the milk slowly, stirring as you go. The rice will be creamy but still soft, not stiff.
Cook gently, stirring every 2 minutes, until the rice is very soft and the mixture is thick and porridgy, about 12 minutes. Add salt to taste.
If it's too thick, add a splash of warm milk. Serve hot in bowls.

notes: Make it ahead and reheat gently with a splash of milk, it keeps for 3 days in the fridge.
If you can't find broken rice, crush short-grain white rice coarsely with your hands or a rolling pin before cooking.

recipe.title: Ajiaco Colombiano
recipe.summary: Hearty potato and chicken soup with corn and cream, comfort in a bowl.

items.raw: 1 kg chicken thighs, bone-in and skin-on
400 g floury potato, cut into chunks
200 g sweet potato, cut into chunks
2 corn cobs, cut into 5 cm pieces
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Put the chicken thighs, onion quarters and crushed garlic into a large pot. Cover with the chicken stock and bring to a boil, then reduce the heat and simmer gently for 15 minutes. Skim off any foam that rises to the top.
Add the floury and waxy potatoes to the pot. Simmer for another 10 minutes until they start to soften.
Add the sweet potato and corn pieces. Continue to simmer for 8–10 minutes until all the potatoes are tender and the corn is cooked through.
Remove the chicken thighs and set aside to cool slightly. Once cool enough to handle, shred the meat into bite-sized pieces, discarding the skin and bones.
Return the shredded chicken to the pot. Stir in the cream and season with salt and pepper to taste. Heat through gently without boiling.
Ladle into bowls and serve hot with fresh coriander if you have it on hand.

notes: Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

recipe.title: Blackened Catfish
recipe.summary: Catfish fillets crusted with Cajun spices and seared hard in a cast-iron frying pan until smoky and crispy.

steps.text: Mix paprika, cayenne, cumin, onion powder, garlic powder, thyme, oregano, black pepper and salt in a shallow dish.
Pat the catfish fillets dry with paper towels. Coat both sides generously with the spice mixture, pressing it on so it sticks.
Heat the oil in a cast-iron frying pan over high heat until it's smoking and a drop of water beads and rolls across the surface, about 2 minutes.
Add the butter and swirl it through the hot oil. When it's foaming and just starting to brown, lay the catfish fillets in the frying pan, they should sizzle hard.
Sear without moving them for 3 to 4 minutes, until the crust is dark brown and charred. Flip carefully.
Sear the other side for another 2 to 3 minutes, until the fish is cooked through and flakes easily with a fork. Serve hot.

notes: Serve with white rice, collard greens or a simple slaw to cool the heat.
The frying pan must be smoking hot, don't skip this step or you won't get that proper blackened crust.
Swap catfish for any firm white fish fillet.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Kopytka
recipe.summary: Little potato and flour dumplings tossed with caramelized onions and mushrooms.

items.raw: 500 g floury potato, peeled and halved
2 brown onions, sliced into thin rings

steps.text: Boil the potato in salted water until tender, about 12 minutes. Drain well and pass through a ricer while still hot into a large bowl.
Add the flour, egg, and salt to the potato. Mix gently with your hands until just combined, it should feel a little soft and slightly sticky, not smooth. Don't overwork it.

Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Dust the work surface lightly with flour. Break off a piece of dough about the size of a walnut, roll it roughly into a stick about 5 cm long, and press gently with your thumb to make a small indent (this is the little hoof). Drop each kopytka into the boiling water as you shape them. They will sink, then float to the surface; cook for 2–3 minutes after they float. Drain and spread on a tray to cool.

While the kopytka cook, heat the oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms and fry, stirring often, until they are golden and any liquid has evaporated, about 8 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Lower the heat to medium and add the onions to the same pan. Cook, stirring now and then, until they are soft and deeply golden, about 12 minutes. Add the garlic and thyme, if using, and cook for another minute.
Return the mushrooms to the pan with the onions. Add the drained kopytka and toss gently until everything is warm and coated. Season with salt and black pepper. Serve hot.

notes: Kopytka can be made ahead: shape and boil them, then store in the fridge for up to 2 days. Toss with the mushrooms and onions to warm through.
The dough should stay slightly loose, too much flour and the kopytka become heavy. If it's very sticky, dust with a little more flour, but resist the urge to knead.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Atole de Chocolate
recipe.summary: Thick, creamy corn masa drink with Oaxacan chocolate and cinnamon, warm for breakfast.

items.raw: 250 g fresh masa (corn dough), or masa harina mixed with warm water
items.prep: or masa harina mixed with warm water

items.raw: 100 g Oaxacan chocolate (tableta), chopped (such as de agua o de metate)
items.note: tableta; such as de agua o de metate

steps.text: In a heavy-based pot, heat the water and milk together over medium heat until steaming but not boiling, about 5 minutes.
In a small bowl, whisk the fresh masa with 1 cup of the warm liquid to dissolve it completely, breaking up any lumps. (If using masa harina, mix it with the liquid until smooth.)
Pour the masa mixture slowly into the pot, stirring constantly to avoid lumps. Add the cinnamon stick.
Continue stirring over medium heat until the mixture thickens and coats the back of a spoon, about 8 minutes.
Add the chopped chocolate and sugar. Stir well until the chocolate is completely melted and the atole is smooth and frothy.
Taste and adjust sugar and salt as needed. Remove from heat.
If you have a molinillo (traditional wooden whisk), hold the pot and roll the molinillo between your palms to make the atole frothy and light. Otherwise, whisk vigorously for a minute.
Serve hot in bowls or mugs, and drink while it's warm.

notes: Fresh masa is best, but masa harina (corn flour) works well too: use about 125 g mixed with a little warm water to a smooth paste.
Oaxacan chocolate is grainy and textured, sold as tablets, seek it in Latin or Mexican markets, or use good dark chocolate with a tiny pinch of ground almond added.
A molinillo whisk creates the traditional frothy top, but a regular whisk does the job.

recipe.title: Rajas Poblanas
recipe.summary: Roasted poblano strips in a creamy sauce with jalapeños, onion and cheese.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Hold each poblano over a gas flame or under a hot grill, turning with tongs, until the skin is blackened all over, about 3–4 minutes per chilli. Place in a plastic bag for 5 minutes to steam, then peel away the blackened skin under cool running water.
Slit each poblano lengthwise and gently remove the seeds and white membrane, keeping the chilli in one piece. Cut the roasted poblanos lengthwise into 1 cm strips.
Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Cook the onion, stirring, until soft and translucent, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and diced jalapeño, and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the cream and stir through the cheese until melted and the sauce is smooth, about 2 minutes. Season to taste with salt and pepper.
Gently fold the poblano strips into the sauce and warm through for 2–3 minutes. Serve hot as a main or side dish.

notes: Rajas poblanas can be served as a main dish with warm tortillas, or as a side to grilled vegetables or eggs.
If you cannot find poblanos, use large green capsicums; they will be milder but the dish still works well.

recipe.title: Mì Xào Rau Muống
recipe.summary: Stir-fried wheat noodles with water spinach, garlic and ginger, simple temple food, weeknight done well.

items.raw: 400 g fresh wheat noodles (or dried, cooked and cooled)
400 g water spinach (rau cần), cut into 5 cm lengths
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: If using dried noodles, cook in boiling salted water until just tender, drain well and spread on a tray to cool. Fresh noodles can be used as they are.
Heat the oil in a large wok or wide frying pan over high heat. When shimmering, add the sliced garlic and ginger. Stir-fry for about 1 minute until fragrant but not brown.
Add the water spinach and toss constantly for 2–3 minutes until it begins to wilt but the stems still have a gentle firmness.
Add the cooled noodles to the wok, breaking them apart gently with chopsticks or tongs as you toss. Stir-fry for 2–3 minutes until heated through.
Pour the soy sauce and rice vinegar over the noodles and toss well for another minute, letting the flavours coat everything evenly.
Taste and season with salt and black pepper. If you like heat, sprinkle with dried chilli flakes.
Serve at once, while the noodles are still warm and the spinach stems hold their slight crispness.

notes: If water spinach is hard to find, use baby bok choy or broccolini cut into shorter lengths; they cook in the same time.
The noodles should be completely cool before stir-frying so they don't clump and stick together.

recipe.title: Granita di Mandorla
recipe.summary: Icy almond milk drink with a brioche, how Sicilians really start the day.

steps.text: Pour the water into a bowl and add the ground almond. Stir well to combine, breaking up any lumps. Let sit for 10 minutes so the almond releases its flavour and begins to soften.
Strain the mixture through a fine sieve or muslin cloth, pressing gently to extract all the almond milk. Discard the solids (or save them for baking if you wish).
Stir the caster sugar, milk and vanilla extract into the almond milk until the sugar dissolves completely. Taste and add a pinch of salt to enhance the almond flavour.
Pour into a shallow freezer container and freeze, stirring with a fork every 30 minutes for the first 3 hours to create a slushy, granular texture. Then leave undisturbed overnight until firm.
To serve, scoop the granita into glasses. Top with a little cold milk if you like, and serve with a brioche bun on the side for dunking.

notes: Granita keeps well in the freezer for up to a week. Scoop it out as needed; if it hardens too solid, let it sit at room temperature for 5 minutes before serving.
For a richer granita, use equal parts almond milk and full-cream milk in the base instead of water and milk.
Some Sicilians make a thinner granita by adding a splash more milk at serving time. Do whatever feels right to you.

recipe.title: Mackerel Rundown
recipe.summary: Mackerel cooked down in coconut broth with green bananas and yam.

items.raw: 2 fresh mackerel, cleaned and cut into chunks
1 green banana, peeled and cut into chunks
200 g yam, peeled and cut into chunks
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the onion and garlic, and cook, stirring, until soft and fragrant, about 5 minutes.
Add the mackerel chunks and cook for 2 minutes on each side to seal them, then remove and set aside.

Pour the coconut milk into the pot and stir well to mix with the onion and garlic. Add the green banana and yam chunks, and drop in the whole scotch bonnet if using (it will flavour the broth without breaking apart).

Return the mackerel to the pot and add the dried thyme. Bring to a gentle simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cover and cook for 20 to 25 minutes, until the banana and yam are tender and the mackerel is cooked through.
Taste and season with salt and pepper. If you used the whole chilli and want more heat, carefully break it open and stir in the seeds. Stir in the spring onions and cook for 1 minute more.
Ladle into bowls, making sure each serves gets fish, vegetables and plenty of broth.

notes: Make it a day ahead if you like, the flavours deepen overnight. Reheat gently on the stove.
The scotch bonnet stays whole while cooking so you control the heat. Leave it out if you prefer a gentler dish.

recipe.title: Ezogelin Çorbası
recipe.summary: Light Turkish lentil soup with bulgur, tomato and warming spices.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic and tomato paste, stirring constantly, until fragrant, about 1 minute.
Stir in the lentils and bulgur, coating them with the oil. Add the cumin and dried mint, stirring to combine.

Pour in the tinned tomatoes and stock. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat to medium-low and simmer, stirring occasionally, until the lentils and bulgur are tender and the soup is creamy, about 25–30 minutes.
Taste and season with salt and black pepper as needed.
Ladle into bowls and top with fresh mint or parsley if you like.

notes: Make it ahead: this soup keeps well in the fridge for 3 days, and the flavours deepen as it sits. Reheat gently with a splash of water or stock if it's too thick.
For extra depth, add a splash of red wine vinegar or lemon juice just before serving.

recipe.title: Steak and Ale Pudding
recipe.summary: Beef and ale filling in suet pastry, steamed in a pudding basin, proper old-school comfort.

items.raw: 800 g beef chuck, cut into 3 cm cubes
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. Season the beef with salt and pepper. Brown the meat in batches, about 3 minutes per batch, until well coloured on all sides. Set aside.
In the same pan, cook the onion until soft, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and tomato paste, stir well, and cook for 2 minutes more.

Return the beef to the pan. Pour in the ale and stock, scraping the bottom of the pan. Add the bay leaves and thyme. Bring to a simmer, then remove from heat and leave to cool completely, at least 1 hour. The filling needs to be cold before you add it to the pastry.

While the filling cools, make the suet crust. Mix the flour and salt in a large bowl. Add the suet and stir until it's distributed evenly. Add the cold water a little at a time, stirring with a knife until a soft, slightly sticky dough forms. Knead gently until just combined; don't overwork it.

Lightly flour a work surface. Roll out two-thirds of the dough into a circle about 40 cm across and 5 mm thick. It should be large enough to line a 1.5-litre pudding basin with some hanging over the edge.
Use this large circle to line the pudding basin, leaving the excess hanging over the rim.

Strain the cooled filling, reserving the liquid. Discard the bay leaves and thyme. Spoon the beef and onions into the lined basin, then pour in enough of the reserved liquid to come halfway up the filling (about 200 ml). Save the rest for serving.
Roll out the remaining dough into a circle about 25 cm across, 5 mm thick. Lay this on top of the filling. Fold the overhanging pastry inward over the lid, pressing down to seal.
Cover the pudding with a pleated piece of baking paper (the pleat allows for expansion), then a pleated piece of foil. Tie both down with string under the lip of the basin.

Place the pudding basin in a large pot and add enough boiling water to come halfway up the sides of the basin. Cover the pot with a lid. Steam for 3 hours, checking every 45 minutes and topping up the water if needed, it should stay at the same level.
Carefully remove the pudding from the pot. Let it rest for 10 minutes. Warm the reserved liquid in a small pan.
Turn the pudding out onto a warm plate or serving bowl. Serve with the warmed gravy poured over the top, and mashed potato on the side.

notes: If you don't have a pudding basin, a 1.5-litre heatproof bowl wrapped in foil will work, though you may need to adjust the steaming time slightly.
Leftovers can be reheated gently in the steamer for 30 minutes, or covered in foil in a 150°C oven for about 45 minutes.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

recipe.title: Semlor
recipe.summary: Soft cardamom buns filled with almond paste and whipped cream, a Swedish fika favourite.

steps.text: Mix the warm milk, yeast and a pinch of the caster sugar in a bowl. Let sit 5 minutes until foamy.

Add the remaining caster sugar, softened butter, salt, cardamom and egg yolk. Stir well, then gradually work in the flour until a soft dough forms. Knead for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic. The dough should be slightly sticky.
Place in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with a clean tea towel, and leave to rise in a warm place for 1–1½ hours, until doubled in size.

Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured bench and divide into 8 equal pieces. Roll each into a ball, place on baking trays lined with baking paper, cover loosely, and leave to prove for 30–40 minutes until puffy.
Preheat the oven to 200°C. Brush each bun with beaten egg, then bake for 12–15 minutes until golden and a skewer inserted into the centre comes out clean.
Once cool enough to handle, carefully slice the top third off each bun and set aside. Scoop out a small amount of crumb from inside each bun to make room for the filling.
Mix the almond meal, icing sugar and water to a paste. Divide evenly among the buns, spooning into the cavity.
Whip the cream with the caster sugar until soft peaks form. Top each bun with a generous dollop of cream, then replace the lid at an angle.
Serve at room temperature the same day.

notes: Make the dough the day before if it suits you, cold dough ferments gently overnight. Shape and prove the next morning.
If you grind whole cardamom pods yourself, use about 1½ tsp of pods; they're more fragrant than pre-ground.
Semlor are best eaten the day they're made. Store in an airtight container for up to a day, but the bun will soften.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Sandesh
recipe.summary: Cardamom-scented cottage cheese sweet, the Bengali classic at the heart of a thousand gentle arguments.

steps.text: Bring the milk to a rolling boil in a heavy-bottomed pan over high heat, until it foams up and rises towards the rim. Once it reaches a full boil, remove from the heat.

Add the yoghurt slowly, stirring gently. The milk will curdle immediately. Let it sit for 2 minutes, then pour through a fine sieve lined with muslin cloth, collecting the whey in a bowl beneath. Let it drain for 5 minutes.
Gather the corners of the muslin and hang it to drain for 30 minutes until the paneer is quite dry but still soft.

Turn the paneer into a bowl and crumble it finely with your fingertips. Add the khoya, sugar, cardamom seeds (discarding the husks), and salt. Mix gently but thoroughly until the mixture just holds together.
Divide the mixture into 12 portions and shape each into a small smooth ball or oval with damp hands. You can press each into a small mould if you have one, then tap it out onto a plate.
Chill for at least 15 minutes before serving. Store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days.

notes: If you can't find khoya, reduce 500 ml milk slowly in a heavy pan until it becomes a thick paste (about 30 minutes), then use that instead, it will give you more authentic flavour and texture.
For a softer sandesh (Arnab's preference), use only 50 g khoya and don't chill for as long; for a firmer set (his wife's way), add an extra 25 g khoya.
Regional variations: try adding a few strands of saffron, a tablespoon of mango pulp, or a teaspoon of rose water instead of cardamom, the arguments are endless and that's rather the point.

recipe.title: Seezunge Müllerin Art
recipe.summary: Pan-fried sole with brown butter and lemon, a Northern German classic.

items.raw: 2 whole sole (300–350 g each), gutted and cleaned
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Pat the sole dry with paper towels. Season inside and out with salt and pepper.
Spread the flour on a shallow plate. Lightly coat both sides of each fish, shaking off the excess.
Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat until shimmering.
Lay the sole in the pan and cook, without moving, for 2–3 minutes until the skin is golden and crisp. Flip and cook the other side for 2–3 minutes until cooked through.
Transfer the fish to a warm plate. Reduce the heat to medium, add the butter to the same pan, and let it melt and brown, swirling gently, for 1–2 minutes until it smells nutty and turns golden.
Pour the brown butter over the fish, squeeze lemon juice over the top (it will sizzle briefly), scatter with parsley if using, and serve at once while the butter is still hot and nutty.

notes: Sole is the classic choice, but halibut, plaice or any firm white fish works. You can also cook fillets, they'll need only 1–2 minutes per side.
The brown butter is everything. Don't skip it or rush it; the aroma tells you when it's ready.

recipe.title: Soupe à l'Oignon
recipe.summary: Silky onion soup with fish stock and dark caramelized onions, Dakar comfort food.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large, heavy-based pot over medium heat. Add the sliced onions and cook, stirring often, until they soften and begin to release their moisture, about 10 minutes.

Continue cooking the onions, stirring occasionally, until they are deeply caramelized and golden brown, about 30–40 minutes. This takes patience, but it's where all the flavour comes from. Lower the heat if they start to catch.
Add the chopped garlic and cook, stirring, for 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the fish stock and add the bay leaf. Bring to a simmer, then lower the heat and cook gently for about 5 minutes to let the flavours meld.
Season with salt and black pepper to taste. Remove the bay leaf.
Ladle into deep bowls and serve hot. Tear in crusty bread if you like, and let it soften into the soup.

notes: For extra richness, some cooks stir in a spoonful of crème fraîche or Greek yoghurt just before serving.
Make this ahead and reheat gently, the flavour deepens overnight.

recipe.title: Kalua Pork
recipe.summary: Slow-roasted Hawaiian pork, tender enough to shred with a fork, seasoned the island way.

steps.text: Preheat oven to 160°C. Pat the pork shoulder dry with paper towels.
Mix salt, pepper and crushed garlic together. Rub the mixture all over the pork, getting it into any cracks in the skin.
Line a large roasting pan with banana leaves (or just use the pan). Place the pork skin-side up on the leaves. Cover tightly with foil.
Roast for 7–8 hours, until the meat is so tender it shreds easily when pulled with two forks.
Remove from oven and let rest for 10 minutes, then shred the meat into bite-sized pieces, discarding the bone and most of the skin (save a bit of crispy skin to mix back in if you like).
Serve warm with the pan juices spooned over.

notes: Kalua pork keeps well in the fridge for 4 days, and freezes for up to 3 months. Reheat gently with a splash of water.
Serve with rice, cabbage slaw and gravy for a real plate lunch, or use it for musubi.
The longer you cook it, the more tender it gets, even 8 or 9 hours won't hurt.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part.

recipe.title: Bap with Gochujang Butter
recipe.summary: Rice with a Korean chilli-butter scramble and a fried egg.

steps.text: Mix the butter and gochujang together in a small bowl until combined.
Heat a small non-stick frying pan over medium heat. Crack the egg into the pan and fry until the white is set and the yolk is still runny, about 2–3 minutes.
While the egg cooks, put the rice in a serving bowl.
Transfer the fried egg to a plate and set aside.
Return the frying pan to medium heat. Add the gochujang butter and sesame oil, stirring until the butter melts and the mixture is warm, about 1 minute.
Pour the gochujang butter over the rice and stir through. Top with the fried egg and scatter the spring onion over the top.
Taste and add a pinch of salt if needed, then serve straight away.

notes: Make the gochujang butter ahead and keep it in a pot in the fridge; it'll come together faster in the morning.
Use leftover rice from the night before, or make a quick batch while you wait for the egg to fry.

Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system. Cool any leftover rice quickly and refrigerate it within an hour; reheat it until steaming hot.

recipe.title: Sago Pudding
recipe.summary: Creamy sago with cinnamon, cardamom and rose water, comfort in a bowl.

steps.text: Bring the water to a boil in a large saucepan. Add the sago slowly, stirring constantly to prevent lumps from forming. Cook, stirring often, until the sago is translucent and tender, about 12 minutes.
Add the milk, caster sugar, cinnamon stick and crushed cardamom pods. Stir well and bring to a gentle simmer until the sugar has dissolved and the milk is fragrant.
Cook, stirring occasionally, until the pudding thickens slightly and the sago pearls are completely soft, about 5 minutes. The mixture should be creamy but not stiff.
Remove from the heat and stir through the rose water. Taste and add a pinch of salt to balance the sweetness. Discard the cinnamon stick.
Divide among bowls while still warm and dust lightly with ground cinnamon. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: This pudding can be made a few hours ahead and gently reheated, or served at room temperature.
Use good-quality rose water, it should smell fragrant but not perfumy. Add it slowly and taste as you go.

recipe.title: Arròs Negre
recipe.summary: Catalan black rice with squid ink, fresh squid and seafood on a slow sofregit base.

items.raw: 400 g tinned tomatoes, sieved or blended smooth
Salt and black pepper, to taste
350 g short-grain rice (bomba or paella rice preferred)
300 g fresh squid, cleaned and cut into rings
2 sachets squid ink (4 g total, or fresh ink from fishmonger)
items.note: 4 g total, or fresh ink from fishmonger

items.raw: 750 ml seafood stock (or fish stock), warmed

steps.text: In your rice pan or large shallow casserole over medium heat, warm the olive oil. Add the chopped onions and cook very slowly, stirring often, until completely soft and lightly golden, this is the sofregit, and it should take 12 to 15 minutes. Do not rush it; this is where the flavour lives.
Add the tinned tomatoes to the sofregit and stir well. Cook for another 5 to 8 minutes, until the sauce thickens slightly and the raw tomato taste disappears. Season with salt and pepper.
Stir in the garlic and chilli (if using), and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the rice and stir constantly for 2 minutes, coating each grain with the sofregit and oil.

Dissolve the squid ink sachets in the warm stock until the stock is jet black, then pour the stock gradually into the rice, stirring occasionally. Bring to a simmer until bubbles break across the surface.
Cook the rice uncovered at a gentle simmer for about 15 to 18 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the rice is almost tender and the liquid has been mostly absorbed.

Scatter the squid rings and mussels across the top of the rice. Do not stir them in. Continue cooking for 5 to 7 minutes, until the squid is just cooked through, the mussel shells have opened (discard any that don't), and the rice is tender with a slight bite. The bottom should form a thin, crispy layer (called socarrat).
Remove from heat, cover loosely with foil, and rest for 3 minutes. Scatter fresh parsley over the top and serve at the table in the pan.

notes: Make the sofregit ahead: cook the onions and tomatoes up to an hour before, then reheat gently before adding the rice.
Fresh squid ink from the fishmonger can replace the sachets, ask for 2 sachets' worth (about 4 g). It will be fresher and give a rounder flavour.
Arròs negre reheats poorly, so cook it fresh and serve at once, still warm from the pan.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Banga Soup
recipe.summary: Palm nut soup with stockfish and crayfish, rich and deeply savoury.

items.raw: 1 kg fresh palm nuts, husked and cleaned
4 scotch bonnet chillies, whole (optional, for heat)

steps.text: Pound the palm nuts in a large bowl with 2 litres of hot water (not boiling), working in batches. Press through a fine sieve or colander lined with muslin cloth, squeezing gently to extract all the cream. Reserve this golden liquid and discard the fibre.

In a large pot, bring 1 litre of water to the boil. Add the stockfish, one halved onion, and a pinch of salt. Simmer for 20 minutes, then remove the stockfish and set aside to cool. Strain the cooking liquid and reserve it (discard the onion).
Once the stockfish is cool enough to handle, remove the meat from the bones and break into chunks. Discard the bones.
Pour the palm nut cream into the pot over medium heat. Stir constantly for 3–4 minutes until it thickens slightly and the oil begins to separate on top, this is how you know it's ready.

Add the reserved stockfish cooking liquid, the stockfish meat, dried crayfish, remaining halved onion, and the scotch bonnet chillies if using. Stir well and simmer gently for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking.
Stir in the ground crayfish, salt, and black pepper. Taste and adjust seasoning. Simmer for another 10 minutes, then remove from heat. Remove the onion halves and whole chillies before serving.
Serve hot with boiled white rice, gari, or fufu.

notes: Make it a day ahead and reheat gently, the flavours deepen overnight.
If you can't find fresh palm nuts, use tinned palm cream (about 800 ml), though fresh is far superior. Skip the pounding and straining; just heat the tinned cream gently and follow from step 3.
Stockfish is essential, dried, smoked whole fish. Don't substitute with stock cubes or powder, you'll lose the soul of the soup.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

recipe.title: Chikuwa Don
recipe.summary: Bowl of rice topped with simmered fish cake and egg, quick bento favourite.

steps.text: Combine dashi, soy sauce, mirin and sugar in a small saucepan or shallow pan. Bring to a simmer over medium heat until the sugar has dissolved and small bubbles appear at the edges.
Add the sliced chikuwa and simmer for 2 minutes until heated through.
Lightly beat the eggs in a bowl. Pour into the simmering broth in a thin stream, stirring gently until the egg is just set but still soft, about 1 minute.
Divide the cooked rice between two bowls. Spoon the chikuwa, egg and sauce over the top. Garnish with spring onion if using, and serve hot.

notes: Make ahead: Cook the rice and prepare the chikuwa mixture up to 4 hours ahead. Reheat gently and pour over fresh rice.
Chikuwa keeps in the fridge for up to a week, so this is perfect for bento prep.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Kik Alicha
recipe.summary: Mild yellow split pea wat with ginger and turmeric, Ethiopian fasting-day comfort food.

steps.text: Heat the niter kibbeh in a large pot over medium heat. Add the chopped onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes.
Add the garlic and ginger and cook, stirring, for another 2 minutes until fragrant.
Stir in the turmeric and cardamom, and cook for 1 minute to bloom the spices.

Add the rinsed split peas and water. Bring to a gentle boil, then reduce heat to low and simmer, stirring occasionally, until the peas break down and the wat thickens, about 30 minutes. The peas should be completely soft and the sauce creamy.
Season with salt to taste. If the wat is too thick, add a splash more water. Serve warm with injera.

notes: Make this on fasting days (Wednesday and Friday for the Ethiopian Orthodox calendar). It's just as good made with neutral oil instead of niter kibbeh if you're fasting from animal products.
Kik alicha keeps well in the fridge for 3 days. Reheat gently with a splash of water to loosen the sauce.

recipe.title: Jianbing
recipe.summary: Crispy crepe with egg, spring onions and wonton, Northern China's street breakfast.

steps.text: Mix plain flour and salt in a bowl. Slowly add water, stirring until smooth. Let the batter rest for 10 minutes.
While the batter rests, break the wonton wrappers into rough pieces and fry in a small pan with a little oil until crispy and golden, about 2 minutes. Set aside.
Heat a large non-stick pan or crepe pan over high heat. It should be very hot, test with a drop of water; it should sizzle and evaporate immediately.
Pour 120 ml of batter into the centre of the pan and immediately tilt and rotate the pan so the batter spreads into a thin, even circle about 20 cm across. Work quickly.
Let the batter cook for about 30 seconds until the bottom is set and starts to turn light golden. Crack an egg onto one half of the crepe, then use a spatula to break the yolk and spread it evenly.
Scatter half the chopped spring onion and half the crispy wonton pieces over the egg. Fold the other half of the crepe over to enclose the filling, pressing gently.
Cook for another 30 seconds until the egg is set, then slide onto a plate. Serve immediately with sweet chilli sauce and soy sauce for dipping.
Repeat with the remaining batter, egg, spring onion and wonton to make a second jianbing.

notes: The batter can be made the night before and stored in the fridge, it actually develops better flavour overnight.
Wonton wrappers crisp up quickly, so fry them just before you start making the crepes.
A non-stick or well-seasoned crepe pan is essential. The pan must be hot enough that the batter sets instantly, or you'll struggle to spread it.

recipe.title: Za'atar Bread
recipe.summary: Warm Palestinian flatbread brushed with olive oil and za'atar spice mix.

steps.text: In a large bowl, combine flour and salt. Make a well in the centre and pour in the warm water. Mix with your hand until a shaggy dough forms, then knead for 5 minutes until smooth and slightly elastic.
Divide dough into 4 balls. Cover with a damp tea towel and leave to rest for 10 minutes while you set up to cook.
Toast the za'atar in a dry frying pan over medium heat for about 30 seconds, stirring constantly, until fragrant. Transfer to a small bowl and set aside.

Place the same frying pan over medium heat. Working with one ball at a time, flatten the dough with your hands into a rough oval about 5 mm thick. Cook for about 1.5 to 2 minutes, until it puffs slightly and the bottom is pale golden.
Flip and cook the other side for another 1 to 1.5 minutes. The bread should be flexible, not crispy. Transfer to a plate.
While warm, brush the bread with olive oil on both sides, then sprinkle generously with the toasted za'atar and a pinch of salt. Repeat with remaining dough balls and serve warm.

notes: Make the dough ahead: prepare through step 2, cover, and refrigerate overnight. Bring to room temperature before cooking.
Za'atar is a Palestinian blend of thyme, sumac and sesame. Look for it in Middle Eastern grocers or make your own by mixing 1 tbsp dried thyme, 1 tbsp sumac and 1 tbsp toasted sesame seeds.

recipe.title: Buniga ni Lolo
recipe.summary: Fijian eggplant braised in coconut milk with spices, tender and rich.

items.raw: 3 medium eggplants, cut into 5 cm chunks

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic and ginger, and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Stir in the cumin, coriander and turmeric, and cook for 1 minute to release the spices.
Add the eggplant chunks and stir to coat in the spice mixture. Cook for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Pour in the coconut milk and bring to a simmer until gentle bubbles appear and the sauce is slightly thickened. Add the chopped chillies and stir well.
Reduce heat to low and simmer gently, uncovered, for 20 minutes until the eggplant is very tender. Stir occasionally.
Taste and add salt as needed. Serve hot, scattered with fresh coriander if you like.

notes: Serve with roti, dhal puri or rice.
You can add 2 or 3 curry leaves and a sprig of fresh coriander in the last 5 minutes of cooking if you have them.

recipe.title: Bánh Nậm
recipe.summary: Folded rice cakes with pork and shrimp filling, a Central Vietnamese specialty.

items.raw: Banana leaves, cut into 15 cm squares (about 8 pieces), or plastic wrap
items.prep: cut into 15 cm squares, or plastic wrap

items.raw: Pickled mixed vegetables (pickled daikon and carrot, pickled onion, or pickled mustard greens)
items.note: pickled daikon and carrot, pickled onion, or pickled mustard greens

steps.text: Make the rice cake batter: Mix rice flour and salt. Gradually add water, stirring until smooth. The batter should be thin and pourable, like crepe batter. Let it rest 10 minutes.

Make the filling: Heat 2 tbsp oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Add shallots and garlic, cook stirring for 2 minutes until fragrant. Add pork mince, breaking it up as it cooks. After 5 minutes, add chopped prawn, fish sauce and black pepper. Cook, stirring, for another 3 minutes until the prawn is just cooked through. Taste and adjust seasoning. Set aside to cool slightly.
Prepare banana leaves or plastic: If using banana leaves, blanch them briefly in hot water to soften, then lay flat to cool. If using plastic wrap, cut into squares and lay flat.

Cook the rice cakes: Lightly oil a non-stick frying pan (about 20 cm) and heat over medium-high heat. Pour about 60 ml of batter into the pan, tilting to spread it into a thin, roughly square sheet about 3 mm thick. Cook for about 1 minute until the edges lift and the top is just set but still pliable. Slide onto a banana leaf or plastic, cooked side up. Repeat to make 8 cakes.

Fill and fold: While still warm, place about 2 tbsp of cooled filling in the centre of each rice cake. Fold one corner over the filling, then the next corner, then the next, creating an envelope. The final corner should tuck under. The rice cake should be soft enough to fold without cracking.
Set the bánh nậm: Let each folded cake sit on its banana leaf or plastic for a few minutes to firm up slightly. They can be eaten warm or at room temperature.

Serve: Arrange bánh nậm on a platter with pickled vegetables and fresh herbs on the side. Make a simple dipping sauce by stirring a small amount of fish sauce into water (about 1 part fish sauce to 3 parts water). Serve with rice paper crisps if you like extra crunch.

notes: Make the rice cakes up to 2 hours ahead and keep them at room temperature, covered with a damp cloth. Assemble and fold just before serving so they stay pliable.
If you can't find banana leaves, plastic wrap works fine, or serve the bánh nậm on a plate with lettuce underneath instead.

Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C. Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

title: Slow-Roasted Tomatoes and Onions with Oregano

recipe.title: Slow-Roasted Tomatoes and Onions with Oregano
recipe.summary: Slow-roasted tomatoes and onions collapse into soft, silky jam with olive oil and oregano.

items.raw: 4 brown onions, sliced into thick rings

steps.text: Preheat the oven to 180°C. Arrange the tomato halves cut-side up in a large baking dish, nestling the onion rings between and around them.
Drizzle generously with olive oil and scatter the dried oregano over everything. Season with salt and pepper.
Roast, uncovered, for 90 minutes, stirring gently halfway through. The tomatoes should collapse and release their liquid, and the onions should soften and begin to caramelize at the edges.
The gemista is ready when the tomatoes have broken down completely and the liquid has reduced to a thick, jammy consistency. Serve warm with crusty bread.

notes: Serve warm or at room temperature with crusty bread for scooping.
Keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days and tastes even better the next day.
The notebook's version with dried tomatoes works too, reduce the roasting time to about 45 minutes if using them.

recipe.title: Lentil Kibbeh
recipe.summary: Bulgur and red lentil shells stuffed with spiced lentil filling, baked instead of fried.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: For the filling, heat the oil in a large pan over medium heat and cook the onion until soft and lightly golden, about 5 minutes. Add the cumin, coriander and allspice, stirring until fragrant, about 1 minute. Add the brown lentils and cook, stirring occasionally, until just tender and any liquid has been absorbed, about 20 minutes. Stir through the pine nuts, then season to taste. Set aside to cool.

For the shells, heat the olive oil in a large pan over medium heat and cook the brown onion until soft, about 5 minutes. Add the cumin, coriander, cinnamon and cayenne, stirring until fragrant, about 1 minute. Add the red lentils and cook, stirring often, for 2 minutes. Pour in the vegetable stock and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the lentils are completely broken down and the mixture is thick and creamy, about 15 minutes. Stir through the bulgur until fully incorporated, then remove from the heat and let it cool for 5 minutes. Season to taste.

Preheat the oven to 200°C. Once the shell mixture is cool enough to handle, wet your hands lightly and form a spoonful of the mixture into an oblong shell shape. Make an indentation in the centre with your thumb, fill with about a teaspoon of the cooled lentil filling, then press the opening closed and shape into an oval or leaf. Repeat with the remaining mixture.

Lightly oil a baking tray and arrange the kibbeh on it in a single layer. Bake for 35 to 40 minutes, until the kibbeh are firm and lightly golden on the outside. Serve warm with fresh lemon and a simple salad.

notes: The kibbeh can be assembled up to 4 hours ahead, covered and chilled. Bake just before serving.
Serve with tahini sauce, hummus, or a squeeze of fresh lemon and a simple salad of tomato, cucumber and parsley.

recipe.title: Saganaki
recipe.summary: Fried halloumi cheese that squeaks between your teeth, golden and crispy with lemon.

items.raw: 250 g halloumi, cut into 8 mm slices

steps.text: Heat a shallow pan over medium-high heat. Pour in enough oil so it's about 5 mm deep, then get it really hot, it should shimmer and just start to smoke.
Dust the halloumi slices lightly in flour on both sides, shaking off any excess.
When the oil's smoking, carefully lay the halloumi slices into the pan. You should hear them sizzle immediately. Don't move them.
Cook for about 2 minutes until the underside is deep golden. Flip and cook the other side for another 2 minutes until it's the same colour. It should squeak when you bite into it.
Transfer to a plate, season with salt, and serve straight away with lemon wedges on the side. Squeeze lemon over each piece and eat it hot.

notes: Halloumi must be proper Cyprus halloumi, soft halloumi will melt and won't squeak. Find it at the deli counter or with the international cheeses.
Eat it straight from the pan while it's still hot and squeaky. Once it cools, it toughens up.
This works as an appetiser before a big feed, or as a quick snack with cold beer on a Saturday arvo.

recipe.title: Shami Kebab
recipe.summary: Spiced ground meat and lentil kebabs, pan-fried until golden and crispy.

steps.text: Boil the lentils in 400 ml water with a pinch of salt until very soft and the water is absorbed, about 20 minutes. Cool completely.
Mix the cooked lentils, beef mince, chopped onion, garlic, ginger garlic paste, green chillies, coriander and mint in a large bowl. Add the cumin, coriander, garam masala, turmeric, salt and pepper.
Beat the egg lightly and mix it into the meat mixture until well combined. Cover and refrigerate for at least 15 minutes (this helps the mixture hold together).
Wet your hands lightly with water. Divide the mixture into 8 portions and shape each into a tight oval patty about 7 cm long and 3 cm thick.

Heat 2 tbsp oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. When the oil is hot, carefully place 4 kebabs in the pan. Fry for 5 to 6 minutes on the first side until golden and crispy, then flip and fry the other side for another 5 to 6 minutes until cooked through.
Transfer the cooked kebabs to a plate lined with paper towel. Repeat with the remaining 4 kebabs, adding another tablespoon of oil if needed.
Serve hot with mint chutney, sliced raw onion and lemon wedges on the side.

notes: Make ahead: Shape the kebabs up to 4 hours ahead, cover and refrigerate until ready to fry.
For extra flavour, add 1 tbsp of tamarind paste to the mixture before shaping.
These freeze well raw: freeze shaped kebabs on a tray, then transfer to a container. Fry from frozen, allowing an extra 2 to 3 minutes per side.

Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Huîtres gratinées au beurre et persil

recipe.title: Huîtres gratinées au beurre et persil
recipe.summary: Oysters baked with herb butter and crispy breadcrumb topping

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Preheat the oven to 200°C. Shuck the oysters, keeping them in their bottom shell and reserving any liquid.
Mix the softened butter with the parsley, garlic, salt and pepper until well combined.
Arrange the oysters in their shells on a baking tray. Top each with about 1 tsp of herb butter.
Sprinkle the breadcrumbs evenly over each oyster, pressing gently so they stick to the butter.
Bake for 8 minutes, until the breadcrumbs are golden and the butter is bubbling around the edges.
Serve at once, with lemon wedges on the side.

notes: The oysters must be eaten as soon as they come out of the oven, while the butter is still foaming.
If shucking oysters yourself, chill them in the freezer for 15 minutes first, they open more easily.
You can make the herb butter a few hours ahead and chill it, then scoop it on to the oysters just before baking.

title: Crispy Tofu Rice Paper Rolls with Chilli Dipping Sauce

recipe.title: Crispy Tofu Rice Paper Rolls with Chilli Dipping Sauce
recipe.summary: Fresh rice paper rolls with fried tofu, herbs and quick sweet chilli sauce.

steps.text: Cut the pressed tofu into 16 rectangular fingers, about 1 cm thick. Heat the oil in a frying pan over medium-high heat. Once hot, fry the tofu in two batches for 2–3 minutes each side, until golden and crispy. Set aside on paper towel.
While the tofu cools, make the dipping sauce by stirring together the sweet chilli sauce, rice vinegar, soy sauce and sesame oil in a small bowl. Stir in the sliced chilli if using.
Fill a shallow bowl with warm water. Dip one rice paper into the water for 2–3 seconds until just pliable, then lay it flat on a clean board.

Arrange 2 tofu fingers down the centre of the paper, then top with a small handful of salad leaves, a few mint and coriander leaves, and some cucumber and carrot matchsticks. Add a piece of spring onion.
Fold the bottom edge of the rice paper up and over the filling, fold in the sides, then roll forward tightly until sealed.
Place seam-side down on a plate and repeat with the remaining rice papers and filling.
Serve the rolls immediately with the chilli dipping sauce on the side.

notes: Press the tofu overnight or for at least 2 hours before cooking so it fries crispy and stays that way. You can make the filling components ahead and assemble the rolls right before serving.
Swap the herbs for whatever's fresh, Thai basil works beautifully, or try rocket for something peppery.

recipe.title: Squid and Chilli
recipe.summary: Quick-fried squid with local chilli, garlic and lemon.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Score the squid tubes in a fine crosshatch, cutting about halfway through the flesh. Pat dry with paper towel and cut into bite-sized pieces (about 4 cm square).
Place a large frying pan or wok over high heat until it's smoking hot, about 2 minutes.
Add the olive oil, then immediately add the squid pieces, chilli and garlic. Stir constantly for about 2 minutes, the squid will curl and become opaque.
Season with salt and pepper to taste, then squeeze lemon juice over and toss through.
Serve immediately, scattered with fresh parsley if you like, with extra lemon wedges on the side.

notes: Don't overcrowd the pan, if you're cooking for more than 4, cook in two batches so the squid fries rather than steams.
Squid cooks fast: longer than 3–4 minutes and it toughens. In and out.
Serve with crusty bread to mop up the pan juices.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Tortelloni di Ricotta e Spinaci
recipe.summary: Hand-folded ricotta and spinach pasta with brown butter and sage.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Make the pasta dough: tip flour into a mound on a work surface, make a well in the centre, crack in eggs, add oil and a pinch of salt. Work with a fork until shaggy, then knead for 8 minutes until smooth. Wrap and rest 20 minutes.
While the dough rests, make the filling: mix ricotta, spinach, parmesan, egg yolk and garlic. Season generously with salt, pepper and nutmeg, taste it, it should be well-seasoned.
Dust your work surface. Roll the dough to the thickness of a coin (about 1 mm). Using a 7 cm round cutter, stamp out circles.

Place a small spoonful of filling (about ½ tsp) on one half of each circle. Fold in half, press the edges to seal, then fold the corners up and press them together to make a purse shape. Place on a floured tray as you go.
Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Melt the butter in a separate pan over medium heat until it turns golden and smells nutty, 5 minutes. Add the sage leaves.

Drop the agnolotti into the boiling water. They'll sink, then bob to the surface after 2–3 minutes. Cook for another 2 minutes, then remove with a slotted spoon and add to the brown butter. Toss gently.
Divide among bowls. Add a pinch of salt and grate parmesan over the top.

notes: Make the pasta and filling up to 2 hours ahead; keep the cut agnolotti on a tray in the fridge, uncovered, until you cook them.
If your filling is too wet, the agnolotti will split. If the ricotta is very creamy, drain it in a sieve lined with kitchen paper for 10 minutes first.
For a vegetarian version, use a vegetarian hard cheese (made without animal rennet).

recipe.title: Mee Goreng Mamak
recipe.summary: Spicy stir-fried noodles with egg and prawns, Malaysian street food done at home.

items.raw: 250 g fresh egg noodles (or cooked noodles)
2 spring onion, cut into 3 cm lengths
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Blend or pound the garlic, chillies, sambal oelek, tomato paste and turmeric into a rough paste.
Heat the oil in your best pan over medium-high heat. Add the paste and fry, stirring, until fragrant and the oil starts to separate from the paste, about 2 minutes.
Add the prawns and stir-fry for 2 minutes until they just start to turn pink.
Push everything to the side. Crack the eggs into the cleared space and let them sit for 30 seconds, then scramble them lightly and mix with the prawns and paste.
Add the noodles and break them up as you stir-fry, coating them with the paste, about 2 minutes.
Pour in the soy sauce and kecap manis, toss until the noodles are coated and heated through, about 1 minute.
Remove from heat. Stir through the lime juice, bean sprouts and spring onion. Taste and add salt and pepper as needed.
Serve hot with lime wedges and coriander, if using.

notes: Use fresh egg noodles from the fridge section if you can, they won't clump. No fresh? Cooked noodles work fine; just break them up as you add them.
The paste can be made 30 minutes ahead and kept in a bowl.
Push for medium heat, you want the paste to fry properly but the noodles not to burn on the bottom.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

recipe.title: Cavolfiore Affogato
recipe.summary: Cauliflower braised in tomato and garlic until it falls apart, a southern Italian vegetable dish.

items.raw: 1 medium cauliflower, about 800 g, cut into florets
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the sliced garlic and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 3 minutes.
Add the cauliflower florets and stir to coat in the oil and garlic. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 5 minutes.
Pour in the crushed tomatoes and dried oregano. Stir well to combine. Season with salt and pepper.

Bring to a gentle simmer, then reduce the heat to medium-low. Cover and braise for 25–30 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the cauliflower is very tender and beginning to break down. The sauce should be thick and fragrant.
Taste and adjust the seasoning. Serve hot, scattered with fresh parsley if you like, with good bread to soak up the sauce.

notes: Best served warm with crusty bread to soak up the sauce.
Keeps well in the fridge for 3 days. Reheat gently on the stove, adding a splash of water if it's too thick.

recipe.title: Naam Tok Gai
recipe.summary: Grilled chicken with lime dressing, fish sauce, fresh herbs and crispy rice powder.

steps.text: Toast the jasmine rice in a dry frying pan over medium heat, shaking often, until it turns golden and smells nutty, about 3–4 minutes. Let it cool, then pound it in a mortar until it's crumbly with some fine powder, not flour-fine, but grainy.

Pat the chicken dry and brush lightly with oil. Heat a chargrill or barbecue to high, then grill the chicken, turning once, until cooked through (75°C inside), about 8–10 minutes. Let it rest for 2 minutes, then slice into bite-sized pieces.
Whisk the lime juice, fish sauce and sugar together in a small bowl until the sugar dissolves.
Put the warm chicken in a large bowl with the dressing and toss well. Add the toasted rice powder, green chilli, coriander, mint and spring onions, and toss again.
Taste and add salt or a squeeze more lime juice if you need it. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: The toasted rice powder is the heart of this dish, make it fresh each time you cook. It won't keep.
Naam tok is best eaten warm, but it's fine at room temperature too. Leftovers don't hold up overnight.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Grilled Lapu-Lapu with Vinegar Dip
recipe.summary: Whole reef grouper char-grilled and served with a sharp vinegar, chilli and garlic dip.

items.raw: 1 whole grouper (1–1.2 kg), scaled and gutted
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Make the vinegar dip: combine vinegar, garlic, chilli and a pinch of salt in a small bowl. Let it sit for 5 minutes so the flavours come together.

Pat the grouper dry inside and out. Make three shallow scores across each side of the fish – this helps it cook through and caramelises the skin. Brush lightly with oil and season generously with salt and pepper, inside the cavity and on both sides.
Heat a large char-grill or grill plate to high until very hot and smoking lightly. Oil the grates well.

Place the grouper on the grill and cook without moving it for 8–10 minutes, until the skin is charred and crisp and releases easily from the grate. Flip carefully and cook the other side for 8–10 minutes, until the flesh near the backbone is opaque and cooked through (check by inserting a knife at the thickest point).
Transfer to a warm plate, squeeze lime over it and serve at the table with the vinegar dip on the side for each person to help themselves.

notes: Best cooked and eaten the same day the fish is caught or bought. The fresher the grouper, the sweeter the flesh.
If you don't have a char-grill, use a heavy-bottomed frying pan over high heat, or cook the fish wrapped in foil in a hot oven at 200°C for about 20 minutes.
The vinegar dip keeps for a few days in a jar in the fridge – use it with other grilled fish or seafood.

recipe.title: Snags and Onion Gravy
recipe.summary: Quality sausages with caramelised onion gravy.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat oil in a large heavy pan or cast-iron frying pan over medium-high heat. Brown the sausages all over until golden, about 8 minutes. Set aside.

In the same pan, add the sliced onions and reduce heat to medium-low. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the onions are soft and deep golden brown, about 20 minutes. Be patient, this is where the flavour comes from.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 1 minute, then add the beef stock and worcestershire sauce. Return the sausages to the pan.
Simmer gently for 15 minutes until the sausages are cooked through and the gravy has thickened slightly. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Serve the snags on a plate with the onion gravy spooned over.

notes: Mash or mashed potato on the side soaks up the gravy beautifully.
Use a good butcher's sausage, it makes all the difference.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

recipe.title: Cassava Cake
recipe.summary: Grated cassava baked with coconut milk and sugar, dense and chewy.

items.raw: 1 kg cassava, peeled and finely grated

steps.text: Preheat the oven to 180°C. Line a 20 cm × 30 cm baking tin with baking paper.
Squeeze the grated cassava firmly over a bowl to remove excess moisture, this is important for the right texture. Transfer to a large bowl.
Add the coconut milk, caster sugar, vanilla extract and salt. Stir well until the sugar is dissolved and everything is combined.
Pour into the prepared tin, spreading evenly.
Bake for 45–50 minutes, until the top is golden and a skewer inserted into the centre comes out clean.
Cool in the tin for 10 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack to cool completely. Cut into squares to serve.

notes: Store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days, or refrigerate for up to a week.
This cake is best made a day ahead, the flavour deepens and the texture becomes even better.
Don't skip squeezing out the moisture from the cassava; it makes all the difference to how the cake sets.

title: Barramundi with Thai Basil and Chilli

recipe.title: Barramundi with Thai Basil and Chilli
recipe.summary: Pan-fried local barramundi finished with fragrant holy basil and fresh bird's eye chilli.

items.raw: 4 barramundi fillet, 150–180 g each, skin on
Salt and black pepper, to taste
2 birds-eye-chilli, sliced into rings (seeds removed for less heat, optional)
1 cup fresh Thai basil leaves (or 3/4 cup if using regular basil)
items.note: or 3/4 cup if using regular basil

items.raw: 1 lime, cut into wedges, to serve

steps.text: Pat the barramundi dry with paper towel. Season skin side lightly with salt and pepper.
Heat 1 tbsp of oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. When the oil shimmers, place the barramundi skin side down. Cook for 4–5 minutes without moving it, until the skin is crisp and golden.
Flip the fillets gently and cook for a further 2–3 minutes, until the flesh is just cooked through (it should flake easily but still be moist inside). Transfer to a warm plate.
Reduce heat to medium. Add the remaining oil to the same pan, then add the garlic and sliced chilli. Cook, stirring gently, for about 30 seconds until fragrant.
Tear in the fresh basil, pour the fish sauce over it, and toss through for about 10 seconds until the basil just wilts.
Spoon the basil and chilli mixture over the barramundi and serve at once with lime wedges on the side.

notes: Barramundi is best when fresh and cooked simply. If you can't find barramundi, use any firm white fish fillet like snapper or bream.
Serve with steamed jasmine rice and a quick salad of cucumber and lime to cut through the richness.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

recipe.title: Lumpia Goreng
recipe.summary: Crispy fried spring rolls stuffed with cabbage and tempeh.

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp oil in a pan over medium-high heat. Add garlic and cook, stirring, for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add tempeh and cook, stirring occasionally, for 3 minutes until it starts to brown.
Add cabbage and cook, stirring, until soft and any liquid has evaporated, about 5 minutes. Season with soy sauce, pepper and salt. Transfer to a plate and cool for 10 minutes.
Lay a lumpia wrapper on a clean surface with one corner pointing towards you. Place 1 tbsp of filling in the centre.

Fold the bottom corner up over the filling, then fold in the left and right corners. Roll tightly away from you, then wet the top corner with water and seal. Place seam-side down on a plate. Repeat with remaining wrappers and filling.
Heat 1 cm of oil in a deep frying pan to 180°C. Working in batches, fry lumpia for 2 to 3 minutes on each side until golden and crispy. Drain on paper towel and serve hot.

recipe.title: Perlou
recipe.summary: One-pot Low Country rice with chicken and sausage, simmered in savory broth.

items.raw: 400 g good-quality pork sausage, cut into 2 cm pieces
600 g chicken thigh, cut into 4 cm pieces

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large cast iron pan over medium-high heat. Brown the sausage pieces until golden on all sides, about 5 minutes, then remove and set aside on a plate.
Add the chicken pieces to the pan and brown until golden, about 8 minutes. Remove and set aside with the sausage.
Lower the heat to medium. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft and translucent, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for another minute until fragrant.
Add the rice to the pan and stir constantly for 2 minutes, letting the grains toast lightly in the oil.
Pour in the chicken stock and stir well, scraping up any browned bits from the bottom of the pan. Return the sausage and chicken to the pan, along with any juices. Add the salt and pepper.
Bring to a simmer, then reduce the heat to low, cover with a lid or foil, and cook for 25 to 30 minutes, until the rice is tender and has absorbed all the broth. Stir once halfway through cooking.
Remove from the heat and let rest, covered, for 5 minutes. Fluff gently with a fork, top with fresh parsley if you like, and serve straight from the pan.

notes: Use bone-in chicken thighs if you can find them, they add more flavour to the broth as everything cooks.
This keeps well in the fridge for up to 3 days and reheats gently on the stove with a splash of water.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Horenso No Ohitashi
recipe.summary: Blanched spinach dressed in cold dashi, bonito and soy, the quiet vegetable side that never fails.

steps.text: Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Cook the spinach, stirring gently, until tender and wilted, about 2 minutes. Drain in a colander.
Gather the spinach into a ball and gently squeeze out excess water with your hands. Do this carefully, the leaves should stay tender. Set aside to cool.
Combine the dashi, soy sauce and mirin in a bowl. Chill in the refrigerator until cold.
Once the spinach has cooled, cut it into 4 cm lengths and arrange in a serving bowl or on a plate.
Pour the cold dashi dressing over the spinach just before serving, or let each person pour their own at the table. Top with bonito flakes.
Serve immediately, chilled.

notes: Make ahead: prepare the dashi dressing the night before and keep chilled.
The spinach must be cooled completely before dressing, or the dashi will warm and lose its clean taste.
Serve in shallow bowls if you have them, obanzai looks best on good ceramics.

recipe.title: Gat Kimchi
recipe.summary: Mustard leaf kimchi with gentle bite and deep, funky fermented flavour.

items.raw: 800 g mustard greens (gat), leaves and stems separated
2 spring onions, chopped into 3 cm lengths

steps.text: Make the paste: whisk glutinous rice flour, water and sugar in a saucepan. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring constantly, until thickened and translucent, about 3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in the garlic, ginger, gochugaru and fish sauce. Set aside to cool slightly.
Prepare the gat: cut the stems into 5 cm lengths. Leave the leaves whole or tear into 10 cm pieces if very large. Rinse well under cold water.

Salt the gat: layer the stems and leaves in a large bowl, sprinkling 2 tbsp of salt evenly as you go. Let sit for 15 minutes, then massage gently with your hands, turning the leaves over to coat all sides. The gat will soften and release liquid, this is correct. Drain off most of the liquid.

Season: add the cooled paste to the salted gat along with the spring onions and sesame seeds. Using clean hands, toss and massage everything together for 2 minutes so every leaf is coated. Taste a small piece: it should taste pleasantly salty now, but not salty enough to eat as is, the flavour will develop as it ferments.

Pack: transfer the gat kimchi into a clean glass jar, pressing down so the vegetables are submerged under their own liquid. Leave a 5 cm gap at the top. If there isn't enough liquid to cover, sprinkle the remaining 1 tbsp salt over the top and leave for 10 minutes to release more brine.

Ferment: seal the jar loosely (not airtight) and leave at cool room temperature or in the cold part of your kitchen for 3 days. After day 1, open the lid to let gas escape. By day 3, it will have a gentle fizz and a deep, funky flavour. Taste it, when it suits you, seal it tightly and refrigerate. It will keep for up to 3 weeks.

notes: Make sure your jar is very clean and dry before packing. A sterilised jam jar works perfectly.
The 3-day fermentation at cool room temperature is ideal. In summer, ferment in the coldest part of your fridge and add 1–2 days.
Once fermented and refrigerated, open the jar every few days to release gas, or it will build pressure.

recipe.title: Masgouf
recipe.summary: Grilled whole fish with spiced tamarind marinade, the Baghdad way.

items.raw: 2 whole barramundi (or carp), about 600 g each, cleaned and gutted
items.prep: about 600 g each, cleaned and gutted

steps.text: Make the marinade: whisk together pomegranate molasses, tamarind paste, oil, garlic, cumin, coriander, Aleppo pepper and salt in a small bowl.
Prepare the fish: lay each fish on a cutting board and, using a sharp knife, cut down the spine from head to tail. Gently press the fish open so it lies flat like a butterfly, skin side down.
Rub the marinade all over the fish, inside and out, making sure to coat the flesh well. Let sit for 10 minutes.
Heat oil in a large heavy-based pan or cast iron frying pan over medium-high heat until shimmering. Carefully lay the fish skin side up in the pan.

Cook for 6–7 minutes without moving, until the skin is golden and crispy. Gently flip and cook the other side for another 6–7 minutes until the flesh is opaque and cooked through (the flesh should flake easily when pressed with a fork).
Serve hot with lemon wedges and fresh parsley scattered over.

notes: If charcoal is available, this is traditionally cooked over open flame. Adjust your grill or pan to get good colour without burning the delicate flesh.
Carp is the traditional Baghdad fish, but barramundi or any firm white fish works well. Ask your fishmonger to clean and gut the fish for you if you prefer.

recipe.title: Beef and Burdock Don
recipe.summary: Thinly sliced beef cooked down with earthy burdock root, quick weeknight donburi

items.raw: 400 g beef sirloin (or rump), thinly sliced
300 g burdock, scrubbed and cut into matchsticks

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large frying pan or wok over high heat. Cook the beef in batches until browned on the outside, about 2 minutes per batch. Set aside.
Add the burdock and onion to the same pan. Stir-fry for 2 minutes until the onion softens slightly.

Return the beef to the pan. Add the soy sauce, mirin, sugar and water. Bring to a simmer and cook, stirring occasionally, until the burdock is tender and the sauce has reduced by half, about 5 minutes.
Divide the hot steamed rice among bowls. Spoon the beef and burdock mixture over the top and scatter with spring onions. Serve straight away.

notes: Shave the burdock on a mandoline or with a vegetable peeler to keep the pieces thin and cook evenly.
You can make this with chicken thigh or thinly sliced pork instead of beef, same cooking time.
Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done.

title: Mashed Potatoes with Crispy Onions and Dill

recipe.title: Mashed Potatoes with Crispy Onions and Dill
recipe.summary: Buttery mashed potatoes loaded with fried onions and fresh dill, a side dish that becomes dinner when you're lazy.

items.raw: 900 g waxy potatoes, peeled and halved
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Add potatoes and cook until completely tender, about 15 minutes. Drain well in a colander.

While potatoes cook, heat 2 tbsp oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Add onions and cook, stirring occasionally, until they're golden and crispy, about 12 minutes. Season with salt and transfer to a paper towel.

Mash warm potatoes with butter and milk until creamy but still with a little texture. Fold in most of the crispy onions and all the dill, reserving some onions for the top. Season generously with salt and pepper.
Transfer to a serving bowl and top with reserved crispy onions. Eat immediately.

recipe.title: Pipi Soup
recipe.summary: Creamy broth with pipis, kumara and fresh herbs from the kai moana.

items.raw: 400 g kumara (sweet potato), peeled and cut into 1 cm cubes
items.prep: peeled and cut into 1 cm cubes

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
1 lemon, cut into wedges, to serve

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring often, until soft and fragrant, about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic and cook for another minute until it smells good. Stir in the kumara and cook for 2 minutes to warm it through.
Pour in the stock and bring to the boil. Reduce the heat and simmer until the kumara is tender, about 12 minutes.
Add the pipis and the cream, stirring gently. Cover and simmer until all the pipi shells have opened, about 5 to 8 minutes. Discard any that don't open.
Taste and season with salt and black pepper. Scatter the spring onion and coriander over the top and serve hot with lemon wedges.
Squeeze the lemon over the soup before eating to brighten the broth.

notes: Buy the pipis the day you cook and keep them on ice. Tap any open shells, they should close; if they don't, discard them.
You can make this with mussels or littleneck clams if you can't find pipis.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Taro and Pisupo Bake
recipe.summary: Taro root layered with corned beef and coconut cream, baked until tender and rich.

items.raw: 1.5 kg taro, peeled and sliced into 5 mm rounds
items.prep: peeled and sliced into 5 mm rounds

items.raw: 400 g tin corned beef, broken into chunks

steps.text: Heat oven to 180°C. Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium heat and cook the onion, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the corned beef to the pan and stir to break it up and warm through, about 3 minutes. Season with salt and white pepper.
In a large baking dish (about 30 × 20 cm), layer half the taro slices in an even layer. Top with the corned beef mixture, then layer the remaining taro slices on top.
Pour the coconut cream evenly over the top, making sure to reach the edges. Cover the dish tightly with foil.
Bake for 45 to 50 minutes, until the taro is completely tender when pierced with a fork and the coconut cream has been absorbed and the top is light golden.
Remove the foil and serve hot.

notes: Pisua is a great make-ahead dish, prepare it and refrigerate for up to a day, then bake when needed (add 10 minutes to cooking time).
Leftovers keep in the fridge for 3 days and are even better reheated gently in a warm oven.

recipe.title: Rabo de Toro
recipe.summary: Rich Andalusian oxtail stew, slow-cooked with tomatoes, wine and warm spices.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot or cazuela over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the oxtail pieces all over, about 3 minutes per side. Set aside.
In the same pot, soften the onions and carrots over medium heat, stirring often, for about 8 minutes. Add the crushed garlic, cumin and smoked paprika, and cook for 2 minutes until fragrant.
Pour in the sherry and scrape the browned bits from the bottom of the pot. Let it bubble gently for 2 minutes.

Return the oxtail to the pot and add the crushed tomatoes, beef stock and bay leaf. Bring to a simmer, season with salt and pepper, then cover and transfer to a 160°C oven for 3 hours, or until the meat is very tender and falls from the bone.
Remove from the oven, taste, and adjust seasoning. Skim any excess fat from the surface if you like. Serve hot with crusty bread, scattered with fresh parsley if you have it.

notes: This is even better made a day ahead. Cool, refrigerate overnight, then gently reheat. The flavours deepen and the fat is easy to lift off the cold surface.
Serve with crusty bread to soak up the sauce, and a simple green salad or steamed greens on the side.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

recipe.title: Corned Beef Silog
recipe.summary: Canned corned beef with onions, garlic rice and fried eggs, the lazy silog when you're running late.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp oil in a pan over medium-high heat. Add the minced garlic and fry, stirring constantly, until fragrant and golden, about 1 minute. Add the chilled rice, breaking up any clumps, and stir-fry until heated through and grains are separated, about 4–5 minutes. Season with salt. Transfer to a serving plate and keep warm.
In the same pan or a fresh one, heat 1 tbsp oil over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook, stirring, until soft and translucent, about 3 minutes.

Add the corned beef straight from the tin, breaking it up with a spoon as it cooks. Stir-fry until the meat is heated through and lightly browned, about 4–5 minutes. Season with salt and pepper to taste.

In a separate small pan, heat 1 tbsp oil over medium heat. Crack both eggs into the pan and fry sunny-side up or over-easy until the whites are set but the yolks are still runny, about 3–4 minutes. Season lightly with salt.
Divide the garlic rice between two plates. Top each with the fried corned beef mixture and one fried egg. Serve immediately while the rice and egg are still warm.

notes: Use day-old rice for the best texture, fresh rice tends to clump when fried.
The corned beef tin is already cooked, so you're just heating and browning it for flavour.
Swap the fried egg for a sunny-side up or poached egg if you like, but that runny yolk over everything is the proper way to do it.

Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system. Cool any leftover rice quickly and refrigerate it within an hour; reheat it until steaming hot.

recipe.title: Chili Oil Chicken
recipe.summary: Poached chicken in aromatic chili oil with Sichuan peppercorns and fresh herbs.

items.raw: 1 whole chicken, about 1.5 kg, cut into pieces
2 spring onions, cut into 5 cm pieces
4 dried red chillies, halved and deseeded
Fresh chives, cut into 3 cm pieces

steps.text: Bring the 6 cups water to a boil in a large pot. Add the spring onion pieces, ginger slices, smashed garlic and salt. Simmer for 2 minutes to infuse the broth.

Add the chicken pieces to the simmering broth and return to a gentle boil. Skim any scum that rises. Reduce heat to a low simmer and poach until the chicken is cooked through (check the thickest pieces reach 75°C inside), about 15 minutes. Remove the chicken to a plate and let cool slightly, then shred or cut into bite-sized pieces. Discard the poaching liquid.

While the chicken cooks, make the chili oil. Heat the neutral oil in a small pan over medium heat. When it shimmers, add the Sichuan peppercorns and dried chillies. Toast, stirring gently, for 2–3 minutes until fragrant and the oil is a deep amber, do not let it smoke or burn.
