Remove the pan from heat. Add the doubanjiang, sliced garlic, sliced ginger, star anise and cinnamon stick. Stir well and let it infuse for 1 minute off the heat. The residual heat will open the flavours without charring them. Taste and add salt to balance.
Arrange the shredded chicken on a serving plate. Pour the warm chili oil (including the aromatics and spices) over the chicken.
Scatter with fresh coriander, chives, sliced spring onion and black sesame seeds if using. Serve warm or at room temperature with steamed rice.

notes: The chicken can be cooked and shredded up to 1 day ahead; reheat gently in a low oven before plating. The chili oil keeps in a clean glass jar in the fridge for up to 2 weeks, use it on tofu, greens, or noodles.

Doubanjiang is spicy fermented bean paste from Sichuan; if you can't find it, skip this step rather than substituting, as it's essential to the flavour. Without it, this becomes a different (still good, but different) dish.
The numbing comes from the Sichuan peppercorns, not heat. If you prefer less mala, reduce them to 2 tablespoons.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Pig's Blood Cake
recipe.summary: Grilled QQ rice cakes with blood cake inside, coated in peanut powder and coriander.

items.raw: 300 g tinned pig's blood cake, cut into 2 cm cubes
200 g glutinous rice cake (mochi), cut into 2 cm cubes

steps.text: Mix the soy sauce, sesame oil and white pepper in a small bowl.

Heat a little oil in a non-stick pan over medium-high heat. Working in batches so they fit in one layer, grill the blood cake cubes for 2 minutes on each side until the edges are golden and crispy, then set aside on a plate.
In the same pan, grill the glutinous rice cake cubes, 2 to 3 minutes per side, until they're golden and the outside is just starting to char while the inside stays QQ (soft and chewy).
Toss both the blood cake and rice cake with the soy sauce mixture.
Transfer to a plate and coat with the peanut powder and fresh coriander. Serve warm.

recipe.title: Cendol
recipe.summary: Sweet green rice flour noodles in coconut milk and palm sugar syrup.

items.raw: Pandan leaves, 3 or 4 leaves, tied in a knot (for colour and flavour)
items.prep: 3 or 4 leaves, tied in a knot

steps.text: Make the syrup first: In a small saucepan, combine the palm sugar and 200 ml water. Stir over medium heat until the sugar dissolves completely, about 5 minutes. You should have a thick, smooth golden syrup. Remove from the heat and let it cool to room temperature.

Make the cendol batter: In a bowl, mix the rice flour, 200 ml water, salt and the pandan leaves together, stirring until smooth and lump-free. The batter should be thin, like condensed milk in consistency. Remove the pandan leaves and set the batter aside.

Bring a large pot of water to the boil (about 2 litres). Place the cendol maker (a special mould with holes, or use a sieve with small holes) over the boiling water. Working in batches, pour the batter slowly through the mould so the thin noodles drop straight into the boiling water. They will sink at first, then float to the surface in about 1 minute, that is when they are cooked.
Remove the cooked cendol with a slotted spoon and place them immediately into a bowl of ice-cold water to stop the cooking. Drain well and set aside. Repeat with the remaining batter.
In a small saucepan, warm the coconut milk gently over low heat until steaming, do not let it boil. Add a pinch of salt and stir. Let it cool to room temperature.

To serve, divide the cendol noodles among four glasses or bowls, pour a little of the palm sugar syrup over them (about 50 ml per serving), then pour the cooled coconut milk on top (about 100 ml per serving). Fill each glass with ice and serve immediately, ice-cold.

notes: If you don't have a proper cendol maker, use a fine sieve or even a ladle with small holes; the noodles don't need to be perfect, just thin.
Everything must be ice-cold before serving, chill the glasses if you want to be proper about it.

recipe.title: Gado-Gado Bali
recipe.summary: Mixed vegetables with rich peanut sauce tempered by base genep and palm sugar.

items.raw: 1 cm piece fresh galangal, roughly chopped
150 g long bean, cut into 5 cm lengths

steps.text: Grind the garlic, shallots, chillies, turmeric and galangal together with a mortar and pestle (or in a food processor) until you have a fine paste. This is your base genep.
Heat the oil in a large pan over medium heat. Add the base genep and cook, stirring, for 2 to 3 minutes until fragrant.
Grind the roasted peanuts finely. Add to the pan along with the palm sugar, tamarind paste and coconut milk. Stir well and simmer for 3 to 4 minutes. Taste and adjust salt.

Bring a large pot of salted water to the boil. Add the cabbage and long beans, and cook for 4 to 5 minutes until tender-crisp. Add the bean sprouts and spinach, and cook for a further 1 to 2 minutes until just wilted. Drain well.
Add the cooked vegetables to the peanut sauce and toss gently to coat. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: The base genep can be made a day ahead and stored in an airtight container in the fridge.
Gado-gado tastes equally good warm, room temperature, or even chilled the next day.

recipe.title: Ikan Sambal Matah
recipe.summary: Pan-fried white fish topped with a sharp raw sambal of shallots, garlic and bird's eye chillies.

items.raw: 2–3 bird's eye chillies, finely sliced (adjust to taste)
800 g white fish fillets (barramundi, snapper or similar), skin on

steps.text: Make the sambal: combine the shallots, garlic, chillies, lime juice, oil and salt in a bowl. Taste and adjust the heat or salt as needed. Leave it at room temperature while you cook the fish.
Pat the fish dry with paper towel and season both sides with salt.
Heat a little oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. When it's hot, add the fish skin-side down and cook without moving it until the skin is crispy and golden, about 4–5 minutes.
Flip the fish carefully and cook the other side until just cooked through, about 2–3 minutes. The fish is done when it flakes easily with a fork.
Transfer the fish to a serving plate and spoon the sambal matah generously over the top. Scatter with coriander if you like, and serve with lime wedges on the side.

notes: The sambal can be made up to 2 hours ahead; keep it at room temperature so the flavours stay fresh and sharp.
Any firm white fish works here. Adjust cooking time by a minute or two depending on thickness.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Kongnamul Muchim
recipe.summary: Warm soybean sprouts with toasted sesame oil and ginger, nutty and grounding.

steps.text: Bring a pot of water to the boil and blanch the bean sprouts for 3 minutes until just tender but still bright. Drain well and squeeze gently with your hands to remove excess moisture.
In a large bowl, combine the warm sprouts with the sesame oil, ginger, and salt. Toss gently until the sprouts are evenly coated.
Transfer to a serving plate and scatter the toasted sesame seeds over the top. Serve warm or at room temperature as part of a Korean meal.

notes: This banchan keeps for up to three days refrigerated. It's equally good cold, straight from the bowl.
The quality of your sesame oil matters here, use a good toasted variety for the full nutty flavour.

recipe.title: Cơm Tấm Sườn Nướng
recipe.summary: Saigon broken rice with grilled pork chop, fried egg and caramelised fish sauce.

items.raw: 2 pork loin chops, about 200 g each

steps.text: Make the fish sauce caramel: add sugar to a small pan over medium heat. Once golden, about 2 minutes, add fish sauce slowly (it will bubble), then stir in the garlic and chilli. Remove from heat and set aside.
Marinate the pork: mix fish sauce, sugar, garlic and black pepper. Coat the chops well and leave for at least 15 minutes (or up to 2 hours in the fridge).
Cook the broken rice: rinse in a sieve, then cook in boiling salted water, about 12 minutes, until tender but with a slight bite. Drain well and set aside.

Grill or pan-fry the pork: heat 1 tbsp oil in a heavy-based pan over high heat until smoking. Cook the chops, without moving them, for 3 to 4 minutes until the edges char. Flip and cook for another 3 to 4 minutes (they should still be slightly pink inside). Rest for 5 minutes, then slice.
Fry the eggs: in the same pan, heat a little more oil and fry the eggs until the whites are set but the yolks soft, about 3 minutes.
Assemble: divide the rice between two bowls, top with sliced pork, a fried egg, cucumber and pickled vegetables if using. Drizzle with fish sauce caramel, scatter spring onion and serve.

notes: The broken rice should have a slight bite, don't overcook it. If you can't find it, use jasmine rice but reduce the cooking time to 10 minutes.
Make the fish sauce caramel up to a day ahead and store in a jar; reheat gently before serving.
Pickled daikon and carrot (cà chua cà rốt) from the supermarket are traditional but optional, they add a salty, vinegary edge.

Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Larb Het
recipe.summary: Northern Thai mushroom larb with lime, herbs and toasted rice powder.

items.raw: 400 g mixed mushrooms (button, shiitake, oyster), finely chopped

steps.text: Toast 2 tbsp white rice in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring often, until golden and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Tip into a mortar and pestle or spice grinder, and grind to a coarse powder. Set aside.
Heat the oil in a large pan over high heat. Add the garlic and chilli, and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 30 seconds.
Add the chopped mushrooms and cook, stirring often, until they soften and release their liquid, about 5 minutes. The mushrooms should be tender and any liquid should have mostly evaporated.
Remove from the heat. Stir in the lime juice, tamari, toasted rice powder and sliced onion. Taste and adjust the lime, tamari or chilli to your preference.
Transfer to a serving plate. Tear over the coriander and mint, and serve with cos lettuce leaves to wrap, if you like.

notes: Make the toasted rice powder ahead and keep it in a jar, it will keep for weeks and makes larb het much quicker on the day.
Larb het is best served at room temperature or warm. It doesn't keep well, so make it just before you want to eat.
Make a batch on the weekend and freeze unbaked. Bake straight from frozen—add 5 minutes to the cooking time.
The dough must be cool enough to handle before you add the egg, or it'll scramble.
Use a mix of mozzarella and parmesan for the best stretch and flavour; fresh mozzarella works best.

steps.text: Preheat the oven to 180°C. Line a baking tray with baking paper.
Heat the milk and oil in a saucepan over medium heat until steaming (don't boil). Remove from heat.
Stir the cassava flour and salt into the hot milk and oil until a thick, sticky dough forms. Let cool for 2 minutes.
Beat the egg in a small bowl, then stir it into the dough until well combined.
Fold the mozzarella cubes and most of the parmesan into the dough gently but thoroughly.
Working with wet hands (the dough is sticky), shape into 12 golf-ball-sized portions and place on the baking tray, leaving 3 cm between each.
Sprinkle the remaining parmesan over each pão de queijo.
Bake for 20–25 minutes until golden brown on top and a skewer inserted into the centre comes out clean.
Cool for 5 minutes before serving warm.

recipe.title: Pão de Queijo
recipe.summary: Warm, cheesy cassava flour rolls with a gooey centre, a Brazilian breakfast staple that's gone in minutes.

items.raw: 150 g whole milk mozzarella, cut into small cubes

recipe.title: Kanji Vada
recipe.summary: Crispy lentil fritters soaked in spiced carrot pickle and mustard oil.

items.raw: 1 cup urad dal (white lentils), soaked for 30 minutes
500 g carrot, cut into thin sticks
4 dried red chillies, broken into pieces

steps.text: Make the kanji first. Heat the mustard oil in a pan until it just smokes, then remove from heat. When it has cooled to warm, add the mustard seeds, fenugreek seeds, and dried chillies. Let them crackle for a few seconds, then stir in the asafoetida. In a jar, combine the carrot sticks with salt, then pour the hot oil and spices over them. Add the citric acid, stir well, and set aside to cool completely.
Drain the urad dal and grind it to a thick, smooth paste using a wet grinder or food processor, adding just a splash of water if needed, the batter should be light and fluffy, not wet.
Transfer the batter to a bowl. Fold in the rice flour, green chilli, cumin seeds, and salt, mixing gently to keep the batter airy.
Heat the oil for frying in a large, heavy pan to 180°C (a small piece of batter should sizzle and rise to the top immediately).

Wet your fingers and shape small balls of batter about the size of a walnut, then gently slide them into the hot oil. Fry in batches until golden and crisp all over, being careful not to crowd the pan.
Fry for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring gently and turning the vada so they brown evenly. They should be golden and crispy. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towel.
Once the vada have cooled to room temperature, add them to the kanji jar and mix gently so each one is coated with the pickle. Cover and leave for at least 4 hours, or overnight, before serving.

notes: The kanji keeps in the fridge for up to 10 days, and the vada soften into it beautifully.
If you don't have a wet grinder, a good blender works fine, just be patient and add water slowly so the batter stays light.

recipe.title: Abgoosht
recipe.summary: Persian meat and chickpea broth served two ways: the broth first, then pounded solids on bread.

items.raw: 800 g beef chuck, cut into 4 large chunks
400 g tinned chickpeas, drained and rinsed
3 medium waxy potatoes, peeled and halved
Fresh herbs (coriander or parsley), to serve (optional)

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large heavy pot over medium-high heat. Brown the beef chunks on all sides, about 8 minutes total. Don't rush this step.
Add the onions and turmeric, stirring, until fragrant, about 2 minutes.
Pour in the water and bring to a boil. Skim any foam from the surface until the liquid looks clear. Add the black pepper and a pinch of salt.
Reduce to a low simmer, cover, and cook for 45 minutes.
Add the potatoes and chickpeas, and simmer, covered, for another 45 minutes until the meat is very tender and the broth is rich and deep in colour.
Taste and adjust the salt. You should have a clear, flavourful broth and very soft solids.
To serve, ladle the broth into bowls as the first course. Pour the remaining broth over the meat and vegetables.

Pound the cooked meat and potatoes with a wooden spoon or potato masher directly in the pot until roughly crushed. Pile onto toasted bread, drizzle with a little broth, and serve as the second course. Garnish with fresh herbs if you have them.

notes: This is traditionally made in a heavy pot called a dizi. An enamelled cast iron or stainless steel pot works just as well.
Some cooks add dried limes (loomi) or a pinch of saffron for extra depth. This version keeps it simple.
The broth keeps well for 3 days in the fridge, and tastes even better the next day.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

recipe.title: Rad Na Gai
recipe.summary: Silky tapioca gravy over soft noodles and chicken, a one-burner Bangkok dinner.

items.raw: 2 tbsp tapioca starch, mixed with 3 tbsp water

steps.text: Bring a pot of salted water to a rolling boil. Cook the egg noodles until soft, about 3–4 minutes, stirring gently to prevent sticking. Drain and tip into a bowl.
In the same pot (no need to rinse), heat the oil over medium heat. Add the minced garlic and fry gently until fragrant and golden, about 1 minute, don't burn it.
Pour in the chicken stock and bring to a simmer until the sauce is bubbling gently. Add the soy sauce and sugar, then taste. Adjust salt and white pepper to your liking.

Stir the tapioca starch mixture to recombine it (it will have settled), then slowly pour it into the simmering stock while stirring constantly. Keep stirring for 1–2 minutes until the gravy thickens and turns glossy and translucent.
Add the shredded chicken and stir to heat through, about 1 minute. The gravy should be thick enough to coat the back of a spoon but still pour easily.
Place the soft noodles in a bowl and carefully pour the hot gravy over them. Top with fried garlic, fresh coriander if you have it, and pickled chilli if you like heat. Eat while it's hot.

notes: Cook from leftover rotisserie chicken or use tinned tuna (drained) for a different angle.
The gravy thickens as it cools slightly, aim for thick but pourable at the stove.
Scale up easily: double the stock and starch for two bowls, cook noodles separately.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

recipe.title: Miso Soup with Hamaguri
recipe.summary: Delicate clam miso soup, a weekend breakfast ritual

items.raw: Small piece fresh ginger, peeled and sliced thinly (optional)

steps.text: Bring the dashi to a gentle simmer in a pot until tiny bubbles rise at the edges.
Add the cleaned clams and a thin slice of ginger if using. Cover and simmer until the clams just begin to open, 3 to 4 minutes.
Scoop the clams into serving bowls as they open (don't wait for all of them; they open in stages).
Dissolve the white miso in a small bowl with a ladle of the hot broth until smooth, then pour it back into the pot. Stir gently, do not let the broth boil or the miso flavour will flatten.
Add the mirin to the pot and taste. Add a small pinch of salt if needed.
Pour the broth over the clams in each bowl, scatter the spring onion on top, and serve immediately.

notes: Clean the clams by scrubbing them under cold water and soaking in salted water for an hour if you have time; this helps them expel sand.
Make-ahead: prepare the dashi and have the clams cleaned and ready the night before. The soup itself takes just 15 minutes on the day.
If clams are very large, you can halve them after opening for easier eating.

Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through. Throw away any mussels or clams whose shells stay closed after cooking.

recipe.title: Chupe de Camarones
recipe.summary: Creamy Peruvian shrimp and potato chowder with ají amarillo and fresh cheese.

items.raw: 600 g waxy potato, peeled and cut into 2 cm cubes
items.prep: peeled and cut into 2 cm cubes

items.raw: 400 g raw prawns, peeled and deveined
150 g fresh mozzarella (or quesillo), torn or cubed
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Stir in garlic and ají amarillo paste, cooking for 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in stock and bring to a simmer. Add potato and capsicum, then stir in cumin. Cook for 12–15 minutes, until potato is just tender.
Season with salt and pepper. Add prawns and cook, stirring gently, until they turn opaque and firm, about 3–4 minutes. Do not overcook.
Remove from heat. Divide fresh cheese among serving bowls, then ladle the hot chupe over it, the cheese will soften and melt into the broth.
Top each bowl with two egg halves and garnish with coriander if you like. Serve immediately.

notes: You can make the broth a day ahead; store it in the fridge and add the prawns just before serving.
Quesillo or fresh mozzarella works best here, it melts into silken clouds in the hot broth. Avoid hard cheeses.
If you can't find ají amarillo paste, substitute 2 tsp of ají amarillo powder mixed with a little water.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Dhal and Jaggery
recipe.summary: Creamy red lentil curry with coconut and a touch of jaggery sweetness.

steps.text: Rinse the lentils under cold water until the water runs clear. Set aside.
Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and let them crackle for about 30 seconds.
Add the chopped onions and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic, ginger and red chilli, stirring constantly, for 1 minute until fragrant.
Stir in the ground coriander and turmeric, cooking for another 30 seconds.
Add the rinsed lentils and water, bringing to a simmer. Cook uncovered for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the lentils begin to break down.
Pour in the coconut milk and stir well. Continue to cook for another 10 minutes, stirring often, until the lentils are completely soft and the curry is creamy.
Stir in the palm sugar and salt to taste. Cook for 2 more minutes, then taste and adjust the seasoning if needed. The curry should be creamy, not thick; add a little warm water if it's too dense.

notes: Keeps well in the fridge for up to 3 days. Reheat gently with a splash of water.
Serve with steamed rice, hoppers or roti to soak up the sauce.

recipe.title: Jaew Makhuea Thet (Charred Tomato Jaew)
recipe.summary: Smoky charred tomato and chilli dip with lime and fish sauce.

items.raw: 2–3 birds eye chillies (adjust to your heat)

steps.text: If you have a gas stove, char the tomatoes, chillies and garlic directly over the flame, turning with tongs, until blackened and soft all over, about 10–12 minutes. If you only have electric, use a grill pan or cast iron over high heat, turning often, until deeply charred. The darker the better.
Let cool for a minute, then peel away the charred skin from the tomatoes and discard. Peel the garlic cloves.
Pound the charred tomatoes, chillies and garlic in a mortar and pestle until you have a rough paste, it should be chunky, not smooth.
Stir in the lime juice and fish sauce. Taste and add salt if needed. The dip should be smoky, hot and sharp all at once.

notes: Serve with sticky rice, grilled chicken, prawns or crispy pork, and plenty of fresh vegetables.
You can make it an hour ahead and it keeps fine in the fridge, but the smokiness is best fresh.

recipe.title: Chapli Kebab
recipe.summary: Spiced minced lamb kebab with pomegranate seeds and fresh herbs, crispy outside and juicy within.

steps.text: In a large bowl, combine the lamb mince, pomegranate seeds, green chilli, onion, garlic, fresh coriander, mint and egg. Add the ground cumin, ground coriander, chilli powder, garam masala and salt. Mix gently with your hands until just combined, don't overwork it or the kebabs will be dense.
Divide the mixture into 8 equal portions. Wet your hands lightly and shape each portion into a thick oval, pressing gently but firmly so it holds together.
Heat a large frying pan or tawa over medium-high heat and add 2 tbsp oil. Once shimmering, carefully place 4 kebabs in the pan without crowding.

Cook for 5 to 6 minutes on the first side until golden brown and crispy, then flip carefully. Cook for another 3 to 4 minutes until the second side is golden and the meat is cooked through (the internal temperature should reach 75°C).
Transfer to a paper-towel-lined plate and cook the remaining 4 kebabs in the same way, adding a little more oil if needed, until each is deep golden brown and crisp at the edges.
Serve hot with lemon wedges, sliced onions and yoghurt on the side.

notes: Make ahead: Shape the kebabs up to 4 hours ahead and refrigerate on a lined tray, covered.
For extra crunch, add 2 tbsp finely chopped pistachios or almonds to the mince.
Serve with naan or flatbread, sliced onions, lemon and a dollop of cooling yoghurt.

recipe.title: Wattleseed Shortbread
recipe.summary: Buttery shortbread with wattleseed flour and a hint of lemon myrtle.

steps.text: Preheat your camp oven (or conventional oven to 180°C) with a tray inside.
Cream butter and caster sugar together in a bowl until pale and fluffy, about 3 minutes.
In another bowl, whisk together plain flour, wattleseed flour and lemon myrtle if using.
Fold the dry ingredients into the butter mixture until a soft dough forms.
Transfer dough to a sheet of baking paper. Press into a 20 cm square (about 1 cm thick), prick lightly with a fork, and scatter flaky salt over the top.
Slide onto the hot tray in the camp oven and bake for 18–22 minutes, until pale golden at the edges but still soft in the middle.
Remove from oven and let cool on the tray for 5 minutes, then cut into 12 pieces while still warm.
Cool completely on a wire rack before serving.

notes: Store in an airtight container for up to 5 days.
You can make this in a conventional oven at 180°C if you don't have a camp oven, bake for 18–20 minutes.
If you can't find wattleseed flour locally, use the same weight of plain flour instead, though you'll lose the earthy, distinctive flavour.

recipe.title: Lentil Ladera
recipe.summary: Brown lentils braised in tomato and onion until they become their own sauce.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Rinse the lentils well under cold water and pick through for any stones. Heat the olive oil in a large pot over medium heat.
Add the chopped onion and cook, stirring occasionally, until very soft and golden, about 10 minutes. The onion should be completely tender.
Stir in the lentils and cook for 2 minutes, then add the crushed tomatoes and oregano. Stir well to combine.
Add 750 ml of water and bring to a simmer. Reduce heat to low and cook, stirring occasionally, for 35 to 40 minutes, until the lentils are very soft and beginning to break down.
The lentils should create their own sauce as they cook and soften. If the mixture becomes too thick, add a little more water. If it's too thin, let it simmer uncovered for a few minutes longer.
Taste and adjust the seasoning with salt and black pepper. Serve warm or at room temperature.

recipe.title: Dhal Puri
recipe.summary: Fluffy roti stuffed with spiced yellow split pea filling, crispy and golden.

items.raw: 1½ cups yellow split peas, soaked for 20 minutes

steps.text: Make the dough: mix flour and salt in a bowl. Make a well, add oil and water gradually, mixing with your fingertips until you have a soft dough. Knead for 5 minutes until smooth. Cover and rest for 15 minutes.

Meanwhile, make the filling: heat oil in a pan, add cumin seeds and let them crackle, about 30 seconds. Add garlic and green chilli, stir for 1 minute. Add drained split peas, turmeric, spring onions and salt. Cook on medium heat, stirring often, for 10–12 minutes until the peas are soft and break easily. The mixture should be thick and hold together. Let cool for 5 minutes.
Divide dough into 8 equal balls. Divide filling into 8 portions.

On a lightly oiled bench, roll one ball of dough into a thin circle, about 15 cm across. Spread a portion of filling on one half, leaving a 1 cm border. Fold the other half over the filling to make a half-moon, press the edges gently to seal, then roll carefully into a thin round paratha shape, about 20 cm across, being gentle so the filling doesn't escape.

Heat a tawa or flat frying pan over medium-high heat. When hot, cook one dhal puri for 1–2 minutes on each side, until golden and crispy spots appear. Press gently with a cloth or spatula as it cooks to help it puff slightly. Transfer to a plate and keep warm. Repeat with the remaining dough portions.
Serve hot, ideally with curry or with just butter and salt on the side.

notes: Make the filling ahead: it keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days. Warm it gently before stuffing.
If you don't have a tawa, use a flat non-stick frying pan or cast iron frying pan.
The dough can be made and left covered for up to 1 hour before rolling.

recipe.title: Mboga ya Managu
recipe.summary: Sautéed amaranth greens with tomatoes and onions

steps.text: Wash the amaranth greens well and roughly chop them.
Heat the oil in a large saucepan over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the tinned tomatoes, breaking them up with a spoon. Simmer for 3 minutes.
Add the chopped greens, salt and pepper. Stir well to combine. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the greens are tender and cooked through, about 6 minutes. The mixture should be saucy but not soupy.
Taste and adjust the seasoning. Serve hot with ugali or rice.

title: Grilled Fish Wrapped in Vine Leaves

recipe.title: Grilled Fish Wrapped in Vine Leaves
recipe.summary: Whole fish sealed in grape leaves on the charcoal, herbs and lemon steam inside.

items.raw: 2 whole white fish (400 g each), gutted and cleaned
12 grape vine leaves, rinsed and patted dry

steps.text: Light your charcoal and let it burn down to glowing coals. You want heat, not flame.
Pat the fish dry inside and out. Season the cavity with salt, pepper and a pinch of oregano. Stuff each fish with 2 lemon slices and 1 oregano sprig.

Lay 6 vine leaves on a work surface, overlapping them to form a base. Place a fish on top, then fold the leaves up and around it, tucking and overlapping to seal it completely. Do the same with the other fish.
Brush each parcel lightly with olive oil. Place on the grill grate over the coals and cook until the leaves are charred and the fish flakes easily and is opaque inside.

Cook for 10–12 minutes until the vine leaves are charred black on top. Flip the parcel carefully, then cook for another 8–10 minutes on the other side until the second side is charred and the fish is cooked through (the flesh should be opaque and flake easily at the thickest part).
Slide onto a plate and let rest for 2 minutes. Unwrap at the table. The leaves are burnt, but the fish inside is perfect, steamed in its own juices with lemon and herb.

notes: Use jarred vine leaves if fresh aren't available. Rinse off the brine and pat dry.
Any whole white fish works: bream, snapper, flathead. Aim for 350–450 g per fish.
The blackened leaves are not meant to be eaten. Unwrap carefully and discard.

recipe.title: Lamb and Cumin Hand-Pulled Noodles
recipe.summary: Chewy hand-pulled noodles tossed with cumin-spiced lamb, a Western Chinese favourite.

items.raw: 2 tbsp neutral oil, plus extra for kneading

steps.text: Make the dough: mix flour and salt in a large bowl. Pour in warm water and 2 tbsp oil, stirring with your fingers until it comes together into a shaggy mass. Knead on a lightly oiled bench for 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. The dough should feel slightly tacky but not sticky. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

While the dough rests, cook the lamb: heat oil in a wok or large frying pan over high heat. Add lamb, breaking it up with a spoon, and cook until just cooked through and starting to colour, about 5 minutes. Add garlic, ground cumin and cumin seeds, stirring constantly for 1 minute until fragrant. Add chilli flakes and spring onions, cooking for another minute.
Pour in soy sauce and black vinegar, tossing everything together. Season with salt and white pepper to taste. Transfer to a serving bowl and keep warm.

Divide rested dough into 4 equal pieces. Working with one piece at a time, use your hands to stretch it gently, then hold it up and let gravity help pull it into a long, thin noodle. If it springs back, rest it for a minute and try again. Lay stretched noodle on a floured bench and repeat with remaining dough pieces.
Bring a large pot of salted water to a rolling boil. Add noodles one at a time, stirring gently. Once water returns to boil, cook for 2–3 minutes until chewy and cooked through. Drain well.
Toss hot noodles with the warm lamb mixture and serve immediately in bowls.

notes: The dough can be made up to 4 hours ahead and kept covered at room temperature. If you're short on time, you can stretch the noodles thinner and cook them a little faster, just watch they don't break.
You can use beef mince instead of lamb; the cumin-to-meat ratio stays the same. Some cooks add a handful of fresh coriander or a drizzle of chilli oil to finish.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

recipe.title: Kokotxas en Salsa Verde
recipe.summary: Hake jowls in a silky parsley sauce, expensive, delicate, worth every euro.

items.raw: 30 g fresh flat-leaf parsley, roughly chopped

steps.text: Put the kokotxas in a wide, shallow pan with the white wine and fish stock. Bring to a gentle simmer and poach for 3 to 4 minutes, until just cooked through, they should be opaque but still delicate. Carefully transfer the kokotxas to a warm plate with a slotted spoon, keeping the cooking liquid in the pan.
Heat the olive oil in another pan over low heat. Add the sliced garlic and cook gently, stirring, until it is just starting to soften and colour, about 2 minutes. Do not burn it.
Pour the cooking liquid (about 300 ml) into the pan with the garlic and oil, and bring to a simmer. Add the chopped parsley and cook for 1 minute.

In a small bowl, beat the egg yolks lightly. Remove the pan from the heat, let it cool for 30 seconds, then slowly pour in the egg yolks while whisking constantly, this makes the sauce silky and rich without scrambling the eggs. Taste and season with salt and white pepper.
Gently return the kokotxas to the pan and warm through for 30 seconds without letting the sauce boil, until the fish is just opaque and the sauce is glossy.
Divide among four bowls, pour the salsa verde over and around the kokotxas, and serve with crusty bread to soak up every drop.

notes: Kokotxas are expensive and seasonal. Buy them very fresh from a good fishmonger, or ask them to order them in.
The sauce must never boil after the egg yolks are added, or it will scramble. Keep the heat low.
Don't skip the white pepper, it's gentler than black and won't speckle the delicate pale sauce.
