recipe.title: Kaeng Ho
recipe.summary: Layered clay pot curry with mushrooms, noodles and vegetables in creamy coconut sauce.

items.raw: 2 tbsp fish sauce (or soy sauce for fully vegan)
items.note: or soy sauce for fully vegan

items.raw: 200 g fresh egg noodles (or rice noodles)
300 g mixed mushrooms (oyster, shiitake, button), thickly sliced
2 cups bok choy (or spinach), roughly chopped

steps.text: Heat the oil in a clay pot (or heavy-bottomed pot) over medium heat. Add the curry paste and sliced garlic, stirring gently until fragrant, about 2 minutes.
Pour in the coconut milk, vegetable stock, fish sauce and palm sugar. Stir well and let it come to a gentle simmer until bubbling lightly and the palm sugar has melted.
Layer the noodles evenly over the curry sauce. Don't stir, just press them down gently so they're submerged.
Layer the potato slices over the noodles, then add the mushrooms, capsicum and bok choy in separate layers on top. Pour any remaining sauce over everything.
Cover the pot and simmer gently for 20 to 25 minutes, until the potatoes are tender and the noodles have absorbed the sauce. Peek at it after 15 minutes, it should smell deeply fragrant.
Gently stir everything together just before serving. Taste and adjust the seasoning. Serve hot, topped with fresh Thai basil and coriander if you have them.

notes: For a fully vegan dish, use soy sauce instead of fish sauce and check that your curry paste and coconut milk are vegan-certified.
You can prep all the vegetables ahead of time. Layer them in the pot just before cooking.
Leftovers keep well for 2 days in the fridge. Reheat gently on the stove with a splash of water.

recipe.title: Stewed Saltfish
recipe.summary: Salt cod stewed with onions, peppers and tomatoes, served with provisions and roti.

items.raw: 500 g saltfish, soaked overnight and bones removed
Salt and black pepper, to taste
4 green fig (plantain), peeled and cut into chunks
400 g dasheen (taro), peeled and cut into chunks

steps.text: Soak the saltfish overnight in plenty of cold water, changing the water twice. Drain, rinse and pick through to remove any bones. Break into large flakes.
Boil the green fig and dasheen separately in salted water until tender, about 20 minutes. Drain and keep warm.
Heat the oil in a large saucepan over medium heat. Fry the onion and red capsicum, stirring, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes.
Add the garlic and green chilli, cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and cook, stirring, for 3 minutes until they start to break down.

Add the saltfish flakes and 300 ml water. Bring to a simmer and cook gently for 20–25 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the saltfish is very soft and the sauce has thickened. Season with salt and black pepper to taste.
Serve the saltfish stew hot with the boiled green fig and dasheen, and warm roti on the side.

notes: Saltfish needs to be soaked overnight to remove excess salt. If you're short on time, use 400 g fresh white fish fillet instead, add it to the stew in the last 5 minutes of cooking.
Green fig is unripe plantain, boiled until tender. Look for it in Caribbean or Latin markets, or swap for potato or sweet potato.
The stew tastes better the next day. Keep it in the fridge for up to 3 days and reheat gently on the stove.

recipe.title: Crêpes aux pommes et cidre
recipe.summary: Buckwheat crêpes with spiced apple compote and cider cream.

items.raw: 15 ml melted butter, plus extra for cooking

steps.text: Make the crêpe batter. Whisk together the buckwheat flour, plain flour and salt in a large bowl. In another bowl, whisk the eggs and milk. Pour into the dry ingredients and whisk until smooth. Stir in the melted butter. Let the batter rest for 15 minutes.

Meanwhile, make the apple compote. Melt the butter in a heavy-bottomed saucepan over medium heat. Add the apple slices, sugar, cinnamon stick and cloves. Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until the apples break down into a soft compote, about 15 minutes. Stir in the cider and cook uncovered for 2 more minutes. Remove the cinnamon stick and cloves.
For the cider cream, whip the thickened cream with the cider and caster sugar until soft peaks form. Set aside.

Heat a 25 cm non-stick crêpe pan or frying pan over medium-high heat. Lightly butter it. Pour in 60 ml of batter and tilt the pan to spread it into a thin, even circle. Cook until the underside is lightly golden, about 1 minute. Flip and cook the other side for 30 seconds. Transfer to a plate. Repeat with the remaining batter, buttering the pan lightly between crêpes.
Warm the compote gently if it has cooled. Spoon compote onto each crêpe, fold into quarters, and serve with a dollop of cider cream.

notes: The batter can be made several hours ahead and chilled.
The apple compote keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days and can be gently reheated.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Canh Chua Chay
recipe.summary: Vietnamese sour broth with mushrooms and vegetables, aromatic and herbaceous.

items.raw: 200 g firm tofu, pressed and cut into cubes
250 g mixed mushrooms (shiitake and button), halved
100 g pumpkin (or kabocha), cut into thin slices

steps.text: Bring the vegetable stock to a gentle simmer in a large pot. Stir in the tamarind paste and palm sugar until dissolved, about 2 minutes. Taste and adjust the balance of sour and sweet, it should brighten your tongue but not overwhelm it.
Add the pumpkin slices and simmer for 5 minutes until they are just tender but still hold their shape.
Add the mushrooms and tofu cubes. Simmer gently for 8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the mushrooms are soft and the tofu has absorbed some of the broth's flavour.
Add the tomato wedges and season with salt and black pepper. Simmer for 2 more minutes until the tomatoes are softened, the tomatoes should be warm but still hold their shape.
Remove from heat and stir through most of the fresh dill and coriander, reserving some for serving. Taste once more and adjust the seasoning if needed.
Ladle into bowls and garnish with the remaining herbs and red chilli slices if using. Serve at once, while the broth is still steaming.

notes: The balance of tamarind to palm sugar is personal. Start with equal parts and adjust to taste, some prefer it more sour, others more rounded.
Make the vegetable stock a day ahead if you can; let it chill overnight so any sediment sinks to the bottom, and the broth will be clearer.

recipe.title: Tepsi Galay
recipe.summary: Baghdad baked vegetables and lamb casserole with potatoes and okra

items.raw: 750 g lamb shoulder, cut into 3 cm cubes
600 g potatoes, peeled and cut into 3 cm cubes
items.prep: peeled and cut into 3 cm cubes

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large heavy-based ovenproof dish (about 30 cm × 20 cm) over medium-high heat. Brown the lamb in two batches, about 6 minutes each, until golden on all sides. Set aside.
Add the onion to the same dish and cook, stirring, until soft and lightly golden, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute more.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 2 minutes, then add the crushed tomatoes, cumin, black pepper, cayenne and salt. Bring to a simmer, stirring.
Return the lamb to the dish and add the water. Stir well. Arrange the potato cubes on top of the lamb and sauce (don't stir them in). Cover tightly with foil.

Bake at 180°C for 45 minutes. Remove the foil, scatter the okra over the top without stirring, and bake uncovered for another 15 minutes, until the lamb is very tender and the okra is just cooked through. Serve straight from the dish.

notes: Tepsi galay is best served warm from the dish. If you don't have an ovenproof dish, brown the meat in a frying pan and transfer to a large baking dish before adding the other ingredients.
The okra really does need to go in at the end, if you add it earlier it will break down and make the sauce slimy. Don't stir once the okra is in.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Sambal Matah
recipe.summary: Raw Balinese shallot and chilli relish, essential with rice and grilled fish.

steps.text: Combine the sliced shallots, chopped bird's eye chillies and sliced garlic in a mortar or bowl.

Using a pestle or the back of a spoon, gently pound to release the oils and aromas, about 1 to 2 minutes, until the ingredients are bruised, glistening and beginning to break down. You want them bruised, not completely crushed.
Stir in the lime juice, neutral oil and salt. Taste and adjust salt or lime to your liking, it should be sharp, hot and bright.
Leave to sit for a few minutes before serving so the flavours marry, then stir through fresh coriander if you like. Serve at room temperature with rice, grilled fish or sate.

notes: Make it fresh each time, sambal matah is best eaten within an hour of pounding, while the shallots still have bite.
Adjust the heat by using fewer chillies, or add a splash more lime juice if you prefer it sharper than hot.

recipe.title: Labaneh with Za'atar
recipe.summary: Strained yoghurt cheese rolled in za'atar and olive oil, served with warm bread.

steps.text: Line a fine sieve with cheesecloth or a clean tea towel. Pour the yoghurt into it, add the salt, and stir gently to combine. Tie the corners of the cloth together and hang it over a bowl (or suspend it in the fridge) to drain overnight, or for at least 12 hours, until the whey has stopped dripping. You want all the whey to drip away; the longer it strains, the thicker and more cheese-like the labaneh becomes.

Once drained, the labaneh will be thick and creamy. Scrape it into a bowl and stir it smooth. You can serve it at this point, or for a richer texture and more authentic presentation, roll it into balls about the size of walnuts. Chill them for at least 1 hour so they hold their shape.

Just before serving, arrange the balls on a plate or in a shallow dish. Sprinkle the za'atar evenly over the top, then drizzle generously with olive oil. The za'atar will stick to the oil and stay bright. Serve immediately with warm flatbread or pita for dipping, the bread is how you eat labaneh, never with a spoon alone.

notes: Labaneh keeps in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 1 week before rolling. Once rolled and dressed, serve the same day for the best texture and flavour.

recipe.title: Mukimo
recipe.summary: Creamy mashed potatoes, peas and maize with buttery onions.

items.raw: 800 g potato, peeled and cut into chunks
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Put the potato chunks in a large pot of salted boiling water and cook for 15 minutes until very tender.
Add the corn and peas to the pot and cook for 3 more minutes, until heated through.
While the vegetables cook, melt the butter in a separate pan over medium heat. Add the onions and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Drain the potato, corn and peas well, reserving 60 ml of the cooking water.
Return the drained vegetables to the pot and mash together, adding the cooked onions and butter. Add enough of the reserved cooking water to make a creamy consistency (you might not need it all).
Season with salt and pepper to taste. Serve hot.

notes: Mukimo is best eaten fresh and hot. Leftovers can be reheated gently in a pan with a splash of water or milk.
You can use fresh potatoes, corn and peas if they're in season, but frozen work just as well.

recipe.title: Kyoto-Style Tofu Pockets
recipe.summary: Inari sushi: sweetened tofu pouches filled with seasoned rice and market vegetables.

items.raw: 300 g sushi rice (or short-grain white rice)

steps.text: Rinse the sushi rice under cold water until the water runs almost clear. Cook in 360 ml water in a rice cooker or pot, about 15 minutes for a cooker or 20 minutes on the stove with the lid on.

While the rice cooks, bring the dashi, soy sauce, caster sugar, mirin and sake to a gentle simmer. Carefully open each tofu pouch along the folded edge with your fingernail or a small knife, then slide them into the liquid. Poach for 8 to 10 minutes until they absorb the broth and soften, turning halfway. Set aside to cool until you can handle them, about 5 minutes.

As the rice finishes, whisk the rice vinegar, salt and caster sugar together. Turn the hot rice into a shallow bowl and gently fold in the vinegar mixture, using a wooden spatula to cool it as you fold. This takes about 5 minutes. Let it rest while you prepare the filling.
Dice the carrot, daikon and mushroom very finely, about the size of a sesame seed. If you like, blanch them in boiling water for 1 minute, then drain well. This keeps them crisp.
Fold the diced vegetables, pickled ginger if using, sesame seeds, salt and white pepper gently through the cooled rice.

Gently squeeze the tofu pockets to remove any excess broth. Hold one open and, using a small spoon, carefully fill each pocket with a modest amount of rice mixture, it should be gentle and not packed tight. The pocket should be full enough to hold its shape but not bursting.
Arrange the filled pockets, seam-side up, on a plate. Serve at room temperature.

notes: Make ahead: prepare the tofu pouches up to a day in advance. Store them in their braising liquid in the fridge, and fill them an hour before serving so the rice softens gently into the pockets.
The rice must be warm when you season it with vinegar, but cool enough to handle before filling the pockets.
Use what the market brings: spring onion greens, tiny diced turnip or lotus root work just as well as daikon.

recipe.title: Cassava Fries with Sea Salt
recipe.summary: Crispy fried cassava sticks, golden and salty, a beloved Fijian after-school snack.

items.raw: 800 g cassava, peeled and cut into thin fries (about 5 mm thick)
items.prep: peeled and cut into thin fries

steps.text: Cut the peeled cassava into thin sticks, about 5 mm thick and 8 cm long. Place them in a bowl of cold water and let them soak for 10 minutes to remove excess starch.
Drain the cassava fries well and pat them dry thoroughly with a clean kitchen towel.
Heat about 2 litres of neutral oil in a large, deep pan or wok to 170°C. To test, drop a small piece of cassava in; it should sizzle immediately and rise to the surface after a few seconds.
Working in batches to avoid crowding, carefully lower the cassava fries into the hot oil. Fry for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until they are golden and crispy.
Remove the cassava fries with a slotted spoon and drain them on paper towels. Sprinkle immediately with sea salt while they are still hot.
Serve hot and crispy with a cup of tea or a cool drink.

notes: Cassava fries are best eaten fresh and hot. If making ahead, reheat them in a 180°C oven for 5 minutes to restore crispness.
Don't skip soaking the cassava, it removes starch and makes the fries crispier.

title: Slow Cooker Lamb Neck with Tomato

recipe.title: Slow Cooker Lamb Neck with Tomato
recipe.summary: Tender lamb neck braised low and slow with tomato and aromatics until it falls apart.

items.raw: 1.2 kg lamb neck, cut into chunks
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat a frying pan over high heat. Working in batches, brown the lamb neck on all sides, about 2 minutes per batch. Transfer to a slow cooker.
Add the onions, garlic, crushed tomatoes, beef stock, tomato paste, bay leaves and oregano to the slow cooker. Stir to combine. Season with salt and pepper.
Cover and cook on low for 8 hours, or until the lamb is tender and falling apart. If you're in a hurry, cook on high for 5 hours.
Skim any fat from the surface if needed. Taste and adjust the seasoning.

notes: Serve with crusty bread to soak up the sauce, or over rice or mash.
Makes great leftovers. Cool and store in the fridge for up to 3 days.
Works just as well in a camp oven at low heat, about 3 hours if the coals are right.

title: Slow-Cooked Beef Cheeks with Native Pepper

recipe.title: Slow-Cooked Beef Cheeks with Native Pepper
recipe.summary: Tender beef cheeks braised low and slow with root vegetables and Tasmanian native pepper.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
1 tsp native pepper (Tasmanian pepper berry), ground, plus extra to serve

steps.text: Preheat the oven to 160°C. Pat the beef cheeks dry with paper towel, then season with salt and pepper.
Heat the oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot or casserole dish over medium-high heat. Brown the beef cheeks in batches, 3 to 4 minutes each side, until golden. Transfer to a plate.
Add the onions to the pot and cook until just coloured, about 4 minutes. Add the carrots and parsnips and stir for 2 minutes.

Return the beef cheeks to the pot. Pour in the tinned tomatoes and beef stock, and add the bay leaves and thyme. The liquid should mostly cover the beef. Bring to a simmer until gentle bubbles break the surface.
Cover and transfer to the oven. Cook for 3 hours, turning the beef cheeks halfway through, until they are very tender and the meat shreds easily with a fork.

Remove from the oven. Stir through the ground native pepper. Taste and adjust seasoning with salt and pepper. Divide among bowls, spoon the gravy and vegetables over, and finish with a light grind of native pepper.
Serve with mashed potato or crusty bread.

notes: Make this a day ahead if you like, the flavour deepens overnight. Reheat gently on the stove or in a 160°C oven until warmed through.
Native pepper is available from good delis and spice shops, but if you can't find it, use a grind of black pepper instead.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Flaki
recipe.summary: Beef tripe stew with paprika, marjoram and a tangy broth, cooked low and slow.

items.raw: 800 g beef tripe, cleaned and cut into strips
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large, heavy pot over medium heat. Working in batches, brown the tripe on both sides, about 8 minutes total. Set aside.
In the same pot, cook the onions, stirring often, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Stir in the paprika and tomato paste, cooking gently for 2 minutes. Pour in the stock, scraping up any brown bits from the bottom of the pot.

Return the tripe to the pot with the bay leaves and marjoram. Bring to a gentle simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cover and cook for 2.5 to 3 hours, stirring occasionally. The tripe should be very tender, almost silky.
Stir in the vinegar. Taste and adjust seasoning with salt and pepper. Serve hot, scattered with fresh parsley if you like.

notes: Flaki tastes even better the next day. Make it ahead and reheat gently before serving.
Tripe should be cleaned already when you buy it, but if you have any doubt, rinse it well under cold water and rub gently with salt.
Some Kraków cooks add a little strong mustard or horseradish at the end. It's optional.

recipe.title: Cullen Skink
recipe.summary: Smoked haddock, potato and onion soup with cream, a North-East classic.

items.raw: 500 g floury potatoes, peeled and cut into 1 cm cubes
items.prep: peeled and cut into 1 cm cubes

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Put the smoked haddock in a large saucepan with the milk and bay leaves. Bring gently to a simmer and cook for 8 minutes until the fish is just cooked through. Lift the fish out onto a plate, discard the skin and any bones, and break the flesh into flakes. Keep the milk in the pan.
In a separate pan, melt the butter and cook the chopped onion gently, stirring occasionally, until soft and pale, about 5 minutes.
Add the diced potatoes to the buttered onion and stir to coat. Pour in the reserved milk with the bay leaves, bring to a simmer and cook for about 12 minutes until the potatoes are tender.
Return the flaked haddock to the pan, add the cream and stir gently. Heat through for 2–3 minutes without boiling.
Season with salt and pepper to taste, go easy on the salt as the smoked fish is already quite salty. Serve hot, scattered with fresh parsley if you like.

notes: This keeps well in the fridge for 2 days and reheats gently, add a splash of milk if it's thickened too much.
Traditionally you'd use the poaching liquid, as this recipe does.

recipe.title: Pasta e Lenticchie
recipe.summary: Rustic southern Italian pasta and lentil stew, thick and warming comfort food.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large heavy-based pot over medium heat. Add the onion, garlic, carrot and celery, and cook, stirring often, until the vegetables are soft and golden, about 8 minutes.

Add the brown lentils and stir through the vegetables for 1 minute, then pour in the crushed tomatoes and vegetable stock. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer gently until the lentils are almost tender, about 20 minutes.

Add the pasta and stir well. Simmer, stirring occasionally, until the pasta is cooked through and the broth has thickened slightly, about 8 minutes. If it's getting too thick, add a splash of hot water.
Taste and season with salt and black pepper. Divide among bowls and serve with fresh parsley and grated parmesan if you like.

notes: Make ahead: This actually tastes better the next day. Cool quickly, store in the fridge for up to 3 days, or freeze for up to 2 months. Add a splash of water when you reheat.
Brown lentils hold their shape better than red; French lentils work too. Skip the fancy stuff, everyday brown lentils from the market are perfect.

recipe.title: Ärtsoppa med fläsk
recipe.summary: Traditional Swedish split pea soup with pork, Thursday's best-loved family dinner.

items.raw: 2 tsp salt, plus more to taste

steps.text: Rinse the split peas in cold water and drain. Place the pork, water, and bay leaf in a large pot and bring to a boil until a grey foam rises to the surface. Skim off any foam from the surface.
Add the split peas, onions, carrots, and celery. Stir in the peppercorns and salt.
Reduce the heat to low and simmer, partially covered, for about 2 hours, stirring occasionally. The peas should break down into the broth and the pork should be very tender.
Taste and adjust seasoning with salt as needed. Serve hot in bowls with rye bread and Swedish mustard on the side.

notes: Best made the day before and reheated, the flavours deepen overnight.
Serve with Swedish mustard, rye bread, and a shot of aquavit if you're so inclined.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part.

recipe.title: Rotkohl mit Äpfeln
recipe.summary: Red cabbage braised with apples and vinegar, bright and substantial enough to anchor a meal

items.raw: 1 medium red cabbage, about 800 g, quartered, cored and sliced into 1 cm ribbons
items.prep: about 800 g, quartered, cored and sliced into 1 cm ribbons

items.raw: 2 medium apples, peeled, cored and cut into thin wedges
items.prep: peeled, cored and cut into thin wedges

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large heavy-based pan or Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until softened and just starting to colour, about 4 minutes.
Add the sliced red cabbage and stir through to coat in the oil. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 5 minutes. The cabbage will reduce in volume.
Pour in the vinegar and water, add the bay leaves and caraway seeds, and stir through. Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to medium-low. Cover and braise for 15 minutes, stirring once or twice.

Add the apples and golden syrup, stir gently, and return the lid. Cook for another 10–15 minutes until the cabbage is tender and the apples have softened into the mix. The liquid should have reduced by half.
Season to taste with salt and pepper. Serve warm, as a side to roasted meat or alongside a good piece of fish.

notes: Keep this in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 4 days, it reheats gently and actually improves as the flavours settle. Make it in bulk and freeze portions.
If you prefer less sweetness, use just 1 tbsp golden syrup, or substitute a splash of apple juice instead.

recipe.title: Halwa
recipe.summary: Sweet semolina halwa with butter, cardamom, and nuts, a Somali dessert for sharing.

steps.text: Heat the ghee in a large, heavy-based saucepan over medium heat. Add the semolina and stir constantly, breaking up any lumps. Toast for 8–10 minutes, stirring often, until the semolina is golden and smells nutty.
Add the crushed cardamom pods and salt, stirring for 30 seconds to release the flavour.
Carefully pour in the water, it will bubble, and stir constantly to combine. The mixture will be thick and pasty.
Add the caster sugar and stir until it dissolves completely into the semolina mixture, about 2 minutes.
Remove from the heat and fold through most of the almonds and raisins, reserving some for the top.
Spoon the halwa into a serving dish and smooth the surface. Scatter the remaining almonds and raisins over the top.
Let it cool to warm, then serve. It sets as it cools but stays soft inside.

notes: Halwa keeps in an airtight container for 3–4 days. You can reheat it gently in a pan with a splash of water if it dries out.
The toasting of the semolina is important, it takes time but the flavour change is worth it. Don't rush it.

recipe.title: Filé Gumbo
recipe.summary: Dark roux gumbo with chicken, sausage and the holy trinity, thickened with filé powder.

items.raw: 400 g chicken thigh fillet, cut into 2 cm pieces
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the flour slowly, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon. Keep stirring, don't walk away, until the roux is deep chocolate brown, about 30 to 40 minutes. It'll go from light tan to darker shades; when it smells nutty and toasted, you're close.
Add the onion, celery and capsicum to the roux. Stir well and cook, stirring often, until the vegetables are soft and golden, about 8 minutes.
Add the chicken and sausage. Stir to coat with roux, and cook for 5 minutes.
Pour in the stock slowly, stirring constantly until smooth to break up any lumps. Add the bay leaf, thyme and cayenne. Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low.
Simmer gently, uncovered, for about 40 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through and the flavours have melded. Skim any fat from the surface if you like.
Taste and season with salt and pepper. Remove from heat and stir in the filé powder until smooth. Don't boil after adding filé, or it gets stringy.
Serve in bowls over white rice, scattered with spring onion if you like.

notes: Make this ahead: gumbo tastes even better the next day. Reheat gently on the stove, and stir in the filé powder just before serving.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

recipe.title: Fasolada
recipe.summary: White bean stew with tomatoes, onion and olive oil, soul of Greek Lenten cooking.

items.raw: 400 g tin white beans, drained and rinsed
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the chopped onion and cook gently, stirring often, until softened and pale gold, about 8 minutes.
Add the garlic and tomato paste, stir well and cook for another minute until fragrant.
Add the drained beans, crushed tomatoes, oregano and 250 ml water. Stir to combine.

Bring to a gentle simmer, then reduce heat to low. Simmer uncovered for about 1 hour, stirring occasionally. The stew should be rich and thick, with the beans beginning to break down slightly and thicken the broth. Add more water if it looks too dry.
Taste and adjust the seasoning with salt and pepper. The fasolada should be flavourful and creamy from the beans and oil, not watery.
Serve warm, with crusty bread on the side.

notes: Fasolada is even better the next day. Store in the fridge for up to three days and reheat gently, adding a splash of water if needed.
If starting with dried beans: soak 250 g overnight, then boil for about 45 minutes until tender before starting the recipe. Add the cooked beans at step 3.

recipe.title: Sancocho de Pollo
recipe.summary: Rustic one-pot Colombian chicken stew with yuca, plantain and potatoes.

items.raw: 400 g yuca (cassava), cut into large chunks
400 g plantain, peeled and cut into thick slices
items.prep: peeled and cut into thick slices

items.raw: 3 medium waxy potatoes, peeled and quartered
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Season the chicken with salt and pepper, then brown it in batches, about 8 minutes total. Set aside.
In the same pot, add the onion and garlic, cook until softened and fragrant, about 3 minutes.
Pour in the chicken stock and bring to a boil, then add the browned chicken back in. Simmer for 20 minutes.
Add the yuca and potatoes, return to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer for 15 minutes.
Add the plantain slices and simmer for a further 15 minutes, until the yuca is tender and the chicken is cooked through (75°C inside).
Taste and season with salt and pepper. Stir through the fresh coriander and serve hot, ladled into bowls with plenty of broth.

notes: Tastes even better the next day. Reheat gently on the stove.
Traditional Colombian comfort food: serve with white rice and avocado on the side.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Ful with Egg and Tomato
recipe.summary: Creamy fava bean puree topped with fried egg, tomato and onion.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp oil in a small saucepan over medium heat. Add the drained fava beans and mash with a fork or potato masher until creamy but still a little textured, about 5 minutes. Season with salt and pepper. Transfer to a shallow bowl or plate.

Meanwhile, in another small pan, heat the remaining 1 tbsp oil over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook, stirring, until soft and lightly golden, about 5 minutes. Add the diced tomato and cook for another 2 minutes. Set aside.
In a frying pan, heat a little more oil over medium heat. Crack both eggs into the pan and fry until the whites are set but the yolks are still runny, about 3–4 minutes.
Top the warm ful with the onion and tomato mixture, then place the fried eggs on top. Serve with flatbread on the side.

notes: Make a bigger batch of ful and store it in the fridge for 3 days; reheat gently with a splash of water.
Use tinned or cooked dried fava beans, the tinned kind saves time and money if you're cooking on a weeknight.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Songseun Jjim
recipe.summary: Steamed pine nuts with vegetables, earthy and delicate temple food.

items.raw: 80 g waxy potato, cut into matchsticks
2 spring onions, finely sliced (white and green parts separated)

steps.text: Soak the pine nuts in warm water for 15 minutes, then drain well.

In a bowl, combine the drained pine nuts, shiitake, carrot, potato, and spring onion whites. Stir in the minced ginger, sesame oil, soy sauce, rice vinegar and a pinch of salt until everything is evenly coated.
Prepare a steamer by bringing water to a simmer in a pot until steam is rising steadily. Transfer the pine nut mixture to a heatproof bowl or steaming plate that fits in your steamer.
Steam over simmering water for 20 to 25 minutes, until the potato is tender and the pine nuts have softened but still hold their shape.
Remove from the steamer and let cool to room temperature. Scatter the spring onion greens and toasted sesame seeds over the top.
Serve at room temperature in small bowls.

notes: Songseun jjim is traditionally served at room temperature, which is when the flavours are clearest.
You can prepare this a few hours ahead and let it sit; the flavours develop as it cools.
If you can't find pine nuts, blanched almonds work, though the flavour will be less delicate.

recipe.title: Tofu Katsu
recipe.summary: Crispy panko-crusted tofu cutlet with tonkatsu sauce, a lighter take on the classic.

items.raw: 400 g extra-firm tofu, pressed and cut into 2 cutlets
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Press the tofu between kitchen towels or in a tofu press for at least 15 minutes to remove excess moisture.
Slice the pressed tofu block in half lengthways, then slice each half in half again to create two thick, flat cutlets. Pat dry with paper towels.
Set up three shallow bowls: one with plain flour, one with beaten egg, and one with panko breadcrumbs.
Season the tofu cutlets lightly with salt and pepper on both sides.
Coat each cutlet in flour, shaking off excess, then dip in egg, then press firmly into panko until completely coated on both sides.
Heat about 1 cm of neutral oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat until shimmering.

Once the oil is hot, carefully place the tofu cutlets in the pan and fry for 3–4 minutes per side, until the panko is golden brown and crispy. Don't move them around too much, let them sit so they get a good crust.
Transfer to a plate lined with paper towels to drain any excess oil.
Drizzle tonkatsu sauce generously over the top of each cutlet and serve immediately with pickled cabbage and steamed white rice on the side.

notes: Make sure to press the tofu well, this is key to getting it crispy. Soft tofu won't work; stick with extra-firm.
You can prep the tofu cutlets and coat them hours ahead, then fry just before serving.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Fattet Tammam
recipe.summary: Chickpea and herb salad layered with crispy pita chips and tahini dressing.

items.raw: 400 g tin chickpeas, drained and rinsed

steps.text: Preheat oven to 200°C. Tear pita into bite-sized pieces, toss with 1 tbsp olive oil and a pinch of salt, spread on a baking tray, and bake for 8–10 minutes until golden and crisp. Set aside.
Meanwhile, soak bulgur in 60 ml hot water for 10 minutes until tender. Drain if needed.
In a large bowl, combine parsley, mint, spring onion, tomato, cucumber, soaked bulgur, and chickpeas. Dress with 2 tbsp olive oil and lemon juice, season with salt.
In a small bowl, whisk tahini with garlic, water and a pinch of salt until smooth and pourable. Add more water if too thick.

To serve, spread half the chickpea salad on a platter, drizzle with half the tahini dressing, scatter half the pita chips, then layer the remaining salad, tahini, and chips. Garnish with paprika and serve immediately.

notes: Make the tahini dressing and baked pita chips up to 1 day ahead. Assemble just before serving so the chips stay crisp.
If you can't find fresh mint, use another 100 g parsley. The salad won't be quite as bright, but it'll still be delicious.

recipe.title: Bánh Cuốn Nóng
recipe.summary: Steamed rice paper rolls with minced pork and mushrooms, served hot with fish sauce dip.

items.raw: 200 g mixed mushrooms (shiitake and button), finely diced
2 spring onions, white and light green parts, finely sliced
items.prep: white and light green parts, finely sliced

steps.text: Make the fish sauce dip first: stir together fish sauce, lime juice, sugar, garlic, chilli and water until the sugar dissolves. Set aside.

For the filling, heat 1 tbsp oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. Add garlic and spring onion whites, cook 30 seconds until fragrant. Add pork mince and break it up with a spatula, cooking until no pink remains, about 5 minutes. Add mushrooms and cook, stirring, until they release their moisture and the pan is nearly dry, about 5 minutes. Stir in fish sauce, sugar and black pepper to taste. Transfer to a bowl and set aside to cool slightly.
Make the rice batter: whisk rice flour, water, salt and oil until smooth with no lumps. Let it rest 5 minutes.

Set up your rolling station: place a non-stick crêpe pan or 20 cm non-stick frying pan over medium heat. Have a damp kitchen towel nearby, a plate lined with banana leaf or baking paper, and a small bowl of water for your fingers.

Once the pan is hot, lightly brush it with oil. Pour about 75 ml batter in the centre and immediately tilt and rotate the pan to spread it into a thin, even circle. Cook for about 1 minute until the bottom is set and dry but still pale (it should not brown).

Spoon about 2 tbsp filling along the lower third of the crêpe. Fold the bottom edge up and over the filling, then roll tightly away from you into a log, tucking in the sides as you go. Slide onto the prepared plate.
Repeat with remaining batter and filling. You should make 12 to 16 rolls.

Bring water to a simmer in a large pot or steamer. Arrange the rolls seam-side down on a steamer tray lined with banana leaf or baking paper (steam will cook them gently). Cover and steam for 5 minutes until heated through and slightly firmer (they will still be tender).
Serve hot, sprinkled with coriander, spring onion greens and fresh chilli from the dip, with lettuce leaves and the fish sauce dip on the side for dipping.

notes: Make the rolls up to 3 hours ahead and keep them covered with a damp cloth at room temperature. Steam just before serving.
If you don't have a non-stick crêpe pan, use a small non-stick frying pan and work quickly, the batter sets fast.

Bánh cuốn freezes well before steaming: place rolls on a tray lined with baking paper, freeze until firm, then pack in an airtight container for up to 1 month. Steam straight from frozen, adding 2 to 3 minutes to the cooking time.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

recipe.title: Escabeche
recipe.summary: Sweet and sour fried fish with pickled vegetables, vinegar-forward and meant for sharing.

items.raw: 800 g firm white fish fillets (barramundi, flathead or snapper), skin on
Salt and black pepper, to taste
1 medium red capsicum, cut into strips

steps.text: Pat the fish dry with paper towel. Season both sides with salt and pepper. Dust lightly with flour, shaking off excess.

Heat oil in a large frying pan over high heat until just smoking. Working in batches if needed, fry the fish skin-side down for 4 minutes until the skin is crispy and golden. Flip and cook for 3 minutes more until just cooked through. Transfer to a shallow dish.
In the same pan, reduce heat to medium. Add the sliced onions and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic and ginger, cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the carrot and red capsicum. Cook, stirring, for 3 minutes until just starting to soften.
Pour in the cane vinegar, water, brown sugar, salt and bay leaves. Stir to combine and bring to a gentle simmer. Simmer for 2 minutes, then remove from heat.
Pour the hot vinegar mixture and vegetables over the fish. Let it cool to room temperature, then cover and refrigerate for at least 2 hours, or overnight. The flavours develop as it sits.
To serve, bring to room temperature or serve cold. Spoon the fish onto a plate with the vegetables and vinegar sauce. Garnish with fresh coriander if you like.

notes: Escabeche is even better the day after you make it, the fish stays moist and the flavours marry beautifully. Cover and keep in the fridge for up to 3 days.
If you can't find barramundi or flathead, any firm white fish works well. Avoid delicate fish like basa.
This is a dish built for sharing. Take it out of the fridge 20 minutes before serving to let the oil loosen up a bit.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

recipe.title: Andouillette à la moutarde
recipe.summary: Chitterling sausage with a silky Dijon mustard and cream sauce.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large heavy-bottomed frying pan over medium-high heat. When it shimmers, add the andouillettes and fry for 3–4 minutes on each side until the skin is deep golden and crispy. They should smell wonderful. Transfer to a plate and keep warm.
In the same pan, reduce heat to medium. Add the shallot and cook, stirring, until soft and just starting to colour, about 2 minutes.
Pour in the white wine and use a wooden spoon to scrape up the fond stuck to the bottom of the pan. Let it bubble and reduce by half, about 3 minutes.
Add the chicken stock and bring to a simmer. Let it reduce gently for about 5 minutes to concentrate the flavour.

Whisk the Dijon mustard into the cream in a small bowl until smooth. Remove the pan from the heat and stir in the mustard cream. Add the butter and stir until it melts. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Slide the andouillettes back into the sauce, turn to coat them, and warm through for 2 minutes over low heat. Do not boil, or the cream will split.
Serve immediately on warm plates with the sauce spooned over and around the sausages.

notes: Andouillettes are sold fresh at good butchers and some French delis. If you can't find them, they're not worth substituting, save this recipe for when you do.
The success of the dish depends on getting the sausage skin crispy in the pan. Don't crowd them, and don't fidget with them while they cook.
Serve with mustard-roasted potatoes or a simple green salad to cut through the richness.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Food safety:

recipe.title: Arancini di Ragù
recipe.summary: Golden-fried risotto balls stuffed with meat ragù, peas and mozzarella.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
Salt and black pepper, to taste
150 g fresh mozzarella, cut into 12 small cubes

steps.text: Make the ragù: heat oil in a heavy-based pot, add diced onion and cook gently until soft, about 5 minutes. Add beef and pork mince, stirring to break it up, until browned, about 8 minutes. Pour in wine and let it bubble away for 2 minutes. Add crushed tomatoes, season with salt and pepper, then lower heat and simmer gently, uncovered, for at least 30 minutes (longer is better). The ragù should be thick and the flavours rich. Let cool completely.

Make the risotto: bring stock to a gentle simmer in a separate pot and keep it there. In a heavy-based pan, melt butter over medium heat, add diced onion and cook until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add rice and stir constantly for 1 minute until the grains are coated and lightly toasted. Pour in wine and stir until absorbed.

Add stock one ladleful at a time, stirring often, letting each addition absorb before adding the next. After about 18 minutes, the rice should be creamy and just tender. Stir in parmesan and season with salt and pepper. Spread the risotto on a large tray to cool to room temperature, about 20 minutes.

Once risotto is cool, mix in 200 g (about half) of the ragù and all the thawed peas. Wet your hands and shape the mixture into 12 balls, each about the size of a golf ball. Make an indent in the centre of each ball with your thumb, press in a cube of mozzarella and a generous pinch of the remaining ragù, then seal the opening and reshape into a smooth ball. This takes patience but it's what keeps the filling hidden inside.

Set up three shallow bowls: one with beaten eggs, one with panko breadcrumbs, and one empty. Roll each arancino ball in egg, then roll in breadcrumbs until well coated. Place on a tray and chill for at least 30 minutes (or up to 12 hours) so the coating sets firmly.

Heat oil in a deep, heavy-based pot or deep-fryer to 170°C. If you don't have a thermometer, test with a wooden spoon handle: it should sizzle gently at the edge of the oil. Fry arancini in batches of 3–4, turning occasionally, for 3–4 minutes until golden brown all over. Don't crowd the pan. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towel.
Serve warm, while the mozzarella inside is still soft and the outside is crispy. Arancini are best eaten fresh but are still good at room temperature.

notes: Make the ragù on Sunday to let the flavours deepen overnight. You'll have leftovers, which freeze well.
If you don't have fresh mozzarella, use fior di latte or even a cube of cold butter instead.
Arancini can be coated and refrigerated for up to 12 hours before frying. This actually helps them hold their shape better.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Bacalao al Pil-Pil
recipe.summary: Salt cod emulsified with garlic and olive oil into a creamy, silky sauce.

items.raw: 600 g salt cod loin (skinless and boneless), soaked overnight
1 small red chilli, deseeded and chopped (optional)

steps.text: Drain and pat the salt cod dry. Cut into 4 thick pieces, about 150 g each.

Heat 100 ml olive oil in a wide, shallow earthenware dish (cazuela) or heavy-based pan over very low heat. Add the sliced garlic and red chilli (if using). Cook gently, stirring, until the garlic is fragrant and just beginning to soften, about 2 minutes. Don't let it brown.

Lay the salt cod pieces skin-side up in the warm oil. The oil should just barely cover them, add a little more if needed. Keep the heat very low and poach gently, uncovered, for 5–7 minutes. The cod will begin to flake at the edges and turn opaque.

Now the critical part: remove the pan from the heat and let it cool for 1 minute. Using a wooden spoon or your wrist in a smooth, circular motion, begin tilting and rotating the pan while gently stirring the cod in the oil. The gelatine from the fish will start to emulsify the oil into a creamy sauce.

Return the pan to very low heat and continue this tilting and stirring motion. Gradually add the remaining 100 ml olive oil in a thin stream while rotating and tilting, as if you were making a sauce. The emulsion builds slowly, this is the pil-pil. Keep going for 8–10 minutes until the sauce is pale, silky and creamy.
Taste and season with salt if needed. Serve in the pan, spooning the creamy pil-pil sauce over the cod. Scatter with fresh parsley if you like.

notes: The salt cod needs overnight soaking in plenty of cold water (change it a couple of times if you remember). If you're short on time, use 2 changes of water and soak for at least 8 hours.
The whole secret is low heat and patience. Rush it or turn the heat up and the emulsion breaks. If it does, start the oil again in a fresh pan and gently fold in the broken sauce.
An earthenware cazuela looks better and conducts heat more evenly, but a heavy stainless steel or cast-iron pan works just as well.

recipe.title: Baklava
recipe.summary: Layers of yufka and pistachios soaked in honey syrup, baked until shatteringly crisp.

steps.text: Make the syrup first: combine water, sugar, cinnamon stick, cloves and lemon slice in a saucepan. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer for 10 minutes. Remove from heat, stir in honey, and set aside to cool to room temperature.
Preheat oven to 175°C. Mix pistachios with caster sugar and ground cinnamon in a bowl.
Brush a 33 x 23 cm baking dish generously with melted butter. Lay down one yufka sheet and brush with butter. Repeat until you have 6 layers, this is your base.
Spread a thin, even layer of pistachio mixture over the top sheet. Layer 2 more yufka sheets on top, brushing each with butter.
Repeat the pistachio layer and 2 more yufka sheets. Keep going until you've used most of your pistachios, finishing with at least 6 yufka sheets on top, each brushed with butter.
Using a sharp knife, cut the baklava into diamond or triangular pieces all the way through to the base, about 20 pieces total. Pour any remaining melted butter over the top.
Bake for 35 to 40 minutes, until golden brown and the edges are darker. You'll hear it starting to crisp as it cools.
Remove from oven and immediately pour the room-temperature syrup slowly and evenly over the hot baklava. It will sizzle and soak in. Let cool completely in the pan, at least 2 hours, before serving.

notes: Baklava keeps in an airtight container for up to 5 days. The pastry stays crisp and the flavours deepen.
Use room-temperature syrup on hot baklava, not the other way around, this is what makes it properly absorb.
Pistachios are traditional, but walnuts or almonds work if that's what you have. Just chop them fine.

recipe.title: Bandeja Paisa
recipe.summary: The legendary Medellín feast: beans, rice, meat, egg, arepa and chicharrón all on one plate.

items.raw: 400 g tin red kidney beans, drained and rinsed
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: For the beans: heat 1 tbsp oil in a pot over medium heat. Add the onion and garlic, and cook until soft, about 5 minutes. Add the drained beans and 200 ml water, bring to a simmer, and cook gently for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the beans are creamy but still whole. Season with salt.

For the rice: heat 1 tbsp oil in a separate pot over medium heat. Add the chopped onion and cook until soft, about 4 minutes. Add the rice and stir for 2 minutes until translucent at the edges. Pour in the stock, bring to a boil, then cover and reduce heat to low. Cook for 15–18 minutes until the rice is tender and the liquid is absorbed. Season with salt.

For the meat: heat 1 tbsp oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the onion and cook until soft, about 4 minutes. Add the garlic and cumin, cook for 1 minute. Add the beef mince, breaking it up with a spoon, and cook until browned through, about 8–10 minutes. Season with salt and pepper.
Fry the eggs: in a separate pan, heat 2 tbsp oil over medium heat. Fry the eggs to your liking (typically over-easy or sunny-side up), about 4–5 minutes.
Warm the chicharrón and arepas gently while you finish the other components.

To serve: arrange each component on a large plate: a portion of beans on one side, rice on another, the seasoned mince, the fried egg, a piece of chicharrón, and a warm arepa. Garnish with fresh coriander if you like. Serve hot.

notes: Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Bánh Hỏi Nướng
recipe.summary: Charred grilled thin noodle cakes topped with prawns and crispy pork belly, dipped in tangy fish sauce vinegar.

items.raw: 250 g raw prawns, peeled and cleaned
150 g pork belly, thinly sliced (5 mm)

steps.text: Pour chicken stock into a saucepan and bring to a simmer. Add rice vermicelli and cook until just tender, about 3 minutes, stirring occasionally. The noodles will be soft and may break slightly, this is right. Drain in a fine sieve and spread on a tray to cool to room temperature, about 10 minutes.
While the noodles cool, make the dipping sauce: stir fish sauce, lime juice and sugar together in a small bowl until the sugar dissolves. Set aside.

Divide the cooled noodles into 8 equal portions. Take one portion and press it gently on an oiled piece of baking paper, forming a flat rectangle about 15 cm × 10 cm and roughly 1 cm thick. Do not press too hard or the cake will become dense. Repeat with the remaining noodle portions.
Heat a large grill pan or outdoor grill to medium-high heat until very hot and a drop of water sizzles on contact. Brush the grill grates lightly with oil.

Carefully transfer one noodle cake to the hot grill (start with the baking paper if using, then slide it away). Grill until the underside is golden and charred in patches, about 3–4 minutes. Flip carefully and grill the other side until golden and crispy, another 2–3 minutes. Transfer to a warm plate. Repeat with the remaining noodle cakes.

On the same grill or a separate pan at medium-high heat, grill the pork belly slices for 2–3 minutes per side until the fat has rendered and the edges are crisp and caramelised. The pork should be cooked through with no pink remaining. Transfer to a warm plate.
Grill the prawns over medium-high heat for 1–2 minutes per side until they are opaque throughout and have a light char. Transfer to a warm plate.

Arrange one noodle cake on each serving plate. Tear or arrange the grilled pork belly and prawns over the top. Garnish with fresh coriander if using and serve immediately with lime wedges and the fish sauce dipping sauce on the side.

notes: The noodle cakes can be formed up to 2 hours ahead; stack them between sheets of baking paper and refrigerate. Grill straight from the fridge, adding 1–2 minutes per side.
If your grill pan is small, grill the components in batches and keep them warm on a plate in a low oven (120°C) while you finish cooking.
The pork belly will spit as the fat renders, keep the heat steady and watch closely after the 2-minute mark to avoid burning.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part.

recipe.title: Bánh Mì Thịt Nướng
recipe.summary: Charred pork shoulder bánh mì with pickled daikon, coriander and fish sauce mayo on crusty bread.

items.raw: 1 lemongrass stalk, white part only, finely chopped
2 small baguettes (or 1 large baguette), halved lengthways
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Mix fish sauce, palm sugar, garlic, lemongrass and ground coriander in a bowl. Add the pork slices and toss to coat. Let sit for at least 15 minutes (or up to 2 hours in the fridge).
Combine mayonnaise, fish sauce and lime juice in a small bowl, stirring until smooth. Taste and adjust seasoning.

Heat a large frying pan or grill pan over high heat until it's smoking hot. Working in batches if needed, cook the pork until the edges are charred and caramelised, about 2–3 minutes per side. Don't move the pieces around, let them sit so they get a dark, crusty exterior. Set aside on a plate.
Lightly toast the baguette cut-side down in the same hot pan for about 1 minute, until golden and crispy.

Spread the fish sauce mayo on the cut side of each baguette. Layer the charred pork, then pickled daikon, fresh coriander and chilli. Season with salt and pepper. Serve immediately while the bread is still warm.

notes: Make the fish sauce mayo and prepare the pickled daikon up to a day ahead; toast the baguette and cook the pork just before eating.
The pork can marinate for up to 2 hours in the fridge for deeper flavour, but 15 minutes is enough for a quick lunch.
If you can't find pickled daikon, use pickled mustard greens or a mix of pickled vegetables, the acid and brightness matter more than the exact vegetable.
Cook pork until it reaches at least 70°C in the thickest part (75°C for mince and sausages).
Food safety:

recipe.title: Beef and Black Bean Stir-Fry
recipe.summary: Thin-sliced beef tossed fast with fermented black beans and garlic in the wok.

items.raw: 500 g beef sirloin, thinly sliced across the grain
3 tbsp douchi (fermented black beans), rinsed and roughly chopped

steps.text: Slice the beef thinly against the grain and set aside. Rinse the black beans, drain well, and chop roughly. Slice the garlic and chilli.
Heat the wok over high heat until smoking, about 2 minutes. Add 1 tbsp oil, swirl to coat.
Working quickly, add half the beef and let it sit for 30 seconds without stirring, this helps it catch colour. Toss for 30 seconds, then transfer to a plate. Repeat with the remaining oil and beef.
Return the wok to high heat. Add the garlic and chilli, toss for 10 seconds until fragrant. Add the black beans, toss for another 10 seconds.
Return all the beef to the wok with the oyster sauce and sesame oil. Toss everything together for 30 seconds, until coated and heated through.
Serve immediately over steamed rice, scattered with spring onion.

notes: Slice the beef when it's partially frozen (about 30 minutes in the freezer) for cleaner, thinner cuts.
This is best served immediately. The beef toughens if it sits in the wok too long, aim for 2 minutes total cooking time from wok to plate.
If you can't find fermented black beans (douchi), use 2 tbsp more oyster sauce and a pinch of extra salt, though it won't be quite the same dish.
Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done.

recipe.title: Bún Bò Huế
recipe.summary: Spicy beef noodle soup with lemongrass and blood sausage, a Central Vietnamese classic.

items.raw: 600 g beef shin (or chuck), cut into chunks
6 stalks lemongrass, white part only, bruised
200 g pork blood sausage (lạp xưởng), sliced (optional)
300 g fresh rice noodles (or dried rice noodles)
Pickled turnips (cà chua đắng), to serve (optional)

steps.text: Toast the coriander seeds and annatto seeds in a dry pan over medium heat for 2 minutes until fragrant, then crush lightly.

Place beef shin, pork knuckle, bruised lemongrass, ginger, onion, and crushed spices in a large pot with 2 litres water. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 60 minutes until the beef is tender, skimming foam from the surface occasionally.
Add the whole red chillies and fish sauce, and simmer for another 10 minutes. Taste and adjust salt if needed.
If using pork blood sausage, add to the broth in the last 5 minutes of cooking until warmed through.
Cook the rice noodles according to packet directions. If using fresh noodles, blanch in boiling water for 1 minute.
Divide noodles into serving bowls. Pour the hot broth over the noodles, ensuring each bowl gets beef and a piece of sausage if using.
Serve with lime wedges, fresh coriander, mint, and pickled turnips on the side.

notes: Make the broth a day ahead for deeper flavour; reheat gently and add the sausage and noodles to serve.
The blood sausage is traditional, but if you can't find it, add extra beef shin or pork instead.
Central Vietnamese bún bò is spicier than northern versions, add more chillies to your bowl to taste.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

recipe.title: Ceviche de Corvina
recipe.summary: Raw white fish cured in lime juice, ají amarillo, and red onion, bright, clean, and classically Peruvian.

items.raw: 500 g sashimi-grade white fish fillet (corvina or snapper), cut into 2 cm cubes
4 ají amarillo (yellow Peruvian chillies), stems and seeds removed

steps.text: Soak the sliced red onion in salt water (about 1 tsp salt per 250 ml water) while you prepare the fish. This takes the edge off the raw onion and cures it slightly, about 5 minutes.
Blend the ají amarillo with the garlic clove and 2 tbsp of the fresh lime juice until smooth. Pass through a fine sieve if you want a completely silky sauce.

Put the fish cubes in a glass or ceramic bowl. Add the ají amarillo paste, the remaining lime juice, and a pinch of salt. Stir gently to coat all the fish. Let sit for 10–15 minutes, the lime juice will turn the fish opaque and firm. Taste and adjust salt.
Drain the cured red onion and gently fold it into the ceviche just before serving, along with any juice from soaking.

Serve in chilled bowls with fresh coriander and toasted corn kernels scattered over the top. Eat while the ceviche is at its brightest, don't leave it sitting or the acid will keep breaking down the fish.

notes: Use only the freshest sashimi-grade fish. Ask your fishmonger for corvina or snapper that's been kept for raw preparation.
The ceviche is at its best eaten within 30 minutes of mixing, the acid continues to work and the texture gets softer the longer it sits.
Make the ají amarillo paste fresh if you can find the chillies; if using paste from a jar, start with 3 tbsp and adjust to taste.

The fish here is eaten raw or only cured in citrus. Buy sashimi-grade fish from a fishmonger, keep it cold and eat it the same day; skip it for anyone pregnant, very young, elderly or with low immunity.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

recipe.title: Char Koay Teow
recipe.summary: Stir-fried flat rice noodles with prawns, cockles, bean sprouts and egg.

items.raw: 300 g fresh thick rice noodles (kway teow)
100 g cockles (if fresh), or tinned cockles, drained
2 spring onions, cut into 3 cm lengths

steps.text: Set a large wok over high heat until it's very hot, you'll feel the heat rise from it. Add 1 tbsp of the oil and swirl to coat.

Push the noodles into the wok. They'll clump at first, but keep them moving with your spatula, breaking them apart, until they're loosened and just beginning to brown at the edges, about 2 minutes. Push everything to the side of the wok.
Add the remaining oil to the empty side. Crack in the eggs and scramble them quickly with the back of your spatula until just set, then mix them through the noodles.

Push everything to the side again. Add the garlic to the empty spot and cook, stirring constantly, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Then add the prawns and cockles, tossing them with the garlic for 1 minute until the prawns turn pink and opaque.
Add the soy sauce, dark soy sauce and oyster sauce, tossing everything together. The noodles will darken and smell wonderful, this takes about 1 minute.
Add the bean sprouts and spring onions, tossing for another 30 seconds. If using fresh chilli, toss that through now.
Taste and add more soy sauce if you need it. Divide between bowls and serve straight away, while it's still hot and the edges are a bit charred.

notes: The noodles need to be fresh and thick (kway teow), sold in the refrigerated section, they're usually stuck together in a slab. If you can only find thin dried rice noodles, use them, but fresh ones give you that lovely charred edge.
The heat and speed are everything here. Once you start cooking, don't stop stirring. A slow char koay teow is a sad char koay teow.
Cockles are traditional, use fresh ones from the fishmonger if you can find them, or tinned ones from the Asian aisle. If you really can't find them, use more prawns instead.

recipe.title: Curry Duck
recipe.summary: Tender duck slow-cooked in fragrant spiced curry, a Trinidadian special occasion dish.

items.raw: 1 whole duck (about 2 kg), cut into 8 pieces
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Dry-roast the coriander and cumin seeds in a small pan over medium heat, stirring, until fragrant, about 2 minutes. Grind to a fine powder and set aside. Mix the ground roasted spices with the crushed garlic and grated ginger to form a paste.

Pat the duck pieces dry with paper towel. Season with salt and pepper. Heat the oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the duck on all sides, about 3 minutes per side. Set aside.

In the same pot, add the diced onions and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add the curry powder and tomato paste, stirring constantly, for 1 minute until fragrant. Add the spice-garlic-ginger paste and cook, stirring, for 2 minutes.

Return the duck to the pot. Pour in the coconut milk and chicken stock. Add the whole green chillies and curry leaves. Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low, cover, and cook gently for 1½ hours, or until the duck is very tender and the meat pulls easily from the bone.

Taste and adjust seasoning with salt and pepper. If the sauce is too thin, uncover and simmer for a further 10 minutes to reduce. Serve the curry duck hot with warm roti, using the bread to soak up the rich spiced sauce.

notes: Make this the day before and reheat gently on the stove; the flavours deepen overnight.
Whole green chillies stay mild if you don't break them open; remove them before serving if you prefer no heat.
Duck makes this special, but chicken thighs work if duck is hard to find. Reduce the cook time to 45 minutes.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

recipe.title: Dolma
recipe.summary: Grape leaves stuffed with herbed rice and meat, slowly simmered until tender.

items.raw: 400 g jarred grape leaves, drained and rinsed
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp oil in a frying pan over medium heat. Cook the diced onion until soft and translucent, about 5 minutes.

Add the lamb mince and cook, breaking it up with a spoon, until browned, about 8 minutes. Stir in the rice, mint, parsley, cumin and allspice. Cook, stirring, for 2 minutes. Season with salt and pepper. Remove from heat and cool slightly.

Lay a grape leaf flat, shiny side down, on a clean surface. Place 1 tbsp of filling near the base of the leaf. Fold the sides in, then roll tightly from the base towards the tip, tucking in the sides as you go. Repeat with the remaining leaves and filling.
Line the base of a heavy pot with any remaining or torn grape leaves. Arrange the dolma seam-side down, snugly packed in a single layer (or two layers if needed).
Pour the stock around the dolma. Drizzle with the remaining 1 tbsp oil. Place a plate or small lid directly on the dolma to keep them submerged.
Bring to a simmer over medium heat, then reduce heat to low. Cook, uncovered, for 35 to 40 minutes, until the rice is tender and the leaves are soft. The stock will reduce and mostly be absorbed.
Let rest for 5 minutes, then serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: Make ahead: Roll the dolma up to 1 day ahead and store in the fridge. Cook just before serving.
Room temperature: These are just as good served at room temperature the next day, making them perfect for packed lunches.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.

recipe.title: Dolma Garaz
recipe.summary: Grape leaves stuffed with spiced meat and rice, served with tomato and yoghurt.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute. Stir in the mince and cook, breaking it up with the spoon, until browned, about 6–8 minutes. Drain off any excess fat.
Stir the rice, cumin, coriander, cinnamon, cayenne, salt and pepper into the mince. Cook, stirring, for 2 minutes. Remove from heat and let cool slightly.

Lay a grape leaf shiny side down on a clean work surface. Place about 1 tbsp of filling near the base of the leaf. Fold the bottom edge over the filling, then fold in the sides and roll tightly away from you. Repeat with the remaining leaves and filling. You should have about 20 dolma.

Wipe out the pan and add the remaining 1 tbsp oil. Working in two batches, arrange the dolma seam side down in the pan and cook, without stirring, until lightly golden on the bottom, about 2 minutes per batch. Transfer to a plate.

Return all the dolma to the pan, seam side down. Pour the tomatoes and stock over them. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, then reduce to low. Cover and cook gently for 30 minutes, until the rice is tender and the sauce has thickened slightly.
Transfer the dolma to a serving plate and spoon the warm sauce over them. Serve with Greek yoghurt on the side.

notes: Make ahead: prepare the dolma up to the end of step 3, then cover and refrigerate for up to 24 hours before cooking.
Swap the beef for lamb mince for a richer flavour, which some prefer.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.

recipe.title: Fatteh Hummus
recipe.summary: Crispy pita chips over creamy chickpea purée with yoghurt alternative, olive oil and pine nuts.

items.raw: 400 g tin chickpeas, drained and rinsed
2 tbsp extra virgin olive oil, plus more for drizzling
200 g unsweetened soy yoghurt (or other plant-based yoghurt)

steps.text: Preheat the oven to 180°C. Cut the pita breads into triangles, lightly brush or toss with a little olive oil, and scatter on a baking tray. Bake for 8–10 minutes, stirring halfway, until golden and crispy. Set aside.

While the pita crisps, make the hummus. Combine the chickpeas, tahini, lemon juice, garlic and 2 tbsp olive oil in a food processor. Blend until completely smooth, adding 2–3 tbsp water as needed to reach a creamy consistency. Taste and season with salt.
Spread the hummus onto a shallow bowl or plate, creating a well in the centre with the back of a spoon.
Dollop the soy yoghurt into the well and drizzle generously with extra virgin olive oil.
Top with the warm pita crisps, toasted pine nuts, and sumac and parsley if using. Serve immediately.

notes: Make the hummus up to a day ahead; store it covered in the fridge and bring to room temperature before serving.
Toast your own pine nuts in a dry pan over medium heat for 2–3 minutes if you have time, it makes a real difference.
This is just as good made with tinned chickpeas as it would be with soaked dried ones.

recipe.title: Gatsby
recipe.summary: Cape Town's legendary split loaf stuffed with fried chips, meat sauce and cheese

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat oil in a large pot or deep fryer to 180°C. Fry the potato chips in batches until golden and crispy, about 4 minutes per batch. Drain on paper towel and season with salt while still hot.
Meanwhile, heat a tbsp of oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Cook the onion, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute.

Add the beef mince and cook, breaking it up with a spoon, until browned through, about 5–6 minutes. Stir in the tomato paste, cumin, coriander and chilli powder, cooking for another 2 minutes until fragrant.
Add the beef stock and simmer, stirring occasionally, until the sauce is thick and coats the back of a spoon, about 8–10 minutes. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Lightly butter the inside of each bread roll. Warm the rolls under the griller or in a hot oven for 1–2 minutes until soft.
Layer the hot chips into each roll, then spoon the meat sauce generously over the top. Scatter the grated cheddar on top and place under the griller for 2–3 minutes until the cheese melts.
Serve immediately while hot and the cheese is still melted.

notes: You can prep the meat sauce ahead and reheat it just before assembling.
If you don't have a deep fryer, use a deep heavy-based pan with at least 8 cm of oil. Use a thermometer to check the temperature.
Some Cape Town versions add sliced cheese or a fried egg, feel free to customize.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
